Charles Maurice Wollenberg.
Grand Master 1929-1930

In the little city of Castroville, on the 13th day of March,_ 1873,
there was born to Louis Wollenberg and his wife Fannie, a man-child
who was gi¥en the name Charles Maurice Wollenberg., and who was
destined to become the sixty-third Grand Master of Masons in California.
This youngster was in his early youth taken by his parents to Prescott, Arizona, where he attended the public schools, and later returning
to California, he matriculated at the University of California at Berkeley', ..
from which institution he was graduated in 1904 in pharmacy. From
then his activities have been various. After graduation he entered the
drug business at San Francisco, and during the tragic days immediately
following the ·great fire and seismic disturbance that practically destroyed the City of San Francisco, he was selected by the Red Cross
society to take charge of the great relief and refugee camps, hastily established to care for the thousands of homeless people who were for a
time sorely in need of food and shelter. In this work he found his
forte, and so well did he perform the arduous duties incident to the
care of the poor, so manifest was his genius for organization, that in
1908 he was appointed Superintendent of the San Francisco Relief Home,
an institution that maintains a staff of nearly two hundred physicians,
nurses, and other necessary employes, for the care of some seventeen
hundred of the dependent poor of the city.

In addition to the manifold duties incident to the superintendence of
public relief, Brother Wollenberg for the past fourteen years has been
a Director of the San Francisco Chapter of the Red Cross; for several
years was President of the Social Workers Alliance; Chairman of the
Budget Committee of the Community Chest; a member of the Board
of Governors of the Commonwealth Club of California. In fact, he is
and has for the last twenty-odd years, been active in all public and private
endeavors that pertain to the welfare of the poor. His friends marvel

Brother Wollenberg's Masonic career began in 1906, in Starr King
Lodge No. 344. He received his first degree March 14; second, April
11; third, May 30, 1906. He became active in Lodge work, and passed
through all the chairs, being Master in 1913. In 1909 he received the
Scottish Rite degrees to the .32d in the San Francisco bodies No. 1 ;
served .as Venerable Master and Master of Kadosh; and in 1925 was
crowned as an honorary 33d. For years he was a director· and chairman of the Scottish Rite relief committee and also of the Sciots Foundation for convalescent children.
In 1917 Brother Wollenberg was appointed a member of the Board
of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, and was President of
the Board from January, 1919, until his election as Grand Master in
October, 1929. At the annual meeting of the Home Trustee.s, held October 17, 1930, he was again elected President.
On September 17, _1899, our prother was un1ted in marriage to Miss
Romilda Judell, who has proved to be most helpful and sympathetic in all
her husband's welf;re work: She is a woman of splendid ·c haracter and
greatly loved by her legion of friends. Two fine boys have been born
to the Wolle~bergs-Albert C., who is at present Assistant United States
District Attorney, and Harold, an electrical expert who bids fair ·to
become eminent in his chosen profession. Both these boys are. members of the craft.

"Gone across the dark river
· And into the land of shadows."
The able ·committee on Necrology will report to you in detail the
list of our members who have passed to the realms beyond mortal
ken, but I will here mention the names of three distinguished brethren
who have held office in Grand ~odge:
Motley Hewes Flint, who served as Grand Master for the year
commencing October, 1905, was murdered in the city of Los Angeles
on the morning of July 14, 1930. Past Grand Master Flint for many
years was an active, energetic and most useful member of Grand
Lodge. During the dark days following the destruction of San Francisco and other cities of California by fire and earthquake, his genius
for organization and his untiring and intelligent labors in the work
of relief stand out as a monument to his zeal for Masonry and humanity, Later his ability for organization was displayed in his great
work for the Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes. In all, his
long life in California was devoted to constructive work.
John H. Logie, Junior Grand Steward, died suddenly in Glasgow,
Scotland, July 19, 1930. Brother Logie was a singularly sweet character, loved by all who knew him, useful as a man and Mason, utterly
without guile, and who always gave freely the best that' was in him
for the good of his fellow. men.
Rabbi Jacob Nieto, one of the best-known members of the craft,
died at San Francisco March 26, 1930. He had served the fraternity
and mankind faithfully for many years, and was a sturdy champion
for righteousness and decency i;'i the individual and in governmental
affairs. He was charitable of the weaknesses of mankind, condoning
the sinner but relentless in his condemnation of sin. As an orator he
was in demand, and gave freely of his time and talents not alone in
Masonic circles, but in the larger field of general social and civic
activities. Brother Nieto was Grand Chaplain of this Grand Lodge
for three terms-1903, 1904 and 1905. In 1906 he was appoin ted Grand
Orator, and at the special services in honor of our soldier dead in
1923 was the eulogist of the occasion. He was truly a good and useful
man.
"Thus passes life.
The joys of youth-bright beauties of the springGrow dim and faded; and the long, dark night ·
Of death's chill winter comes. But as the spring
Rebuilds the ruined wrecks of winter's waste,
And cheers the gloomy earth with joyous light,
So o'er the tomb the star of hope shall rise
And usher in an ever-during day."

Grand Secretary
I want at this time to acknowledge my indebtedness to our be!oved Brother, John Whicher. Grand Masters come and go, but it is
mdeed fortunate that our beloved Grand Secretary goes on forever.
Giving his entire time to his office, he is brought in intimate
contact not only with the Grand Lodge officers but wi th our subordinate Lodges, and to him all bring their perplexing problems.
An untiring student of Masonry, thoroughly conversant with the
· Constitution, Regulations and Landmarks of our California jurisdictio1i, he is a fount of Masonic wisdom to whom we safely look for
counsel and advice to keep us clear of all entanglements.
John Whicher is known not only to the brethren of our California
Lodges, but regarded as one of the valuable Grand Lodge Secretaries
throughout our great country.
In February each year there is held a conference of Grand Secretaries in the City of Washington, D . C. California has never been
represented. May I recommend at this meeting tha t we send our
Grand Secretary to this conference in 1931. I kn ow that a personal
acquaintance with those with whom Brother Whicher is in correspondence will greatly add to h is efficiency, if such were possible,
and also redound to the benefit of the Grand L odge.

pleasure.

Bi-Centenary of American Masonry

On June 5, 1930, the following cablegram was received :
"Grand Master, Masonic Temple,
San Francisco, California.
"On the eve of the two hundredth anniversary of the first Grand
Lodge recognition of American· Freemasonry by constituting a Provincial Grand Lodge for New England, I wish to congratulate all our
brethren in the United States on the great Masonic progress they
have made. I reiterate my fraternal good wishes and sincere desire
for their continued happiness and prosperity. It remains my earnest
hope that the tenets of our Order may assist still further to strengthen
the bond of friendship and good will which so happily exists between
our two nations, and I shall continue to watch with sympathy every
endeavor on both sides of the Atlantic to promote those feelings by
"the development of Freemasonry in its purest and highest forms.
"ARTHUR, Grand Master."

Visit to Grand Lodge of Arizona
The Grand Lodge of Arizona invited the Grand Master of California to attend the fiftieth anniversary of the chartering of Arizona
Lodge No. 2 by the Grand Lodge of California. As the Lodge organizing in the city of Phoenix in March, 1880, once owed obedience
to the Grand Lodge of California, I deemed it fitting to accept, and
requested Deputy Grand Master, John Stewart Ross, to represent us.
That he fittingly did so is indicated by the following extract from a
letter dated November 27, 1929, from M.'. W:. Amos A. Betts,
Grand Master of Arizona:
"Your own distinguished associate, the R ight Worshipful John
St~w~rt Ross, Deputy Grand Master of California, was of course the
principal speaker, and I assure. you that he acquitted himself in a
manner to reflect credit and glory upon his worthy chief and his
Grand .Lodge. In a very h.appy vein he conveyed your greetings and
best wishes to your old-time fellow-Hassayampers. We are sorry
to have been deprived of your personal presence but since we were
denied that pleasure we were happy that you se~t Brother Ross as
your representative.''
Conference of Grand Masters
On February 20, 1930, I attended, as 'your Representative, the
Annual Conference of Grand Masters of the United . States. I was
accompanied by M:. W:. Albert E. Boynton, Past Grand Master,
who is a member of the Board of Directors of the George Washington National Memorial Association.
·
There were forty Grand Juri.sdictions represented by thirty-six
Grand Masters and four Deputy Grand Masters.
··
The first topic discussed, that of Masonic Education, clearly indicated that no jurisdiction had developed a satisfactory programme
hut all were busily seeking, .as are we, for something that will create
increased interest in the membership and inculcate a desire for more
light.

I feel that our programme, as adopted by Grand Lodge of Cali~
fprnia, plus the district officers meetings, which have been developed
since our last communication, are as satisfactory .as any presented.
The discussions on Lodge and temple finances indicated that
many jurisdictions were realizing the need of Grand Lodge control.
The amendment to our Constitution in 1928, by which investment in
Masonic temples was controlled by a committee of Grand Lodge,
received general commendation.
.•
Dual membership, and organizations whose membership is, based
on Masonic affiliation, were also discussed. Both are troubling many
jurisdictions. I will take. up the question of dual membership later
in this report.
Visits by Distinguished Masons
\Vhile attending the .conference of Grand Masters, Past Grand
Master Melvin M. Johnson, of the Grand Lodge of Masons of .the
Commonwealth of Massachusetts, one of the most distinguished
Masons of the Eastern Section of our country, a Masonic authority
and the author of "The Beginnings of. Masonry in America," a book
found in all Masonic libraries, informed me that he would vis!f
California in March.
The time of his arrival was coincident with my visits to the
Lodges of the Sixty-second, Twenty-eighth, Fifty-third and Fiftyfourth Districts, and I invited Brother Johnson and his good wife to
accompany me and see something more of California than the usual
beaten path. We drove first to Fresno, then to Angels Camp, Yosemite and San Jose and. thence to San Francisco.
I am sure the Masons who were fortunate enoug~ .to ·hear B_rother
Johnson will not forget his visit, and I doubt if' he will soon forget
the ride from Sonora to Ange\s, his visit to .the "Mother Lode"
country, where Bret Hart and Mark Twain lived, and wbere the
latter served in various stations in Bear Mountain Lodge at Angels;
then to the southland, where they were shoyvn that section of our
State. Both in San Francisco and Los Angeles Brother Johnson left
·
his impression, and his visit will long be remembered.
On July 30th Grand Master Herbert C. Dean, accompanied by
Grand Marshal Balcom, Mrs. Dean and Mrs. Balcom, arrived in San
Francisco on the last leg of a trip around the world, during which he
had visited the Lodges under Massachusetts jurisdiction situated in
China.
Many of the Grand Lodge officers a-nd brethren enjoyed meeting
Brother Dean, and his word picture of Masonry in China and . the
situation of California Masons residing there was a strong argument
for dual membership.

Brothers Dean and Balcom attended the reception. to the Grand
Master by' Spe'ranza Italiana Lodge, and I am sure they enjoyed the
coiitact with our Italian brethren-to say nothing of the raviolas. ·
Brother Dean's talk carried a strong undercurrent favoring· dual membership.an'd his hearers- gained more insight in things Masonic in China

Two hundred years ago the first regular constituted Lodge in
the American colonies was chartered by the Grand Lodge of England
in the Massachusetts Colony. If the brethren who have led Masonry
in Massachusetts through all these years measure up to Brothers
Johnson, Dean and Balcom, its leadership in things Masonic can be
well understood. We congratulate Massachusetts on its representatives who visited us this year. We wish them God-speed and hope
they will come soon again.
The George Washington Memorial Association
In company with Past Grand Master Albert E. Boynton, I attended the meeting of the George Washington Na tional Masonic
Memorial Association at Alexandria, Virginia, February 21 and 22.
One can not help being struck with the magnitude of the monument. ~t is truly a stupendous undertaking and when completed will
be the finest memorial of its kind in the world.
. I.ts cost ·of over three million dollars seems large, but when we
consider that it is not only a monument to the memory of Washington, but also a landmark of American Masonry, bringing together
the forty-nine jurisdictions of the U nited States in a com mon activity,
providing a meeting place and a shrine for American Masonry, this
can be over.looked, for in fact it represents less than one dollar for
each Master Mason in the United States.
It is hoped . to complete the exterior by FebrQary 22, 1932, marking
the two hundredth anniversary of the birth of George Washington.
Congress has created a committee to arrange that this date be fittingly
celebrated, and it is expected that the dedication of this monument
will be one of the outstanding features of the "Washington year."
To finance the completfon many ·of the jurisdictions are pledging
a support eq1:1ivalent to two dollars per member and in addition one
dollar for each initiate, for future maintenance. California has
pledged. one dollar· per member, payable twenty cents a year.. To date
we have made three payments and I recommend these contributions
be continued.

The geographical extent of our Masonic jurisdiction and the
number of Lodges contained therein, preclude the pos.sibility of the
Grand '.Master attempting to visit even a majority of the Lodges
during the year, and it is unfair both to him and the other Lodges of
the State for an individual Lodge to expect his presence except on
unusual occasions.
I accepted invitations and was present at the 75th anniversary
of the following Lodges:
·
Morning Star Lodge No. 68, Stockton, December 14, 1929.
Ertterprise Lodge No. 70-, Yuba City, January 4, 1930.
Yolo No. 81, Yolo, January 24, 1930.
Bear Mountain No. 76, Angels Cainp, March 22, 1930.
·P etaluma ' No. 180, Petaluma, May 24, 1930. ,.
Joint meeting of Ione No. 80, Ione; Volcano No. 56, Volcano;
Amado.r No. 65, Jackson; at Volcano, June 1, 1930.
N;l.val No. 87, Vallejo, July 21, 1930.
The 80th anniversary of Benicia No. 5, Benicia.
They were all enjoyable and interesting, bringing back the days
of the early SO's, and the brethren of these pioneer Lodges are to be
complimented on the interest shown in commemorating the birth of
Masonry in their communities.
· On January 29th I installed the officers of Confidence Lodge
No.' 203 at Castroville. This visit was· of a peculiar interest to me, as
the minutes of January 29, 1872, when read, brought forth the fact
that on that day, fifty-eight years ago, my father was raised to the
degree of Master Mason, and on January 29, 1873, was installed as
Secretary of the Lodge. He was a member o~ the building -committee
in 1872 that built the hall we were then in, and the minutes contain a
resolution of thanks for his purchase of a carpet in San Francisco.
That carpet is still on .the floor of the hall and is just the age of your
Grand ·Master. Here, I truly felt the significance of the closing part of
our instaHation service, "May your children's children .c elebrate, with
jay and--gratitude, the annual recurrence of this auspicious solemnity."
On April 26th, accompanied by Mrs. Wollenberg, I sailed for the
Hawaiian Islands, and oi1 the 30th arrived at Honolulu after an
enjoyable and smo~th passage. There we were met by our. Grand
Senior "Deacon, · Brother Chas. C. Pittam, and Brother John A. Madden, Ins.pector of the One Hundred and Third District.
ffr~ther Pittam, with Inspectors Madden and Shepherd, had '
arranged our itinerary, and it was truly 'one continuous round of
pleasure. Ncit only did we have our official visits to the eight Lodges

situated in the four islands of this group, but for three weeks we
enjoyed continuously the beauties of the gems of the Pacific, and at
the same time the open-hearted hospitality of the Masons within its
borders. To attempt to thank those individuals who gave of their
time and hospitality, would be to name the officers and many members
of the Lodges.
May I ask you who represent our Hawaiian Lodges at this communication to take back to my brethren and their good ladies who
were so generous to Mrs. Wollenberg and myself, our "Aloha."
Everywhere, Lodges and brethren have been most cordial in
their reception to me, and I hesitate to mention any one event.
Yet, there were two receptions which I feel I might be pardoned
for mentioning. That of the brethren of Los Angeles on June 12th,
when a reception was tendered by the seventy-two Lodges 'at the
Shrine Auditorium, and that on October 13th, the Fairmont Hotel.
tendered by the Masons of San Francisco.
I would again tender the sincere appreciation of M rs. Wollenberg
and myself, not only for the courtesies extended on these occasions,
but more particularly to the brethren and their ladies of those Lodges
where on occasion Mrs. Wollenberg has accompanied me.

Lodges Constituted

Dedicating Masonic Club House, Los Angeles
A very interesting ceremony was that of the dedication of the
Masonic Club House of the University of California at Los Angeles.
The trustees of this Club are to be complimented on the very
beautiful building designed to meet the needs of the students of
Masons attending College.
There, as at the club house located at the University of California
at Berkeley, a splendid work is being carried on for the spiritual,
mental and social welfare of the students of Masonic families. And
in order that the brethren of the jl,lrisdiction might know of the advantages of these club houses, I issued a circular letter under date of
August ·l, 1930, as follows:
San Francisco, August 1, 1930.
To Masters of All Lodges in the Jurisdiction:
With a view to calling attention to the two splendid Masonic
club's being maintained for the benefit of students at the University of ·
California at Los Angeles and the University of California at Berke~
ley, I earnestly request that Masters advise their brethren of the fact
of these two clubs and of the benefits to accrue to their student children by affiliating with one or the other of them.
These two clubs are functioning in a practical manner, and every
Mason in our jurisdiction, having children in attendance at the University should urge membership. Co-operation on the part of the
parents is desirable, not merely for the success of the clubs, but for
the social and moral advantages of the students.
Our brethren should be reminded that these clubs are housed in
beautiful and comfortable buildings, and that the privileges extend to
the sons, daughters, sisters, brothers, nieces, nephews, and grandchildren of Masons. It has been said, and with truth, that the clubs
are havens for boys and girls who are away from home and home
influences; that they are places for clean social diversion, for relaxation from college activities, and where the homesick and lonesome
student may be associated with those whose business it is to serve
them and direct them and keep them happy.
The good hostesses who are in charge of our Masonic University
club affairs have been chosen for their peculiar fitness for the work
of looking after the young students; they have the happy faculty of
getting close to the hearts of the members; they know and can advise
concerning the many little problems that puzzle boys and girls-and
the Mason whose children are in attendance at either State University
would do well to encourage them to take full advantage of the privileges offered.
. I confidently rely on the Masters to convey to their membership
the above information.
Fraternally yours,
C. M. WOLLENBERG, Grand Master.
The trustees of both these clubs will report later on their activities
to Grand Lodi'e.

Restoration of Charter of Seal Rock Lodge No. 536
On the 24th day of September, Grand Master H utaff arrested
the charter of the above named Lodge. In his report to Grand Lodge
he stated:
"During the past ten months, due to the existence of two factions
who have embarrassed Masonry generally, the conditions prevailing
in Seal Rock Lodge No. 536 have been a source of much anxiety to
the Grand Master and other Grand Lodge officers.
"At my request, Brother Chas. M . Wollenberg, Deputy Grand
Master, visited the Lodge on February 6, 1929, as my representative
and endeavored, to the entire satisfaction of all concerned, to adjust
the existing differences. As a result of this conference and in an effort
to bring about a conciliation, the Worshipful Master resigned.
"After conferences with the officers of the Lodge, the granting
of special dispensations to reballot on candidates and to hold an
election to elect a Master caused by the resignation of the former
Master, it has been impossible to bring peace and harmony within the
portals of the Lodge, and the conditions seem to grow worse each
· month.
"I sincerely regret that the real offenders cannot be segregated,
thereby preventing the duty which I feel is incumbent upon me, and
it is only after careful consideration that, under date of September
24, 1929, I ordered the .arrest of their charter, and recommend that
this order be kept in force until the next communication of our Grand
Lodge; unless the incoming Grand Master shall in the meantime
become satisfied that the members of the Lodge are making a conscientious effort to uphold the principles of Masonry and work in
harmony. In which event he be authorized to return to the Lodge
its charter. In order that the property and business affairs of the
Lodge be properly conserved, I specially exempted from suspension
Brothers Walter Grant Campbell and the Treasurer and Secretary.
"Following is the text of my letter to the Master and members
of the Lodge:

"'The foregoing facts have been established through very careful
investigation. It is evident that under these conditions the usefulness

Masonic Library of Southern California
In April I received a communication from the Secretary of East
San Diego Lodge No. 561 calling attention to a circular of the "Masonic Library of Southern California, Inc." suggesting by way of
financial assistance a "contribution of one cent per capita monthly"
and asking if such a contribution could be made by the Lodge.
My reply was that such a contribution by a Lodge would be in
contravention of the provisions of Section 88 of the Constitution and
could not be permitted.
This led to a considerable correspondence with the President of
the Library, and finally a meeting at the library in Los Angeles.
There is no question that a Lodge could spend its funds for the
purclJase of books and maintenance of a lib.rary for the benefit of its
members, and that likewise several Lodges could unite in such an
acti.vity.
This library, however, is a private corporation, and although
organized by the Lodges of Southern California, it is no longer under
their control.
The Masonic Library of Los Angeles is a necessary institution,
and should be of great. value to the brethren of the southern part of
the State, and the programme of the Directors of the Corporation is
one that deserves support of the Lodges.
•
They recognize that the value of a Masonic library consists in a
great degree upon its accessibility to those who have the desire or
the necessity to consult its volumes.
Their present financial set up does not make this, the largest
collection of books on Masonic subjects in our State, as accessible as
they should be.
I therefore recommend that legislation be enacted at this cession
of Grand Lodge, enabling two or more Lodges to join in the Library
Association and providing for the su 1port of such Association from
the funds of the Lodge.
Dispensation to Form New Lodges
Shortly after the close of Grand Lodge last year I received a
petition for a dispensation for the formation of a Lodge at Willow
Glen in the county of Santa Clara. After a visit to San Jose, at which

"In my judgment this is the best method yet suggested for the
proper education of the officers of the Lodges. A young man going
through the chairs will thus be fairly well informed by the time he
reaches the responsible office of Master.
"Frank and friendly discussion around a dinner table, directed by
an able Inspector, will accomplish much, and I believe t hat in a few
years the troubles which some L odges experience, due largely to a
lack of knowledge on the part of the Master, will be things of the past.
" I direct that this practice be at once established in every Inspection district, excepting those where the distance or modes of travel
between Lodges may render it impracticable."
This has resulted in the formation of many additional district
officers' associations, and wherever formed information comes from
both officers and our Inspectors of the increased interest that is
being developed.
These meetings have brought out the fact that the junior officers
of the Lodges, with few exceptions, have failed to interest themselves
in a11ything but ritual until just previous to their installation in the
;Master's chair. It is at this time we qualify them on Masonic law
under' Section 137 of the Constitution.
The incoming Master, taking over the control of his Lodge and
all its pl'oblems for the first time in his Masonic career, is forced to
hastily comb through the Constitution in order to answer the questions on Constitution and Regulations.
I believe better results could be obtained were we to qualify the
\Varden~, and thus reduce the number of questions to the Master.
In other words extend this examination over three years ancl
thus create continued interest in the subject.
To this end I propose the following amendment to the Constitution:
Amend Section 137 by addi.ng after "First Degree," line 8 and
after "Second Degree," line 11:
"And that he is thoroughly proficient in those portions of the
Constitution and General Regulations of the Grand Lodge which
relate to the government of a Lodge."
R.". W:. Brother John Stewart Ross has volunteered to compile
the laws cited in our digest, so that our decision would be accessible
to all officers in our jurisdiction, and I feel that if his very generous
offer, one entailing a search of our proceedings from the year 1850 to
date, is accepted there will be no excuse for the officers of a Lodge
not knowing our laws.

Officers' Clubs
Within the year I have received many requetss from Lodges for
, interpretation of questions of Masonic law and custom. With few
exceptions all could have been readily answered by reference to the
Constitution and to decisions heretofore made.
·
The number of letters received by the Grand Master, to say nothing of the large number that come to the Grand Secretary, in4icate
either the need of a revision of the Constitution so that the layman
can obtain the information required or the education of the officers
of the subordinate Lodges in Masonic law and custom.
·
With this thought in mind, on January 1st I wrote the Inspectors'
of the several' Masonic districts as follows:
"I take pleasure i11 handing you herewith your commission as
Inspector for the. year 1930, and with it I take occasion to observe
that in many Inspection districts a most commendable practice is in'
vogue of holding monthly or bi-monthly meetings attended by the
Inspector and all the officers of the Lodges within his district, the
purpose being the discussion of Masonic law and custom as well as
ritual.
"No better p'..an for the Masonic educatio~ of Masters and Wardens particularly and other officers generally has been suggested, and
I heartily commend it to all Inspectors.
"Each Inspector should arrange· to meet the officers of all the
Lodges in his district, at dinner at least every two months, and more
frequently if circumstances appear to justify or demand it. Such
gatherings will afford the officers of the several Lodges opportunity
to become acquainted with their fellows during the service of the
dinner. After the dinner, from one and half to two hours may be·
taken up with discussion of Masonic subjects concerning basic and
Constitutional law, Regulations, and ritual: At no such time should

Degree Teams
While I knew that many degree teams were operat'ing in the
jurisdiction, it was not until I read a leaflet originating in Los Angeles, headed "The Association of Masonic Industrial Clubs-A
Confidential Message from the President," that I discovered a most
amazing and highly irregular and unmasonic method of operation.
This leaflet disclosed many disturbing facts: First, that some thirtyfive industrial organizations were represented by Masonic clubs or
degree teams; second, that while many promises were'made as to the
future activities of the Association in the way of social events, entertainment, publicatiol\ of a magazine, employment bureaus, relief, etc.,
a most specious promise was made concerning the future financial
welfare of the brethren who should join, by "pooling savings and
investments, whether large or small, under our plan of centralized
organization under the direction of competent trustees or managers,
whereby the individual member would receive the full- profit of his
investment." And then goes on to show the highest form of investment is in the "Southern California Trust Estates; so e.,ach· member
of the Association of Masonic Industrial Clubs is to subscribe for at
least one unit of beneficial interest ·at $25.00 per unit, which not only
takes care of yo'u r dues in your Club, but gives the member an assured
income of 12 per cent on the $25.00."
I summonsed the President and other officers (all Past Masters)
of this Association to meet me, and as a result .cif this interview, on
November 30, 1929, it was disbanded.
Another serious breach of Masonic custom, if not indeed of law,
was reported to me in March of this year, that two degree teams representing organizations which required as a prerequisite to membership that their petitioners should be Master Masons, were conferring
degrees in Lodges and immediately following the ceremony of conferring the third degree presenting to the newly-raised brethren, post'aated six ~10nths, petitions for the d~grees in their respective organizations. On investigation I found the facts to be as reported, and all
such petitions were returned to the deluded applicants and destroyed.
Other complaints came to me from Inspectors and Masters concerning the activities of degree teams, and I deemed it necessary to
order the discontinuance of the certificates of proficiency heretofore
permitted to be issued by Inspectors, a copy of which order, which
was directed at Inspectors and Masters, is as follows:
"It is well-settled by our Constitution and Regulations that the
Master may invite any qualified brethren to confer a degree, he of
course remaining present. This responsibility is committed entirely

25

to the Master and it is his duty to see that the work is performed
's trictly according to our ritual. The same is true· whether one or more
temporary officers participate.
"There have· grown up in some parts of the jurisdiction wh.a! ~re
known as 'degree teams,' organiz.ed for the express purpose of v1s1tlng
Lodges other than those to which. the membe~s _of such teams a_re
members and conferring degree~. Here\ofore, in order to assist
Masters ~f Lodges in determining the qualification~ .o.f members. of
the team and thus relieve the Masters of the respons1b1hty of examining the degree-team members as to their qualificat ions, the <;irand
Lecturer was authorized to delegate 'to Inspectors the authority to
examine and issue certificates of qualification to the teams, after due
examination by the Inspectors. This practice is now ordered to be
discontinued.
"On and after this date, if and when any Maste: .reque~ts or
permits any brother or b_reth_ren to confer o~ to parhci_Pate in the
conferring of any ·degree in his Lodge, excepting the officers of another Lodge holding obi;d!ence to our _Gra~d Lodge, he a~cepts the
responsibility of determining the quahficat10ns of sue~ brother or

and until the Master has so satisfied himself he cannot lawfully invite

.Lodges, to participate in degree work.

"Dated March 31, 1930."

Suspension and Restoration of a Master
Under date of December 11, 1929, I suspended from office the
Master of Anaheim Lodge No. 207, for reasons stated in the following lett~r, the original of which was directed to Darrol D. Webb, then
Master of said Lodge:
"For gross violation of Masonic law you are hereby suspended
from the office of Master and from the exercise of all powers and
duties of the office of Master of Anaheim Lodge No. 207, F. & A. M ..
of the jurisdiction of California.
"At your stated meeting for November, 1929, you caused a ba,llot
to be taken on seven petitioners collectively. A ~lac_k .ball appe~rmg,
you directed an individual ballot to be had on. an indi_vidual candidate.
As a result of this ballot you declared a candidate reiected. You then
proceeded with balloting until all the petitioners were balloted upon.
A recess · was then declared · during which time several brethren
entered the Lodge room and 'others retired, in the proper be)ief that
balloting had closed. During th~ if!termissioi:i your attention was
called to Section 104 of the Constitution. You declared the ballot on
the theretofore rejected candidate null and void and ordered another
ballot thereon, which appeared clear; whereupon you promptly de-

Under our law the effect of this suspension, had it been allowed
to extend beyond the time the Master's successor had been elected

Misrepresentation in Petition
During the year a num,ber of instances were brought to the attention of the Grand Master wherein candidates had applied for admission and had been elected to receive the degrees in various Lodges,
who· had failed to state in their petitions that they had been previously
rejected for the degrees in another _Lodge.
.
In four of these instances the candidate had received the first or
first and second degrees before this was discovered.
In several instances a trial was held. In one case the candidate
was able to convince the trial c.o mmission that he had been advised
that it was not necessary to answer the question truthfully or that he
did not know he had been rejected, and he apparently had the sympathy of all the members of the Lodge in which he had been elected.
The prosecutor was the Junior Warden of the Lodge and very littl e,
if any, attempt was made to convict, and it resulted in a verdict of not
guilty.
After 'careful consideration of this action, the Grand Master felt
that more could be accomplished by issuing an order to the Lodges
involved, as follows:
" Information has been ' lodged with the Grand Master that

on or about.. ......................................................... ., for the degrees of Ma-

Transcripts of Trial Records
Many times during the year I have received letters asking whether.
or not charges had been preferred against men who were undergoing
trial or had been convicted in the courts. In a number of instances
these were cases that had attracted more than usual attention, due
to the •impor·t ance of the case and its publicity in the newspapers.
Under our law, Grand Lodge is informed of a trial ~fter . its conclusion, and then only if a verdict of guilty and a judgment of suspension or expulsion has been .found.
I can see no objection to a copy of all charges of unmasonic
conduct being filed in the Grand Secr~tary' s office, and at the conclusion of the trial the transcript of same, whether resulting in acquittal or otherwise, being so filed.
This would enable the Grand Master to. know what was going on
in our jurisdiction; encourage officers of Lodges to do their duty, and
oftentimes prevent injustices.
.
I ask Grand Lodge to approve this policy, and recommend that
Section 207 of the Constitution be amended as, fo~lows:
.
In the first paragraph the words "thirty days" 'be changed to
read "ninety days," thus giving ample time for the. Grand Master to
direct an appeal - to the Grap.cl Lodge if he deem.s such· procedure
proper under .the circumstances of the particular case. ·
And in the next to last sentence of the first paragraph, strike out
the word "appealed" in the phrase "in all appealed cases" and the
words "in all cases of expulsion or suspension" immediately following.
The result would be that in all cases the transcript would have to be
prepared and forwarded to the Grand Secretary, giving opportunity
to the Grand Master or some one delegated by him to look ove.r the
record.

Public Schools Week
One hundred and thirty yeats ago there existed in this country
of ours a· number of schools, but with one exception all were connected with various religious denominations, and but three per cept
of our population was afforded an opportunity for education, and this
not free.
·
The leaders in this Republic early realized that if it was to continue, it would be necessary to establish a system of free educ.ation
through public schools, where distrust and intolerance would be
removed from the minds of the future citizens of our land, by intimate
contact in the school yard and the school room.
The result of this was the establishment of our Public Schools
System; one in which Masonry had a large part in bringing into being.
T~e vari~us deno.nii~ati'qns that maintained private schools in
connection with their churches in 1800, for the most part accepted
the public school system, at least in the elementary and secondary
grades. One great religion only maintains a system of sectarian
schools, and the head of that religion has lately issued an encyclical
pointing out that the "Education of the young is a matter for the
church; the right of the parent therein is secondary and the State has
no right at all." If such a theory were to prevail in our country a
most dangerous condition wo,uld arise. No longer would we ·have
harmony, toleration and democracy. And so 1• commend to you the
idea of a Public Schools W t:ek, the creation of Past €;rand Master
Adams some ten years ago, and give it to you in charge as Masons
individually, to display your interest in the Public Schools System,
not only in the one week set' aside for this observance, but throughout the fifty-two weeks of the year, thus displaying your good
citizenship.
I ask that you lend careful ear to the report of our Committee on
Public Schools Week This activity deserves the commendation of
our craft.

Politics
Immediately after my return to San Francisco from the annual
communication of Grand Lodge at Los Angeles, my attention was
called to a so-called. Masonic ticket for municipal offices in the election
to be held in San Francisco in November.
The word Masonic did not appear on this ticket, but it is a fact
that candidates were approached and solicited for funds to "help pay
the cost of printing" and were told it would be distributed at Masonic
Lodge meetings and to some 75,000 Masons and their famiiles.
The originator 'of this ticket, in his correspondence with candidates for office, used letter-heads on which was printed his Masonic
titles, and used his title in Masonry after his signature, although
letters were sent to non-Masons.
In two instances members of the craft refused to allow their
names to appear on this ticket, and non-Masons were substituted.
In an interview with the brother responsibl e, I pointed out that
the brethren generally resented the efforts of this group to link
Masonry with local partisan politics; that his denial meant nothing,
as the use of his Masonic letter-hea.ds and Masonic titles was for the
deliberate purpose of linking M~sonry to his so-called Masontc ticket,
and that if it continued I would be forced to take active steps to
prevent its re-occurrence.

Dual Membership
At the conference of Grand Masters at Washington, D. C., February 20th, this subject was ably presented by Grand Master McFadden, of Virginia. It created a great deal of interest, and .it is being
discussed in many American jurisdictions at this time.
Grand Master Dean, in his address to the officers of Grand Lodge
and Past Grand Masters, at a luncheon in San Francisco, brought
home to us the value of dual membership to those who are temporarily living in foreign lands.
In order that the brethren here assembled may give this subject
thought and have the facts before them, I here quote from the address
of the Grand Master of New York, 1927, the following, relating on
this subject:
·
"It is my purpose to call your attention only to one or two outstanding features which the question presents.
"First, ~ingle or exclusive membership is largely an American
custom and 1s not therefore a Landmark of the Craft. Some American
ju_risdictions have used a plural system for many years, apparently
with good results. To adopt plural membership therefore would
not be an innovation in the body of Masonry.
'
'
"Second, brethren coming from other jurisdictions who may
desire membership in one of our Lodges must first make sure that
their possible affiliation with us will not be in violation of the laws of
their home jurisdiction.
"Third, he who would join Lodges other than his Mother Lodge
must present his petition, which shall be the official form used by the
~rand Lodge of the State of New York, pass the ballot, and qualify
m every respect under the By-laws of the Lodge he would join and
the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of the State of New York.
"F?~rth, after being duly elected, he would have th~ same rights
and privileges as any other member of the Lodge with which he
becomes connected.
"The question may be argued both affirmatively and negatively.
but after all is said and done, the positive arguments seem to preponderate, whereas the negative arguments are more or less technical
and easily overcome."
The report of the Special Committee on the above was as follows:
. "We have considered carefully the situation referred to in ·fu
said address, the history of Lodge membership, single and plural
the material available contributed by Masonic students and thoughtfui
Masons, b<?th in recent publications and in the general history of
the fratermty, and have to some extent canvassed the opinion of
members of the fraternity both in this and other jurisdictions.
"The advantages of plural membership in our opinion exceed the
disadvantages.
"Many are the cases of Masons, who, moving from their old
home and the neighborhood of their Lodge to a location distant
frequently, in another State and Masonic jurisdiction, and 'desirous

37

naturally of Masonic intercourse, discover a group in the neighborhood in which they have established themselves with which they
delight to foregather but find, as is natural and manly, embarrassment
by reason of the fact that they have no status, are merely guests, and
hesitate to wear out their welcome. Whether Masonic hospitality is
all-extensive as distinguished from normal human relations may be
debatable, but we doubt it. We see no reason why the Masonic relation should so transform. the human creature, as to make him an
unending and great welcomer of the visitor who pays nothing, who
bears no burdens, who take no part in activities, who has no status.
And it seems self-evident that the lack of opportunity to bear burdens,
assume responsibilities, to render service, and to take active part in
Masonic life inevitably soonor later saps and kills Masonic vitality.
Indeed, we consider it axiomatic that upon activity, responsibility,
right and duty to perform service depend Masonic life, and that the
Mason out of touch is dying or dead. The army of unaffiliates doubtless grows in some measure from this cause.
"A frequently heard objection to participation in the formation
of a new Lodge is the fear of an unwillingness to be weaned and
severed from one's Mother Lodge.
"Massachusetts has planted Freemasonry in several parts of the
world distant from its section, notably the Canal Zone, Chile and
Shanghai. This was a partial cause for the adoption of plural membership by that jurisdiction."
"Rhode Island adopted dual membership in connection with the
establishment as a regular Lodge of its War Lodge, which operated
at Coblenz, but made the privilege of dual membership available
generally within that jurisdiction, limiting the privilege to two
Lodges within the jurisdiction.
"New York has planted the seeds of Masonry in Finland, Roumania and Syria, an act and an activity which suggests the propriety
of affording the opportunity of plural membership on that account;
but we take the view that there is now no, or should be no, serious
objection to membership in two or more Lodges of different obediences, with appropriate regulation governing discipline and limitation as to Mastership.
"We, therefore, recommend that plural membership both within
and without the jurisdiction be permitted."
The recommendation was adopted and New York now permits
not only dual but plural memberships.
I believe that dual memberships would not affect many in our
jurisdiction. Lodges would still have control and would make the
same investigation as in all cases of affiliation, and could and should
keep out those who would become charges on the Lodge or be otherwise undesirable.
The man who will se~k dual membership is the active man of
affairs, removed through business from his home Lodge, who, loving
Masonry, desires to have contact with his brethren of the fraternity;
or again, the brother of our own jurisdiction who, raised and passing
through the chairs in one part of the State, has for one reason or
another made a permanent home in another section.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

38

39

PROCEEDINGS OF 'l'HE

His love for his Mother Lodge, the obligation due it for the
honors eonferred on him, and perhaps its need of his financial support,
prevent him from dirnitting, and it is therefore, embarrassing for him
to partake of the hospitality of the Lodge in his new home.
He wants to be active in Masonry, and Masonry needs him. Will
you again give some thought to the qu~stion of dual membership?
And in order that it be brought forward for discussion at this
communication of Grand Lodge, I would recommend the amendments proposed in 1923, by the Jurisprudence Committee, with some
slight changes, that is, amending Section 157 of the Constitution to
read as follows:
"No Mason shall be a member of more than one Lodge of this
jurisdiction, but may in addition maintain membership in Lodges of
other jurisdictions whose Constitution permits dual membership, and
a brother of a foreign jurisdiction which permits dual membership
may affiliate with a Lodge in this jurisdiction without withdrawing
from such Lodge. He shall be subject to the provisions of the Constitution regarding application, references, report and ballot, if such
membership be permitted by the law of the jurisdiction of any Lodge
of which he is a member at the time of application for affiliation in
another Lodge, and in such event he shall be entitled to the same
rights and privileges and be subject to the same duties, prohibitions
and liabilities in each Lodge as attach to membership therein; provided, that if he shall be expelled or suspended for any reason by any
Lodge of which he is a member, he shall thereby stand expelled or
suspended from all such Lodges and shall not be reinstated in any
Lodge until the Lodge by which he was expelled or suspended shall
have reinstated him to membership, and provided further, that he may
withdraw from any Lodges of which he is a member.
Resolved, further, that Section 161 of the Constitution be amended
by striking out the last sentence of the first paragraph thereof and
inserting in lieu thereof the following:
"If the applicant be elected, he shall become a member of the
Lodge so electing him by signing its By-laws; provided, however,
that an applicant for affiliation who has given to any Lodge of which
he may be a member, notice of his intention to withdraw therefrom.
shall not be permitted to sign the By-laws and become a member of
any other Lodge until after the issuance of the certificate of his
withdrawal from such Lodge, which shall be immediately issued by
the Secretary upon due notice of his election by the Lodge with
which he desires to affiliate; and provided further, that every applicant shall state in his application for affiliation whether or not he
desires to withdraw from the Lodge of which he is at the time a
member."
Be it further resolved, that the second paragraph of said Section
161 be amended by inserting after the words "ipso facto cease" the
following words :
·
"Unless he indicate upon the petition for dispensation that it is
his intention to retain his m embership in the Lodge or Lodges of
which he is a member."

Expense of Grand Master
I would ask Grand Lodge and the Finance Committee to give
consideration to the appropriation of funds to cover the traveling
expenses of the Grand Master.
For many years an annual appropriation . of $2,500.00 has been
made for this purpose. I know that those Grand Masters who met
the demands on them by the Lodges of the jurisdiction, attended the
conference of Grand Masters at Washington, D. C., and visited the
Lodges of the Hawaiian Islands, spent a great deal more than this
allowance, the -deficit coming from their own funds.
To be Grand Master is a privilege and an honor, and the incumbent gives freely and gladly of his time. But I doubt if our brethren
expect him to pay the expenses necessitated by the discharge of the
duties of the office.
With the understanding that this applies to the future only, I
recommend the adoption of the following addition to the usual annual
resolution of the Finance Committee:
"The actual individual expenses, not to exceed $5,000.00 per annum of the Grand Master in the discharge of his duties appertaining
to his office, shall be paid. He shall submit to the Grand Secretary,
a statement, and after approval by the Committee on Accounts, the
Grand Secretary shall draw a warrant on the Grand Treasurer in
payment thereof."
Conclusion
In concluding, I beg of you to accept all the thanks that a heart
full of gratitude can offer.
My experience as Grand Master has been a happy and profitable
one to me, and I hope of some small value to the Masonry of our
jurisdiction. I have tried to be fair to all men, always having in mind
the best interests of Masonry.
The brethren have at all times been kind, courteous and generous,
and have ever shown me the very highest respect.
The elected and appointed officers of Grand Lodge, our tireless
Inspectors, the chairman and members of our committees and the
Masters of the various Lodges have always and cheerfully met every
request of the Grand Master, and I take this occasion to tender to
them my sincere thanks.
The opportunity of meeting and becoming acquainted with men
of such high character has been a great privilege, and I trust that the
friendships made will continue through life.
I have had many invitations to visit Lodges that I was unable
to accept. This is a large jurisdiction and no Grand Mas ter can cover

40

GRAND LODGE OF °CALIFORNIA

it in a year. Perhaps those Lodges whose invitations I was forced to
decline will at some future date give me an opportunity to greet them
as a Past Grand Master.
·
Brethren, such is the report of my stewardship. Let us proceed
with the business that brings us here.

First: That Public Schools Week commencing on the 21st day of
April, 1930, be observed by all our Lodges and their members according to custom.
Second: That in every community in Ca}ifornia and the Territory of Hawaii in which there exists a Lodge of Masons there be held
during that week at least one public meeting or gathering through
which the attention of the people may be focused on the public
schools.
Third: That no "work" be done i.n any L odge on the night on
which any meeting for the observance of Public Schools Week is held
in the city or town in which the Lodge is located.

GRAND LODGE, F . & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
CHARLES M. \VoLLENBERG, Grand Master

SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA

PROCLAMATION
ELEVENTH A N NUAL OBSERVANCE PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

To all Masons in the Jurisdiction:
If it be true, as has been said, that "the startling advancement of
education in the West has imperiled the intellectual leadership of the
Eastern states," it is undoubtedly due to the attitude of the public.
In the support of its public schools California occupies a particularly enviable position. There is no other State in the Union in which
the people seem to be more genuinely interested in their schools and
more willing to provide the necessary support.
It may be only a coincidence that there is no other State in which
the people know more of the aims, purposes and achievements of their
schools than they do in California; but it is more than likely that it
is because here an especial effort has been, and is still being, made to
keep the people informed, and to establish · a close contact between
the schools and their patrons. In this work the Masonic Fraternity,
even with becoming modesty, may justly claim to have played no
small part.
Public Schools Week has become a community affair and is no
longer merely a Masonic event ; but our task is far from completed.
We must continue to foster the observance, willingly and gladly
joining with the civic organizations in the larger communities, carrying on alone if, and only where, compelled so to do, and everywhere
being willing to bear the burden and heat of the day, while generously
giving credit to all who labor in the vineyard whether or not they be
of our number.
Now, therefore, I, Charles M. Wollenberg, Grand Master of
Ma'sons in the jurisdiction of California, do proclaim, request and
direct as follows:

Dated at San Francisco California, this 17th day of February,

JOH N WHTCHER,

Grand Secretary.

C. M . WOLLENBERG,

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the M:. W:. Gran.1 Lodge of California:
Herewith is presented my twenty-third annual report informing
you of all moneys received for. account of Grand Lodge, the Masonic
Homes and the Emergency Relief Fund, and a summary of disbursements. The Constitution requires that the detail of all expenditures be filed with the Finance Committee, which has been don e.
Membership
The membership of chartered Lodges for the year ended July
31, 1929, was 138,456, and of Lodges under dispensation, 196, a total
of 138,6S2, a_ net gain over the previous year of 4,350.
For the fiscal year ended July 31, 1930, chartered Lodges reported
a membership of 141,926 and the three Lodges under dispensation,
reporting as of September !, 1930, have 136 members, the total
membership now being 142,062, a net gain of 3,410 over last year.
There are only five jurisdictions in the United States having a
larger membership than ours; and our percentage of net increase is
exceeded only by the District of Columbia, New Mexico and Arizona.
There are S77 chartered Lodges on our registry, and three
Lodges under dispensation.

Meetings on Holidays
There appears to be much misunderstanding reg~rding the
amendment last year to Section 1 of Article III of the Uniform Code
of By-Laws, and members generally do not know, or remember, just
what holidays are excepted from stated meeting dates. I reco~men~
that either the amendment of 1929 be repealed or that certain holidays be specifically named in the Section, so that all Lodges will be
definitely advised.

To the Finance Committee, Grand Lodge of California.
Following your authorization we have audited the accounts of the
Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31,
1930. We present herewith the attached statements:

Grand Treasurer's Report of Cash Receipts and DisSchedule of Assets.

Comments
The audit covered an examination of the cash funds received during
the year ended July 31, 1930. In the case of annual returns received
from the various Lodges, the cash received was applicable to the annual
reports for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1929, and did not cover any
moneys received on account of annual returns or reports for the fiscal
year ended July 31, 1930. Cash received reported as dues from the
Lodges for the year under review, total $129,978.43, of which $1.63 was
for the prior period. These total receipts were proved with the total
membership and all such funds were completely accounted for.
We certify that the attached statements were compiled from the
books of account and records of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of
California.
Respectfully submitted,
RUCKSTELL & LAND, Certified Public Accountants.
By FLOYD T. WEBB.

merit.

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Past Grand Masters,
Officers and Brethren of the Grand Lodge of Masons of California.
In accordance with honored custom the 81st communication of
the Grand Lodge pauses in its deliberations to listen to a message
from its Grand Orator.
Because of the honor bestowed on me one year ago by our
Most Worshipful Grand Master, I appear today as your Orator,
and I trust all present will believe and understand that I approach
this moment with due humility, realizing that in addressing the select
men of 580 Lodges, representing 144,000 good men and true who
constitute the body Masonry in this great State of California, that
proverbially speaking I am "carrying coal to Newcastle."
While I am sincerely grateful for the high honor which this
h~ur affords I am also deeply moved in the august presence of
these honor~d Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters, who, each in
his time guided our destinies with a wisdom and foresight that has
made our great Brotherhood the most honorable and respected institution in this glorious State.
We feel a great pride in our affiliation with this Brotherhood,
and well we may, for nothing in history furnishes a parallel to its
unselfish purpose in behalf of mankind or its universality. It is said
to exist where Christianity has not gone, and its claims are respected
where even the superior claims of religion would fail. May not the
reason for this be found in the fact that Masonry is neither a religion nor a cult, yet it has consistently guarded the one essential
of religion, namely, that great Central Truth, that God lives and
is the universal Father of all mankind, and as such, we are the
object of his love and mercy and entitled to equal considerations as
members of the same great family.
Permit me to carry you back a few brief moments to review in
retrospect the struggle and the evolution of man out of the abyss
of darkness to the light of our day, because this struggle and this
evolution have a direct bearing upon Masonry so far as its origin is
concerned, and also on the influence it has exercised in the upbuilding M the human race. We review the past, not in order that we
may return to it but that we may fincl in what direction, straight
and clear, it points to the future.
The age of Speculative Masonry is satisfactorily fixed in our
minds so far as the order of the present day is concerned, but the

70

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

antiquity of the "principle" on which our Speculative Masonry is
founded reaches back to the dim and distant past, to the time when

Moses, Buddha, Mohammed, or Christianity. That is why we find
today representatives in goodly number of all these faiths, votaries
of Masonry.
· Wisely King Solomon said: "We walk upon the ashes of the
generations who have gone this way before us and to which in
turn our ashes contribute." In other words, we have advanced because of the experience of those who have gone before and to which
our achievements will in turn contribute for the benefit of those who
follow us.
These things we must also bear in mind in connection with the
present mental status of man, particularly in his outlook upon nature
when compared with the dim and distant past, and the evolution of
the Masonic principle.
Even in this Twentieth Century, mankind en masse, in its attributes and in its thoughts is largely controlled by inherited beliefs
and impulses, which countless thousands of years have ingrained
in his nature, like instinct.
With all our vaunted civilization in this Christian era there is
still being used over vast regions of our earth amulets, charms, magic,
and incantatio11s as the chief weapon of defense against malignant
nature.
Is it any wonder that primitive man sought in the supernatural
an explanation of the phenomena of life? No, it was but natural
that he should people his world with spiritual beings, defying objects
of nature and assigning to them benign or malign influences which
he could invoke or propitiate.
To primitive man life seemed "full of sacred presences" which
he began early to deify, so that until quite a recen't period his
story is mainly associated with a Pantheon of greater and lesser
gods which he manufactured wholesale.
Xenophanes (536 B. C.) was the earliest philosopher to recognize and write of man's practice of making gods in his own image
and endowing them with human faculties and attributes. The
Thracians he said made their gods blue-eyed and red-haired; the
Ethiopians, snub-nosed and black.
And so, all through early history we find a pantheon full to
repletion bearing testimony no less to the fertility of man's imagination than to the hopes and fears which led him in his exodus from
barbarism.
It is marvelous what a long line of superhuman powers, major
and minor, man has invoked of his gods. We find in Tyler's definition of religion one outcome of a belief in spiritual being has been
"that man has built an altar of righteousness in his hear,t."

man first learned to communicate his thoughts to his fellowman.
No sage of the past nor philosopher since history. has been
recorded, has been able to testify to its antiquity, for in every age
and in every civilization there is evidence that great secret orders
existed that taught a faith in God above and a moral law within.
Zoroaster more than ten cen.turies before our Christian era taught
a dual philosophy of good and evil and of light and darkness; the
Egyptians, Greeks and the Romans, as well as other ancient peoples,
all had their secret orders and their mysteries.
Some of these teachings in man's past seem to us perverted efforts, cruel and barbaric, yet the germ principle was to make life
tolerable and offer happy hopes for the hour of death. If recorded
history speaks of them, then surely we may infer that this principle
of which I speak far antedates man's ability to write.
Plato in his histories tells us the Mysteries were established by
men of great genius who in the early ages strove to teach purity
and a higher life. Cicero speaks of the high purpose of the mystic
· orders of his day, all of which bear mute testimony that from the
very beginning there arose out of conflicting faiths, that were based
upon fears and superstitions, a Divine urge that impelled men to
t<?il in behalf of a brotherhood that could &atisfy man's craving for
freedom and unity.
When we begin to study the history of man, whose mundane
story scienists are just beginning to unravel, we can scarcely comprehend the vastness of time which has elapsed.
It takes us back two millions (and some claim three millions)
of years. Back to the Pliocene or Miocene period when man lived
and moved and had his being; while modern history, as we know
it, embraces that b.rief space of time that has elapsed since the
earliest Egyptian ·and Babylonian records were made.
With this knowledge before us, so patiently and so painstakingly drawn from the footprints and markings in the rocks and sands
of time, we are justified in the conclusion that the principles of
Masonry arose out of the wants and very needs of man's nature,
out of the beatings and pulsations of the heart of a common humanity
and the deep seas of human sympathy and which the secret orders
and the mysteries failed to recognize and failed to satisfy.
Masonry and the principle on which it is founded have no creed,
no dogma and offers no religious formula by which the benefits of
religion may be secured, whether it be the religion of Confucius,

71

72

PROCEEDINGS Olt THE:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Ray Lankaster in his Romanes Lectures "Nature and Man"
(Oxford University Press, 1905, p. 21) remarks that a man is nature's
rebel * * *. The mental qualities which have developed in man,
though traceahle in a vague and rudimentary condition in some
of his animal associates, are of such an unprecedented power and
so far dominate everything else in his activities as a living organism,
t?at they have to a large extent. cut him off from the general operation of that process of natural selection and survival of the fittest
which up to the appearance of man had been the law of the livin~
world.
They justify the view that man forms a new departure in the
gradual unfolding of nature's predestined scheme, for to man
only .has been given the attributes of Knowledge, Reason, Selfconsc1ousness and Will.

tempt that was made, will live the true value of P ythagoras, Plato,
Aristotle, Pericles, Socrates and the other great Greek thinkers and
writers.
It is not that they answered questions, but they dared to ask
them. Never before their time had man challenged his world or
the way of life to which he was born.
Never before had he said or thought that he could alter his
condition by shattering traditions to which seemingly necessity bound
him and still live.
Hence there is no measuring of the debt which our generation
owes to those apostles of light nor to those others of the middle
ages of our own era:--Shakespeare, Goethe, Pasteur and a host of
others.
They were pioneer heroes in life's evolution whose daring, for
the purpose of comparison, was greater than that of an Amundsen,
a Peary, a Byrd, or a Lindbergh.
It is a far cry from the day when man wit!\ his stone implements, gutteral speech and crude drawings banded with a few others
for protection, to the highly complex civilization composing our modern society, wi th its achievements in the arts and sciences.
The social mind of modern society required many centuries of
warfare against darkness, superstition and intolerance to the acceptance of the new consciousness that recognizes every man, no matter
how high or how low in the scale of development, as our brother and
entitled to the same protection, sympathy and kindness we expect
from and give to our equals.
.
Slowly to be sure, but very positively, increasing numbers of
peop}e and more nations are apprehending the reality of a human
brotherhood, the needlessness of wars, of cruel ties and oppression
and the possibilities of the common purpose for all mankind.
In this' uplifting and development of the race, Masonry has
played a most important role. We can trace, like a golden thread
woven into the warp of a fabric, all down the line of receding ages
into that dim obscurity of an unrecor.ded past and behold e.merging
with the first rays of dawning light, the principles and tenets that
form the broad foundation of our institution.
The thread is buried for a time by ignorance, intolerance or
tyranny, but is never lost, nor was the interval of its suppression
wholly wasted, for in these periods of rest, like a tree in winter
which stores its energy in · its roots, so too were the truths of its
tenets, the justice of its principles, stored in the heart of man, to
burst forth like Springtime with new vigor, and like the tree,
bear new and better fruit.

God by God flits past in thunder till his glories turn to shades

hm1t her scope, and transform her energies.
The victory is so recent that the mental attitude of the race is
not yet wholly adapted to the change.
Man wandered the earth for ages seeking to find himself. The
lamp of reason, lighted in his soul at birth, even in his darkest period,
has never been wholly extinguished, but re-trimmed and re-furnished
hy his indomitable energies, it now shines more and more toward a
perfect day.
The slowness of its arrival is explained by Jung in his Psychology of the Unconscious, when he says the difference between ancient

was undirected thinking, the latter directed thinking. In other words,
the one was · a thinking in images, a world of subjective fantasies
like the world of children that creates not science, but mythology:
and the other is an orderly direction of thought.

Beecher said: "We sleep but the loom of life never stops and the
pattern which was weaving when the sun went down, is weaving
when it comes up tomorrow."
So it is with the generation that is, as it was with those that have
passed into history. There is as great a need for the ministry of
Masonry in the complex life of our day as there was twenty centuries ago, and we who stand today the successors of those early
brethren who formulated the ideals under which we work, cannot lose
sight of their true significance. The institution we have inherited
must be kept at all times in the forefront of progress, for ours becomes a greater duty, because the vastly greater numbers in our
world have brought to us greater opportunities and greater responsibilities.
Our world is far from the ideal of civilization, yet there is hope,
for as man develops he places a greater value upon his own rights;
liberty becomes for him a grander and diviner thing and he begins
to value the rights of others, but only .when all men give to all
others the rights they claim for themselves, will this world become
civilized.
Masonry, therefore, has an important role to sustain. Its symbolism and its teachings are directed toward the individual and not
toward the State; its function is to inculcate the moral principles
that build character.
Her deep truths are drawn from that inexhaustible fountain, the
Holy Bible, which is always open upon our altar; she has always
preached the sanctity of the home and the purity of life. Her name
will always be coupled with obedience to law and order, to loyalty ·
to government and all that citizenship under that government stands
for.
Masonry has for over 200 years in this great U~ion of ours, not
only builded mankind, but she has been the champion of light, as
reflected in our public school system, and has consistently . supported the building of those indissoluble monuments of civilizationfreedom of speech, of the press and a religious liberty.
Monuments that will serve the generations who shall be our
heirs as keys to unlock the fetters of ignorance and tyranny, no
matter what form they seek to assume; she is a believer in the fundamental rights of liberty of man within the full meaning of freedom, provided he does not use his liberty as a cloak for a maliciousness
that subverts human rights or loyalty to the Flag of Country.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M: .w:.Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit my twenty-third Annual Report as Grand
Lecturer. The most satisfactory experience about my years of
service has been the wonderful assistance and hearty co-operation
of the Inspectors and Brethren, who have at all times been most
anxious and willing to serve, which compensates in no small degree
for my efforts in bringing up and maintaining the standard of the
ritual, and it is with genuine pleasure that I can testify to the loyal
co-operation of my Brethren. This is very gratifying.
I have received reports from all the Inspectors, and they report
their Lodges to be in excellent condition, with the exception of a
few Lodges in small communities that are fast becoming depopulated, and some others that have heavy financial burdens in Temples.·
But, on the whole, a very satisfactory condition exists in the Jurisdiction.
The new Funeral Ritual, adopted at the last session of the Grand
Lodge, is proving satisfactory, judging from the reports of the
Inspectors and the favorable comments of the Brethren. One
Brother writes : "In my humble opinion, the new service is about all
that could be asked for in a funeral ceremony. With the elimination
of the expression of those doleful and depressing thoughts which

81

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

were conveyed in the old service, the present ritual is now a work of
solemn beauty and carries with it a simple, dignified expression of
love and sympathy. Properly rendered, it should be an inspiration
of hope to the heart burdened with sorrow ..
Fraternal visits between Lodges are productive of much good
and arc to be highly commended and encouraged. But the so-called
Degree Teams are out usually to cover themselves with glory and
are mostly of spectacular makeup, which is not the intent and purpose of Masonry. "Light with dignity will travel farther than sound
with jazz." I would suggest that, if a group of Brethren, for instance
the co-workers of the candidate, desired to visit the Lodge in which
he was taking his degrees, in a body, and after the degree was over,
to present him with a Bible or a pin or something of that nature, it
would add to the dignity of the occasion and have far greater effect
than attempting to confer the degree. The whole proposition of
degree teams is in the hands of the Master of the Lodge. This is
pursuant to an edict of the Grand Master. Some legislation should
be enacted to relieve the Master of this embarrassment. This could,
in my judgment, very easily be done ·in the following manner: When
a group desires to put on a degree in a Lodge, they would make the
request of the Master and, if acceptable, he would then in turn seqd
the request to the Grand Lecturer, who would instruct the Inspector
of the District to examine the group and, if found proficient, issue
them a certificate which would be good for the balance of the year
in which it was issued. As it is now, when a request is made to the
Master, he either denies the request or else he lets the group go
ahead and put on the degree without examination, he having no time
in which to make the examination.
I have accompanied the Most Worshipful Grand Master on many
of his visits throughout the State. He has been enthusiastically received everywhere, and has left a message to the Brethren that was
thoroughly enjoyed. These visits are very much appreciated by the
Brethren and are a great stimulus to the Lodges, particularly those
of the smaller Districts.
I owe much to the V.'.W.'.Grand Secretary and his assistant,
Brother Hobbs, for the many courtesies extended to me in his office
during the year. They both have been most kind.
The Officers of the Fifty-Second District will exemplify the
Third Degree on Thursday, October 16th, the candidate being furnished by Crockett Lodge No. 139.
In conclusion may I say, as someone has aptly said : "It is my
joy in life to find at every turning of the road the strong arm of a
comrade kind to help me onward with my load. And since I have no

gold to give, and love alone must make amends, m y only prayer is,
while I live, God make me worthy of my friends."
Thanking the Grand Lodge and the Brethren of this Jurisdiction for their consideration an d confidence placed in m e, which is
greatly appreciated.
