REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M.'.W.' .Grand Lodge of California:
Your com mittee on Masonic H is tory begs leave to submit the
following report of its activities during the past year, together with
its recommendations as to further action on the part of your most
worshipful body :
At the last Annual Communication you directed the committee
to continue its work of gathering and preserving material relating
to the history of Masonry in this State and appropriated $3,000 for
carrying out your instructions. We have obeyed your mandate, and
beg to report tha t we have ex pended a little less tha n $ 1,800 of th e
appropriation.
In our report to this Grand Lodge last year we requested the
assistance and cooperation of the Inspectors in the selection of committees among the constituent Lodges, these com mittees to work
under the direction of your History Committee in searching throug h
their Lodge records for the desired data and information contained
therein. This request met with your approval.
Immediately following the adjournment of Grand Lodge, we
requested the Inspectors to appoint such committees and to direct
and instruct them in the work. We are pleased to report that we
received almost unanimous cooperation from the Inspectors and secured the appointment of committees in approximately seventy-five
per cent of the Lodges. W e wish at this time to express our appreciation to the Inspectors and L odge officers for the cooperation and
assistance rendered in selecting the local committees and in following up their work. Your ·committee also addressed special instructions to each local member appointed, outlining the work proposed
and giving examples of the information and .d ata we required. The

82

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

work of these committees has not progressed as rapidly as we anticipated. We realize that this is due largely to the difficulty of searching back into the records of the past, and the fact that few members
have the available time for such a research. However, the material
and partial reports received from them leads to the conclusion that
the continuance of these local committees is well justified and will
be of valuable assistance to the Grand Lodge Committee.
During the past year members of your committee have visited a
number of Lodges and localities where Lodges at one time existed,
searching records, investigating numerous traditions and stories,
and assisting and advising the local workers.
The desire of the present committee to make definite progress in
this work, and the inability of its members to take time from their
own business, impressed us with the need for a trained research
worker. We therefore sought the services of a competent brother
to act in the capacity of full time investigator. Several brothers were
tried with varying degrees of success. However, last May we succeeded in securing the services of Brother Chas. R. Ingram, a recent
graduate of the University of California, who had engaged in extensive historical research. Brother Ingram was born and raised on the
Mother Lode, has served fo the offices of his own Lodge and has had
several years of valuable newspaper experience. We felt that his
training, qualifications and experience admirably fitted him for the
work. Our dealings with him and the results of his .efforts during
the past several months have more than vindicated our judgment.
His work has been eminently satisfactory.
The committee has centered its attention on the Lodges of the
Mother Lode because there the greatest fire hazard exists. We
deemed it highly advisable to search these records first and then follow with investigations in other parts of the state. We are pleased
· to report that the work of collecting material on the Mother Lode is
completed and we have on file excerpts from the minutes, and stories
of Masonry in the several communities covering that interesting section of California. These reports cover many of the earliest Lodges
in the State and bring to light important historical facts.
· All information received by the committee is promptly filed
where it is safe from loss or destruction. Three typed copies of
every item of information are made. Original reports are placed in
a safe depository in the office of the Grand Secretary, while the two
remaining copies are filed in offices of the members of the committee.
The information is so indexed that it is readily available for use
from time to time, and when the Grand Lodge feels that it should be
coordinated and written into an historical volume.

83

We have found that much of our most valuable material is
locked up in letters, bills, warrants and manuscripts. In many cases
discarded books and papers, considered of purely local significance
and of little value to a Statewide study, contain information and
stories hot recorded in the minute books of the Lodges. Ofttimes
an unpretentious receipted bill or a cancelled note reveals the full
story of the charity work of a Lodge and its members. We have discovered letters reposing in garrets and cellars and out-of-the-way
places which disclose incidents of real Masonic significance. These
have greatly assisted us in a proper interpretation of entries in the old
minute books which had long puzzled those who had perused them.
Frequently a second or third visit to the Lodge room is necessary to
link together obscure passages jotted down in the minute books.
As a result of investigations carried on during the past year, we
are able to give you much of the true history of Masonry in this
State that was formerly known only as vague rumor.
A few matters of Masonic interest may be here mentioned:
We find that it was an almost universal custom among the old
Lodges to vote on applications for affiliation at the meeting the applications were received, without resorting to the formality of committee action.
It was not at all uncommon among the old Lodges to have a
standing committee on "reform," whose duty it was to see that the
brethren refrain from an excessive use of intoxicating liquors. The
Lodge thus attempted to set a good example in the community where
excess was common.
One Lodge for the first ten years of its existe11ce had the unpleasant experience of hearing charges of unMasonic conduct preferred against one or JJ.nother of its members at practically every
meeting.
Many of the old Lodges in the mining camps re1quired non·
affiliated Masons living within their jurisdiction to either affiliate,
pay dues or refrain from visiting the Lodge. The reason for this
requirement was . that calls for charity were so frequent and were
such a heavy burden, that the small local membership could not support the load without assistance from non-affiliates. The non-affiliates were most frequently those in need of charity.
Jn many local jurisdictions the receipt of notice of a Lodge
meeting was considered a summons, and a Mason either a member
of the local Lodge or a non-affiliate must obey the summons or present a reasonable excuse for his non-attendance. We found a letter
at Ione in reply to notice of a Lodge meeting in which a brother informed the Master that it would be difficult for him to attend the

84

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

stated meeting of the Lodge to be held that night because he had
broken his leg and could not walk, and that he hoped the Master
would accept that as a legal excuse.
One Lodge in 1860 issued scrip to fund its debts and regularly
paid interest thereon.
Another Lodge paid wages and expenses to its first Master during the time he was perfecting qimself in the work.
We find that following the Civil War, discord arose in. several
Lodges over questions involved in that conflict, resulting in the formation of a number of new Lodges.
·
In San Francisco a Masonic brother, Robert Tiffany, and his
family were saved from mob violence by the intercession of his
Masonic brethren. Tiffany was falsely accused of being a cousin of
the slayer of President Lincoln and in sympathy with him. The infuriated mob stormed his house and threatened violence to him and
his family until quieted by several Masons who circulated through the
crowd and established the falsity of the charge.
Also we find that in 1856 one brother escaped the vengeance of
the San Francisco Vigilantes Committee through the. good work of
a Masonic brother, an influential member of that organization.
The recqrds of Corinthian Lodge No. 9, of Marysville, disclose
the fact that in 1853 John A. Sutter was elected to receive the degrees . of Masonry in that Lodge, but we are unable to find any record
of the conferring of the degrees.
In 1870 trouble arose between the San Francisco Lodges and
St. Mary's hospital by reason of the insistence of hospital authorities
in burying as Catholics many Masons who died in that institution.
The Masons in San Francisco were at one time compelled to forcibly
remove the body of a brother who died in the hospital, in order that
it might be interred with Masonic honors. One brother went so far
as to prepare and file an affidavit with his Lodge expressing his desire to be buried by the Masonic fra-ternity, irrespective of any claoim
or proof presented to show that he had embraced the Catholic faith
on his death bed.

Our records disclose the fact that all of the charter members of
one of our Lodges were operative as well as speculative Masons.
This very unique situation occurred at Penrhyn, when the quarries
of that place were in operation. Their temple was built of stone
taken from the quarries near there.
We find in the records of some Lodges applications fo r the
" degree of Master Mason's Daughter," but as yet we are unable to
ascertain just what the degree signified. [Probably "Jephthah's
Daughter," by Rob. Morris- Grand Sec.]

85

In the early days many sons of Masons were recognized as
"Lewis Masons." One of them , 19 years of age, was raised to the
sublime degree of Master Mason by a Sacramento Lodge.
General Joh n Bidwell was an enthusiastic and active Mason for
many years. He constructed a large two-story building in Chico
and furnished the upper floor as a Lodge room. Suddenly he turned
against the fratern ity and had one of his workmen set all Lodge
furniture and pa raphernal'a on the street in frorit of the building.
The opposition grocer across the way noted this action and offered
to lease his own building to the Lodge for fifty years for one dollar.
The offer was accepted. The Lodge later purchased the building.
We are at present endeavoring to fi nd the cause of Bidwell's peculiar
actions. Recently we came into possession of facts which we hope
will lead to a solution of this perplexing question.
We are often asked the question, " Is it true that the Masonic
signal of distress has been given to Indians and recognized as such
by them?" Many instances of this kind have occurred. One of
them may be mentioned:
In 1849 Brother James Hodge Watson. the founder of Watsonville, was crossing the plains with an emigrant party. They were
attacked by a band of Indians which gr!'!atly outnumbered them. It
looked as though the heroic band of gold seekers wou ld shortly be
annihilated, when Brother Watson, as a last resort, gave the Masonic
sign of distress. The Indian Chief immediately ordered a cessation
of hostilities, escorted the entire party to his camp an d entertained
them royally for three days. He then gave them safe conduct
through his section of the country.
We find that Masonry was the greatest stabilizing force in California life for several decades, and Masons were the most active
agents in establishing a degree of permanency in the State. In the
mining camps the Masonic hall was usually the first permanent
building erected. Those who took the lead in drafting local mining
regulations were members of the fra ternity, and it was s uch men and
Masons as Abel Sterns, Dr. B. F . Keane, William A. January, Robert
Semple, Stephen J. Fields, John W . Geary, S. C. Hastings and Myron
Norton who laid the solid foundations of our State government.
The research of your committee has disclosed many facts of
unusual interest to California historians aside from matters connected
with Masonry. One example will suffice: In a letter written by a
Mason dated "Yerba Buena, June 14, 1843," is disc losed the fact,
hitherto unauthenticated, that prior to 1843 the priests at the Mission
were aware of the existence of gold in central California but had

PROCEEDINGS OF 'l'HE

GRAND LODGIG OF CALIFORNIA

suppressed the .d iscovery through fear that its disclosure would result in a great influx of gold seekers and thus undo much of their
work among the Indians.
Your committee has also instituted research to ascertain littleknown and unpublished facts in the lives of some of the early California Masonic characters, among them being Kit Carson, ·William
A. January, John W. Geary, Jsaac Roop, Peter Lassen and Dr.
B. ·F. Keane.

prepare slides and arrange material for use among the Lodges, · so
the story of Masonry in California may be made immediately available to the craft.

During the past year your committee discovered a printed circular which had been sent through the mails by Mountain Shade
Lodge in 1852, setting forth certain specific unMasonic acts on the
part of the Grand Master of that year, committed within its jurisdiction. The character of acts were quite similar to those which formed
the basis for the charges preferred by California Lodge No. I against
the same Grand Master at the special communication of Grand Lodge
held during 1852.
The Masonic celebration held at Coloma in 1928 was preeminently a success, and has been a subject of constant discussion
among the craft. Many brethren have expressed a desire to witness
other celebrations or pageants of like kind and cha.r acter. During
the coming year several of our L odges will probably observe their
75th anniversaries, and we s~bmit for their consideration the advisability of presenting a pageant similar to the one staged at Coloma.
Should any Lodge or .g roup of Lodges decide to present a pageant
or celebration representing or depicting any phase or period of California Masonic history, we feel that the History Committee to be
appointed by your incoming Grand Master will be pleased to furnish
facts and data necessary to guarantee success in that undertaking.
We find that many of the older Lodges in the State are housed
in frame buildings and are so situated as to constitute extremely
dangero~s fire hazards. Many of the communities wherein they
are situated are without adequate water system~ to afford proper
protection in case of conflagration. In most cases the books are
kept in the L odge rooms and consequently may a t any time suffer
the same fate that has befallen some of our most important historical
records. In view of this fact, we respectfully suggest that such
Lodges keep their valuable books and records in fire-proof vaults
or safes.
During the past year members of your committee have accepted
invitations from many Lodges to deliver talks on Masonic history.
At these meetings unusual interest in our Masonic past has been
shown by the brethren. It has been suggested many times that we

We feel that what has already ·been accomplished by the committee and those assisting it has fully vindicated the Grand Lodge
· in its efforts to perpetuate our Masonic history; that the funds used
by the committee have been economically and efficiently expended;
and that the work should be continued along the same lines until
such time as all available material has been collected and the several
sources of information exhausted. We believe that during the coming year we will be able to place in our files all of the essential facts
contained in the records of the subordinate Lodges.
We recommend that the Grand Lodge continue the activities of
the Committee on Masonic History, and we feel that if the work
of that committee is to be successfully continued it will require the
same appropriation as was made available last year. We therefore
recommend that Grand Lodge appropriate for the use of the committee the sum of $3,000, of which $1,20.0 shall be the surplus saved
this year. To effect th is we have prepared a resolution which we
here respectfully tender for your consideration.
R esolved, that the sum of $3,000 be set aside and appropriated
to the work of the Committee on Masonic History during the ensuing year, $1 ,200 of said sum being the surplus yet on hand from
the appropriation made for the work of said committee for last year.
Said committee is directed to continue the work of ga thering and
preserving information and data that is in danger .of ·becoming lost
and to place the same in permanent and accessible form, and that
the various Inspectors are requested to cooperate with the committee
and assist the local Lodge groups in their research.

REPORT OF EDUCATIONAL COMMITTEE
To tM M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee for 1930 has pleasure 111 presenting its sixth
annual report of its activities.
The work of this committee has been confined to a slightly
different manner of activity than in prior years, and the experiences
of this past year, added to those of the five preceding years, we feel
are invaluable in reaching certain conclusions with respect to the
efforts of this Grand Lodge to pursue its forward step along the .
lines of offering more light to its votaries.
This year the committee published six papers for use of the
Lodges and a revised reprint of the pamphlet for use of local Lodge
committees in imparting information to candidates. The correspondence in the Executive Director's office has been as large as in former
years, reaching into thousands of letters, and you brethren would
probably be astounded to witness and experience the interest in this
phase of your endeavors evidenced by the members of the craft at
large in writing into the office asking questions and in most cases
acknowledging the reply which is promptly forthcoming. I might
say that the full time of our office stenographer is utilized practically every day in writing letters dictated by Brother Blight.
Your chairman has conferred with members of the committee,
both here and in Los Angeles, and desires at this time to express his
personal appreciation of the cooperation of all the members thereof.
Early in the year, after the various districts of the State had
been allocated to members of the committee, our Grand Master
caused a letter to be sent to the Lodges notifying them as to who
was the member of the committee who would serve them, and bespeaking their cooperation. In a very large measure this cooperation has been afforded, and at this point we desire to say, as we
have said in every previous report, that wherever and whenever the
officers of a Lodge have enthusiastically cooperated and lent the
same efforts towards the progress of this program as towards other
phases of their work, this work has been eminently successful. Your
chairman has in mind a larg.e number of instances where he has personally spoken with candidates . newly raised, and the expressions of
interest in the instruction they received, based upon the candidate's
pamphlet, have in every case been little short of astonishing. This
thought brings us to the focal point with respect to a bureau of
information such as this committee represents. It is· this: No argum ent is needed to support the statement that if we interest a man

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

89

while he has the enthusiasm of newness in his contact with us we
are able to work with him with little or no trouble. We, all of us,
have obser_ved men without number who have come into our Lodges,
and I believe none will deny that irrespective of whatever their
background may be, or however large or diversified their activities,
they have an unmistakable interest and enthusiasm for the new
organization; its work, its associations and the teachings it imparts
to them. That is the time and those are the circumstances under
which it is well to attract them further. We fully believe that one
of the reasons that some of the enthusiasm is apparently lost (although
we equally believe that their interest is never lost) is because these
men who come into the Institution are brought up to a certain point
by our work and that point is not quite far enough, in that it does
not focus their ideas so that they can draw a conclusion with satisfaction. The fact of the matter is, our work does give them all that
could possibly be desired, but does not explain why this information
is ~iven them in the manner t hat it is as distinguished from being
plamly presented. You and I know the reasons for this, and we
also know that the reasons are sound and admit of no denial; but
we alsC! know that if we can add to the work as presently given, we
enable each man within the limits of his own ability to draw such
deduction_ as he sees, and thus, in his own mind, put himself in
a~co~d with the very thoughts and sentiments which we have given
hun 111 :1 covered manner. If, therefore, we will consistently, and as
a matter of routine, take hold of every candidate as he comes into
our Lodge and tell him something of the history of this Grand
Lodge, its purposes, its accomplishments, and possibly some of its
outstanding individual characters; tell him something of his own
Lodge along the same lines, laying stress upon its local accomplishments; point out to him the interpretation of some of the more
salient points of each degree as he goes through; answer by anticipating some of the usual and very natural questions which so many
candidates ask; explain some of the apparently difficult passages in
the lectures_ which he learns; and having done these things, review
them all with him by asking him questions in return designed to
test how much he has gathered from the information thus afforded
him; there ·can be no question that we will be creating a body of
Masons who, first, will be better informed; second, better able to
instruct their successors; and, third, more greatly interested. You
and I have seen, time after time, that the candidate who has his
candidate's lectures the best is the man whose interest is maintained
not only in himself but by having his good wo rk called to the atten~
tion of the officers.
The conclusion to be drawn from these observations is and this
committee recommends, that for the coming year and 'currently

90

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

thereafter there be an Instruction Committee, who, having informed
themselves as to the information to be given the candidates (just as
the coaches have learned their catechism) shall meet with candidates
as they are going through the degrees (at similar rimes and manner
as the coaches do), and impart to the candi'dates such information;
that thereafter the candidates shall, in effect, pass what might be.
termed an examination before · such committee, and for the satisfaction of the Master and the Lodge, the committee shall report such
fact to the Master. How excellent a thought it is to contemplate
that a candidate not only shall be able to recite that portion of his
lecture of the third degree describing the second section thereof, but
in addition thereto be able to tell something of its tremendous lesson!
In order that the Lodge may know that this work is going on, it
might be well occasionally to have a candidate or two pass this socalled examination in open Lodge.
The presentation of papers which have from time to time been
offered to the Lodges is another phase of this bureau of information.
It is designed to afford to all present at a meeting, in a short time,
something of interest concerning our work. We believe this observation is correct: The manner in which these papers is pre·sented to
the Lodge ninety per cent determines whether it succeeds or fails.
All of us know that one man can read such a paper or relate the
substance of it in such a manner as to challenge the attention and
interest of his listeners, and that another man can not do this. May
we say, therefore, that it is of prime importance that the Master
carefully choose the brother who is to present this paper. Surely
there are many men, at least half a dozen, in every Lodge who have
the ability to present it successfully.
The sum and substance of these observations, in the final analysis revolves about the amount of thought and effort which the leader
of' the Lodge gives to the program. He is careful in his choice of
investigating committees; he is careful at the beginning of his year
in his choice of coaches; he is careful in his choice of committeemen
for other work; he is careful in checking on the work of his subordinate officers; he is extremely careful in his appointment to the
lowest office of the man who will some day succeed him .. If he will
be equally careful in his designation of his Committee on Information
for candidates. and his choice of those who present the papers furnished, this phase of his work will not only meet with equal success,
but will challenge the interest and excite the approbation of his
brethren. We can say what we please about effort and expense, and
whether it is worth it and all such, but the fact remains that we are
engaged in a long crusade for the dissemination of light, and every
step which adds brilliance to the flame is a s tep in the forward

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

91

movement. Six years ago the Grand Lodge of California took its
stand on this subject, and under the leadership and recommendation
of every Grand Master has pursued this course. It is not a program
in which the results can be tabulated at the end of a year; but just
as the fruits we enjoy today are the results of the great difficulties
of our brethren of decades ago, who probably questioned some of
their efforts at that time, so will the real fruits of this ac tivity of ours
influence and succeed amongst those who are to come after us, and
who, doubtless, will evolve something further for their successors.
Your committee therefore respectfully recommends:
1. That the program laid down by this Grand Lodge in 1925 be
continued;

2. That the Grand Master be authorized to appoint a committee
of such number as he deems advisable for the carrying on of the
program ;
3. That the sum of Eight Thousand Dollars ($8,000.00) be appropriated for the use of the Committee under the direction of the
Grand Master.
EDUCATIONAL COMMITTEE OF 1930.

Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and Finance.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES MASONIC HOMES
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
We present herewith, as required by the Constitution, a report of
the Homes for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1930, with a roster of
residents to August 31, together with a statement of revenues received since the close of the fiscal year, to September 30.
Pursuant to Constitutional requirement, immediately following
the close of Grand Lodge in October, 1929, the Trustees met and
organized as follows :
President, James B. Gist, term expires 1931;
Vice-President, Albert E. Boynton, term to 1930;
Samuel E. Burke, term to 1932;
Chas. Albert Adams, term to 1933;
John Stuart Ross, Deputy Grand Master;
Robert B. Gaylord, Senior Grand Warden;
Frank W. Mixter, Junior Grand Warden;
Treasurer, William Parker Filmer;
Secretary, John Whicher.
Five meetings of the Board were held in the year-three at Los
Angeles and two at San Francisco. Weekly meetings were held at
Los Angeles by the Los Angeles members of the Board and weekly
meetings were likewise held by the San Francisco members, for
routine business.
Residents
On the first of September there were 299 residents at the Decato
Home-155 men and 144 women, a net increase for the year of 36.
Death took its toll of 26 men and 7 women, a total loss of 33-17 less
than the previous year. The admissions were 41 men and 28 women.
The average age of those who passed away was 77.7, and the average
of those now resident there is, men 77, women 73.8.
Five of the men residents and eight of the women are less than
60 years of age, and your Trustees are seriously considering whether
an age limit should not be fixed.
Outside relief is being granted to 60 Lodges for the care of 32
adults and 57 children, at a present expense of $2,305.00 a month.
At the Covina Home there are 98 boys and 77 girls. Nine boys
and three girls are being cared for in private homes, under the &,.upervision of the Superintendent and his staff. During the year, 18 boys
and 14 girls were admitted, and 16 boys and 22 girls dismissed.

uRAND LO DGE OF CALIFORNIA

Four boys and nine girls were graduated from the Covina High
School in June. A detailed statement relating to these graduates and
provision for their future appears in the interesting report of Superintendent Downen, attached. hereto.

At the close of the year the fund was practically all expended,
there being a balance of only $787.74. Just how much assistance
should be given to a child, after leaving our Home, and how best to
provide for its future, is sometimes a difficult problem to solve. All
of them manifestly are not mentally fit for University training. But
beneficiaries are selected with care, and with the sole idea of affording worthy children the opportunities for advanced schooling-either
mechanical or scholastic-they would have if their parents were living.
It is hardly necessary to state that the financial assistance to
these children aggregates considerable money, all which heretofore
has come from voluntary donations of Brethren and Lodges, and
none from funds paid for maintenance. The fund is at the present
time exhausted, and donations will be most welcome.

PROCEEDINGS OF' 'l'HE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Buildings at Decoto

They have scrutinized every item of expenditure and have urged the
Superintendents to observe the strictest economy in their expenditures
for supplies and clothing. We believe those two excellent brethren
are not only competent but conscientious in the discharge of their
responsible duties, and no complaint of extravagance can be justly
lodged against them.

The building program approved by the Grand Lodge in 1921
is now fully completed, with the exception of one dormitory back of
the south wing, which building will not be needed for several years.
The first contracts were entered into (on competitive bids) in April,
1922, and you now have a group of buildings, all as nearly fireproof
as mechanical ingenuity can provide, that are not only an ornament
to the landscape, but a visible monument to the generosity and
thoughtfulness of the craft for those of its members who, by the
variations and vicissitudes of fortune and the ills incident to old age,
have not been able to accumulate funds sufficient to maintain them,
and who must perforce of evil circumstances seek a haven a home
provided by their brethren.
'
'

The income for the maintenance of the Home is derived from a
per capita tax of 25 cents, and the revenue from initiates. The income
from the per capita tax is small, and the maintenance of the Home
rests primarily on the revenue from initiates. For several years the
number of initiates has fallen below the preTious year. In 1921, when
our building program was approved, Lodges reported 9,208 initiates;
in 1929 there were 6,789, and in 1930 there were 5,800. The year 1931
doubtless will show a further decline in accessions to our Lodges.
This is in the face of the fact that California is the only jurisdiction
in the world which shows any material gain in membership; many
jurisdictions are actually losing.
From revenues available for that purpose, the group of buildings
at Decoto has been built and paid for, with the exception of an
indebtedness of $280,000.00, which the trustees believe can be cancelled within the next four years. The Homes, however, cannot be
maintained on the present basis of per capita tax unless through some
unexpected revival the number of initiates is increased.

In 1921 the Decoto Home housed a family of 138. Now 299
residents are domiciled there. Jn 1921 there were 513 Lodges on our
registry, with 85,000' members. In this good year of 1930 there are
580 Lodges, with a membership of more than 142,000. Inevitably,
the demands of the Lodges on the two Homes have increased and
witt continue to increase, and the cost of maintenance has mounted
from a gross expense of $103,000 in 1921, to $243,000 in 1929 and
$267,000 for the year just closed.
The decrease in yearly revenue and the steadily mounting cost
of maintaining our two Homes have engaged the serious and thoughtful consideration of the several members of the Board of Trustees.

At the present time the current expenses of the Homes exceed
the revenue available for that purpose. Either the revenue must be
increased, or the Trustees must find some means to reduce the expenses. The only source of additional revenue is an increase in the
per capita tax. In view of present depressed financial conditions, the
Trustees do not feel justified in recommending an increase in the per
capita tax at this communication of Grand Lodge, but the fact remains
that we cannot continue indefinitely to expend for maintenance more
than our current revenue. The alternative between reducing expenses
and increasing the per capita tax is an issue which in the near future
must be determined by Grand Lodge. We feel that the general
situation should be reported now, so that when the time for decision
arrives there will have been a sufficient opportunity for proper consideration and for a determination which meets the approval of the
Masons of California.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The making, ma.rking ~nd mending of linen, s heets, pillow-slips,
table cloths, preserving fruits, etc., is attended to by the women of
~he Horr_ie. They also assist in preparing fruit and vegetables, work
in the kitchen and in the dining room, and take care of their rooms,
halls and 1aundry and general household duties.
At this season of the year the natural supply of water is lower,
and there has been a decrease _in service given by the deep well pump.
It has been necessary to connect with the Niles water supply and
by means of an auxiliary pump we have been able to keep our reservoirs full at all times and equal to any demand made upon them.
Library and Club Rooms-There are now 5,600 books on the
shelves of our new main library and branches located in the club
rooms and hospital department. The Masonic Hill branch of the
Alameda County Free Library continues to be well patronized and
enables our family to obtain many of the latest books. In addition
we are the re~ipients, through members of the fraternity, of daily
papers, magazines and periodicals, which are placed on the tables
of t~e men's club rooms and ladies' reading and social rooms. A
reading class for those with impaired eyesight, or entirely blind
me~ts daily. in the main library. At that time the daily papers and
subiects of interest are read to them by good readers selected from
members of the Home.
Soci~l Life-The members of the Home have, during the past
y~ar, enioyed many splendid programs and stage plays provided by
!ru~nds, who are int~rested in their welfare. These evening gatherm~s often c~ose :v1th dancing.. Every Thursday evening we all
enioy a moving picture entertainment. Every Tuesday evening a
social is held in the Assembly Hall where tables are provided for
card&, chess, checkers, etc. Choir practice every Friday evening
The usual services are held every Sunday afternoon. These service~
are often conducted by ministers, accompanied by the choirs of their
churches, after which a few musical numbers are given by the
Home orchestra.
A_number of the members of the Home have radio sets i~stalled
.
in their roo~s. This privilege is particularly appreciated by those
who. are bhnd and those who are ·confined to their beds in the
hospital department.
..
~II holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. Th~
specials _were those which were held on New Year's Eve, New Year's
Day, Lincoln and Washington's birthday, Easter, Memorial Day,
Fourth of July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Farm-There has been no change in the management of the
farm. ~he greater part of the hill ranch has, as in the past, been
leased either on shares or cash rental. Our share has been more

than sufficient for the needs of the farm department, the surplus
being sold in the local market. The orchards have supplied plenty
of fruit for table use, the surplus being preserved or sent to the
<lrier and stored for future use. The garden has furnished a variety
of vegetables and greens. The chicken ranch has supplied all eggs
for table use; air over and above our needs have been preserved in
water glass or sold in the San Francisco market.
Arrangements have been made whereby members of the family,
a few ·at a time, may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest.
During the year many trips are made to Oakland, San Francisco
and towns in the vicinity of the Home.
Grand Master Charles M. Wollenberg and officers of the Grand
Lodge have made a number of visits to the Home during the year
and a large number of brethren from various Lodges have spent
many pleasant hours with us. The number of visitors and donations received this year indicates an increasing interest in the welfare of the Home family.
I wish to extend my appreciation of the loyal services rendered
by the officers and employees throughout the year, and express to
the Board of Trustees my sincere gratitude for the friendly advice
and support they have at all times given me.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK B. HARTMAN, S11pcrilltende11t.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of Superintendent, Covina
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
You are already familiar through monthly written reports from
this office, with many of the details which go to make up the sum
total of a year's achievement in caring for and training 180 boys
and girls whose lives have been entrusted to our keeping.
A recent classification of the children under our charge shows
the following:
Percentage of children having both parents dead ............ 13.4
Percentage of children having one parent dead ................ 79.3
Percentage of children having both parents living ............ 7.2
The 79.3% having one parent dead is made up as follows:
Father dead ................................ 54.7%
Mother dead ........................... ,....24.5%
In the 7.2% having both parents living, in practically every
case one parent is totally disabled and therefore unable to contribute
toward the child's maintenance.
D~ring the past year, through the employment ofa field worker,
we have been able to keep in touch with the families of the children
in our care, and in a number of instances have been able to place
the children back with their own relatives. There is a tendency,
once a child is placed in the Home, to leave it chere indefinitely,
regardless of changed conditions which would justify its ret1;1rn to its
family. Whe~ ;uch conditions exist, .it has been our eff?rt to ?is- ·
cover them and bring them to your attention for appropriate act1,on.
Our experien~e :. convincingly indicates that it is demoralizing to a
parent for the fraternity t'o continu_e to care for a child after that
l?a.rent,' throu~h improved. economic. conditions, has become ab_le_ to
resume 'responsibility.
There i~ a~other · class of cases in whi~h the parent, though
.unable tb rec~ive the child back home, is enabled through our caring
for the child to improve his qr her financial conditio~ to the extent
that some montl.~y payment toward the child's maintenance may
justly be expecte<i. It is a poor parent who is not willing to pay
what he can in the behalf of his child.
I.o s'o me instances we have been able to place the child back
under its mother's care, the Home allotting a small sum monthly
toward its maintenance there. Where the mother is well qualified
persqnally to care for .her child, poverty alone is not sufficien~ reason
for separating them. 3.5% of the children under our care are now
with their own mothers, we maintaining supervision.

139

We have also placed a small percentage of our children (4.6%)
in foster homes, where we pay for their maintenance, and give them
superv1s1on. Some of these are older children, who need to be in
Los Angeles to receive vocational training to prepare them to earn
their own living; others are younger children who present special
problems of disposition, which render them unfitted for life in the
large group in the Covina Home.

The general progress and development of the children during
the year has been most satisfactory. Thirteen boys and girls were
graduated from the Covina High School; and one boy was graduated
from the Frank Wiggins Trade School in Los Angeles. · All of
these have been assisted in working out their plans for the future.
Some have entered directly into gainful employment, while others
will take further vocational training, assisted in some cases by
allot~ents from Masonic Scholarship Fund. The plans of these boys
and girls are indicated in the following summary:
One boy talented in art, has entered an art school in San Francisco, working part time to help maintain ,himself.
. One boy will enter Whittier College, receiving $300.00 aid; and
working for the balance of his expenses.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LOD GE OF CALIFORNIA

One girl expects to take training as a dentist's assistant.
One girl has secured a position in a business office.
The system of training the older children in the use of money,
by giving them opportunities for earning within the Home and
requiring them to buy their own clothes, etc., has been continued,
with excellent results. We find this a valuable aid in teaching one
of life's great practical lessons.-the value of a dollar.
The physical plant of the Home has been maintained in excellent
physical condition. The twenty-one buildings comprising Camp
Tucker at Balboa, where the children spend the summer months,
have been painted, re-roofed and repaired. At Covina the most noteworthy improvement is the construction of a swimming pool, made
possible through a bequest from Mrs . Almina Runyon. The pool is
30 x 60 feet in size, is finished in tile, and equipped with devices
for filtering and purifying the water, so as to comply fully with the
requirements of the California State Board of Health. Its location
and the landscape gardening surrounding it, are such as to make it
a pleasing ornament to the grounds. This pool fills a long-felt want
on the part of the children, and will afford healthful recreation during
many months of the year.
In all that we do the governing aim is to make the institution
at Covina a real home for the children, wherein they can live happy
lives and develop qualities of · character that will enable them to
succeed in later life.
In 1929 we graduated a girl, the oldest of a family of four
children, who may here be called Katie. She made a splendid record
and is now in college. In 1930 we graduated her sister Martha.
The third is Jack, a boy of fifteen, now in his second year of high
school. Then there is Alice, now twelve, and still in grammar school.
We quote from a letter which Jack wrote to Martha when she
graduated and left the Home:
"Dear Sister Martha: I sure have been bawled out a lot
by you, but guess I deserved it. Anyway, Marth, I'll try to be a
good boy, because I wouldn't want to spoil such ·a famous
reputation that you and Katie have made for yourselves at
Covina and the Home. I'll try and help Alice, like you and
Katie have helped me, even though . I get mad at her every once
in a while, but I guess I was that way when I was her age.
Don't forget all ·the swell times we have had at the Home with
all the kids. Love from your brother, Jack."
·
In this boy's unstudied words is pictured in some degree the
life of one family in the Home during the last five years-the preservation of a strong sense of family life within the Home, the boy's

pride in the family record, his feeling of responsibility for his younger
sister, his inspiration for achievement, and a suggestion of the good
times and happy life in the Home. Who can measure the value of
what has been done and is being done for this group of four fatherless children?
·
A little girl, twelve years old, ~ecently wrote, for the Home's
weekly newsletter, the following .lines, which are interesting as
showing a child's conception of what is being done for the children
at Covina :

140

''How the Masons established the Masonic Home
I will tell you in this little poem.
A group of men who Joyed girls and boys
Realized that some had no childish joys.
So being Masons they called on their brothers
And told them to assemble all of the others.
They made up a plan, these kind-hearted men,
That was all for us children from beginning to end.
They planned several houses and built them of brick
Taking extra precautions that the foundat!ons were thick.
Each building was furnished wit\1 the greatest of care
From bedding and dressers to fine silverware.
All over California was spread the Home's name
And along with that its very great fame.
Then into this Home the children did flock,
Some came with one shoe, and some with one sock.
They were well taken care of in this beautiful home,
Found plenty of pleasure and cared not to roam.
Though many happy years have now passed away
Yet still they add to our comfort and play, ·
Till this year we have a new swimming pool
In which on hot days we can quickly get cool.
And we thank the Masons who love girls and boys
That planned for our health and comfort and joys."
]oHN M. DowNEN, Superintendent.

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CONSTITUTION
The following resolution.s proposing to amend the Constitution were presented, all being referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and Jurisprudence.
To the M.'.TV.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Resoi<'cd, That Section 93 of the Constitution be amended by
adding the words "or within" after the word "from" in the second
line of said section.
C. H. ECKERT,
Past Master, Holtville Lodge No. 425.
We, the undersigned, present the following preamble, covering
residential qualifications of persons in the service of the United States
Navy:
1. WHEREAS, A person presenting his petition to a Masonic
Lodge within the jurisdiction of the State of California must comply
with the residential qualifications as contained in Section 96 of the
Constitution, and
2. WHEREAS, This requirement sometimes causes the petitioner
to forego presenting his petition for the reason that his ship may
not be in port long enough to allow the Lodge to take proper action,
it being necessary for ·the Lodge to receive the request, vote for a
special dispensation and apply for same to the Grand Master at one
stated meeting and at the next receive the petition and then another
month is required for the proper investigation, and
3. 'NHEREAS, During the intervening weeks the ship on which
petitioner resides and calls his home, has left port and it is sometimes six or eight months, and in some cases even longer, before the
candidate is in a position to present himself for the first degree.
4. We, therefore, offer the following resolution for an additional
section to the Constitution to be known as Section 96-A, and recommend its adoption.
5. Resofr1ed, That Section 96-A be added and made a part of
the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California; said section to read as follows:
"Section 96-A. The home port of a vessel belonging to the
United States Navy (said port having been designated by the

GRAND J,ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

167

United States Navy Department) shall be considered as the
bona fide residence of any of its crew, and any person attached
to said vessel for the six months last past may petition for and
receive the degrees of Masonry in any Lodge having jurisdiction of the home port of the vessel, without the necessity of the
Lodge securing a special dispensation to receive the petition."
DAVID L. POTTER,
Master, Naval Lodge No. 87.
RUSSELL C. ]ONES,
Master, Solano Lodge No. 229.
JOHN K. HARRISON,
Master, Vallejo Lodge No. 487.

The following proposed change in the Constitution of
this Grand Body is submitted for your consideration.·
Group Balloting, Section 103)/,. First paragraph, line 3. Changing the word "three" to read "two." It now reads, "Where three or
more petitions are to be balloted upon, the Master shall" etc. If
changed as proposed it will then read, "Where two or more petitions are to be balloted upon the Master shall read the names," as
at present re.quired, etc.
No good reason appears to the proposer for requiring separate
ballots when but two petitions are to be balloted upon, when a collective ballot is all that is required when three or more petitions
are to be balloted upon.
The proposed amendment meets with the approval of all with
whom it has been discussed and in the opinion of the proposer
should be adopted as a matter of uniformity in balloting for candi dates.
'c. P. LYNDALL, P. M.,
Arlington Lodge No. 414.

Resoh•ed, that Section 119 of the Constitution he amended to
read as follows:
Providrd, that should any member neglect for the period of two
years to pay said dues or have the same remitted by his Lodge, the
Secretary shall notify him by registered letter that unless at the next
stated meeting his dues are paid he will automatically be dropped from
the rolls without further reference to the Lodge, and such member
may not be restored except by three-fourths vote by ballot of all the
members present at the next stated meeting after the petition for
restoration is presented.

REPORT OF U. C. L. A. CLUBHOUSE
To the M: .w : .Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Director s of the Masonic Club of the University
of California at Los Angeles fraternally submit their report .for the
year ending October 1, 1930. In ou r report of last year we estimated
the cost of the building together with the site therefor at the sum of
$104, 172.20. It now appears from the Balance Sheet annexed to and
made a part of this report that the total cost of land and building is
$107,271.64. We also estimated the cost of furnishings in the sum of
$19,934.57. Aside from the lighting fixtures for the stage and additional ones for the study rooms, w hich have not as yet been purchased,
the same balance sheet discloses a total of $17,653.18 laid out for that
purpose. There remains in the fund contributed for the erection and
equipment of the clubhouse the sum of $8,457.84, and outstanding in
pledges, $8,089.60. We have thought it best to defer certain impr_o vements until we shall know more concerning the results of the ·pledges
outstanding. It has always been the policy of your Board not to Incur
indebtedness until we had the money on hand to make payment. When
the outstanding pledges shall have been paid we can the more intelligently and economically adjust contemplated improvements and
furnishings. Furth er information concerning the general 'fit1ani:;ial

175

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

situation of the clubhouse is contained in the report of Brother Roger
Prior, certified public accountant, but the foregoing covers' the salient
features.
Grand Lodge appropriated the sum of $9,000 for the purpose of
maintaining the clubhouse, to which should be added the sum of
$152.60, interest earned thereon, and we are happy to report that we
have during the past year been able to operate more economically
than was anticipated. Of the sum set aside for this purpose there
remained on hand as of October 1, $1,063.22. We have so far been able
to economize by the employment of student help as superintendent
nf the building and by no'n-employment of office assistants. Also we
have not felt the advisability until now of increasing the salary of the
resident hostess to the amount estimated, not because she is not fully
competent and capable but rather because during the early part of
the year and the summer session her responsibilities we're not pressing. However, her burdens are greater at this time, and the Board
has increased her salary to the sum of $1800 per year, effective
October 1, 1930. Mrs. Kempton is really an ideal woman, as indicated
by the . fact that many of the students constantly address her as
"Mother Kempton." She seems thoroughly to understand them,
sympathizes with their problems and enjoys their confidence to such
a degree as to make of the whole a very happy family.
General upkeep shows an expenditure in excess of that estimated,
for the reason that it was necessary during the summer to completely
waterproof the building on account of rain driving through some of
the joints between the concrete tile. By contract we are now guaranteed against a repetition of leaks for at least three years.

Dedication of Clubhouse
On March 27, just one year to the day after ground was broken
for the structure, the Grand Master, together with other Grand Lodge
officers, dedicated the clubhouse in due and ancient form to the purposes for which it was constructed. The ritual of that ceremony
follows:
The Grand Marshal announced "The Grand Master and Officers
of the Grand Lodge."
GRAND MASTER: We read in the Holy Writings that when all
the work that Solomon made for the house of the Lord was finished,
h~ assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the
chiefs of the fathers of the children of Israel; and then the house
which was erected to God was dedicated in His Holy Name. We
have gathered this evening in imitation of the children of Israel to
dedicate this building, thus perpetuating a custom which has come
clown to us from time immemorial. Among the ancients, every temple,
altar ~nd statue was dedicated to some divinity. The Hebrews extended this ceremony even to their private houses; and it was a
custom in Israel to dedicate a new house to God with prayer, praise
;ind thanksgiving; and this was done in order to secure the Divine
presence and ·blessing; for it was believed that no pious or sensible
man could expect to dwell safely in a house which was not under
the immediate protection of God. They made a distinction between
~onsecration and dedication; for sacred things were both consecrated
and dedicated; while profane things, such as private dwelling houses,
were only dedicated. This distinction has always been observed
;unong nations generally, many of whom (and in the early ages all)
consecrated their churches to the worship of God, but dedicated them
to, or placed them under the especial patronage of, some particular
saint. A similar practice prevails in our Institution; and while we
consecrate our Lodges to the honor and glory of God, we. dedicate

176

l'IlOCEEDlNGS OF THE

them to the memory of the Holy Saints John. Our buildings are
dedicated to the purpose for which they are set apart.
"Masonic Lodge halls are dedicated to Freemasonry, Virtu.e and
Universal Benevolence; and you may be interested in knowing that
this was the form of dedication of the first edifice ever erected as a
Masonic hall of which we have authentic information ; and that the
ceremony of that first dedication in 1774 was in all its essentials
identical with that which will be performed today. To those unmindful
of its symbolism, it will be nothing but an unmeaning form; but it
is in truth and fact, as are all our ceremonies, fraught with significance.
"The Biblical and Masonic elements of consecration are corn,
wine and oil. In devoting anything to religious purposes, the anointing
of oil was considered as a necessary part of the ceremony. The tabernacle in the wilderness, and all its holy vessels, were by God's express
command anointed with oil; and hence 'Free Masons' Lodges, which
are but temples of the Most High, are consecrated to the sacred purposes for which they were built by strewing corn, wine and oil upon
the emblem. The corn alone is carried in a golden pitcher; the wine and
oil being contained in silver vessels. It is to remind us that the first,
as a necessity and the 'staff of life' is of. more importance and more
worthy of honor than the others, which are but comforts. In the
dedication of halls set apart for the uses of Masonry, a procession
forms a part of the ceremony. It will here be omitted, but its symbolism may be explained as a reminder that in the pilgrimage of life,
as each proceeds along the path allotted to him, he should share his
last crust of bread with the hungry, cheer the sorrowful, and pour
the healing oil of consolation into the wounds which sickness has
made in the bodies or affliction has rent in the hearts of his fellow
man. This brief explanation will, we hope, bring a clearer understanding of the significance of the ceremony."
Music (suggestion): "Opening the Gates of the Temple."
The Chairman of the Board of Directors then addressed the
Grand Master as follows:
"Most Worshipful Grand Master, the men of the Craft in the
jurisdiction of California, animated with a desire to promote the honor
and .glory of our ancient Institution, and to establish a home for the
promotion of the mental and moral well-being of the students of
Mas~nic families attending the University of California at Los
Angeles, have erected this edifice for their comfort and care, where
relaxation from the activities of campus life may be found , and where
those who may need consolation or advice may come with full assurance of finding the same amid surroundings touched by the spirit

and atmosphere of Masonry. The Clubhouse and the plan upon which

"THE GRAND MASTER: Having h eretofore made an inspection,
and the building and the plan upon which it is constructed meeting
with our unqualified approbation, it gives us great pleasure to comply
with the desires of the brethren and to discharge the impor tant and

It is interesting to observe that this dedication immediately preceded the dedication of the campus of the university, and was participated in by the director and vice president of the University, Dr.
Ernest C. Moore, who, although not a member of the fraternity, paid
tribute to our contribution to the cause of education generally, and
specifically to the mental and moral welfare of the students by the
erection and maintenance of the building. He spoke as follows:
"It is to me a rare privilege to have been with you as you went
through your moving ritual. This great order which is doing this
· thing today seems to me to stand for three . things. I am very glad to
stand with you for all of them. The fir st is construction. We must
build homes in which to live; temples in which to worship; schools
t o be educated in. I understand that this beautiful place has been
built that young hopes may flourish, that they may be lifted up, may

180

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

mount up on wings as eagles mount toward the sky. To have them
helped to do that will be a great thing in years to come. The people
of this great commonwealth of California have built a University
just across the street. This Masonic house will do a most helpful
work for that University. The second thing in connection with this
order is its love. of education. Masons champion the work of the
schools everywhere, and to one who has devoted his whole life to
the service of education it is an inexpressible privilege to welcome
this effort on your part to be of assistance in the work of the U niversity. The third thing that you fight for is our country. Education
would be impossible but for the country which makes it possible, and
in supporting our country we support all the good things of this life.
Most Worthy Grand Master, it has been a great privilege to be here
today and a great pleasure to see this fine building. We shall think
of you as fellow educators and ask you to pray for the welfare of the
University as you do for our country and for men."
It has been found advisable during the year for the council to
propose and the Board to approve amendments to their by-laws, by
which the four constituent organizations are welded into one large
organization while preserving the identity of the four within the
larger. Under the present system the one large organization is responsible to a great degree for all student activities, and we find more
harmony and efficiency existing. In order that you may know the
approximate size of this organization we are informed by Mrs. Kempton that at the close of the college year in June they had a membership of 750, the greater number of whom were active. And to more
accurately convey the use to which the clubhouse is put her report
also shows that from March 4 to June 16, 15,048 contacts were made,
or in other words that an average of 140 students per day made use
of the clubhouse. This number is exclusive of visitors. While the
Wednesday afternoon informal dances, with an. average attendance
of 250, accounts in a measure for the use of the facilities offered, it
will be readily appreciated that it fails to account for 'the total. Mrs.
Kempton also reports that there is an ever increasing use of the
study and conference rooms, the students expressing a preference
for the peace and quiet thereof. Another thought that will convey to
you the value of this undertaking is this: we have had instances
where students coming from the east have been directed by railroad
officials to the clubhouse and who have found themselves immediately
in the hands of sympathetic and helpful friends instead of being alone
in a strange land. As further evidence of the part you are playing in
endeavoring to mold the character of these young men and women it
should be stated that the clubhouse has been recognized by the as-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

181

sociated women students as a legitimate student activity, and the
president of the Council has been invited to participate in the deliberations of that body.

REPORT OF U. C. BERkELEY CLUBHOUSE
To the. M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of
California, Inc., submits herewith its report of the affairs of the
institution, together with its financial statement. The latter is embodied in the report of N ormaIJ MacEachen, certified public accountant of San Francisco, who has audited the books of the corporation
for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1930. [Exhibit A attached
hereto.] The report, together with exhibits consisting of balance
sheet as of said date and statement of income maintenance expense
for the fiscal year, has been submitted to the Finance Committee of
Grand Lodge for its examination and consideration.
It is reported by Mr. Mac Each en that all cash received was
properly deposited in bank, and all disbursements were supported by
approved vouchers. He also reports that "the books continue to be
neatly and accurately kept and all information requested was promptly
furnished."
The generous provision made by Grand Lodge at its session one
year ago not only made possible the payment, on October 28, 1929,
of the balance of $9,350.90 due on the unsecured note held by the
First National Bank in Berkeley, but provided the greater portion
of the current operating expenses for the year. In order to completely
meet the last item, however, it was necessary for the trustees to
withdraw $1,300 from the Depreciation Fund, with the result that
the trustees have not now on hand any amount to meet those
necessary items of depreciation which are apt to be required at any
time, in view of the fact that the clubhouse and its equipment have
reached the stage where some depreciation and replacement must, of
necessity, be a matter for consideration.
Fire insurance in the amount of $90,000 is carried on the clubhouse building, and $12,500 on furniture, fixtures and equipment.
Workmen's compensation and public liability insurance are also
carried.
The Trustees have prepared and submit herewith Exhibit B, an
itemized budget for the ensuing fiscal year amounting to $12,010.
Activities have been conducted at the clubhouse during the year
with the same efficient management by the hostess, Mrs. J. H. Quinn,
under the direction of the executive committee of the Board of Trustees. Peace and harmony have reigned in every department of the
work, and the influence of the institution on the student body has been
probably greater during the period than in previous years because of
the fact that the clubhouse has become an established and accepted in-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

183

,.titution in the activities of the University. Its position in the affairs
of the student body and of the individual students who are so fortunate
as to come within its influence continues to rec~ive commendation
from the president and other officials of the University. The number
of those availing themselves of the opportunities for social activities
and personal use of the clubhouse has increased during the year, as
our Masonic brethren throughout the State are coming to realize
more and more how helpful the clubhouse and those in charge there
can be to the young men and young women attending the University.
Your Board of Trustees, therefore, asks that its report be received
and approved, and .that the present generous provision for the support and maintenance of the Masonic Clubhouse at the University of
California be continued.
