REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON ELEVENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
SAN FRANCrsco, October 14, 1930.
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge Ji. & A. M. of California:
Again this year, as has been the case each year for several years past,
your Committee on Public Schools vVeek is able to report that from
every point of view the latest observance was the most successful ever held.
Last year the reports received from the lodges might have seemed to
indicate that the peak had been reached; but even the extraordinary success of the Tenth Annual Observance was eclipsed this year. In one of
the first reports received, the Master in commenting on the result of his
observance described a situation which other reports indicated was general throughout the state when he said:
"The interest, with the consequent attendance at the public
meeting, is increasing yearly until now there remains no covered gathering place of sufficient size to accommodate the crowd."
There were several reports in which the belief was expressed that to
accommodate the increasing attendance it would be necessary to hold more
than one public meeting. Never before was it so evident that what in its
origin was a purely Masonic event has become in the true sense of th~
phrase "a community affair"; and an extremely popular one.
While everywhere the Masonic Lodge, or the Masters and Wardens
Association, was of course the motivating factor in the observance, there
were few communities, and those only very small ones, in which active
cooperation was not received from organizations such as the Parent
Teacher Association, the American Legion, Chambers of Commerce,
Service Clubs and other fraternal and civic organizations. In some instances these were all represented on the committee through which the
arrangements were made, and in others they joined in sponsoring the

187

Local Posts of the American Legion, as would be expected, have
always when requested cooperated in the observance; but this year for
the first time there was a pledge of support by the State Department. In
a letter received from the Department Commander, Clarence L. Kincaid,
he wrote:
"You may depend upon our complete and wholehearted support in the movement. We of the American Legion, are deeply
interested in every movement which has as its objective the
furtherance of the public school educational system."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As has been the case for several years, the California Parent Teacher
Association joined wholeheartedly in the observance. In a public announcement Mrs. Robert L. Cardiff, the President, said:
"In California there are 181,000 members of the California
Congress of Parents and Teachers . . . . This group is solidly
back of the public schools and actively supporting Public Schools
Week."
Further evidence of the recognition of the observance as a community
affair is furnished by the official· proclamations which were issued. First
and foremost, of course, was the fine proclamation issued by Governor
Young in which he stated that although he had theretofore steadfastly
declined to issue proclamations with respect to all celebrations or observances of special days or weeks, except for such nationally observed
holidays as Thanksgiving, Armistice Day and the like, he felt constrained
to call public attention to the Eleventh Annual Observance of Public
Schools Week; and commending its purpose, he urged the people of the
State to avail themselves of the opportunity that would be afforded during
that week to obtain first hand information of the methods, aims, purposes
and achievements of the modern school.
In addition to the Governor's proclamation, and as the result of a
suggestion emanating from the League of California Municipalities, there
were proclamations issued by the Mayors and City Councils of nearly one
hundred municipalities. The Superintendent of Public Instruction also
issued a circular letter addressed to all Superintendents, County, City and
District, and to school principals calling their attention to the observance,
and expressing the hope that this year every school in the state would
actively participate.
In our report last year we referred to the great interest that is now
being evinced by the school people. The cordial, hearty and extremely
valuable cooperation received from them would of itself indicate that
those best qualified to form an opinion were convinced of the worth of
Public Schools Week to the school system of this state; but if anything
more were needed, it is found in the reference to the observance made by
the Superintendent of Public Instruct.ion, as Director of Education, in his
April report to the Governor's Council. The following is a quotation from
Superintendent Kersey's report:
"The annual observance of California Public Schools Week
has just closed. The week of April 21 to 25, in which this observance was held, provided opportunities for closer cooperation
and mutual understanding between the public schools and the
people of the state. Throughout California public mass meetings,
luncheon club programs, special columns in local newspapers,
demonstrations of teaching and learning procedures and activities,

am! school-room visitations have all served to bring before the
the people of this state the great service performed by the public
schools.

188

189

"It is fitting that a week should be devoted each year to a
clearer understanding of the needs, purposes and ideals of our
public school system. The averagt parent and citizen is most interested .to know just what the children are doing daily in the
classroom. Such an observance provides opportunities for more
accurate information concerning the schools. The underlying purpose of the observance has been to present the regular activities
and the normal school life to the patrons of the public schools.
"The value of California Public Schools Week can probably
be best measured in terms of the continued support of our public
schools by the citizens of each community. It is hoped that California Public Schools Week will continue from year to year to
oontribute its due service toward the maintenance of California's
educational leadership."
In this connection, in passing, we may refer to a signed statement of a
City Superintendent of Schools published in a newspaper in his city which
always has been particularly generous in the amount of space devoted to
the observance. He said :
"The public schools arc so frequently asked to lend themselves to so many different weeks and days in the interest of so
many different interests and events that it is indeed a fine thing
to have a week set aside by a great organization outside the
schools in the interest of the schools themselves.
"So Public Schools Week sponsored by the Masonic Grand
Lodge is worthy of great commendation."
Expressions similar to that just referred to appear in scores of editorials in newspapers thtoughout the state. The following are typical of
many which might be quoted:
"Weeks are set apart to various institutions for publicity
purposes. Some of them are well worth while. None of them is
more so than that which commands the attention of the people
this week as Public Schools Week."
"This is Public Schools W eek---one of the special 'weeks'
that is not foolish or unnecessary. It serves a fine useful purpose.
It is a week set aside for the establishment of a closer contact, a
better understanding, between the public and the public schools.

mo

PROCEEDINGS OF THI!;
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"That understanding is essential. It is essential also to keep
in mind that education is the first business of Americans ; and to
remember the wisdom of Napoleon who said, 'Education is the
first business of any republic.'
"Public Schools Week helps us to remember that."
"Next week is Public Schools Week. So many weeks have
been set aside for special observance that the thing has become
somewhat monotonous; but this is a week that should appeal to at
least every parent and it would be good business if everyone gave
it some attention; for the schools of the Nation are its hope for
the future."
In our report of the Ninth Annual Observance we made mention in
detail of the extraordinary amount of newspaper publicity that had been
received, and in referring to this last year we called attention "to the fact
that the press of the state, both metropolitan and rural, had been even
more generous in the amount of space devoted to school matters, and to
awakening the interest of the people in their schools; but never before was
so much attention given to the observance by the newspapers as was
evident this year. It was what theatrical people term a "wonderful
press"; and a striking feature of the publicity was the number and extent
of the editorials in addition to the space in the news columns. The remarkable publicity received is evidenced by the fact that the first news column
story sent out, the Grand .Master's Proclamation, had a return of one
hundred and twenty-four clippings. Other news stories such as endorsements by the President of the State P. T. A., the Commander of the
American Legion, the President of the California Teachers' Association,
and the Superintendent of Public Instruction received almost as much
publicity.
The editorials covered not only the observance itself, but all phases of
the public school system including taxation for school purposes, new
buildings, trends of education and similar topics; and it was extremely
valuable not merely because it awakened the interest of the people in
their schools and thus furthered the purpose of Public Schools Week, but
also because it gave assurance to the school people of the great interest
and concern of the public in the work in which they are engaged.
Wherever visits to the schools constituted a feature of the observance
the people were urged to avail themselves of the opportunity presented.
The following is quoted from what might be said to be a typical editorial
on this phase of the observance :
"Next week is Public Schools Week in California and a fine
time for patrons of our schools to learn more of what goes on
inside the classroom. The public realizes that it has good school

191

buildings, but most of us take the · actual work of teaching, the.
real school, as a matter of course.... Next week is a good time
to get acquainted with the work of our teachers, to voice a bit of
encouragement and appreciation cif the institution which is preparing our children to take thefr places in the world. It is a good
time to quit finding fault and to give recognition to the merits
of the public school system, an institution which is directly responsible iri a large measure for our national progress."
No inconsiderable part of the newspaper publicity received was due
to the contact made by the local publicity committees with the newspapers
published in their communities. In accordance with the request made
by our Director of Publicity to the Master of every Lodge, there were
forty-nine local publicity committees in touch with him. Last year there
were but four. I t is hoped that next year will show a corresponding increase in the number of local committees which will apply for and receive
material which they may furnish their local newspapers in addition to
material sent them by our Director of Publicity.
In concluding our reference to the publicity, mention should be made
of the fact that in some instances the newspaper clippings attached to
the reports, in compliance with the request made by our committee, were
more valuable in indicating the result of an observance than was the
report itself. For instance, the Master of one Lodge was apparently a
little doubtful of the success of his observance which he said was "only
fair" because the attendance at the public meeting was not as large as he
had expected; but the newspaper clippings attached to his report furnished
evidence of the great amount of publicity the observance. had received and
which must have re~ulted in focqsing the attention of the people on their
schools, and also showed that during the week a .large number of people
had visited the schools and thus receiv.ed first-hand information of what
they were doing. It was thus apparent that the real purpose of the observance had been achieved and the Master's doubt of its success was really
without warrant even though the public meeting was not as largely attended as he thought it should have been.
No one who has not had the privilege of carefully reading the reports
from the Lodges can have an adequate conception of the growth and development of this movement. Perhaps one of the most interesting things is
to compare the reports from year to year from the same Lodge, and to
note . the comments of the different Masters. For instance, this year a
Master. reported that his community was so small and his members so
scattered that he did not believe he "could hold a successful observance·
but our files include a report from that Lodge showing that a very sue~
cessful observance had been theretofore held following a personal letter
written the Master that year expressing the hope that he would be among

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

192

193

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

those to whom especial credit would be due for success achieved in spite
of the obstacles confronting them.
It is perhaps not generally known that as the reports from the Lodges
are received they arc carefully analyzed, particularly those indicating that
the observance had not been as successful as was expected. If we find, as
we usually do, that the suggestions made by our committee have not been
followed, we immediately write the Master while the matter is still fresh
in his mind not, as we are careful to explain, by way of criticism of anything done or left undone, but solely with the desire to be helpful and with
the hope that any mistake which possibly may have been made will be
ti1ereafter avoided; and we always ask that our letter be handed the one
1vho will be in charge of the ob, ervance the following year for his guidance in making his arrangements.
Of course we do not ordinarily write Masters reporting even extraordinarily successful meetings. That would be impracticable if not
physically impossible. Occasionally, however, we make an exception
where a successful meeting has been held following failures in the past,
or where, as was the case this year, some little Lodge in a remote community ·holds its first observance and the Master reports that the members
now know that something can be done in a small community and that next
year he expects to .have the .support of other organizations.
As .we have intimated, our letters arc usually prompted by our belief
t}iat the failure to hold a successful observance may have been due to the
fact .that the suggestions made by our committee have not been followed.
One letter written this year was iu acknowledgment of a unique report
of one of the most successful observances anywhere held. The Master
reported that no endeavor had been made to obtain the cooperation of the
civic organizations in the community, nor had any special effort been made
to obtain newspaper publicity, nor to otherwise insure a large attendance;
and the reason he gave for not doing this was that he knew that if any
special effort were made they would be unable to handle the crowd although the auditorium in which the meeting was held is the largest in that
section of the state. That he was entirely correct is evidenced by the fact
that they had a capacity house with one thousand seated and five hundred
standing. The most extraordinary thing in connection with the whole
observance is that the attendance of fifteen hundred reported is equal to
the total population of that community. The Master reported that some of
those In attendance came from a distance as far as twenty miles, notwithstanding the fact that they had stormy weather on the night the meeting
was held. In view of the fact that the Master had reported that with
concentrated effort they could easily fill an auditorium twice as large as
theirs, we suggested that he might consider the advisability of holding

two meetings-one in which the program would be presented by the pupils
of only the elementary schools and the other with the program furnished
by the high schools.
Needless to say we are always glad to receive from any source suggestions or constructive criticism; and always when the matter is brought
t~ our attention in a special communication, and frequently when it appears in a report, acknowledgment is made in a personal letter. Mention
may here be made of a complaint received this year with respect to the
time of our observance. It was unfortunate, of course, that the date fixed
conflicted with the Easter school vacation in some communities, but it was
practically unavoidable. We have learned by experience that the fourth
week in Apr4'1 is the time best suited for all the school districts in the state.
At an earlier date the weather in some communities is inclement and a
later date brings the observance too close to the summer vacation. This
was the first time since the date was fixed for April that the Easter vacation in any way interfered; and it was due only to the fact that this year,
as will be remembered, Easter came very late. We had at first thought of
changing the date, but the Superintendent of Public Instruction, with
whom the chairman of our committee conferred, advised that no change
be made, calling attention to the fact that the Easter vacation was not observed during the same week in all the school districts. In all cases in
which it was asked, permission was given the Lodge by the Grand Master
to hold the observance during the week preceding or following the date
fixed. It will be noted of course that the conflict in dates was with respect
to only the Easter vacation, and not with the observance of Easter which
had been concluded the week before the date of our observance.
Among other suggestions received was one to the effect that the Fraternity might well consider the idea of not confining its efforts in behalf
of the public school system merely to the observance of Public Schools
Week, and that each Lodge might have a Public Schools Week Committee whose efforts should not be confined to a particular period, but extending throughout the year. It had been our intention to present these
suggestions with comment thereon in this report, but for the reason
hereinafter stated consideration thereof perhaps will be better postponed.
It has been our practice in thti past to include in these reports detailed
references to selected observances (without naming or otherwise identifying them) as suggestions of what might be done in other communities. In
some instances, the references were with respect to the manner in which
the arrangements had been made, and in others to the nature of the program. Most frequently it was where an especially successful observance
had been held ·in the face of what had been believed were insurmountable
obstacles. .Our hope was that the Master who received the report would
hand it to his successor for his guidance and that the necessity of issuing

195

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALJl<'ORNIA

a Bulletin of SUilfCRtions each year would thus be avoided. It appears,
however, th11t thiR hu not been done ; and it has become apparent that not
infrequently those in charge of an observance are entirely without knowledge of tht' information contained in these reports. We are therefore of
the opinion that perhaps it will be well for the committee next year to
issue a Bulletin of Suggestions with the first notice sent out. We shall
therefore confine this report in the main to only general statements.
As is always the fact,· the most gratifying reports were those from
communities in which for the first time a successful observance had been
held. One of these was from a comparatively large city where the results
theretofore had never been anything like commensurate with the earnest
endeavor which had been made. The Masters of the Lodges had become
discouraged and were disinclined to essay an undertaking which seemed
foredoomed to failure. With that tine spirit, however, which animates the
Masons of that community an especial effort was put forth this year;
and the result was an extraordinarly successful observance which delighted everyone and ·especially the City Superintendent of Schools. One
of the reasons, by the way, heretofore given for lack of success was that
the Committee of Arrangements had not received from the school people
the support they felt they had a right to· e:x:pect. This year there was not,
and could not have been, any such complaint. Nowhere else was there
tirter cooperation received from the school people. This was the last of a
group of three cities which for one reason or another seemed unable for
several years to hold a. successful observance. As has been heretofore
reported, success first came to one of the others four years ago and to the
third three years ago; and in both these .cities, as we feel certain will be
the case in the one to which special reference has just been made, each
succeeding year has added to the success theretofore achieved.
We may now confidently assert that there is not a large community in
the state, and very few small ones, where Public Schools Week is not now
successfully observed. Indeed we think it is not too much to say that with
the exception of Independence Day, and of course Thanksgiving and
Christmas, there is probably not another anniversary which is so generally
observed everywhere throughout California as is Public Schools Weck.
In the smaller communities the public meeting continues to be the
main, and in some instances the only, feature of the observance. This,
it will be remembereo, was the original form of our observance. The trend,
however (referred to in our report two years ago), in the .d irection of
having the public meeting only one of the features of the observance has
continued; and this year was particularly evident. Instances in which the
observance extends over the entire week have become so general as to no
longer occasion comment. The public meetings are only incidental features
of a week's program which includes visits to the schools with practical

demonstrations of the actual work being done, exhibits of school work of
all sorts and kinds, some of which are extremely elaborate, pageants presented by school children exemplifying school objectives, and special programs appropriate to Public Schools Week at the meetings of the service,
and other luncheon clubs.
Visits to the schools with a demonstration of the modern methods by
which the so-called fundamentals are taught, and with the opportunity to
learn at first hand something of what is being done in social studies, and
to meet the school faculty, apparently received more newspaper notice
than any other feature of an observance; and no better method could be
devised for insuring that close contact between the schools and the public
wpich is of course one of the primary purposes of Public Schools Week.
The following is a quotation from an editorial with reference to a program
of that sort:
"One of the outstanding achievements of the week was the
closer understanding between those who conduct the affairs of our
schools and the patrons thereof. Meetings like that of Thursday
night make history in school work and likewise encourage to
greater efforts in the efficient education of the youth. Those
responsible· for the observance of Public Schools Weck in - - are to be congratulated."
As we have repeatedly said in these reports, we are steadfast in the
belief that there is no town nor hamlet in California having a public school,
and where the~e is located a Masonic Lodge, which cannot hold a successful observance of Public Schools Week. It is, however, undoubtedly true
that there are certain very small communities where the conditions are not
favorable for a public observance of any sort. It is in these communities,
however, that there is the greatest need for such a movement as that in
which we are engaged. Due to our traditional form of school administration with the district as the unit, those who need the most receive the
least. It is in the remote, sparsely settled community with the little rural
school, that the teacher and children need most the sympathy, aid and encouragement which result from the observance of Public Schools Week.
There is here no magnificently appointed auditorium, no well equipped
gymnasium, no domestic science nor manual training class. Nothing but
a bare room with the teacher and a handful of children who are handicapped in the race for life by reason of the fact that they did not happen
to be born in a community providing those things of which they are deprived, but to which they are no less entitled than are their more fortunate
brothers and sisters. Here is a fine opportunity for our great Fraternity;
and we· must measure up to it. · Our Committee is especially desirous of
being of service ; and we urge the Master of any Lodge in such a neigh-

194

PHOCEEDINGB OF' 'l'HE

196

borhood as we have described to make a special request, and at an early
date, for such suggestions as we might be able to make by reason of our
experience.
It is glorious, of course, to feel that one has had a part in an observance of such magnitude as has attracted the attention of the people
of a large city, with encomiums from the press and the plaudits of a fine,
rich, well-organized school depart~ent that is appreciative of the be~efits
which have come to them, but for lack of which they would not have
materially suffered. It would be, however, a far greate~ satisfaction for
the Master of some little Lodge in a community such as we have described to realize that through his efforts, and those of his brethren, with
such other assistance as he might have secured, the children of that little
rural school had come to realize that they, too, were objects of keen
interest and public attention, and that in the recognition and appreciation of their accomplishments they, too, had been encouraged to a
renewed effort that might not have been induced through mere school
routine. Grand Lodge will do its part; but the burden of the work must
perforce be borne by the Masters of these little Lodges. There has come
to them the challenge of childhood. How they meet it will determine their
claim to be deemed worthy of the leadership with which- they have been
entrusted.
The Fraternity may be justly proud of what it has accomplished in
instituting, and continuing to foster, Public Schools Week. There is, however, more to do than has yet been done; and the task we have undertaken
wiU not be finished until we shall have done all that we can to secure for
all the children of all the people an education appropriate to, and commensurate with, the demands of the age in which we live, and to provide
equal opportunities for all of them.
All of which is fraternally submitted.

In Memoriam Motley Hewes Flint
By WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY
\\Then a man dies, whom we have loved and honored and whose
face and voice we shall sadly miss for many a day, at our meet\ngs,
in our works and when we rest from labor, it is fit that we should
assemble together, and recount the story of his life, make up the
record of his works, and hear spoken of his excellencies and good
deeds. For, after a time, the great void that such a death makes will
be filled, and he will only occasionally be spoken of and remembered;
a~·d this will c:ome to pass also· as to all of us.
'
,
·
Motley Hewes Flint was born in Some.rville, Mass., February
19th, 1865, and died at L.os Angeles July 14th, 1930, aged 65 years.
He received his limited education in . the.public Schools of San
Francisco and at an early age began his business career in that city
by engaging in the wholesale paper business. He removed to Los
Angeles in 1886 when he was just twenty-one years of age and there
resided for the· rest of his life.
He was raised a Master Mason in Sunset Lodge (now Eastgate
No. 290) on August 23rd, 1895, and served that Lodge as Master in
1898, 1899 and 1900. He was High Priest of Signet Chapter No. 57
during the years 1901, 1902 and 1903. He was Knighted in Los
Angeles Commandery in 1896 and joined .the Scottish .Rite in 1905,
being coroneted an Inspector General Honorary of the 33° in 1914.
He was a charter member of San Gabriel Conclave of the Red Cross

202

l'ROC.l!:EDlNGS Ol!' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of Constantine and was its Sovereign in 1922. He was Potentate of
Al Malaikah Temple of the Shrine in 1906, 1907, 1910, 1911 and 1912.
He was Grand Master of Masons in California in 1.905-1906.
While this brief outline of his Masonic record, as preserved in
the archives of the order, indicates long service, high honors and
brilliant achievements, it fails to give more than a suggestion of the
Masonic life of a remarkable man who found in our Institution a
philosophy which he accepted unquestioned to guide and direct his
life and an incentive and opportunity to exemplify in full measure the
benevolent aspirations of a good Mason.
Past Grand Master Flint was Master of his Lodge for three years,
and at a time of general depression and much unemployment. The
membership of his Lodge was composed largely of railroad men,
many of whom had gone on strike. He labored assiduously for his
brethren and secured employment for every member of his Lodge
who needed work. He was Grand Master the year of the San Francisco fire and as soon as he heard of the calamity he went to San
Francisco and devoted his time and efforts for months solely in the
work of succoring and rehabilitating the bereft and needy. Our records disclose the immense labor involved and the hundreds of thousands of dollars contributed by the Masonic world and expended
under his wise direction. This service required not only much time,
but the strain nearly cost. the life of the Grand Master.
For more than a quarter of a century he was President of the
Board of Relief of Los Angeles and in that work of mercy he was
characteristically active, earnest and masterful. The thanks and
prayers of thousands were his reward for his untiring zeal and abiding sympathy for the unfortunate. For twenty years he was the
Shrine Santa Claus and raised funds and dispensed Christmas cheer
to several thousand poor children and to hundreds of necessitous
families. For many years he was a faithful and invaluable Trustee of
the Masonic Homes of California and thereafter Chairman of the
Endowment Fund Committee, which has struggled so long and so
successfully to provide an adeq11ate financial backlog of protection
for our homes for the aged and orphaned.
After expending the efforts of all the years of his manhood in
relieving distress and bringing some comfort and peace into weary
and hurdened lives he left a memorial of his greatness of heart and
the sincerity of his sympathies by dedicating his fortune to charity.
His will created three perpetual trust funds: One of $50,000 to yield
an income to be used for Christmas cheer for poor children, one of
$50.000 to yield an income to be used to provide summer vacations
for poor children, and the third, being the residue of his estate
amounting to several hundred th ousand dollars, to yield an income

to assist deserving boys and girls to get a start in the business world,
and to assist aged men and women fallen upon days of penury and .
want in their · 1ater years. It was like him to provide expressly that
all red tape should be cut out and that the money should go to
those who needed it when they needed it.
Being a restless man of prodigious energy and industry, Motley
Flint found time for many civic activities. He was s uccessful in
bringing conventions and large meetings to California and was indefatigable in providing shows and entertainment for them. For many
years he was facile pri1~ceps in this work and was the responsible host
to Knight Templars, Shriners, Elks, Bankers, Educators and other
large groups. He had genius for this as for other things. He devoted
much time in aiding to secure the motion picture industry for Los
Angeles, in striving for a people's harbor, in acquiring an adequate
water supply for the city and in the dissemination of information for
the development and upbuilding of the Commonwealth he loved so
much and served so patriotically.
He was imbued with a deep and ardent love for his country and
his State and was always a loyal citizen and a staunch advocate of
what he conceived to be the public weal. He accepted his citizenship
as an obligation and instead of being passive and indifferent in
political concerns he was alert and diligent and demonstrated a
thoroughgoing Americanism.
Soon after his removal to Los Angeles he became a clerk in the
postoffice and in 1887 was appointed Assistant Postmaster. In 1890
he was appointed Postoffice Inspector., In the performance o{ the
duties of thi's position .he trave led constantly 3-nd extensively throughout the west .and developed ~ 'w idespread circle of friends and acquaintances. He was an outstanding figure in this branch of the
Government service and was selected to install the postal system of
the Hawaiian 'Islands when they were annexed to the United States.
He was appointed Postmaster of Los Angeles in 1904 and resigned
after six years of service to become President of the Metropolitan
Trust Company. When this company was consolidated with the Los
Angeles Trust and Savings Bank he became Vice President of the
bank and continued as Vice President, and afterwards as Executive
Vice President of that ba nk and its successors for more than twenty
years. His industry, sound judgment, keen powers of analysis, sterling honesty, positive character, understanding of human nature and
spirit of helpfulness won for him a m erited success and an important
place in the financial world. His duties at the bank were arduous
and the responsibilities great and it was only because of a strong
will and unusual vigor that he was able to devote much time and
energy to such varied business, civic, charitable and fraternal activities.

Motley Flint had an extraordinarily large number of friends and
a.cquaintances throughout every State in the Union. His business,
fraternal and civic activities brought him into contact with thousands
of men who were impressed and drawn to him by his positive character, outspoken manner, earnestness of purpose, straightforward
manliness, strict integrity, social disposition and genial nature. He
was a fast and staunch friend. He made enemies, as men of strong
will and positive convictions win always surely do, but he plotted no
harm against anyone and sought no revenge. He was sometimes
brusque and often misunderstood, for his acts and words were frequently impulsive; but at heart he was sound and kindly. His abruptness masked a keenly sensitive nature and a profound love for his
felloVI man. He suffered deeply when unjustly criticized and his later
years brought him great sorrow because of unwarranted misrepresentations and unmerited attacks of which his well known life and
noble character offered a sufficient refutation.
In 1928 Motley Flint retired from business with the purpose of
devoting his time to the pursuit of living values and pleasures that
had been denied him by his active and strenuous business career. He
wished to travel abroad and by observation and experience partially
to make up for a limited education. He also wanted to develop his
modest and beautiful home at Flintridge, where it was his custom
and greatest delight to assemble and entertain his family and friends.
But all the cherished hopes and plans for the expected leisure of his
declfoing years were shattered by an assassin's bullets, which struck
him dow_n in a court of law whence he had been called as a witness.
While in good physical and mental health, and pursuing his lawful.
O!=casions, he was killed by an entire stranger, whom he had never
met or wronged. Thus tragically, and inexplicably ended the life of
a Master Craftsman-a great and goo<l n:ia11.
. May his memory be a blessing to those who cherish and treas•.
ure it! .

In Memoriam Jacob Nieto
By WILLIA M A. SHERMAN
We cannot approach Jacob Nieto, man, Mason, rabbi, along the
beaten paths of eulogy or satisfy ourselves with the empty civilities
of commonplace funeral tributes, for he did not make his life journey
over main traveled roads nor was he ever commonplace. Cold for"
malities would be unsuited to him. His manner and mode of life
reflected the highest culture and finest nature. Like Cromwell, he.
would always have said, "Paint me as I am."
Rabbi Jacob Nieto was born of a well known, long established
family , with every facility for education. He belonged to an old
aristocratic line in Israel. He traced his ancestry back to the days
of the Spanish Inquisition. · He was born in London, England, December 22, 1863. He was educated at the Collegiate School of
Kingston, Jamaica, British West Indies, at the College of the C.ity
of New York and the J ews College of London, England, from which
he received his degree as Bachelor of Hebrew and Rabbi. He came
to California in May, 1893, as Rabbi of Congregation Sherith Israel,
San Francisco, and continued as its leader until his death on March
26, 1930.
Brother Jacob Nieto had a distinguished and impelling personality. He was an impressive figure to behold, tall of form, rare and
unique in manner and appearance. Wherever he might be he was
always a marked man. By education, experience and analysis he was
unquestionably one of the best informed and most cultivated of men.
His mind was a treasure-house of universal learning. H is ability to
express himself made him one of the outstanding orators of his time.
He had a profound insight into human nature and a sympathy for
erring mortality which was noble, inspiring and constructive. He
had a great and sympathetic soul and was truly one "to whom the
burdened heart could pour out its sorrows, one to whom distress
could prefer its suit, one whose hand was guided by justice and
whose heart was expanded by benevolence." No one who sought his
guidance, counsel or assistance was turned away if it were within
his power to help. No problem was too intricate to r eceive his humane
consideration.
Brother Jacob Nieto was always a champion of youth. He had
a parti.c ularly peculiar and penetrating understanding and insight into
the life and mental processes of the growing boy. As one 0£ the
original members of the San Francisco Council, Boy Scouts of
America he contributed largely to a community service which has
inspired 'and developed into useful citizens, thousands of boys. His

207

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ability to analyze the qualities and abilities of youth is forcibly emphasized in one outstanding incident-his selection of a poor boy
for higher education. This boy was in an orphan asylum and through
the efforts of Brother Jacob Nieto was educated at the Hebrew
Union College in Cincinnati. It was Brat.her Nieto's ambition. that
this boy should be a rabbi, but when the youth told his benefactor
that he'preferred the law to the synagogue, he accepted the decision
as an evidence of individuality which he admired and was satisfied.
That boy today is one of the lea·ding lawyers of the country.
· He contacted the civic and political life of the State at a thousand
points. For nearly four decades he was a powerful element in shaping public opinion. He always spoke frankly and his opinions were
widely quoted. No cause of liberal or humanitarian impulse lacked
his championship. The under-privileged w ere always uppermost with
hinr and he gave them the full strength of his advocacy. He was a
great frie·n d of the labor groups and championed their principles in
bold and forthright fashion . During the San Francisco catastrophe
of ·1906 he proved a tower of strength and service in the hour of
crisis and the period of reconstruction which followed. He had an
enormous amount of courage and nothing ever overwhelmed . his
great spirit. He knew full well the burdens, opportunities and responsibilities of his calling and performed his duties faithfully and
well.
Brother Jacob Nieto loved his fellow man and responded
promptly to the· ideals of fraternal service. Masonically, he received
the Blue degrees in Fidelity Lodge No. 120 io 1897 and immediately
commenced a ·Masonic career that ended only with his death. He
passed through the chairs of Fidelity, becoming its Master in 1905.
Becoming eligible-. to p·articipate in the deliberations of this Grand
Lodge in 1903 as junior ·warden of his Lodge, he at once took an
active part. He was appointed Grand Chaplain at that session and
continued in that place for three years. In 1906 and 1907 he was
Grand ·orator and inspired and instructed the brethren with his might,
eloquence and learning. In 1923 he was the eulogist at the soldier
metnorial·services conducted by 'Grand 'Lodge. Through all the years
his voice was often heard in this Grand Body in support of its great
huma:nitllrian principles and ideals. He once said, "No occasion and
no place seem to inspire me to reach my greatest heights than a
Masonic gathering."
He was alfo -a · member· of San Francisco Chapter No. 1, Royal
Arch · Masons, ~rid ltal\fotnia Council No. 2, Royal and Select Masters. In the Scottish Rite he attained the exalted rank of the thirtythird deg'ree and was the· orator of Islam Temple of the Shrine, in
which he ·took a·ri active part. In ·all the activities of Masonry he was

always a willing worker and was ever giving of his great oratorical
ability. He was past president of the District Grand Lodge No. 4,
lndependent Order B'nai Brith. He was an organizer and past president of the Jewish Educational Society of San Francisco and President of the Board of Rabbis of Northern California and of the
Western Association of Jewish Ministers. As the leading Rabbi in
years of service on the Pacific Coast he held the affection and esteem
of his colleagues.
Brother Jacob Nieto was an able writer. His writings were
touched with wit, often with sarcasm, but always with kindliness.
His opinions were logical and sincere. He was the author of "The
H.omance of Poverty," editor of the "New Occident" and contributing editor of the Jewish Journal and at one time feature writer for
the San Francisco Bulletin.
Brother Jacob Nieto·'s home life was happy. Mrs. Rose Nieto,
his widow, two daughters, Miss Anita Nieto and Miss Julie Nieto,
and a son, John Nieto, also three sisters, Mrs. Albert Lucas, Miss
~1irriam Nieto and Miss Sarah Nieto, survive him.
Brother Jacob Nieto's friends were legion. He had an unbounded capacity to draw people to him. The funeral services in
Congregation Sherith Israel were attended by thousands in all walks
of life, who thronged the vast structure and packed the streets surrounding the Temple as the funeral cortege passed. In the passing
of Brother Jacob Nieto, San Francisco and the State lost one of its
best known and best loved citizens. He was the type of human
kindly man upon whom could be justly attached the title "One who
walked with kings, but never lost the common touch."
His place in the minds of the public was splendidly and truly
expressed by Brother Eugene Block of the San Francisco CallBulletin in an editorial of that paper, as follows: "There went a man
who was truly a friend of the under-dog-Rabbi Jacob Nieto--for
nearly forty years a beloved figure in his adopted San Francisco.
He had a shining intellect and an understanding heart and all manner of men mourn his passing and regret that such good men cannot
live forever. In mentality he was an aristocrat, but within himself
he was utterly democratic. The forsaken, the forlorn, and the broken
made persistent and powerful appeal to Rabbi Nieto's spirit. He
understood and sympathized. If his tongue spoke cynically at times,
his heart never did."
On our personal friendship I shall not dwell. To me the beauty,
the charm, the spiritual value of that unfaltering, unwavering love is
a sacred thing, not to be· talked of, but rather as the years go on to

206

208

PR OC EEDINGS OF THE

r ecall to the mind's eye, to sense again and again and say to myselfmy life has been rich indeed, Brother Jacob N ieto was my friend.
To speak of one who has been so much of one's life, and not
lose one's sen se of restraint is difficult indeed. The temptation to
burst the bounds and perhaps grow inarticulate is too strong and so
I close having left untouched, I feel, the real beauties of that fine
character. I fe el with Ingersoll that if every one for whom Brother
Jacob Nieto had done a kind deed. would bring a blossom to his grave,
he would sleep tonight beneath a paradise of flowers .

In Memoriam John H. Logie

By OAKLEY K. MORTO N
During the past year the silent messenger entered the official
family of Grand Lodge. No more can we have the hearty hand-clasp
and exchange welcome greetings with Brother John H. Logie, Junior
Grand Steward.
After enjoying a visit to his birthplace and boyhood surroundings in the Orkney Islands, the final call came to him suddenly on
July 19th, 1930, at Glasgow, Scotland. Although seventy years of
age, life had been generous to John Logie, and he was privileged to
he active and enjoy health until the influenza, during the epidemic a
few years ago, took heavily of his vitality and his last years were not
so free of interruptions.
In 1880 he came to Canada, then 19 years of age; two years
later he moved to Duluth, Minnesota, and in 1903 moved to California, locating at Redlands, San Bernardino County. John Logie
was always one of the influential citizens of Redlands. Many sought
his counsel, for the saying was "John's advice is always safe." He
maintained a quiet but active interest in the public schools. All
school observances received his full cooperation and he viewed with
intense satisfaction the erection of the fine school buildings of Redlands. He was particularly happy to arrange for the laying of each
corner stone with the proper dignity by his beloved Masonic fraternity.
In our Masonic Ritual the name John carries a reverence and
deep significance. Brother Logie merited his name of John and when
he was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason on March 2, 1889,
Masonry gained another John that it could always be proud of. From
the date of his initiation to his death his interest in Masonic principles never waned. He was passed to the degree of Fellowcraft on

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

209

May 6th, 1889, and raised a Master Mason on May 20th, 1889, in
Palestine Lodge No. 79, A. F . & A. M., in Duluth, Minnesota. He
served as Secretary of this Lodge for some years.
For ten years he edited the Redlands Commandery Monthly
Bulletin, which carried the meat of all Masonic activities of that
city, as well as interestfog educational items of Masonic doings about
the world. It was always enjoyable to read John's review of Masonic
functions.
He was a Past Commander of Redlands Commandery No. 45,
K. T., which Commandery he helped organize, and served as its
first Recorder. For three years he served as an Illustrious Master of
Valley Council at San Bernardino. He was also a Past High Priest
of Redlands Chapter No. 77. For many years he was President of
the Gateway Scottish Rite Club, comprising San Bernardino, Riverside and Redlands. He was elected to receive the 33° in the
Scottish Rite on October 20th, 1923, and was coroneted a 33° on
January 12th, 1924.
A wonderful tribute and fitting climax of his Masonic endeavors
came in December, 1928, when he was elected, from the floor, Master
of Redlands Lodge No. 300 with the unanimous approval of the
officers. Although hesitant to accept this honor, his year was filled
with constructive activity and sincere service, thus laying a foundation from which the Lodge will long benefit. During his year as
Master many outstanding candidates were admitted into Masonry
under his guidance. Sorrow& and tribulations also came to him for
advice, and he many times said that he valued his year as Master
above all his other Masonic service, as it gave him a deeper insight
into the real functionings of a Masonic Lodge and the service that
it was possible for the Master to render. One outstanding evening
of his year in the East was the vis!t to his Lodge of his admirers
and close personal friends in Scottish Rite Masonry. Each station
was filled by a 33° brother. The Sovereign Inspector General, a
Past Master of Ohio, occupying the East. Brother Logie, the surprised and honored guest of the evening, was deeply affected by this
expression of the love and affection of his Masonic associates. At
the October, 1929, annual communication of Grand Lodge he was
honored by the M.'.W.'.Grand Master, Charles M. Wollenberg, with
the appointment of Junior Grand Steward. He was thus honored
with the opportunity to ~ervo in the highest Masonic body during
hi~ final year with us.
Brother Logie realized the value of church life in a community
~nd he gave of his time and ability to his office as Warden of the
Trinity Episcopal Church of Redlands. Shortly prior to his trip

210

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

abroad he worked out the details for the fulfillment of the Masonic
desires of five ministers of his city, who took the Order of the
Temple together at a wonderfully impressive ceremony. He was not
narrow in his church views, but felt there was a real need for united
Christiari effort between the denominations in any community. Anything that he could do to promote united Christian activity received
his immediate active approval.
Brother Logie is survived by ·his wife, Alice L. Logie, and their
two daughters, Helen a nd Marguerite, both now married. His home
life was ideal and he was fortunate in having a family that appreciated and shared his interest in our fraternity.
He stood forth as a noble example of the principles of Masonry.
His craft knowledge indicated his tireless. research. In 1927 he discovered that the Great Seal of Grand Lodge was not correct according_ to the rules of Heraldry. A special committee was appointed, of
which he was a member, and he canvassed the world in gathering
data from which to design the present Grand Lodge seal. His book
on Heraldry presented to Grand Lodge last October contains information on that subject and Masonic se·a ls from every country on the
globe. The design which he submitted was checked by English,
Canadian and A ustralian authorities on Heraldry, and approved and
adopted by Grand Lodge at the 1929 communication and is now the
seal in use.
In all his activities of life, whether domestic social business
religious or fraternal, he was at all times a loyal,' earnes~ and con~
scientious man. He seemed to understand t_h e spirit and truths of
Masonry; he was one of whom it could· be truly said: "Modest,
earnest, industrious, with the fear of God and the love of mankind in
his heart, he was one of our most useful citiiens."
.

Is spent in. duty to God and man.
Beautiful calm when the ·course is :run
Beautiful twilight at·· set of ·sun ·
· Beautiful death with a- life well done."

the Grand Lecturer's Report pertaining to degree teams be referred
to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to be considered
by them in connection with that portion of the Grand Master's
Message pertaining to the same subject.

any other position on the degree team than that designated in the
certificate, until the Master has satisfied himself that the brother is
proficient in the work of such other station.
The high standard of the ritualistic work th~oughout the state
· bespeaks the untiring efforts of our Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M:.W:.Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee on Returns herewith submits its report.
The slump in the stock market, the business depression and the
increase in unemployment appear to have affected the work of the
Lodges. There has been a noticeable falling off in the number of
those petitioning for the degrees.
During the year 6,21S candidates were raised to the Sublime
Degree of Master Mason. This is 409 fewer than the previous year.
The net increase in membership for the year is 3,410, which is more
than twenty per cent less than the increase of a year ago. This is
not a matter of great concern.
Of all the Grand Lodges in the United States, California has
the largest increase m membership. Some 17 Grand Jurisdictions
report a decrease. The total increase in membership throughout the
country is given as, only, 676. Other fraternal organizations report
decreases in membership.
We ought to remember that it is tqe quality of the candidates
that <;ounts and not the number. With fewer candidates the Lodges
should he able to act with greater care. They may be able to make'
Masons and not merely make members. And with less work the
members of the Lodges will have more time to devote to sociability
and the joys of getting well acquainted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCING
MASONIC TEMPLES
Io the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California :
During the year, eighteen Lodges, or hall associations, have conducted correspondence with your committee. Some of these were
only inquiries as to how to proceed to raise funds for their projects.
The committee has reviewed and approved the following buildings :
Santa Ana Masonic Temple Association, located at Santa Ana,
conducted a campaign and raised $174,715.00 in pledges, for the purpose of erecting a new building. On September 30, 1930, $94,563.00
had been collected on their subscriptions, and the contract for the
erection of the building had been let. This, we believe, has been the
largest project undertaken during the past year.
The South Pasadena Masonic Temple Association conducted a
campaign and raised $105,000.00, and arc proceeding with the erection
of their building.
Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, located in San Diego, conducted a
campaign and raised $75,000.00 for the financing of their Temple.
The committee app.roved the purchase of a lot and erection of
a building by Santa Paula Lodge No. 291, to cost $55,000.00.
The committee approved the proposition of La Mesa Lodge No .
407. located at La Mesa, to expend $23,500.00 in the· erection and
furnishing. of a new Temple.
Permission was given to Altadena Lodge, U. D.. located at
A ltadena, to purchase a lot and construct a building costing approximately $13,500.00.
Approval was given to Santa Maria Lodge to remodel their olrl
huilding at a cost of approximately $15,000.00.
Permission was . given to Beverly Hills Masonic Temple Association to. purchase a lot costing $10,000.00
Permission was given to Bell Masonic Temple Association, located at Bell, to purchase a building which had already been erected
for hall purposes, the purchase price of which was $21 ,602.00.
Permission was granted to San Buenaventura Masonic Temple
Association at Ventura, to borrow an additional $6,000.00 on }heir
building, which had just been completed.
Brother Greig, of our committee, handled the following projects,
and on his recommendation, approval was given :
Hiram Lodge No. 43, located at Eldorado. Permission to expend $500.00 in remodeling their hall.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

230

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Martinez Lodge No. 41, located at Martinez. Permission was
g'.ven to erect a new building costing not to exceed $43,500.00
Escalon Lodge No. 591, located at Escalon. Permission was
given to erect a building costing $8,500.00, the lot for same haying
been donated by Brother Otto Peterson.
Correspondence was had, or interviews held, with the following
Lodges who have been contemplating building, but have, so far, not
asked for permission to expend funds.
Alta Loma Lodge o. 64.3, Long Beach.
Searchlight Lodge No. 567, Long Beach.
Orange Grove Masonic Building Association, located at Orange.
Glassell Park Lodge No. 605, located in Los Angeles.
Tuscan Lodge No. 261. located in Williams, has been granted
permission to proceed with a building program to the extent of
approximately $25,000.
Your committee feels that the brethren in general are pleased to
cooperate with the committee in the matter of the construction of
Masonic buildings, the principal idea being. how to raise the funds
with the least possible effort and expense. Somt: funds have been
raised by the sale of stock, others by the sale of certificates which
the Lodge or building association agrees to redeem on the death of
the subscriber, and others by outright donation. Of course, the latter
is the most desirable way to raise funds, if the Lodge can develop
th e proper, giving spirit.
The principal aim of your committee is to be helpful and constructive, keeping in mind the one thought that as little money a~
possible should be raised by mortgages.
ROBERT GREIG,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
At the 79th Communication of Grand Lodge, the M.'.W.'.Grand
Master Will H. Fischer reported the activity of some Clandestine
Bodies in California and recommended the appointment of the Committee to investigate and repo rt upon the matter. Owing to a change
in the personnel in this Committee the work was not actually
entered upon until the early part of this year. However, although
the difficulties confronting your Committee were great we have been
able to collect concrete evidence of the existence, identity and activity
of all of the Clandestine Bodies now operating in this State.
There is. some Clandestine activity in the northern part of the
State but most of this irregular Masonry is centered in the Sau
Joaquin Valley and south of the Tehachapi.
Other than the membership in the co-M<1sonic Bodies, there are
very few of the White Race participating in this Clandestine activity,
most of it being among Negroes, Filipinos and Mexicans.
We find that the Clandestine Bodie.s opera ting in California are
made up of the following:
1. Twenty Lodges chartered by the so-called Supremo Gran
Oriente de! Rito
acional Maxicano, having headquarters in San
Bernardino, and of which one, Samuel W. Kelly, a Mexican, in
spite of his name, was the Deputy Grand Master. We are lately informed that Mr. Kelly has recently died, and so far as your Committee has learned, there seems now to be no head to the organization
in California.
2. Three subordinate Lodges operating under charters granted
by the Grand Lodge "Benito Juarez" of Torreon, State of Coahuila,
Mexico.
3. One colored Grand Lodge known as Most Worshipful
Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge , Ancient Free and Accepted Masons.

This spurious Grand Lodge is not to be confounded with the
Most Worshipful Sovereign Grand Lodge of F ree and Accepted
Masons, which, while a colored organization, has received quasi recognition of our Grand Lodge.
4. Certain Lodges of which we have identified three in Southern California, though there are doubtless many others operating
under charters granted by a so-called co-Masonic Grand Lodge with

Lo"dge is headed by one, Louis Gazieu, and whose title is "Most

and still later to a Lodge known as "Oriente," No. 41 of San Pedro,
California. The Master of Hiram Lodge, No. 45, at San Bernardino, is Peter Samano. The Master of Oriente Lodge No. 41 is
Rafael Martinez and Antonio Estrada is Secretary. These three
Lodges s'e em to be in charge of one Emelio Espinoza of Los Angeles,
residing at 2121 E. Florence Avenue, that city, under the title qj
Deputy Gr.and Master. Their Rite is said to consist of nine degrees. Their initiation fee is $70.00. We are informed that th~ir
membership fotals about 7 5 for all · three Lodges. These Lodges
work in Spanish .and have no American members.
We are informed that the Grand Lodge Benito Juarez of Mexico would like to receive recognition from our Grand Lodge. I was
informed by Mr. Espinoza that his Grand Lodge was withdrawing
the Charters of the three Lodges above named and apparently was
preparing to withdraw from California. This was no doubt a preliminary move toward an application . for recognition to our . Grand
Lodge. ,

3.

As to Negro Masonry:

A Clandestine Negro Grand Lodge known as "The Most Worshipful of Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted
Masons (colored) is operating in California. It was originally organized under the name of "Most Worshipful R. J. Fletcher Grand
Lodge of A. F. and A. M. and incorporated under California law
with offices in Sacramento in May, 1910. Later in 1913, by order
of the Superior Court of Sacramento County, the name was changed
to "Most Worshipful Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge." We are informed that this organization now has some twenty-three
subordinate Lodges scattered throughout the State ranging from Redding on the north to, San Diego on the south. While it was organized originally for Negroes only, we are informed that in 1927 or
1928 certain Filipinos either acquired the Charter of the organization or were granted a dispensation to organize Lodges of Filipinos
or of Negroes and Filipinos. It is said that one L. P. Lee, colored,
is Grand Master. Our last information is that he is employed in
some capacity in the Engineering Department of Los Angeles
County. One W. H. H. Robinson, colored, is his secretary. He is
in the automobile distributing business in Los Angeles.
In June of 1929, this so-called Grand Lodge met in Pasadena,
L. P. Lee presiding as Grand Master. D. E. Taylor, colored, residing at 14570 22nd Street, Los Angeles, is a prominent officer and
was a candidate for Grand Master at the Pasadena meeting in opposition to L. P. Lee.
A Lodge known as "Ezra," No. 11, was organized in Stockton
in 1926 or 1927 by one H. M. Fieldhouse (white), assisted by a
Filipino named "Karp." They initiated about 35 men, mostly Filipinos. They meet at 114 South America Street, Stockton, California. A formal installation of the officers of this Lodge was conducted
by said Fieldhouse upon December 15, 1928, at the old Auditorium,
134 N. Eldorado. Stre_et, Stockton.
We are -informed that one H. M. Fairfield (white) and the Filipino Karp have instituted the following Lodges of Filipinos or mixed
Filipinos and Negroes: "General Antonio Luna," No. 15, at Salinas;
Aklan Lodge, U. X. p., near Livermore, California; "Luana Lodge/'
U. D .. Carpenter Hall, Valencia near Market Street, San Francisco.
Fieldhouse seems to be in considerable authority and his address is
gi~en us as 3476 18th Street, San Francisco.
In June of 1930 this organization held its meeting in Los
Angeles with about 250 delegates attending. A Los Angeles Lodge
of this group is named "Malachi," No. 9, composed of Negroes and
Filipinos. There are numerous other Lodges in Fresno and surrounding Valley towns.

!l3ii

Hiram of Tyre Grand Lodge is said to be affliated with the
Grand Lodge of the. Uni.ted States" with headquarters at
3404 i~t. Antonie Street,. Detroi.t,. Michigan,. .yhere it is said that a
gene'fl assembly is scheduled to lle held in 1932.
A\nother Negro Grand Lodge was organized and incorporated
under the name of "Most Worshipful Alpha Grand Lodge of Ancient
Free and Accepted Masons of California in September, 1923, in Los
Angeles County, with J. W. Dupree, J. F. Purseley, V. M. Cole,
W. H. Prioleau and Houston Mays as incorporators. · It is stated
in the Articles .of Incorporation that this alleged Grand Lodge is a
part of the United Grand Lodge of England and was organized at
the instance of the Most Worshipful King Solomon Grand Lodge,
A. F. and A. M. of Texas. We are unable to find any Lodges
which this Grand Lodge has chartered or any evidence that it is
functioning in any way whatsoever.
There is another Negro Grand Lodge, the formal title of which
is "The Sovereign Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California," which is· quasi-legitimate. It has a sort of qualified standing
with our Grand Lodge. They are also known as the Prince Hall
Masons, which is the name of a holding corporation for their. Grand
Lodge. They seem to have two headquarters, one at 12090 Central
Avenue, Los Angeles, and 1545 Steiner Street, San Francisco. T,'hi~·
group of Masons seem to have organized a complete complement of
York Rite Bodies to-wit: Lodges, Chapters, Councils and Commanderies, also Eastern Star Chapters and a Shrine.
"Ge~eral

4. As to Co-Masonry:. There seem to be two distinct groups of
Co-Masonic Bodies in California. .One of these groups was organized by the various Theosophical societies, but we are informed that
td some extent these Lodges have been dissolved on account of certain conceptions and directions coming to them from the Theosophical societies.
Another group of Co-Masonic Lodges are a part of the National
Co-Masonic Institution with headquarters at Larkspur, Colorado.
The head of this National Institution is one Louis Gazieu, and his
title is Most Puissant Grand Commander. They seem to have a
Rite of 32 ceremonial and one governing degree divided into a system
of Lodges, Chapters, Councils and Areopagus. They have organized
at least three Subordinate Lodges in Southern California, one known
as Hollywood Lodge, located at Hollywood Boulevard and Serrano
Street. Another one is in Long Beach and still another one in San
Diego.
We believe that we have contacted all of the irregular Grand
Bodies which have organized Lodges in California. On account of

I

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I

the difficulties ·st.1rrounding the task it has not always been po~'ible
to obtain as specific and precise information concerning the o cers
of the various Lodges as was desirable. We believe that if this
work is continued full and exhaustive information may be plac~d at
the disposal of Grand Lodge for such action as may be deemed
necessary in the premises. While the work of these Lodges, generally s'peaking, seems to be in the hands of Negroes, Filipinos and
Mexicans, with the exception of the Co-Masonic Lodges, yet it is
apparent that white men and Americans are being drawn into the
Clandestine operations and action of some sort is considered to be
advisable. We do not deem it the part of wisdom for Grand Lodge
to remain quiescent while spurious Masonry is being carried on at
its doors. In this connection we are reminded of the decision of the
United States Supreme Court announcing the principle that a regular and bona-fide organization might be precluded by )aches from
complaining of the piracy of its Ritual, Landmarks, Cerem.:>n,les and
name by a Clandestine and irregular organization.

Smithan, Inspector of the 92 District, for valuable information and
services rendered your committee.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
.M.'.W.'.Gra11d Lodge of California:
our Board of Control presents herewith a report of its activities ince the close of the annual communication of Grand Lodge
in 19 9.
•our meetings of the Board have been held during the year, as
folio s: At Oakland, California, on November 23, 1929; at Los
Angelfs, March 8, 1930; at Fresno, June 14, 1930, and at San Francisco, October 13-14, 1930.
·
In accordance with the custom established, the Board of Control has given notice to the various Boards of Relief of these meetings and in every case the several Boards have sent d.elegates to
attend. The meetings, therefore, in addition to the business transac·
tions, have served as conferences for the interchange of experiences,
and comparisons of methods and we believe have been of service to
the Boards of Relief.
The Board of Control is pleased to report that Boards of Relief
and individual Lodges are now working in complete accord with the
established procedure of this Board, ancl that with efficiency and
regularity have come greater economy.
·
In its four years' existence the Board of Control has submitted
to and has had approved by Grand Lodge plans for more effective
service and for standardization of the work of the Boards of Relief.
The results of its efforts are seen in:
1. Uniformity in annual reports.
2. Uniformity in financial and relief records.
3. Regular annual audit of all Boards.
4. · Uniform By-Laws and compacts.
5. All Board officers now carry Fiduciary Insurance.
6. All Boards now carry Compensation Insurance.
7. Great reduction in the total sums for reimbursement granted
by Grand Lodge.
8. The incorporation in the Constitution of Board of Control
,provisions.
9. The more economical administration of Employment Service
. and Boards of Relief.

and affairs by its own auditor. We believe this to be, not only less

Oakland and Berkeley. The Oakland Board of Relief, known as
the East Bay Masonic Board of Relief, is composed of members from
the blue lodges located in Oakland and Berkeley, and holds one
meeting each month. During .the past year .a per capita assessment
has been levied in the sum of four cents.
There are two paid employees, both engaged in the relief and
employment service. The secretary receives nothing, the assistant
secretary receives $175.00 per month and a typist or clerk receives
$50.00 per month. These · amounts cover the work done for both

Requests for Reimbursement
The total requests for reim.bursement approved this year amount
to $6,881.67, covering 133 cases. In comparison with last year's
requests, we are happy to announce, that this amount is nearly
$700.00 less. This year your Board of Control has had for considerat ion 100 cases from 35 other United States jurisdictions, as against 91
cases from 34 other United States jurisdictions last year; 26 cases
from 9 Foreign jurisdictions this year as against 17 cases from 8
Foreign jurisdictions last year. California cases however, this year
are more than last year, both in number and amount.
This reduction in the amount requested for reimbursement, in
the face of an abnormal economic condition, shows a marked increase
in diligence and efficiency on the part of our various Boards of
Relief, and we desire to commend them highly. Your Board of
Control also gratefully acknowledges the assistance and co-operation
of our M.". W.". Grand Master and our V.".
Grand Secretary. ·
Six of our Boards of Relief request NO reimbursement. This Board
is convinced however, that some plan should be developed looking
to a still further reduction of requests by a definite system of follow-up
by the Grand Secretary or this Board. This is most forcibly brought
to our attention by the fact that we are recommending reimbursement
in 21 cases of other jurisdictions ranging from $100.00 to $400.00 each.
Your Board of Control desires to emphasize the necessity of
information being sent out to all Boards of Relief and Lodges, of
imposters. Several cases of duplication of relief are noted. Most of
such cases appear to be not deserving. Several cases reviewed by
·this Board would indicate a tendency on the part of some of our

A Striking Case
Your Board of Control has had for consideration a request by
the Board of Relief of Los Angeles for reimbursement for funds
expended for the relief of a brother of a Southern California Lodge.
This request commands notice in this report because it is unusual
a nd because it shows ignorance of Masonic duty on th e part of the
Master of the said Masonic Lodge.
The brother in question sought remission of his dues and relief
from his Lodge. It was not the first time that the brother had appealed to his Lodge. In justice (to the Lodge) it must be _said that
relief had bee n granted several times and that perhaps the Lodge
officers felt that the brother's requests were too frqeuent. The fact
remains, however, that neither of the appeals of the brother were
granted, although he was in good standing and in distress. Instead
he was notified on April 16, 1930 that if his 1930 dues "were not paid
by May 2, 1930, he would be suspended." The brother appealed to the
then Acting Grand Master, who immediately communicated with the
said Lodge, ordering that said Lodge take no action in suspending
the brother and that the Lodge comply with its obligation in granting
relief to the brother, his wife and daughter. In the meantime, the
Master and the \Varden interviewed the brother and his wife separately in Los Angeles-the Master refusing at first to reveal his
identity to the brother. Later the Master wrote a most heartless and
uncalled-for letter to the wife and a similar letter to the brother.
Although the officers found the brother and his family in actual need,
the;r first. act, instead of granting relief, was an attempt to get riq _of
the brother and to notify him that he would be suspended.
The brother had applied to the Los Angeles Board of Relief for
assistance. That Board communicated with the Lodge and was
directed to render no relief. But the Board of Relief, acting under
Section 90 of the Constitution and Decisions 343 and 346, and deeming
it necessary to provide food and shelter for the needy brother, granted
him relief in the amount of $110.00. This action was given approval
by the Acting Grand Master and the Board of Control. After a
conference with the Acting Grand Master the Lodge officers notified

257

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Gl1AN[) L ODG ~ O F CALIFORNIA

the Board of Relief to advance $100.00 to the brother and gave
assurance that the $110.00 already paid to him would be returned to
the Board.

San Francisco: E x penses w er e slightly lower owing to the fact
that the Manager took over the duti es of the Secreta ry of the Board
of Relief during his absence fo r several months a nd a substitute was
employed to take care of the Employment Service.

256

But this did not close the matter. The brother is now and has
been since May 16, in need of assistance. The Los Angeles Board of
Relief has been granting this assistance and the Lodge has not
reimbursed the Board except as above noted. The Board of Relief
comes to the Board of Control with a request for reimbursement
for funds expended in the amount of $197.00.
Your Board of Control has gone into this case at length because
it believes it to be a matter of serious concern to this Grand Lodge.
In its continuous ·con~act w ith reimbursement controversies in this
jurisdiction, it has found similar cases but none so aggravated as
this. And this particular case has been submitted for the information
of Lodges as well as a warning to Lodge officers.
The Grand Lodge has clearly defined the duties and obligations
of a Lodge in the matter of relief to a distressed and needy worthy
brother (Sec. 90 and Decision 343-346) , .a nd our custom and procedure
in the matter of charity has become practically a California Masonic
Landmark. Until Grand Lodge legislates otherwise, we must carry on
as we have for four score years. To quote the Deputy Grand Master
"The time when a brother needs and applies for relief is not the time
to det.e rmine whether he is worthy of Masonic consideration. If the
brother is in good standing, the only duty of the Lodge is to determine
if the brother is in need and if it finds that he is to grant him relief."
It is the province of this Board of Control to pass upon requests
for reimbursement and to make recommendations thereon,
vVe, therefore, report that the request of the Los Angeles Board
of Relief for reimbursement in the sum of $197.00 for funds expended
for the relief of Brother
of
Lodge has been denied
and we recommend that said
Lodge be instructed by Grand
Lodge to reimburse the Los Angeles Board of Relief for funds already
expended in the relief of said brother and further that the present
relief be continued by said Lodge under the direction of and through
said Board of Relief with the instruction to said Board, so far as
possible, to keep said r elief expens es at the lowest possible figure.
Employment Service
The reports of our Employment Service reflect the general condition of unemployment that prevails throughout the Nation. In
nearly every case there have been more applicants and fewer placements than last year, which has increased the cost per unit.
Following is a brief summary of the several reports:

Oakland-Berkeley-Richmond: The Employment Service and
Board of R elief are now being operated a nd supported jointly by the
Lodges of the Oakland-Berkeley District. An additional two cents
per member per month is collected toward the expense of t he Employment Service.
This new arrangement is in li ne with the recommendation of the
Board of Co ntrol and is working out very satisfactorily. Two paid
employees serve both th e Board of Relief a nd Employment Service.
The total expense for salaries for the year being $3,475.00 : Rent
$35.00 per month; Applications received, 1978 ; P ositions secured, 764;
Cost per unit for positions filled, $5.84.
Los Angeles: Conditions continue about the same. An unusually
large list of applicants placed a heavier burden upon the office. Lodge
Employment Committees are cooperating.

Recommendations
Your Board of Control is of the opinion that 110 reasonable effort
~hould be spared in emphasizing to employing Masons the need for
greater cooperation in assisting our less fortunate brethren to jobs.
We, therefore, recommend that the Grand Secretary be authorized to have printed a card bearing the name and location of all
Employment Service Bureaus within the jurisdiction. This card to
he sent out by the Secretary of each Lodge with every receip~ for
dues and designed to carry a double message.
It would explain briefly the importance of immediately signing
the r eceipt for dues to prevent improper use of that document in case
it was lost and, it would remind the brother to make use of the
Employment Service wherever possible.
'0l e also recommend that the Committee on Masonic Education
be requested to have preparer! a paper setting forth the functions and
opportunities of our Employment Service, said paper to be used as
one of the regular monthly subjects of that Committee and to be
r ead and discussed in the constituent Lodges.

REPORT OF MASONIC TEMPLE ASSOCIATION

-o

To the M .".W.".Grand Lodge of California:
In presenting the report of the Masonic Temple Association of
California to Grand Lodge we beg to state that there have been extensive improvements made in various parts of the building. The
Lodge room on the fourth floor has been entirely rebuilt. The ventilating system is being replaced and will be completed very shortly
and the northern wall of the building has bP,en faced with composition plast er much in keeping with the stone work on the front of
the building.
Upon the death of Brother Edward Peabody, who was secretary and general manager of the Temple, Brother Frank C. Ruppel
voluntarily offered his services without s·a lary or remuneration and
since that time the affairs of the Temple have been conducted very
much to its benefit. The directors have declared three dividends,
which, whi le small in themselves, show increase of pr_ofits which,
with the trend of business ou t Market street, will slowly continue.
We feel that we should place the credit of the management
where it belongs, and in connection therewith we name the splendid
work done by. Brother Ruppel.
