REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws has had under consideration the
By-Laws of Liberal Arts Lodge and Willow Glenn Lodge, both
under dispensation, and finds them to be in proper form, except as
to Section 2, Article V, and. Section 2, Article VI, which do not
conform to the Uniform Code of By-Laws of Lodges, made obligatory in October, 1898, and as amended to October, 1918, in that they
fail to require the Secretary and the Treasurer to furnish a good and
sufficient bond within fifteen days after installation. The committee
recommends the approval of these . By-Laws subject to correction
thereof, as herein indicated; such amendments to be properly certified and transmitted to the Grand Secretary.
Your committee has also had under consideration various amendments to By-Laws of Lodges and they are found to be in proper
form, and we therefore recommend their approval.
RANDOLPH V. WHITING,

Juuus GABRIEL,
VICTOR R. MCLUCAS,

Committee.

Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California:
This committee, in reports of previous years, has presented the
view that a Masonic Lodge is a strong asset in any new community,
in promoting civic development and moral gain. It is comparable to
those other important moral agencies, the public school and the church,
all being most helpful and so greatly needed, as soon as new towns
and settlements have become well established. However, these observations yield to circumstances such as the present ones of industrial and financial depression.
We want no failures on our r ecord as an Instituticin, and seeking, as we do, quality rather than quantity, it is better that ocasional
petitions for dispensations be denied, as our Grand Master's address
shows he has done this past year, than to grant such petitions with
a possible risk of later circumstances disclosing that the action was
too optimistic. When in any given city or community, there are
enough Lodges, reasonably accessible, to supply the Masonic needs
of the brethren residing therein, no good is gained by giving the
right of life to still more new Lodges.
No business that it can transact, comes to this Charters Committee until after the Grand Master, in his wise discretion and only in

269

cases of manifest propriety and necessity, has granted dispensations
in response to petitions. Thereafter, each Lodge must work a time
under dispensation and each must exhibit satisfactory evidence of its
Masonic capability before this Charters Committee can recommend
. that a charter be issued in lieu of the dispensation under which the
newly organized Lodge has been conducting its affairs.
The Committee makes favorable recommendation in all three of
the cases before it. One of the new Lodges is in a city recently incorporated as such under State laws; the second may best be described
as being in a city within a city; the third is in unincorporated territory
but has been an old settlement for many years.
Willow Glen is a community of homes, adjacent to San Jose in
Santa Clara county and has about 7,000 population. It has recently
been incorporated as a city, but has not been given an independent
post office by the Federal government, the inhabitants receiving mail
through the San Jose post office. T he Lodge is to be called "Willow
Glen."
Westwood (the University city within the city of Los Angeles
that had its origin with the establishment of the "University of California at Los Angeles") is the location of the new Masonic Lodge
that will be called " Liberal Arts" Lodge. It is not intended solely
for men who arc students past majority in that university, but will
serve the Masonic needs of a section of the larger city, estimated a t
12,000 people.
Altadena comprises a closely-built residence community of highest
worth, located adjacent to Pasadena in Los Angeles county, with a
population of about 16,000. It is not a city, being purposely unincorporated. The Lodge is to be called "Altadena."
T hi• Committee on Charters is pleased to report that in the
hearings before it, excellent evidence was given of the ample cooperation and generosity of both brethren and Lodges, toward the three
newly organized Lodges whose representatives were before us. Although created in communities of the large populations already given,
nevertheless the brethren had reverted to the ways of more simple
days, for instead of contributions of money only, had given extensive
personal service to promote the ends desired. Gifts were told of
Lodge furniture, of regalia and particularly of personal effort and
labor in th e new halls or temples a bout to be occupied. In one case
the pedestals for the Wardens were made and given by a brother
who was a cabinet maker ; the Tiler's register beautifully prepared
and bound by one skilled in that work. In another, one I.,odge officer
·was said to be the financial "genius" with an enthusiastic ability to
interest others in giving financial support to the new enterprise
(subsequent, of course, to approval of plans by our special Grand
Lodge Committee on "Financing Building Projects" ) ; the officer
next above him was the able architect of the new Lodge home; and

270

PROCEEDI NGS OF 'l'HE

the Master, a lawyer, gave all the time necessary to take any legal,
steps required. Such team-work, accompanied by zeal and generosity1
i~ indeed Masonry conducted in the true Masonic spirit.
Recommending the issuance of charters to three new Lodges·
only, reveals the least number of dispensations and petitions for
charters on which this committee has worked for many years past.
The total of new Lodges for nine· years, including this year, is 164
or a yearly average of 18 new Lodges. From what has been stated
and from the unusually high character and personnel of the representatives of the new Lodges, and from the exc~llent manner in
which the books of records were kept, we believe that all of the three
will be Lodges of high quality, which is always ou r desire.
In each case, these new Lodges are clear of all debts; have been
conducted in due Masonic manner; are in communities sufficient
both in population and resources to justify the chartering of these
Lodges and they in all respects substantially comply with the requirements of our Constitution.
Your Committee recommends that charters be issued to these
new Lodges in the order of their petitions for charters, with the
following names and numbers:
Willow Glen Lodge No. 676 at \Villow Glen, Santa Clara county;
Liberal Arts Lodge No. 677 at Los Angeles;
Altadena Lodge No. 678 at Altadena, Los Angeles county.
HENRY ErssLER,
LEO BRUCK,

RALPH A. CHASE, Chairnrn.n.

The report was adopted and charters ordered to be issued
therewith.

Respectfully reports that after careful examination it finds thaf
in each case so referred to the committee, there has been at least / a
.substantial compliance with the Constitution and Regulations; that ~n
those cases where the same were not strictly complied with, the errors
in no way prejudiced either the accused or accuser: In none of these
cases was an appeal taken, many of them being under section 192
of the Constitution adopted two years ago, and in each instance the
substantial rights of the parties were safeguarded. It is noteworthy
that in only one instance did the accused, whose case fell under section 192 of the Constitution, providing for automatic expulsion,
where the accused had been convicted of a felony in the courts of
the land, unless the accused, after sixty days' notice, demands a
Masonic trial, demand such trial. The adoption of section 192 has
resulted in relieving the Lodges of a vast amount of trouble and
expense in obviating the necessity of trials, where the final result
was obvious.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption :
Resolt•cd, that the action of the trial commissioners in each of
the cases herein above referred to, be, and the same is hereby approved, sustained and affirmed.

Adopted.
Disapproval of Certain Practices-Your committee desires to
report that while in its omnibus report it sustained the action of the
Trial Commission in case No. 656 from Composite Lodge No. 639,
your committee feels it would be remiss in its duty if we did not
make special reference to the record in this case. It contains about
500 pages of vituperation, wrangling and abuse, and only about 150
pages of actual testimony. Such practice entails useless expense on
the __trial Lodges, creates unnecessary ill feeling and serves no good
purpose. While each side in a Masonic. trial should be given every
~pportunity to ful.l y present its case, this should be done in a gentlemanly and dignified manner. A Masonic trial is no place to vent
personal spite.
We wish here and now to voice our disapproval of such practice
and to caution Masters against permitting the same. We also desire
to call attention to the fact that argument of counsel on objecfions
or in summing up the case are no part of the record, and should not
be taken down by the reporter at the expense of the Lodge. If
counsel desire their arguments to come before this committee, they
may · do so by preparing and filing briefs.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:

\

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

273

Resolved, that the practice of indulging in abuse and personal
animosities at Masonic trials be and the same is hereby disapproved
and condemned.

Adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which has been referred trial
record No. 649, from Los Angeles Lodge No. 42, begs to report as
follows:
This proceeding arises under section 192 of the Constitution,
which specifically r eq uires notice to be sent to accused at his last
known place of address. In this instance the accused was known
to he in San Quentin, but the Secretary inadvertently ignored this
fact, which was known to him , and sent notices to a Los Angeles
address. Whether c Mason be confined to San Quentin or elsewhere
he is entitled to notice of proceedings pending against him, where it is
possible to notify him. Section 192 specifically gives to the accused
the right of electing whether he will stand Masonic trial. It might well
be that if allowed to defend himself, he could adduce exten uating facts
which would give an entirely different complexion to this case. In any
event it is one o f the fundamental principles of our I ns titution that
no m ember shall be deprived of his rights without full notice and op1iortunity to defend himself.
Your Committee, therefore, offers the follow ing resolution and
nwves its adoption:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

276

Resolved, that the judgment of Los Angdes Lodge No. 42 be
and the same is hereby reversed, with instructions to strictly comply
with the provisions of Section 192.

Adopted.

Ybur Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption :
Resolved, that th'e judgment of Sequoia Lodge No. 349 be and

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 640, from El Dorado Lodge No. 26, begs to report t hat the only
evidence produced at the trial, as'i de from identification testimony,
was that by a member of the trial Lodge who read into the record a
report from the District Attorney o f Los Angeles county, which recited in effe ct the plea of guilty of the accused and the r endition of a
suspended sentence by the court. It is with the utmost reluctance
that your committee finds itself compelled to advise that this evidence
was not sufficient to sustain the finding of guilty. The report referred
to was not a properly authenticated court record and was purely
hearsay in· charac't er. This being the only evidence introduced, it
follows that the finding of the trial commission is wholly dependent
upon hearsay testimony for its sup port. Section 202 of our Constitution definitely and positively provides that hearsay evidence is not
admissible. We therefore offer the following resolution and move its
adoption :
Resol7•ed, that the judgment of the trial commission in this case
be and the same is hereby reversed and the matter remanded for a
new trial; that proper opportunity be given to amend the specifications
to charge the commission of an offense, and that the accuser be and
he hereby is, advised to secure and present to the trial commission a
properly authenticated copy of the court record.

Adopted.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
GENERAL PURPOSES
Grand Secretary
1. Your Committee on P olicy and General Purposes approves
the recommendation of the Grand Master that our beloved and
efficient Gra nd Secretary, John \ Vhicher, be authorized and requested
to attend the conference of Grand Secretaries, to be held in Washington, D. C. in 1931. His prese nce there w ill undoubtedly ·redound to
the benefit of and refl ect credit upon this Grand L odge. Out of the
abundance of his wisdom and the p lentitude of his ex perience he will
contribute much to the work of the conference. We recommend that
the subject matter be r eferred to the Finance Committee for an appropriate appropriation.

Adopted.
Cabinets for Lodges
2. Your Committee does not concur in the recommendation of
the Grand ·Master that Grand Lodge install fi'reproof cabinets in
certain Lodges to protect old r ecords and minute books. We agree
with him that many of the Loclge records are precious and deserving
of protection against the hazard of fire, but are persuaded that a due
regard for their preservation by the officers of th e L odges will lead
them to deposit o ld and valuable records in a safe place or to lodge
th em with the Gr and Secretary for preservation. The committee on
History and the Gra nd Secretary are engaged in collecting and
properly caring for r ecords and other objects of historical and Masonic
interest and are prepared to receive a nd adequately protect all such
treasures confined to their care.
We are of the opinion that Grand Lodge should not undertake
to provide furniture and equipment for Loclge uses except in cases of
unusual emergency.

Adopted.

Masonic Library of Southern California
3. Your Committee has considered the report and recommendation of the Grand Master regardlng the Masonic Library of Southern
California, Inc., and the propriety of permitting two or more Lodges
to join in a library association and to support the same from the funds
of the Lodge.
It appears from the Grand Master's report that the Masonic
Library of Southern California, In~., is a corporation and is · not
owned by or controlled by subordinate Lodges of this Grand Lodge.
If the Lodges owned this library they would have an unquestioned
right to support and maintain it, but they are not authorized to pay
Lodge funds for the use and benefit of a private corporation, no matter
how laudable its business. We do not favor the abrogation of a law
which we believe to be salutary and proper.

so filed. He proposes amendments to Section 207 of the Constitution
to effectuate the recommended changes in our trial procedure.
Your committee is of the opinion that the existing law is sufficient and that the suggested changes are unnecessary. The Lodge is
the proper forum for the trial of cases of unmasonic conduct and this
Grand Lodge is the appellate auth'ority to which appeals, in proper
cases, may be brought. Until the appellate jurisdiction of Grand
Lodge is invoked it has no place in the trial and should not be charged
with responsibility for the pleadings or otherwise in the case. The
Grand Master has the inherent power to make such investigation of
the acts of a Lodge as to him seems proper. As a matter of policy
the recommettdation should not be adopted.

Adopted.
Qualification of Wardens
4. Y oui: Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the
opinion that the needs of the craft are satisfied when the Master is
thoroughly proficient in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge which relate to the government of a Lodge
and that there is no compelling reason to exact the same thorough
proficiency of the Senior and Junior Wardens. The Master is the
governing officer of his Lodge, and as the Wardens in time ascend
to the oriental chair, they must exhibit the Constitutional <qualifications
respecting our laws. \Ve think the proposal of the Grand Master for
a change in the law adding to the necessary qualifications of the
Wardens would imp9se burdens upon the Wardens and Inspectors
which are not warranted at this time, and therefore should not be
adopted.

Grand Lodge did not concur in the report of the committee, and the matter was referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence, with directions to present an amendment to
Section 137 of the Constitution, to the effect "that the
Wardens shall be proficient in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations which relate to the government
of a Lodge."

Degree Teams
6. Your committee 1s m full accord with the Grand Master, in
the matter of his order of March 31-, 1930, reported in his annual
message, on the subject of "degree teams." Our law requires that
the Master or one of the Wardens be present at every meeting of a
Lodge and that all work be done by them, or in their pres.ence, and
under their direction. When another person or other persons, excepting the installed officer or officers of another Lodge, perform work
in his Lodge the Master is charged with the responsibility of determining his or their qualification to do the work in accordance with
our ritual and to see that the work done conforms therewith. The
Master cannot delegate his power to the Grand Lecturer nor evade
his responsibility in the premises.

Adopted.
Committee on Education
7. Your committee has considered with care the comments of
the Grand Master and the Report of the Committee on Education,
respecting our educational program, as well as the verbal protests
made by brethren opposed to the program.
The Grand Lodge of California for many years has engaged in
an earnest effort to develop a satisfactory and beneficial educational
work on behalf of Lodges and their members. Thus far that effort
has been experimental and the results have not fully met our expectations, but the committee has been diligent and faithful and has accomplished much in the face of more or less apathy and indifference.

in the ultimate success of this importan t undertaking. The work of
this, the Educational Committee, t o be successful, will require a
sustained and continuing support and cooperation from the Lodges
and if such support is not to be forthcoming, that fact should be made
plain to Grand Lodge.
We recommend the continuance of the Committee on Education
and suggest that during the coming year it make a careful investigation
of the plans and experiences of other jurisdictions in the matter of
Masonic Education. with a view of adopting methods that will be
more productive of r esults than those now pursued.

Claim against Widows and Orphans Fund
8. The Grand Master r efers t o Grand L odge an unfortunate
controversy between the Trustees of the Masonic H omes and Aahmes
Temple of the Shrine, over a death benefit of $1,500 claimed to be

of this Grand L odge.

Long Beach Temple
9. We do not concur in the Grand Master's recommendation

this matter, even if· we were qualified to determine the legal rights
of the Association. It appears to us that th e Association should be
advised in this matter by its legal counsel, rather than by Grand
Lodge.

"Such a restored Mason shall pay as dues $12.00 a year in advance
to the Grand Lodge, the dues beginning on the date of rest oration
by Grand Lodge and continuing until such time as he is elected to
m ember ship in some Lodge. The Grand Secr etary shall issue a dues
receipt for the same, which receipt shall serve to all intents and purposes as a <limit when applying for affiliation. A Mason so restored
who refuses or neglects to pay dues as herein prescribed shall not
receive any Masonic rights, priviliges or charities until he shall have
paid all back dues to the Grand Secretary accruing since his restoration and shall have received permission of the Grand Master to regain
such standing; or until he shall have been elected a member of some

financial distress be shown, the Grand Master may order the dues
remitted, then and there declare such a restored Mason entitled to
all Masonic privileges and benefits an d cause the Grand Ser etary to
issue the receipt as above provided."
Under our ex isting laws the only dues paying members of Grand
Lodge are the m embers of L odges of this Grand jurisdiction. The

Standing of Masons Whose Dues Are Remitted
15. There has been referred to your Committee a proposal to
amend the Constitution to read as follows:
" Section 140: None but members in good standing, whose dues
are .paid, shall be entitled to vote at an election; and every voter shall
be eligible to any office in the Lodge. If the dues of a member have
been remitted, in accord·a nce with the provisions of Section 128, at
any time within one year previous to an election, then such member
shall not be di~qualified from voting at such election, or holding office,
though the dues of such member accruing since such remission have
not been paid."
Also, a resolution to amend Section 2, Article IX, of the By-laws,
to read as follows:
"Section 2: No member, who shall be in arrears for dues at the
time of the annual election, shall be permitted to vote, or shall be
eligible to any office; but such disqualification shall not apply to a
member whose dues have been remitted in accordance with the provisions of Section 128 of the Constitution, at any time within one year
previous to the annual election."
The purpose of these amendments is to provide for the good
standing at the time of an election of a member whose dues have
been remitted. Our present law provides that none but m embers in
good standing, whose dues are paid, shall be entitled to vote at an
election, and also, that a Lodge cannot remit in advance. Therefore,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

286

a Mason whose dues have been remitted cannot vote at an election,
nor be elected to office. The remission of dues should be equivalent
to the payment of the same so far as affects the Masonic standing of
a brother.
The proposed amendments are approved as to form by the Committee on Jurisprudence.
vVe recommend the adoption of the amendment to Section 140
of the Constitution, and also r'ecommend the adoption of the amendment to Section 2, Article IX of th e By-laws.

Report and recommendation adopted , and Section ·140 of
the Constitution and Section 2, Article IX, of the By-Laws
were amended by unanimous vote.
Suspensions.
16. Your Committee has considered the resolution presented by
the Master of Crockett Lodge proposing an amendment to Section
210 of the Constitution.
The proposa l is intended to incorporate in our Law a provision
prohibiting a suspended Mason from applying to the Lodge oftener
than once a year for restoration.
We are of the opinion that no sufficient reason exis ts for the
modification of our present law. There is a single instance in which
a Lodge would be relieved of some possible annoyance by limiting
th e rights of a suspended brother, but that instance does not afford
a justification for the proposed change and we, therefore, recommend
that the amendment be not adopted.

Adopted.

Group Balloting
18. Your Committee is of the opinion that our law on the subject
of group balloting should not be changed to permit group balloting
when but two petitions are to be balloted upon. The purpose of the
statute is to reduce time and labor where there are many petitions
before a Lodge for ballot. No particular burden is imposed upon a
Lodge to ballot twice at a stated meeting.
Your Committee recommends that the proposal of Past Master
Lyndall of Arlington Lodge No. 414, for an amendment to Section
103)1, to the Constitution be not adopted.

Adopted.
Foreign Language Lodges
19. Special Inspector Brother Louis Muller has directed our
attention to what is regarded by some of our members to be an unjust
discrimination against the Lodges working in foreign languages, and
Grand Master Wollenberg, in order that the same be corrected, has
presented a resolution to change the decision embodied in Section 83
of Decisions and Regulations. In 1929 a decision was made that "No
Lodge, other than one expressly permitted to cohfer degrees in a particular foreign language, may allow a degree to be conferred therein
by persons conferring it in such foreign language." Brother Wollenberg's recommendation is that the policy adopted in 1929 be abrogated
and that foreign language Lodges of this jurisdiction be permitted to
confer a degree or degrees upon a candidate of another Lodge in the
Lodge in which such candidate has been elected, when invited to do
so by ·such Lodge, in the language of the foreign languag.e Lodge,
provided the candidate speaks, reads and understands such foreign
language.
Your committee is of the opinion that the present regulation on
this subject is discriminatory and is objectionable to our brethren of

Foreign Grand Lodges:
24. Germany: In 1928 your committee reported in a generat way
respecting the eight Grand Lodges of Germany and directed your
attention to the fact that the National Mother Grand Lodge of the
Three Globes was recognized by us in 1881 and that the Grand Lodge
of California was in fraternal accord therewith.
For some years our harmonious relations with that Grand Lodge
were suspended because of the establishment by it of a Lodge in
New York, but upon a withdrawal of the Lodge and observance of
the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of New York, relations
of amity were renewed. Undoubtedly the confusion resulting from
this epirode is responsible for our error in failing to report in our
Proceedings the fact of our recognition of the National Mother Grand
Lodge of the Prussian States, called of the "Three Globes."
· In 1829 this Grand Lodge recognized the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, the Mother Grand Lodge of the Electic Union, the Grand Royal
York Lodge of Friendship and the National Grand Lodge of All
German Freemasons. ·
Your committee now has before it a request for the recognition
of a sixth of the eight German Grand Lodges, viz.: the Grand Lodge
"Zur Sonne" of Bayreuth. It appears that this Grand Lodge has been
in existence for more than a hundred years and is recognized by and
in fraternal concord and amrty with the other German Grand Lodges
recognized by this Grand 'Lodge. Cordial relations were disturbed
about two years ago because some of the Lodges of the Grand Lodge
"Zur Sonne" were permitted to use instead of the Holy Bible a plain
white book in and on which was no printing except the single word
"God." This white book had been in use for more than fifty years.
In order to preserve peace and harmony and to conform to an essential landmark, the Grand Lodge required all its Lodges to display
the Great Light upon their altars and to discard the white book.
The Grand Lodge has forty subordinate Lodges, many of which
are. located in important cities of Germany, and numbers in excess of
4,000· members. The personnel of the tnembership is reported to us
to he of a very fine character.

291

Adopted .
Czecho-Slovakia: There are two Grand Lodges in the CzechoS lovakian Republic. One of them is styled the Grand Lodge Lessing
"Zu den drei Ringen" (of the three Rings) and the other the National
Grand Lodge of Czecho-Slovakia (Narodni Velika Loze Ceskoslovenska). Both are seated at Prague. Lessing works in the German
language, while the National Grand Lodge works in the Czechian or
Bohemian language.
These two Grand Lodges are in fraternal unity and concord and
each gives full recognition to the other. Grand Lodge Lessing has 23
Lodges and about 1200 members. The National Grand Lodge has
more Lodges and a larger membership.
After an exhaustive examination the Grand Lodge of England on
June 4, 1930, recognized both of these Grand Lcfdges and· they are
recognized by many important American jurisdictions. They are the
sovereign authority of symbolic Masonry in their jurisdiction, and it
appears to your committee that the requests for recognition are entitled to favorahle consideration; it therefore respectfully recommends
that the Grand Lodge of California recognize the Grand Lodge
Lessing and the National Grand Lodge of Czecho-Slovakia.

Adopted.
Switzerland: Swiss Grand Lodge "Alpina." An investigation of
the conditions in Masonry in Switzerland has resulted in satisfying
your committee that the Grand Lodge "Alpina" is a Masonic power
conforming to our standards for recognition; that it is sovereign in
its jurisdiction and is active as a Grand Lodge with many subordinates
and a large membership. It is in fraternal relations with the Grand
Lodges of England, Ireland, Scotland, Alabama, Iowa, Kentucky,
New York, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio and South Carolina.
The chairman of your committee has visited two of the subordinate Lodges of the Grand Lodge "Alpina" and has
several 0£° its
members, and by personal bbservation has satisfied himself of the
Masonic regularity and standing of that Grand Lodge.
No matter how meritorious they may be, the Grand Lodge
"Alpina" should not be confused with the two so-called International
Masonic Associations in Switzerland. These are, the International
Masonic Association of Geneva, · composed of twenty-four Grand
Lodges, and the Universal Masonic League of Basie, composed of

Colombia: Sin'c e 1922 your Committee has had under advisement
the requests for recognition of the three Grand Lodges of the R~public
of Colombia, namely:
·
The National Grand Lodge of Colombia at Barranquilla,
The National Grand Lodge of Colombia at Cartagena, and
. The Grand Lodge of the Republic of Bogota.
The Republic of Colombia is the northwesterly Republic in South
America, bounded on the north by the Caribbean sea and Panama
and on the west by the Pacific ocean. It is a rugged, mountainous
country of vast distances. By reason of the difficulties of cmnrnunication, and barriers between different sections erected by nature, it was
found desirable, if not neces.sary, to establish more than one Grand
Lodge to lead and govern the Craft. This was done by the establishment ·of three Grand Lodges, each having exclusive sovereign juris,
diction over those States of the Republic which compose .its territory.
The three Grand Lodges are bound together by a treaty ,of amity a,nd
work in entire concord and harmony.· Today all the symbolic 1,pdges
of Colombia are obedient to and under Masonic jurisdiction and so
far as we can ascertain there is no confusion in the Craft.
·
Masonry was originally established in Colombia (then New
Granada) in 1833 under the Supreme Council system, and in August,
1922, the Supreme Council relinquished all power arid authority. over
symbolic Lodges and the craft degrees and recognized · the three
symbolic Grand Lodges as sovereign a,nd supreme in their respective
furisdictions. The fairness and friendliness with which our Colom:bfan
brethren approached and solved a difficult problem merits:. our com~
m'e ridation. It was such an unusual method.
. '
Colombia is a growing and progressive State,. and Masonry is
an institutio.n of usefulness there which is also gro~.ing and developing. There are large numbers .o f Americans, English and French who
are members of the sy~bolic Lodges and hope for recog~ition of
their Masonic standing by the Lodges o.f their native lands. There
are English speaking Lodges at Bogota arid elsewhere of which several
native Californians are members.
.

Brazil: Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has
received requests for recognition from
..., The Grand Lodge of Rio de Janeiro
The, Grand Lodge of the State of Parahyba
The Grand Lodge of the State of Sao Paula
The Grand Lodge of the State of Bahia
The Grand Lodge of the State of Para.
In 1925 this Grand Lodge recognized the Grand Orient of Brazil
pursuaiit to a recommendation of this committee, which reported that
the Grand Orient of Brazil was a body founded upon the Supreme
Council system and the only Masonic power in Brazil. Your Committee found that its authority was universally recognized throughout
the Republic and for that reason favored the recognition.
Since the adoption of the report the Masonic conditions in Brazil
have undergone a great change. Until 1927 there existed in Brazil no
independence of ancient craft Masonry, but the symbolic degrees were
ruled by the Grand Orient, which administered many degrees of many
Rites. Moreover, the· executive bodies of the Grand Orient worked,
by force of law, in French, while the language of the country is
Portuguese. In June, 1927, seven symbolic L odges of the Scottish
Rite abandoned the Grand Orient "to follow the regular trail of
Masonry.?.' They formed themselves into the Grand Lodge of Rio de
Janeiro.and took as the basis for its constitution and work the Ancient
Landrparks, the Constitutions of Anderson and the Symbolism of
Maekay.. The Grand Lodge. is absolutely independent and sovereign
and works only in the symbolic degrees.
Following this example, Lodges in the different S tates of the
Republic of Brazil seceded from the Grand Orient and formed Grand
Lodges of symbolic Masonry. Thus far in eight States have such
Grand Lodges been formed, and our requests for recognition come
from five of these eight.
Ari' examination of the constitutions and laws of these new Grand
1:.odges and an inquiry into their present status and claims persuades
us to believe that they arc en titled to recognition in due time. For the

295

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

present they should be allowed to demonstrate their stability and the
allegiance of their membership to the policy and organizations newly
adopted. We are not fully informed respecting the conditions now
prevailing in Brazil as a result of these secessions, which may unfortunately turn out to be a schism instead of a revolution.
Favorable action on the foregoing requests will necessitate withdrawing recognition of the Grand Orient of Brazil. The reason for
that recognition has ceased, and that Power has not the same claims
to our consideration as it had in 1925 when it was the only Masonic
governing body in its jurisdiction; but we think this an inopportune
time to take any action whatsoever because of the negotiations between
the Grand Orient of Brazil and the Grand Lodge of England and
the possibilities of complete accord resulting therefrom in the near
future.

membership, but has heretofore failed to adopt appropriate legislation
to carry the policy into effect. Y our Committee favors the adoption
of Constitutional amendments to permit dual membership.

Suspension of Master

To the M:.w:.Grand L odae of California:
1. With reference to the suspension from office by the Grand·
Master of the Master of one of our Lodges, reported on pages 19.
and 20 of his Message, no claim is made of insufficiency of facts to
suppoct the conclusion that suspension was proper. It appear's
that just previous to the installation of this Master's succe's sor, th.e
Grand Master terminated this suspension, in view of the fact that
the Master had apologized for his actions and that he felt that
further suspensi~n, involving as it would deprivation of his rank as
a Past Master, would be a greater punishment than was wafra.nted
for the offense. In view of all the circumstances we consider this·
action entirely proper.
We recommend that the action of the Grand Master be approved.

Adopted.

Stop Order Relative to Advancement
2. The Grand Master reported in his Message (pages 20 and

Grand Master's predecessors in office. The Grand Master felt that,
under -all the circumstances, the only appropriate authority to deal

it has been presented," is the Grand L odge, and so informed the
Master of West Gate Lodge, with the further information tha.t he
would refer the entire situation to the Grand Lodge and ~ould tak~
no affirmative action in the meantime. This he has done. We believe that his entire action in the matter was proper and should be
approved.

Misrepresentation in Petition
·3. The Grand Master reported in his Message (pp. 21 and 22)
that in four cases applicants for the three degrees had failed to state
in their applications that they had been previously rejected by another Lodge, had been elected to receive the three degrees, and had
received the first or first and second degrees when the matter was
brought to his attention.
As to each of these cases he made a11 order, the form of which
appears on pages 21 and 22 of the Message.
It will be observed that this order, simply because of this defect
in the petition s, in effect tre ats all that has been done under the
petitio1is as in effective for any purpose and void (except that it
recognizes that the applicant by his initiation, or by his initiation
and passing, has been made an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft,
as the case may be), requires the return of the fees , and authorizes
advancement only upon a new petition for the remaining degree or
degrees; and a new unanimous election to receive the same.
Assuming that the actual initiation, passing, or raising, of a candidate whose petition is defective in the respect mentioned, rrtakes
him an Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft or Master Masoh as the
case may be, as is conceded by this order, and by all the decisions,
and as we think is obvious, our Constitutional provis 'ons are so
written that there is no basi s for any distinction, with regard to the
rights of the subordinate Lodge to adv~nce the candidate, between
Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts in good standing whose petitions for the degrees are in due form, and those whose petitions
are not in due form . In the matter of both, the written law as to
advancement is the same. There is nothing in the law as now written,
which would justify a conclusion that a new election for the remaining degrees can be required except in the single case where, by objection made, advancement has been denied by the Lodge, such
denial made under the provisions of sections 109 to 111 of the Constitution being regarded as tantamount to a final rejection for the
remaining degrees.
We have just discussed a somewhat similar question in principle in re W es t Gate Lodge No. 335. In view of what we there said,
and the reaso ns stated in this report, we are forced to the conclusion
th a t the se orders, howe ver laudable their purpose, were not-in accord
with our law as it now is.

No. 620. This Lodge is located in the town of Ocean Beach in San
Diego county on the promontory of Point Loma, by which name it
is generally known, and it is never referred to as a peninsula, while
there are other places in California which are so called. For this
reason it is claimed that the name "Peninsula" is misleading, and the
brethren are desirous of overcoming this difficulty by the change
proposed.
The proceedings are in due form, the name chosen will not conflict with the na~e of any other Lodge, and no good cause appearing
to deny the petition, we propose ·the following resolution and recom. mend its adoption:
Resolved, that the name of Peninsula Lodge No. 620 be, and it
is hereby changed to Point Loma Lodge No. 620, and that the necessary changes be made in its charter, seal and records.

Elk Grove Lodge vs. Harding Lodges
5. Your committee has considered the charges filed by Elk
Grove Lodge No. 173 against Warren G. Harding Lodge No. 579,
in which it is claimed that the latter named Lodge knowingly and
wilfully received and acted upon the petition for degrees of a man
n:siding in the jurisdiction of Elk Grove Lodge, without norice or
r'e quest for a waiver.·
·
It is unfortunate that two Masonic Lodges should arrive at such
a vital difference as to necessitate charges by one against another,
and ' discord permitted to interrupt the harmony that should prevail·
am<irtg ·mel'l and Masons. The charges are sufficient in form, l>ut
we · believe that this is not a matter which should require action by
a commission elected to try the cause, but that if the brethren of
the two Lodges would meet in the spirit of our Institution, they can
adjust their differences amicably and satisfactorily.
We therefore recommend that these charges be ·referred to the
Grand Master for such action as he may deem necessary.

Report adopted.

9. Your Committee on Jurisprudence presents herewith a proposed amendment to section 165 of the Constitution:
Sec. 165. It is the duty of every Master Mason to be a member
of some Lodge, but a non-affiliated Master Mason shall remain in
good standing for a period of one year after the date of his dimit;
provided, that should he fail to become a member of some Lodge
within said period of one year from the date of his dimit, he shall
· be deemed unworthy of Masonic consideration, and shall not thereafter be .entitled to a ny of the rights, privileges or benefits of Masonry.
Upon the r ejection of an application for membership the Lodge shall
return all amounts paid by the applicant.

'A nd ·Section 165 was amended by unanimous vote.

Appeal-Trial Records
12. Your Committee on Jurisprudence, in accordance with the
mandate of this Grand Lodge, offers the following resolution and
recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that Section 207 of the Constitution be amended as
follows:
Strike out the word "thirty" in line 5, page 171, and jn lieu
thereof insert the word "ninety," in 1929 edition of the Constitution;
strike out the word "appealed" in line 14, page 172.
Strike out the words "and all cases of expulsion or suspension,"
on lines 14 and 15, page 172.
The section as amended to read as follows:
Sec. 207. An appeal may be taken to the Grand Lodge by either
party at its next succeeding annual communication, but not unless
a notice of such intended appeal shall be given to the Master, in .
writing, within ninety days after his announcement of the result of
the trial. Any and all additional evidence, which either the accuser
or accused shall desire to have heard on the appeal, shall be taken
and reduced to writing within sixty days from the day on which the
announcement of the result of the trial shall be made by the Master
to the Lodge and all arguments and· representations which it is desired to have considered on the appeal shall also be reduced to writing; and no additional evidence, arguments, or representations shall
be considered on the appeal unless the same shall be reduced to
writing and transmitted to the Grand Secretary at least sixty days
before the commencement of the next annual communication of the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

351

<;rand Lodge. In all cases, whether appealed or not, the Master
cause the Secretary to prepare a transcript of the record of
trial, and immediately transmit it to the Grand Secretary, together
with information of the appeal intended, if any there be. In all cases
where the trial was had in a Lodge other than the Lodge of which
the accused is a member, the Grand Secretary shall notify the Lodge
of which he is a member, forthwith upon the receipt by him of the
transcript of the record of trial.
Every transcript of a trial record, when prepared by the Secre-·
tary of any subordinate Lodge in this jurisdiction, shall, before its.
transmission to the Grand Secretary, be submitted to the Master of
the Lodge, who shall carefully examine the same and see that it is
fairly and legibly written, with sufficient spaces between papers and
testimony; and that it otherwise complies with the Constitution and
Regulations of the Grand Lodge; and said Master shall endorse his
approval ~hereupon.
When a trial is had in the Lodge of which the accused is a
member, or in another Lodge to which the case is transferred, the
Secretary cannot make any charge for serving the summons, or for
writing up the record of the trial, or for writing a transcript or copy
of the record for transmission to the Grand Secretary. ( 1925.)
~hall

Adopted, and Section 207 amended by unanimous vote.

13. Also that Section 189 of the Constitution be amended as
follows : At the end of the section add the following words: "A
copy of such charges shall forthwith be forwarded by the Secretary
of the Lodge to the Grand Secretary."
The s.ection, as amended, to read as follows:
Sec. 189. When any member of a Lodge (except its Master or
the Grand Master) , or any Mason residing within its jurisdiction,
shall be accused of unmasonic conduct, charges to that effect may be
preferred by any Master Mason in good standing; which charges
shall be in writing over his signature, and shall be presented to the
Master of the Lodge having jurisdiction thereof. If facts shall be
brought to the attention of the Junior Warden of a Lodge showing
any member, of whom his Lodge has jurisdiction, to be guilty of
unmasonic conduct, and if, for the period of thirty days following
the bringing of such facts to the attention of the Junior Warden, no
Master Mason in good standing shall have preferred charges against
S"Uch member, then and thereupon it shall become the official duty
of such Junior Warden to prefer such charges, in the manner io this

section provided as for a Master Mason. A copy of such charges
shall forthwith be forwarded by the Secretary · of the Lodge to the
Grand Secretary.

Qualifications of Wardens
17. Your Committee on Jurisprudence recommends that Section
137 of the Constitution be amended to read· as follows:
"Sec. 137. No Junior Warden of a Lodge shall be installed until
he shall have produced to the installing officer the certificate of the
Grand Lecturer. or of the Inspector of the district in which his Lodge
is situated, certifyirtg that he has personally examined such Junior
Warden-elect and that he is qualified to give the work and Lecture
of the First Degree and that he is thoroughly proficient in those portions of the Constitution and General Regulations of the Grand Lodge
which relate to the government of a Lodge ; and no Senior Warden
shall be installed until he shall have produced the certificate of either
the Grand Lecturer or the Inspector of the district in which his
Lodge is situated, certifying that he is qualified to give the work and
lectures of the First and Second Degrees, and that he is thoroughly
proficient' in those portions of the Constitution and General Regulations of the Grand Lodge which relate to the government of a Lodge.
If any Warden-elect fail to procure such certificate within sixty days
of election or such further time as may be, upon a satisfactory showing, granted by the Grand Master, his election shall be invalidated
and a special dispensation issued to hold an election for the place
of su.c h Ward,en; provided, however, that the Warden elected under
such dispensation shali not be the one who had been previously
elected and who had tailed to qualify."

, Adopted, and Section 137 amended by unantmous vote,

Audit of Accounts
5. Your committee; employed Ruckstell & Land, certified public
accountants, to examine the books and records of the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer, as well as those of the Masonic Homes
of California and Endowment Fund. These accountants have certified that · all books and accounts are correct. This audit discloses
that the net worth of the Grand Lodge on July 31, 1930, was $783,379.27, which includes 'Masonic Temple Association stock in the sum
of $588,800.00, a decrease for the fiscal year of $4,532.41. This de- .
crease is caused by a falling off in th e number of candidates and
because of increased appropriations and disbursements, many of
which are, however, non-recurring.

Adopted.

Masonic Homes
11. Your Committee on Finance has had under consideration
the report of the Trustees of our Masonic Homes, and the request
of the Grand Master that we give earnest consideration to their needs.
The two institutions are the pride of Masonry in California, and
we believe every thoughtful Mason in our jurisdiction would approve
of the Homes being run on a plan that will insure happiness and
comfort to the residents and allow the Homes to measure up to the
standard of like institutions in California.
We appreciate the statement of the Trustees wherein they say
that they do not feel justified in recommending an increase in the
per capita tax, and in conference with various Trustees this statement has been repeated. We feel that the Trustees are entitled to
great credit for the unselfish service they render, and the fact that
they expect to curtail expenses wherever possible in an endeavor to
hold down the per capita cost is indeed commendable.
With the feeling that during the coming year much thought and
attention should be given to the matter of curtailment of expenses,
we recommend that the per capita tax for Homes be set at twentyfive cents, as heretofore.

Adopted.

We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its

Resolved, that the sum of $5,000.00 he appropriated from the
funds of this Grand Lodge for the use of the Committee on Education for the ensuing year.

Adopted.

Assistance to Harmony Lodge
13. Harmony Lodge No. 164, located at Sierra City, California,

is one of California's earliest Lodges, having received its charter in
1862 and at which time its hall was built. The Lodge has endeavored
to keep the building in repairs, but is now confronted with the necessity of replacing. the foundation and is financially unable to do so.
Investigation shows that this hall is one of the old landmarks
and one of the few halls in the mother lode country which has not
been destroyed by fire. Harmony Lodge has a membership of only
thirteen and the brethren are striving to keep it alive.
Your committee has before it the request of Harmony Lodge
for an appropriation to replace the foundation of their hall, and the
committee feels that the cause is worthy of support. We offer the
following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that a sum not to exceed $250.00 be appropriated from
the funds of this Grand Lodge for the purpose of replacing the foundation under the hall of Harmony Lodge at Sierra City.

Adopted.
Reimbursement to Welcome Lodge
14. Your committee has before it a request of Welcome Lodge
No. 255 for the reimbursement of Grand Lodge dues for the years
1926-1929 inclusive, paid on Brother E. S. Garrett for the reason that
the Grand Lodge dues on this brother were paid by Riverdale Lodge
No. 496.
From i,1formation furnished, it appears that Brother Garrett
affiliated with Riverdale Lodge, the Secretary of that Lodge overlooking his demit. Welcome Lodge, having no knowledge of his
affliation, voted not to suspend Brother Garrett for non-payment of
dues. As a result, Grand Lodge dues on Brother Garrett were paid
by both Welcome Lodge and Riverdale Lodge.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resol!•ed, that the sum of $6.38, being the amount of Gra.1,1d Lodge
dues paid by Welcome Lodge on Brother E. S. Garrett for the
years 1926-1929 inclusive, be refunded to said Lodge.

Adopted.

Visit to Hawaii by Grand Lecturer
16. The Masonic Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands have requested
the Grand Lodge of California to authori ze the Grand Lecturer to
visit them during the year 1931.
Inasmuch as these Lodges are members of the Grand Lodge of
the jurisdiction of California, your committee feels that they are
entitled to receive instruction from the Grand Lecturer which can
only be obtained through persona! contact. We further feel that a
visit could he made to the Islands every three or four years with the
view of maintaining the ritual to a high degree of efficiency and
benefiting the craft in general.
The present regulations of the Grand Lodge provide that the
traveling exp enses of the Grand Lecturer ·s hall be paid only when
traveling with in the State of California. We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that an amount not to exceed the sum of $500.00 be and
is hereby appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge to defray
the traveling expenses of the Grand Lecturer to the Hawaiian
Islands.

Adopted.

the embarrassing situation confronting this Lodge, over its Masonic
Temple. It has also ·interviewed its Master. It is probably unnecessary to recount the full history leading up to the construction of this
Temple and its present embarrassed financial condition, but it will
probably be sufficient to say that the present indebtedness against
the Temple is approximately $85,000.00, represented by serial bond
issue. There is not sufficient income from the Temple, including
that paid by the Lodge, to pay the interest alone, much less to provide
any funds for the retirement of the bonds. It was the hope expressed
by the Lodge tha·t .Grand Lodge. might be willing to .purchase the
building for the present existing debt and operate the Temple, with
·the thought that some day the .i.,odge might be ·able to redeem. As
much as we· sympathize with the brethren in this Lodge, and as
desitous as we are that some assistance be given, yet your committee

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
REPORT OF THE COMMITTEB ON
CORRESPONDENCE
October, 1930
BY JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith is submitted my Tenth Report as Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee. As usual, the views expressed under
the various topics are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
We also desire to express our thanks to the Secretaries of the
several Grand Bodies and of the Grand Lodges of the United States,
the Editors of Masonic publications, and to other writers who have
directly or indirectly furnished material which has furnished the basis
for some of the opinions expressed in the report.
Consideration of the same general questions and conditions that
have been before the Craft for a number of years are practically
along the same unchanged lines. Generally the subjects such as
lack of attendance, stricter investigation of candidates, the large
number of suspensions and the financial condition of the lodges due
to small dues and building of improperly financed temples are the
ones most discussed. These will be considered in their proper order
in the body of the Report.
·
Within the limits of the Report cannot be considered what might
be termed "minor questions" and for that reason a summary of some
of these are as follows;
CIPHER RITUAL: The use of cipher rituals in practically all
of the Jurisdictions is a Masonic offense. Effort in some of the
Grand Lodges to allow the use of these publications have usually
met with the fate it deserves. As one Correspondent expressed it:
"It is curious how this old predilection for 'mouth to ear' instruction proceeds, and how strong is the fear of the profane obtaining
information of the esoteric side of Freemasonry. In American book
stores the writer has read full and concrete exposes, not only of
Masonry but practically every secret organization in existence."

CLANDESTINE BODIES: Pennsylvania, Colorado, New
y ork and some of the other States are having trouble with these
pests. In Colorado the District Court of the City and C~unty of
Denver ruled against the use of the word Masonry, or anything pertaining thereto, by any organization other than the recogni~ed Grand
Lodge of the State. New York amended their law to read as follows :
"No certificate of incorporation of a proposed domestic corporation and no statement and designation of a foreign corporation having
the name or names 'Masonry,' 'Masons,' 'Masonic,' ' Freemasons,'
'Free and Accepted Masons,' 'Ancient Free and Accepted Masons,'
or the component parts thereof or the significent words therein,.
whether the same are used in juxtaposition or with interspace, shall
be filed or recorded in any office for the purpose . of ..e_ff~cting its .
incorporation, 'or of authorizing it to do business in this state, unless
such certificate or statement and designation. be accompanied by
the consent of' the Grand ·Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of New York. duly acknowledged by- its Grand Master
and Grand Secretary."
In Pennsylvania a verdict was rendered against a clandestine
organization which was functioning there. The case is still on appeal.
CO-ORDINATE BODIES: During the past year there has
been little to disturb the. peace and good harmony prevailing between
the various Grand Jurisdictions and the coordinate Bodies. The
requirements are well understood and established and the reciprocal
fellowship and esteem continues to exist.
The strained relations existing between the Grand Lodge of the
Philippine Islands and the Shrine regarding the holding of Ceremonials in the .Philippines have been satisfactorily adjusted. This
result in a large measure was due to the efforts of the Officers of
Islam Temple of San Francisco.
In our neighboring Jurisdiction of Nevada, trouble arose between
the Grand Commander of the Knights Templar and the Shrine, due
to the latter organization permitting non-memb.ers and profanes to
appear in public in Shrine regalia. We have not learned of the
ultimate outcome of the protest. We believe the principle that no
Mason should bring reproach upon the Fraternity by his actions in
any organization having as a prerequisite membership in the M~sonic
Fraternity is generally' observed. However, it is the exception to
the rule that produces the trouble. As heretofore stated, we think
that discipline through the Blue Lodge, which certainly has the
power to protect Masonry, will be a more salutary .effect than any
other form of procedure.

3

Many of the coordinate bodies are functioning along proper
lines and influenced only by the highest motives. To the Public,
however, no distinction is made, and for that reason the Masonic
organization is blamed for any transgressions of the established
rules of proper conduct. In all such coordinate Bodies or "play
grounds" the present slogan, " Watch your step," should ever be
before the individual Member.
DUAL MEMBERSHIP : Our Reports of 1928 and 1929 included the views both for and against Dual Membership. It is still
a live topic. Many of the Jurisdictions are considering it for future
action. During the past year Alberta. Connecticut. New Jersey,
Oregon and Wisconsin have changed their laws to permit dual
membership.
·
DUES: From the financial reports a large number of individual Lodges in various jurisdictions are operating "on a shoe
string." We cannot see how a lodge can properly function on dues
of $2 and $3 per annum, with low initiation fee. Some of the
Jurisdictions exempt Ministers from paying dues.
Connecticut
exempts all members who have been in good standing for 30 years
from further payment of dues: over 10% of their entire membership
is now exempt. In another jurisdiction one of the subordinate lodges
was so well fixed financially that its members were not called upon
to pay dues. Investigation revealed the fact that the Grand Lodge
was expending several thousand dollars over and above per capita
tax paid by this lodge for taking care of its· stipendaires.
The Grand Master of New York in commenting on lodge
finances, quoted from Charles Dickens as follows : " Annual income
£20, annual expenditures £19.9.6, result Happiness. Annual income
£20, annual expenditures £20.0 and its result-Misery."
EDUCATION: In some of the Jurisdictions the Public authorities have asked the cooperation of the Masonic Fraternity to assist
in the betterment of the Public Schools. Even where not asked
some of the Grand Lodges have followed the example of California
in taking an active part in trying to inform those interested that
the Public Schools are one of the bulwarks of our nation. In a
number of the Jurisdictions Educational Loan Funds to help deserving boys and girls are maintained, with the number availing themselves of the fund increasing each year.
One of the outstanding events was the action of Brother John
Smith of Mount Moriah Lodge No. 125, of Philadelphia, who
bequeathed the residue of his estate of over $1,000,000 to the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania for carrying on the education of its wards.

HOMES : Of the forty-nine Grand Lodges in the United
States, all but eleven maintain Homes for the care of the needy.
There seems to be a general feeling that perhaps instit utional relief
is being carried to extremes, and that the financial question involved
in a number ·Of States is getting to be a serious one as t ime goes on.
Some of the Jurisdictions who have not yet established Homes
are leaning towards the " Iowa plan.'' or taking care of the deserving
through the lodge in the locality in which the party lives and establishing Sanitariums for the care only of the absolutely helpless.
There is also a general tendency to educate the members that they
can perform a true and pract ical Masonic service by remembering
Masonic homes in their last will and testament.

RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES: A large
number of the Grand Lodges are adopting a set of b asic principles
for Grand Lodge recognition. England has recently adopted a test
for regularity of origin. It is practically the same as t hat adopted
by the large Jurisdictions of the United States.
An outstanding piece of work of the year was performed by
Brother Ely P. Hubbel, Chairman of the Foreign Correspondence
Committee of Florida, who compiled a chart showing the recognition of Masonic Grand Bodies by every Grand Lodge in the
world. It is a valuable contribution to Masonic stat istics.
RELIEF: Generally speaking it would appear t hat we have
lost sight of the idea that taking care of dependents is a function
of the individual Mason and the constituent lodge, and is now primarily a Grand Lodge problem. This has fostered the idea that
Masonry is a ben~ciary society, and the view is held not only by
a large part of our membership but also the outside public. The
Reports show cases where lodges have reinstated members who
have been suspended for a number of years, and passed them on to
the Grand Lodge for care. In some cases the family or friends have
attempted to pay all arrearages so that the Brother may avail himself of the beneficences of the particular Jurisdiction. I n other cases
the lodges have apparently pa ssed on to the Grand Lodge cases
that were not entitled to assistance. One Jurisdiction found that a
large number of the residents of their Home were of this type and
it was necessary to establish strict er requirements. Perhaps when
the care of dependents is made primarily the first duty of the lodge
these instances will become fewer.
An idea was suggested to the Masons of Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia that they appoint a Committee to propose
to the War Department a plan for "Welfare Wor k" by the Masons
in those states in time of war. T he Grand Lodge of Indiana refused

to cooperate, and in their report expressed the following sentiment:
"Experience gained in the World War leaches that so-called 'Welfare Workers' represented py any particular race or religious faith
proved a burden and an encumbrance to the Government, rather than
a help to our fighting men and tended to create discord, jealousy
and friction in and out of our Army."
ROUND TABLE CONFERENCE: The Grand Lodge of
Wisconsin experimented by holding a "Round Table Conference,"
open to all the members of the Grand Lodge, on an evening during
their session. It was attended by over 200 members. The time
was taken up in considering various topics on the program with
extended discussion from the floor. Informal conferences followed
on Lodge problems and the result was highly satisfactory.
This resulted in the adoption of a resolution authorizing the
Grand Master to appoint a Round Table Committee for the discussion of lodge problems with power to formulate a program,
subject to the approval of the Grand Master. The Grand Lodge will
set aside one evening during their next Annual Grand Lodge Communication for a Round Table discussion at one or several conferences. This should certainly work for the betterment of the
Craft. .
TRIALS: Whether or not names of those expelled or suspended as a result of Masonic trials should be published in the
Proceedings produces a difference of opinion. We believe that a
man tried and expelled is no longer a member of the Fraternity
and we fail to see where he should be protected, even to the extent
of allowing the general public to labor under the belief that he is
still a Mason.
The reports of the Grievances and Appeal Committees of the
various Jurisdictions continue to show a large number of cases
where reversal of manifestly proper decisions are made on account
of errors in trials or procedure. A number of the Jurisdictions
have adopted the practice of having Trials held before a Commission, appointed by the Grand Master and composed of experienced
members, rather than before the Lodge itself or a Trial Commission
selected by them. It seems to have produced satisfactory results
and materially reduced the work of the G. and A. Committees.

Georgia (1928):
ATTENDANCE
The lack of attendance at Lodge meetings is one of the problems
confronting practically all of the Jurisdictions. The advent of the
automobile was the first contributing factor to stress the appeal of
"the great open spaces." Then came the movies and the talkies,,
which had a great appeal both from an entertainment and educational standpoint. The radio changed this by bringing the member
back to his own fireside. The advent of "Pewee Golf" is perhaps
now having the same appeal as the automobile and the theater.
In this day and age the average person desires chiefly to be
entertained. By reason of lack of finances the Lodge cannot successfully compete with the changing forms of entertainment available through other sources. The constant rendition of ritual, long
and uninteresting meetings, the discussion of abstract educational
topics, does not add to the drawing power of ·what a lodge is
supposed to furnish. With all of the met:;1ods now · in vogue for
disseminating knowledge, the use of lectures, etc., to instruct has
ceased to attract. We believe that if the ritual was shortened, the
size of lodges reduced, and the main object of the meeting made an
opportunity to become personally acquainted with one another,
the conditions complained of could in part be remedied.
If our memory serves us correctly, two Jurisdictions adopted
a requirement that a member must attend his own lodge at least
twelve times during the year, otherwise he would be automatically
suspended. One adopted a regulation that the member must pass an
examination of a lecture of the third degree. These methods have
produced no results and were repealed. As truly said, "you can
lead a horse to water but you can't make him drink."
Alberta (1929):
(Chairman- · Corresp1mdence C ommittce) : There seems to be a
great awakening to the need of greater effort to instruct _the members
of the Craft. Many Grand Jurisdictions are awakening to the fact
that a continual diet of Ritual becomes m onotonous and is apl: to
bring on a mental scurvy and a loss of members. There is the greatest
beauty in the Ritual, but we can get too much of a good thing and
those Lodges which are branching out and encouraging their members
to study Masonry and other subjects akin to it, are, we think, on the
right road to creating greater interest and increasing attendance at
the meetings. The Lodges w ho have a hig h percentage of attendance
have a very low percentage of suspensions for non-payment of dues.

(Grand Master) : Very few persons today are guided in any of
the activities of life through a sense of duty-there must be an appeal
that challenges the interest of the individual and leads him to a
choice among the varied activities of life. We are living in a new
world and we must needs recognize this fact. Tqe traditions of the
past, however sacred they may be to come of us, no longer appeal to
this genera ti on.
·
!'1asonry today must compete with the moving picture, the automobile, the radio, golf, and the many phases both of amusement and
profit to the individual. How she is to do this is far too complex a
problem for any single individual to solve. In this statement we
would not be misunderstood as meaning that the landmarks of
Masonry must be abandoned. We believe that the principles of
Masonry are everlasting, because she has followed the divine order
of nature in laying her foundations in secrecy, where all that is
grand and beautiful and useful is born of night and mystery.
What we need is a new applicatio~ of the truths of Masonry to
the needs of this day in which we live. To do this we must needs
a?op.t modern methods in the administration of our Lodges, and so
v1tahze the work and the meetings as to make an appeal to the
membership.
Idaho (1929):
· (Chairman Educational Committee): The problems of our Idaho

L~dg.es today are quite different from those of a generation ago.
W1th~n the memory of men not yet old, conditions were much simpler.
Men m those days had leisure evenings, and the Lodge room afforded
them a place to spend a pleasant hour. Homes were much more
isolated and roads were of the pioneer type. Having little else to do
in the evening, they enjoyed going to Lodge, where besides disposing
of their Masonic obligations they met congenial spirits and ta lked
over the problems of the day with the neighbors.
Then came the a utomobile, good roads, moving pictures, radio,
and many other modern forms of attraction, and the old days passed
away, never to return. Men are no longer troubled with idle evenings.
There are so many things to do and so many places to go that there
are not evenings enough in the week. In order to attend Lodge now
they must forego some pleasure or business engagement. It is more
interesting to turn on the radio and listen to the varied and attractive
programs that are offered, or step into the car and speed away on a
drive to the neighboring town.
Men no lo nger need to go to Lodge for a diversion. Those who
go must do so for a more substantial reason. It must be more be-

cause of loyalty to the Lodge, love of Masonic principles and teachings, or because of a deeper faith in the fundamentals of the Fraternity. These are new conditions and it can readily be seen that
the problem of Lodge attendance assumes greater importance.
North Carolina (1930):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of
Alabama is also rightly much concerned about problems of larger
attendance. This is indeed a serious matter. As a matter of fact
attendance at meetings of all organizations is a serious matter in this
busy day of over-organization. People do not have time to attend
meetings as they did in the days of the long gone past. No longer
is the Lodge or the church the community center of social activities
and social contacts. On the contrary, the average man or woman belongs to so many different groups which have meetings that it requires much more than seven nights in each week to attend all these
meetings. We know of many men who are scarcely on speaking
terms with their wives and families, and we doubt not that there are
many women also who are scarcely on speaking terms with their
children and home. Small wonder it is therefore that in this vivid
age, Lodge attendance is reported to be small. In the experience of
the average man, the question of what he is going to do with his
evenings means a selection of activities on the basis of relative importance; and on this basis we have to admit that a few Lodge meetings of which we have known could be eliminated.
To be self-perpetuating in the existing social order, any activity,
be it Lodge or something else, must be inherently satisfying. If
Lodge work is satisfying to the individual Mason, he will attend
without urging; if it is not thus satisfying to him, he will attend only
because of some sense of Masonic duty or obligation to do so.
Philippine Islands (1928):

(Grand Lectitrer): Sometimes the "Right Hand of Fellowship"
is remarkably cold when extended to a visiting brother. Every visiting brother should be given the cordial greeting he deserves, and
made free of our Masonic home. Masons are entitled to enter our
tiled doors, and cordiality, courtesy, and hospitality are due to every
brother. He may come with a mind harassed with business worries,
but when he meets with a group of genial and sympathetic men, it
gives him a breathing spell and rest and he goes away feeling glad
that he came.

Washington (1930):
(Grand Master) : Masonry is faced with a condition and not a
theory; a condition that is having a cumulative effect; a condition
under which no other institution could thrive. It has been a common
and easy explanation that the intricate Masonic System furnishes
more attractive fields which lure away our members, but it is my
observation that these fields are no more enthusiastically populated
than are the more somber quarries of the Craft.
It is quite evident that this matter of attendance and interest
and a proper understanding of the nature of the Institution merits
careful and continued consideration on our part. In our efforts to
increase and maintain interest, let us not lay violent hands on usage
and custom and bend the Institution to meet every varying condition
of society. If we do, we have no further right to the nanre of Institution. However, let us not be unmindful of the fact that we are
trying to interest men of intellect with ever increasing demands on
their time and we must make it well worth the time spent, if we
want their time and attention.

Our custom and almost unwritten law that Lodge officers must
be regularly advanced, once appointed or elected, has fastened on
many Lodges a regime of ritualists, mumbling at that, who have
neither the education nor experience needed to fit them to preside
over the affairs of a Lodge with efficiency and dignity. Lodge meetings, carefully planned, efficiently carried out and occupied with the
things of Masonry, ritualistic, fraternal or charitable, can be and are
made well worth our time.
CANDIDATES
The old saying that it is not quantity but quality that counts,
still holds good. From articles in the current Masonic press and the
reports of Grand Lodge Officers and Committees, it would seem
that in a large number of cases there is a tendency to resolve any
question of doubt in favor of the applicant, ra~her than for the
benefit of the Lodge or the Institution. The reports of Grievances
and Appeal Committees are testimony to this fact.
We think that the average Investigating Committee in a large
number of cases has outlived its ·usefulness and ceased to produce
the results it should. A stricter means of investigation should be
adopted.
Some of the Lodges have established a semi-official investigation
committee, which passes on applications before they are presented
to the Lodge. One objection to this is that if the applicant is
rejected by this committee it does not become a matter of record
for the Lodge or the Grand Lodge.
One of the large Jurisdictions is now voting on an amendment
to their Constitution, which provides that there shall be a Standing
Committee of Investigation in each Lodge. When a petition is
presented to a Lodge it is referred to this Committee. The applicant must appear before them and also the members of the Lodge
who recommend him. This method would seem to overcoe the
defects of our present system and is doubtless worthy of a trial.
Masonry should be a select organization and the more safeguards that are thrown around it to produce this result, the better
it will be for all concerned. Brother J. Frank Allen of North
Carolina very aptly covers the present condition we believe when
he says, "there is evidem;:e of Masonic indigestion," due to the
character of candidates accepted.
Ireland (1929):
(Grand Master) : There has been no change of real importance,
with one exception, and that was the amendment of the law which

14

REPOR'l' ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

I moved myself, and which you passed in my absence at the last
communication of Grand Lodge. That was to alter Law 131, the ·
law which forbade a domestic servant or a bailiff becoming a .member
of the . Order. While some very · old and ultra-conservative minds
may not like altering any of these old customs, this must be remembered, that the relations between master and servant are very different nowadays from what they were 200 years ago. A servant was
then thought to be, and was called, a menial. I should be sorry for
anybody to call servants menials in these days. At any rate, I do
not see anything in the profession of a servant derogatory to any
man's dignity in the world. I have met, as I mentioned in the letter
sending the amendment, many men in private houses, in clubs, and
in hotels, wearing a livery, whom I have been proud to call my
friends and my brethren. This was brought very forcibly to my
mind the other d.ay when a well known brother wrote to ask my
advice. He wanted to propose a most desirable and eligible man
for the Order, and I was, very much against the grain, obliged to
write and say t.hat under the existing law it could not be done. Another thing is that in these days it has become an absurdity. It is
difficult to say where a liveried servant begins or ends. We have
been called upon to decide whether a chauffeur is a liveried servant
or not. Some chauffeurs wear livery and some do not. But, a·n yhow,
I think that the whole of them belong to a profession which is just
as good a profession as any other. We were the last Grand Lodge
in the world to keep that law on our Statute Book, and I should have
felt ashamed if my butler came to me and said to me that he wanted
to join the Order and I should be obliged to say "you cannot." That
is all for the best, and I think that it will meet with general approval.
We, and also England and Scotland, make no distinction of
color and race. We admit all colors and all races to the benefits of
Masonry. It is otherwise in America. The Americans have always
told us that we should have trouble with our colored brethren. Well,
we have alw.ays said that we would not, that we had sufficient trust
and confidence in them, but now I do not know what we will say.
I would rather, almost, it had occurred in any other Lodge except
a Lodge of colored men, but if the same thing had occurred in my
own Lodge, or in the most famous and oldest Lodge in Ireland, I
should have considered it my duty to have taken ·exactly the same
step. The first thing to do is to put ·one's foot down absolutely upon
dissension inside the Lodges. And if anything of the sort . has to
be brought to the notice of the authorities, to the notice of the Grand
Master, or to myself, it means that things must be very bad indeed
in the Lodge, because any Lodge that has Masters and Past Masters
should be able to settle those internal differences without having

recourse to higher authorities. I am not reading a lecture to you, I
am only justifying my action in taking the steps I did, and I should
do exactly the same in the case of any other Lodge in t he Jurisdiction.
