Massachusetts (1928):
At 476 Avenue Haig in Shanghai, China, there is an attractive
three-story building, and until recently there was a brass signboard
on the gate reading: "Chinese Freemason." Another sign on the.
same gate reads : "W ootsu Memorial Building," which means that
it is thei memorial building for the Five Ancestors. The Five Ancestors are the Patron Saints of an organization, which includes
hundreds of thousands of Chirtese living in China and in all parts
of the world to which Chinese have gone.
Fifty years ago foreigners coming in contact with this organization stated that they believed that this is the eastern branch, corresponding to the movement known as Freemasonry in western
countries. A closer study, however, of the organization has shown
that it has no historic connections with the Free and Accepted
Order of Masons of Europe and America, but that it originated
in China in the seventeenth century with a group of militant
Buddhist priests who aided the . Manchu Imperial House, but were
later treacherously attacked by representatives of the Manchus. The
survivors of this attack are the Five Patron Saints of the Order,
which for two centuries devoted its energy to the overthrow of
the Manchu dynasty and the restoration of the political control of
the country to the Chinese.
Since the overthrow of the Manchus by the Chinese revolution
of 1911 the society has been gradually developing away from its
political activities of a rebellious nature into a benevolent fraternal
society, devoting itself to the moral welfare of its members and
to the promotion of industry and commerce, and to the cultivation
of better international relations. It has also begun charitable and
relief 'Wbrk for the benefit of members. These things afford inter·
estrng parallels to the qistory of Masonry, which keeps itself free
from po"litical activity in countries where there is political and
refigious freedom.
I
But all well-informed Masons know that in many parts of the
world the freedom of today is the fruit of the work of Masonic
Lodges in the past.
The organization in Shanghai, which is known as "the Chinese
Grand Lodge," dates only since the revolution of 1911, and is the
international headquarters for a group O:to~ganizations which were

CORNERSTONES
In some Jurisdictions the question still continues as to whether
or not the laying of a corner stone is Masonic "labor " or simply
a ceremony. The Church authorities regard the event as a ceremony and the Jurisdictions which hold that viewpoint have complied
with the invitations to lay corner stones on Sunday.
Some of the Jurisdictions try to enforce the requirement that
the corner stone laid by them must bear an inscription relative to
Masonry. As the Chairman of the Correspondence Committe of
Nevada states, this is "pure publicity seeking and nothing else
when applied to public buildings, churches and club houses."
In sonie cases it has become practically impossible by reason
of the present construction of modern steel and concrete structures
to meet the demands laid down in the old rituals.

. THE REAL JACQUES DE MOLA Y
"THE REGISTER," March 13, 1930, Denver, Colo.
To most Americans the term Knights Templars connotes a
l~rge fraternity within the Masonic order. But the original Knights
Templars were a Catholic religious oi:der, one of the military organizations of men under vow that arose as a result of the Crusade
period. Jacques de Malay, the last Grand Master of the real Templars, was put to death by a vicious King of France who was anxious
to gain control of the order's property. His martyr<;lom is commemorated in modern Masonic degree work and his name has been
given . to the society of youths promoted by Masons. Recent discoveries about the real history of Malay are, therefore, of interest
to the general public. The Central Bureau of the Central Verein, in
its editorial service, has just announced :
The results of twenty years of historical research in many instances demand correction of older opinions. To volume ten of the
Catholic Encyclopedia George S. Goyeau, a well-known French
scholar, contributed the article on Jacques de Molay, the last Grand
Master of the Templars. While insisting that Malay was innocent of
the charges brought against him by his accusers, Goyeau assumes this
victim of the ambitious and autocratic Philip IX of France to have
"pleaded guilty to some of the imputed crimes, notably the a.lleged
obligation to the Templars on joining the order to deny Christ and
to spit upon the crucifix." Malay is further accused by Goyeau to
have "repeated these same admissions and denials" ( the latter related
to charges of a sexual nature) also on his second appearance before
the inquisitor general of the kingdom, October 25, 1307. In explanation of this action on the part of so distinguished a knight and man
of integrity the French publicist writes: "It is supposed that his
(Malay's) ~bject in making this partial admission was to save his
comrades from the extreme penalty."
It seems not to have occurred to Goyeau how unworthy of the
subject of his biography this attitude would have been, and how in-

27

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

compatibJe it is with what we know of his char~cter in general.
Father Bernhard Duhr, S. J., a distinguished historian, who refers
to thes~ hitherto dark spots on the noble escutcheon of the persecuted knight-for of course Goyeau merely voiced the opinion of
historians- declares : "So then the Grand Master (supposing the
indictment referred to true) was not alone a contemptible coward,
but also a mean calumniator."
Father Duhr believed it a duty of justice and charity to investigate this phase of the terrible tragedy, one of the saddest of medieval
times. An imperious king, seeking to extend his influence and power,
and a weak Pope, swayed by the will of the headstrong monarch,
expfain to a great extent the events in which both a number of
ecclesiastics and lay1nen took so ignoble a part. Molay, on the other
hand, looms as a man possessed of Christian fortitude, upright and
unafraid, whose reputation was of the highest until the very day on
which he fell into the hands of his enemies. And all through the trial
the members of his order spoke favorably of him. Investigations
conducted outside of Paris in France failed to bring to light anything
but praise for the deposed Grand Master. It is difficult to believe,
therefore, that this man should have confessed falsehoods.
Father Duhr does not, having weighed the evidence, hesitate to
declare the information supplied by the inquisitor, William of Paris,
who, on October 14, 1307, conducted the first hearing of Molay,
entirely untrustworthy. He believes the torture to have been applied
to the Grand Master in spite of certain contentions declaring he had
not made the notorious confessions under duress. The distinguished
Jesuit historian, considers it highly improbable that those acting
under instructions from Philip, to question the prisoners until they
had confessed and adhered to their confessions, should have been
willing to omit the torture while obtaining from so important a
witness, as the Grand Master, the admissions desired by the King.
As to any evidence that Molay was not tortured, Duhr remarks it
does not exist! Pamphlets, and the like, full of exaggerations and
discrepancies, which emanated from sources inimical to the Templars, are not deserving of serious consideration.
Duhr's essay, published in the Jesuit review, "Stimmen der
Zeit," clears Molay not merely of guilt of those crimes for which
ultimately he and a number of other Templars suffered death at the
stake, but als·o of _ the . imputations referred to. He quotes, among
others, the opinion of a Protestant historian, Wenck, who says:
"The execution of the Grand Master was nothing but the last link
of a chain of actions, intended to compromise the order. The King
needed them to vindicate his action in the eyes of the people."
Molay died, thinks Duhr; "for the cause of justice and the innocence

of the ordet-ttuly a real martyr !" And such many of the people of
Paris thought him at the time, since they sought to obtain f~om the
ashes of the pyre on which he expired relics of him and his companion at the stakie, the grand preceptor of the order.
Freemasons have attenipted to claim Jacques de Molay for themselves. The junior branch of the sect bears his name. History
grants them no such privilege. Molay remained a fait hful Catholic ;
while in prison he repeatedly requested that his chaplain be granted
permissio n to read mass in his presence. ~~ and _the _Grder of
Knights Templars were the victims of an amb1t1ous King, Jealous of

Wisconsin (1929):
(Grand Master): Not since the organization .of the Masonic Fraternity back in the centuries has the Craft had an opportµnity of
doing so much good in any one of its activities as is offered in the
p-romotion of the Order of De Malay. It strikes right at the, very

Perfect Ashlars so much needed in the work of rebuilding and

we select the future Mason from our own environment largely
from sentiment and because of the ties of blood and relationship,
whereas the candidate for Masonic honors has no knowledge of
what is before him. Sometimes, many times, he petitions for Masonic
light out of · curiosity, mingled with a desire to follow in the footsteps of those he knows and trusts to help him in the paths he has
not known.
All this is well; but when you begin training your boy in the
tenderest years of his life, to place ·upon him responsibilities connected with mystery, you at once help to broaden him out and
build the foundation of manhood upon a higher plane. Take any
well-conducted Chapter of the Order of De Molay-and be it said
to our shame that only a fraction of the Masons have even ·witnessed the impressive ceremonies of this organization-and you

EASTERN STAR-ORDER OF
When the Grand Master of Pennsylvania, through an Edict,
placed the ban of disapproval on the Eastern Star in his State the
reason was not generally known. The remarks of the present Grand
Master of Pennsylvania before the Grand Lodge of New York sets
forth at length some of the conditions which caused this drastic
action.
The remarks of the Grand Master of Missouri set forth a
similar condition arising there. These instances show to what
extent trouble can arise when organizations who have as a requirement for membership connection with the Masonic Fraternity,
endeavor to trespass upon the rights of the parent body.
The action in both cases, while drastic, seems to have been
deserved.

(Grand Master): During the year my attention was called to an
anonymous pamphlet, saig to have been circulated at the !~st Grand
Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star, with a request that a thorough
investigation be made with a view to finding whether or not such

Growing out of this, and other matters, several law suits have
been instituted. Most of the parties, plaintiff and defendant, are members of the Order of the Eastern Star. Some of them are members
of the Masonic fraternity.
As in all controversies where some personal feeling is injected,
many charges and counter-charges have been made.
Necessarily, I have heard many stories, nearly all of the. st~te­
ments being hearsay. As Grand Master, I confined my investigation
to the strictly Masonic side of the question. I understand that the
Grand Chapter, 0. E. S., has appointed a committee to investigate
the matter.
I have endeavored to make it clear to the Craft that no person,
committee newspaper or organization would be permitted to investigate any' Masonic Lodge in ·the State of Missouri, because that is
the function of the Grand Lodge or its officers. As your Grand
Master, I have made such an investigation.
I found that certain records of the Lodge had been illegally and
unlawfully revealed. But I further found that the officers and members of the Lodge had released such information without knowing
that it was to be published and under a mistaken idea as to its purposes; and that there was no moral t~rpitude inv~lved. Accordingly,
a proper reprimand was administered to certam mem~ers an~ a
definite promise made to m e that never again would any information
be given out unlawfully by that Lodge or any of its members.
Every Freemason knows , or ought to know, that it is improper
for any Lodge, officer or member to reveal the transactions of any
Masonic Lodge to anyone, except - members of the Lodge or the
duly constituted authorities of the Grand Lodge or a legal committee representing the Grand Lodge or the Grand Master. The
same rule applies to divulging any Masonic information.
Having taken the · position that no other organization. wou~d be
permitted to invade the province of the Grand Lodge m this or

any other matter, the same rule should apply to the Grand Lodge

The Grand Chapter can, and will, in due course, properly work

Now, Brethren, those were the things that led us to see that if
we did not do something the Eastern Star would control us and
we would not control them. And, therefore, Grand Master Sell
issued his edict. Our Grand Master has a great deal more power,
as I understand it, than yours here. The Grand Master ·saw conditions and acted, no vote of Grand L odge being required. The
Grand Master issued an edict that all members of Lodges in Pennsylvania had to resign from the Eastern Star within six months,
and those not doing so would be expelled. There was some demurring; there were some who threatened law-suits; but in all only
about a half dozen resigned or were suspended, and later on they
all came back. I think without a single exception every one of them
came back, and begged off; and now we are going along as happily
as ever.
Now, many of them could not see it down there, as probably
many of you cannot see it. I have had men come to me and say,
"Why this edict? What is the matter with the Eastern Star? I go
out with my wife and we have a pleasant evening and she enjoys
these things as well as I do; what is the matter with it?" Well,
when I told them some of the things that I have told you, they
have said, "I see it, and I am satisfied." With · us the Eastern Star
is a thing of the past, and I think we will never go back to it,
because we have seen how it is working out.
We have one Lodge about which I am going to tell you, because
it is of particular interest to you. M cKean County is a county on
the border line of the State of New York, and the county seat of
this county is Smethport. For some reason or other there seemed
to be some unduly zealous members of the Eastern Star in the
Lodge in that town. They kicked up quite a row, and finally about
twenty-five of thern resigned and came over into New York. They
joined one of our Lodges. That was all right-entirely regularwe had no fault to find with this action. But what happened? Why,
the Lodge from which these Brethren resigned began to take on
new life. It had freed itself of the kickers. Those left became more
active and energetic and built a new temple. Then some of those
who left us wanted to come back and join the old Lodge, .but they
were given to understand they would not be accepted. Furthermore,
the Master of the Lodge from which they had resigned felt they
should not even be permitted to visit the old Lodge. That probably
wasn't quite fraternal, Grand Master Dutton, but in our state, as
probably in yours, the Master has it in his power to say who shall
visit his Lodge and who shall not be admitted. For th e sake of
the harmony of the Lodge the Master felt that the Brethren who
had resigned should not even be permitted to visit it.

The Eastern Star is a woman's organization, and I haven't a
word against it as such. The ladies who maintain this organization
have just as much right to be interested in it as we have to be
interested in Masonry. Our experience, however, was clearly to the
effect that like oil and water they do not mix.
EDUCATION-MASONIC
This topic still continues a fertile field for discussion among
those who are in favor of an extended campaign of Masonic education and those who are opposed to it. If those who are opposed to
it are correct, the great body of the Masonic Fraternity are · not
interested in a general movement to educate them either along
Masonic .or other lines.
We believe that perhaps beneficial results could be secured if
when a candidate was initiated he was .presented with some Masonic
work, such as Brother Street's " Symbolism of the 3rd Degree,"
Brother Haywood's "History of Free-Masonry," Brother Newton's
"The Builders," Brother Darrah's "Evolution of Freemasonry,'' or
Brother Tatsch's "Outlines of Masonic History." Before being
passed to the Degree of Fellow Craft the candidate should be required to state that he has read the book presented to him. This

35

plan would furnish the new Mason, who is n~turally enthusiastic
and curious, a means of grounding himself in the rudiments of
Masonry, both as to principles and history.
The presentation of the Blue Book to a candidate after he
receives his 3rd Degree could easily be eliminated.
Canada (1929):

•

(Grand Master) : I am firmly convinced that the time has come
when something more definite and constructive should be accomplished in the line of Masonic education. We find in every other
jurisdiction, where Masonry is alive, a growing demand from the
younger generation of the Craft for some substantial food to satisfy
-their craving for knowledge about Masonic matters. As that great
apostle of Freemasonry, Albert Pike, somewhere says in effect "A
few rudimentary lessons in architecture, a few elementary ins;ructions in symbolism, imperfectly pr epared and undersood, a few casual
hints in moral dogma are no longer enough to satisfy the earnest
inquirer after Masonic truth." The leaders in Masonry everywhere
are recognizing this modern development and are seeking a solution.
We lead the young enthusiast through the triple gates of our
tiled and guarded courtyards into the sacred inner temple, and we
wonder perhaps as he surveys with eager eyes all the r iches of our
treasure house, but when he seeks from us the answers to the thousand questions w hich spring from the. fullness of his desire to learn
more about this great heritage which he now shares with us we
discourage him and blunt the keenness of his longing by our 'lack
of means to answer.
What a wonderful field lies before the student of Masonry! This
great fraternity of ours, with all its complexity of tradition and
history, its ritualistic symbolism and peculiar system of jurisprudence and philosophy, its remarkable line of offices, the variety of
its manifold activities, to say nothing of its concordant organizations
and ramifications, surely somewhere in all this wealth of material
must lie some one thing to attract each one of us.
What is the right line of Maso~c education r Of w hat shall it
consist? How shall it be applied an d administered? What should
be its immediate and ultimate objectives? These are regiti mate questions of great importance which many Grand Lodges are trying to
answer in the present day and which I think we can not ignore.

has first been received into the society. As a matter of fact, at that
time his interest is keen, his enthusiasm is high, and as a result he
wants to know something about the fraternity with which he has
identified himself. It is believed that if some system could be devised
whereby proper Masonic education could be given to the newly raised
Brother it would produce highly beneficial results and perhaps keep
his interest in the fraternity over a long period of time. Educational
programs, no matter how designed, are highly desirable. ·

ETHICS
The fundamental principles of Masonry are and should be well
known to every member. If every member could answer satisfactorily the questions asked by the Grand Master of Arkansas in
his "New Year's Greeting," and live up to the thoughts set forth
by the Grand Master of Tennessee, there would be fewer Masonic
trials. and perhaps some of the general public would have a different
conception of our Organization.

No. 11. I pledge my Masonic Lodge, to which I belong, that
hereafter I will not speak evil of any Brother Master Mason. If I
can not praise him I will say nothing. Will you niake the same

No. 12. From this day hence, I pledge that I will watch myself
more closely and be very guarded and careful to say nothing disrespectful or disparagingly of any person, but more especially of a
Brother Master Mason or any member of his family. Are you willing
to join your Grand Master in this pledge?
No. 13. We are responsible to the higher orders of Freemasonry for the material they use, and we should not be jealous or
envy a Brother because he has the higher degrees in Masonry. He
is a child of some subordinate Lodge; we are responsible for his
Masonic birth, and he has assumed additional obligations of fidelity
which only strengthens him and his parent Lodge, and offers to the
world a picture ·beautiftil and sublime, and builds a sacred temple
dedicated to God and the brotherhood of Masonry in the hearts of
men. Am I right in this statement?
No. 14. Good Masons by the multiplied thousands are suffering
and paying the penalty of those who are sailing under false colors
and who are Masons in name only. What is the remedy? Shall we
turn them out and be more careful hereafter as to whorn we take
into our portals? Let's stop them at the door. Am I right?
No. 15. Our churches are continually reminding us of our duties
to God and our fellow-men. What are we doing along these lines?
No. 16. How many members of your Lodge know their Masonic
obligations? Shouldn't they be repeated in open Lodge until they
learn them? How can they obey if they don't know the command?

(Grand Master) : There are many pastimes and forms of entertainment that have their rightful place in every-day life, but when indulged in in connection with Masonry or in Masonic quarters are
inimical to the. teachings of the fraternity and harmful to the reputation of Masonry.
The habit of playing cards for gain, the games being conducted
in Masonic quarters, seems to be growing among the Brethren of
this jurisdiction. This is a direct violation of Code No. 325, against
which the Brethren have repeatedly been warned, and cannot longer
be tolerated.
In ~ertain portions of the state "athletic nights" are popular in
our Lodges. Boxing and wrestling exhibits are given before the
members, and frequently there is no particular display of science ·
connected with these exhibits. They lower the dignity and refinement of our teachings and principles. The Lodges are fraternally
requested to refrain from holding entertainments of this description.
. Clubs deriving their membership from the Masonic fraternity
are using the name of Masonry for their Sunday outings. A Masonic
Lodge ~ay meet on Sunday for no other purpose than to administer
the last sad rites, and these clubs should refrain from the Masonic
reference in their publicity.
I sincerely trust that the Brethren in Illinois will exercise proper
caution in using the words "Masonry" or "Masonic" in any of their
activities outside of the Lodge.

(Grand Orator): Any organization, secret or public, to justify its

with high resolve. Its history, its landmarks and its traditions should
be a certain guaranty that its future activities will redound to the
honor of its members and result in some good to mankind.
Precept alone, however pure and lofty, means little-fulfillment
means much. A promise by itself means nothing-keeping a promise
means everything.
Nothing injures the good name of the Order (Masonry) or

The best help a member can give to a Masonic rule or obligation is to obey it. The best way to enforce or help any law of the
country is to obey it. You will agree that it is the first duty of a
Mason in his activities as a citizen to set an example of obedience
to the laws of the country.

Why should we, who boast of the uplifting, refining influence
of the· fraternity, longer permit these and other violations to continue if we really desire Masonry to live? Cheapen it, drag its
banners in the mire, expose it to ridicule and misunderstanding, and
you write its epitaph.

There are several organized agencies in this country today
engaged in the commendable endeavor to teach respect for law and
order, and to teach the value of the protection the law gives to
· persons and property; the courts, the church and the home are the
chief and foremost among these agencies. Our institution, founded
on the fundamental truth of the Christian religion and a faith in the
e.xistence and omnipotence of a Supreme Architect of the Universe,.
should be found among these agencies. It should haye a place in
the front rank of these onward marching hosts in defense of .t he
American principle that the laws must be respected until they are
repealed.

Tennessee (1929):
(Grand Master) : All Masons are not members of a Lodge, nor are
all Lodge members real Masons.
A real Mason never talks about what the world owes hini, the
happiness he deserves, the chan ce he ough to have. All that he
claims is the right to live a nd play the man.
A real Mason is ·d ependable. His simple word is as good as his
Bible oath, and he does a little more than he promises. He is just as
honest in the dark, in his own room, as he is in public.
A real Mason does not want something for nothing , nor does
he want pulls, tips, favors; he wants work and honest wages. He
treats his fellow men as he would have them treat him.
A real Mason is loya l to his friends and guards their reputation
as his own. A real Mason honors a woman, any woman. He cannot
hurt a woman, physically or morally.
A real Mason minds his own business. He does not judge other
people or speak unkindly of them. He always has excuses for others,
never for himself. He is patient an d charitable to them; to himself,
he is strict.
A real Mason is glad to live and not afraid to die. He is a real
man, the finest, best, noblest, most refreshing thing on all i h e green
earth, unless it is a real woman.

Post cards advertising the sender's business. On the bottom the

Raffles, public and private, to raise money for one thing and

GRAND LODGE
In a large number of cases sessions of the Grand Lodge consist
of purely routine matters which are monotonous to the Brethren.
Some of the Jurisdictions are attempting to follow the procedure of
the Grand Lodge of England, Ireland and Scotland by concentrating this work in a Board of General Purposes. This allows greater
opportunity for the members at a Grand Lodge Session to become
acquainte~ and availing themselves of the hospitality of the City
wherein they meet.
The high cost of printing Proceedings has eliminated rosters,
detailed financial statements, etc., which makes the task of the Chairman of the Correspondence Committee easier when acting as a
Reviewer. If it has nothing else to recommend it, the smaller size
of the volume does.

Illinois ( 1928) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : It is often said that a
chosen few run the Grand Lodge, and in most instances this is
true. Much of the work of all our Grand Bodies is done in committees. The committees come before the Grand Body and report,
and the Brethren vote yea. Unfortunately, many who serve on
Grand Lodge committees are men who have served their time in
the work of the Fraternity and are in reality on the retired list, and
others who because of personal influence and political pull seek
appointment on committees in order to get their railroad expenses
paid to the city where the Grand Lodge holds its sessions. As a·
result many of our Grand Lodge committees are not made up
of men who are active in the work and who are thoroughly ·acquainted
with the demands of this modern age. As a result they report different matters according to their own notions and the Brethren
vote yea and then go home and criticize the Grand Lodge for action
taken. It is refreshing to notice that in one Grand Jurisdiction this
year that a certain number of Lodges asked for the passing of
legislation which they see.med to think would be a benefit to them.
It was, as usual, referred to a committee. The committee reported
adversely, and the representatives voted down the committee's report by an overwhelming vote, and passed the legislation which
they so much desired. If representatives only knew it they hold
the balance of power. If the platform rules the Grand Lodge it is
generally because representatives haven't backbone enough to stand
up for the things which they believe to be right.

during this year have been agreed upon by these four officers. Generally, the following method has been followed: the Grand Master

and their views have prevailed over what had been the original purpose of the Grand Master.

Texas (1929):
(Grand Master) : On frequent occasions in Masonic discussions and
intercourse we hear the cynical coined expression "the amen corner,"
or "It will never 'get by' the 'amen corner,'" alluding by that term to
· our Past Grand Masters and other permanent membership-Masons
who have borne the heat and burden of the day and wrought well in
the quarries of Masonic endeavor. Brethren, if this is meant as a slight,
rebuke, or criticism, it is wrong, unjust and unMasonic. All honor to
these loyal, veteran Craftsmen whose love, zeal and true devotion to
the tenets and principles of our Institution freely and unselfishly have
given of their time, talents, and substance, many times at a tremendous personal sacrifice, without the hope of fee or reward. Without
them this Grand Lodge would suffer an irreparable loss, I might say,
calamity. Thank God, we are privileged today to be guided in our
deliberations by the wisdom of their experience, to be directed by
their timely advice and counsel, and to be admonished by their brotherly caution.

GRAND MASTER
Proceedings still show many instances where Grand Masters
are called upon to answer questions, wise and otherwise, that might
easily be solved by reference to the printed law.
It· is a heavy burden where the Grand Master endeavors to
satisfy all parties. Education and examination of the Officers
charged with the administrative duties of a lodge is about the only
remedy for this state of affairs. There also appears to be less
inclination among Grand Masters generally to grant dispensations
even where the power is given.
The approval of the decisions of a Grand Master on a set of
facts and as such making them law, has naturally produced a large
amo~nt of special legislation. Making laws by Judicial Decision

50

in our legal system has produced an unsatisfactory condition, and
the same will also be manifested in the Masonic organization if
carried to extremes. It is being done in some Jurisdictions.
Colorado (1929):
(Grand Master) : I have witnessed very little ritualistic work during the year as I purposely requested the Lodges to put on no
degree work at my visitation. I felt that if the Grand Master has
a message for the Brethr!!n he ought not to be forced to deliver
it at the end of a long ritualistic service, when everyone was tired
and after many of the Brethren had gone to their homes. I enjoy
the degree work and I know the Lodges take pride in doing it well,
but I felt that discussion of the work was more especially the
function of the Grand Lecturer.

Grand

"I do not believe that any Grand Master can lay down the

Masons who could well fill the office, who are not and can not in
justice to their families give two years to the work, so that it
might follow that the best man may not be able to accept the office.

North Carolina (1930):
(Chairman CorrisPondence Committee) : We discover a mode of
electing and installing the Grand Master in Rhode Island which
differs from our procedure. Immediately after his election, all of
the Past Grand Masters present wait upon him and escort him into
the Grand Lodge, where he is at once installed by the retiring Grand
Master, who surrenders the gavel. Of course, he is so surprised
at having been elected, and so excited about having been installed,
that he does not feel able to preside during the remainder of the
election of officers, and therefore modestly requests the retiring
· Grand Master to take the gavel again, complete the election and
install the other officers.
The Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania exercises
greater power, perhaps, than any other Grand Master. He is not
troubled by having his acts reviewed by a Jurisprudence Committee
when the Grand Lodge meets. What he does is law unless and until
some succeeding Grand Master shall annul his actions. Thus we find
that the Grand Master sits as a Court of Review in the adjudication
of the qualifications of petitioners for the degrees.

was practically a full report of the proceedings appeared in one of
the evening papers. I want to say candidly this is a Masoriic offense,
and . that if it occurs again it will be my unpleasant duty to take
certain steps in regard to it. I do ask you, Brethren, that you keep
as much of our business as possible out of the papers.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We wonder how a Grand
Master can change the by-laws of a Lodge. We have always felt
that as the by-laws were adopted by the Lodge itself, and were
not dictated to them by Grand Lodge or any other power, that no
one could change them except the body which gave them birth.
We recognize that it is the province of the Grand Lodge or someone
to whom that power is delegated to see that such by-laws are in
accord with the Grand Lodge Constitution, but not otherwise to
interfere. This may be our mistake,, but we cannot see it differently
until we are shown.

LODGES
If we may summarize some of the existing conditions that
affect the efficiency of a Lodge we might say that they generally
consist of too large a membership, advancing Officers by rotation
regardless of executive ability or qualifications, subordinati~g the
practical workings of Masonry to ritualistic work, not adhering to
a budget, and the erection of Temples improperly financed.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Some of these difficulties have been met by the Grand Lodge
who adopted uniform regulations, but in the other instances they
can perhaps be best handled by Experience and Education.

A lodge of 160 members has a site worth $1,500.00, but no money.
Has plans for a $35,500.00 Temple, expecting to sell stock to mem- ·
hers up ·t o 40 per cent of the building cost and secure a loan for the

Iowa (1929):
(Grand Master): Apparently most lodges do not even try to live
within their income, but rather to live at least up to their income.
And their plans, if they have any worthy the name, are made in the
most optimistic spirit of the most prosperous year, with seemingly
never a thought of possible adversity.

I would recommend to them the present-day specific for all financial ills, the budget system; that they figure conservatively the income (not including fees for degrees-an uncertain quantity, at best) ,
and then see that the sum of the expenditures comes well within the
total income, leaving a good margin for safety.
A commodious and elegant home is a fine thing, and to possess
such a laudable ambition, but if secured only with the accompaniment of a bur.densome debt, an ever-present worry and a constant
handicap, 'twere better that a Lodge should live in more m odest quarters, though rented, yet able to carry on.
Some Lodges in the days of prosperity undertook the financing
of Temples entailing debts which now threaten the very existence of
those Lodges. Some have erected or purchased business buildings,
figuring that rentals would pay off the debts incurred, only to find
now, perhaps, empty store room's, converted into liabilities instead of
assets, for taxes, insurance and repairs go right on.
In an affort to meet their obligatio.n s some Lodges have raised
their dues to $10.00 or even more, and their fees in like proportion.
Some think that the Grand Lodge can and should help them. To
these let me say again that Grand Lodge funds are simply the contributions of all the Lodges. And shall we take the money of the
prudent and thrifty ones, some without homes of their own, to provide homes for those which heedlessly get themselves into trouble,
helpless in a maze of debts? I hardly need say that th e Grand Lodge
has no money for such purpose.
Too often these over-ambitious programs are started off with a
big feed, a booster meeting, with a Whoop! Hurrah. Boys! on a wave
of enthusiasm rather than a due consideration of financial conditions.
What a cry went up a few years ago over an additional dollar
in dues for a worthy charity, and yet more than one insta nce of Lodge
building incurred .debt on which the interest alone required $3.00,
$4.00 or even $5.00 from the dues of every member during a term of
years.

annually.
One Lodge by persistent effort has succeeded in paying off
almost 10 per cent of its debt in fifteen years. How Jong to pay the
total debt?
Now·all this has a very close bearing upon one phase of Masonry
-Masonic Relief. Charity, or Brotherly Love, synonymous terms,
one of the most excellent tenets of our profession, should always
have consideration in making up the Lodge budget and due allowance should be made for its possible needs. If a Lodge engages in
undertakings beyond its means, what will it do when some unfortunate Brother needs help? If such improvident Lodge shirks its
duty by shifting the case to the Grand Lodge it bu~ increases the
burden of the other Lodges.
T o sum up all this·, I recommend that the Grand Lodge create a
Board, or Committee, to which all our Lodges shall submit their
plans for financial undertakings of any magnitude. The powers of
such body may be either advisory or mandatory, as deemed best.
Nevada (1929):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): "When Is a Lodge Successful?" The writer's idea of a successful, a prosperous, and great
Lodge is not that Lodge of many members, splendid equipment, and
a big bank account. Even ritualis tic work rendered letter perfect and
with military precision does not make a Lodge great. There may be
a finer spirit of brotherly love and affection, a more convincing power,
in the halting words of a humble tiller of the soil or wielder of ax
or sledge than in the smoothly delivered and faul tlessly pronounced
words of the college professor occupying the East, and work put on
by the light of dim kerosene lamps may be, and often is, more impressive than the same work performe d under brilliant electroliers.
A Mason may be proud of his Lodge because its membership runs
into the thousands and its wealth is a by-word in the Jurisdiction ;
but for love of Lodge, give me the Mason who knows every other
member of his Lodge. We hold with Past Grand Master William R.
Hervey of California that "That Lodge is prosperous an<;I great which
commands the affections of its members, and displays spiritual rather
tha n material wealth."

New York (1930):
(Board of General Activities) : One of our sister Jurisdictions
a<lopted the system a year or two ago of giving each of its Lodges
an efficiency test. This Grand Lodge adopted a standard of what a
Lodge ought to be; appraised that standard at 100%, and then graded
each Lodge according to its success in measuring up to it. We may
not have need in our Jurisdictiol} to adopt such a system; if we <lid
we might set a different standard; but the idea behind it is one that
will instantly appeal to every one of us. Where is there a Mason who
would not be proud to feel that his is a 100% Lodge?
In the very nature of things such a Lodge would be necessarily
many-sided, touching the nature of its members at every point, able
to satisfy all their Masonic needs. It would have a competent official
staff; its treasury would be perpetually solvent; its books would delight the eye of a certified public accountant; its membership would
live and work in harmony where friendship would thrive and good
fellowship would flourish; its rooms would be appropriately furnished
and decorated, arranged for convenience and equipped effectually; its
ritualistic work would bring joy to the Grand • Lecturer ; its charities
would overlook no Brother in sickness or distress; throughout the.
year its communications would be as various in their appeal as dignified in their conduct; the Masonic mind, the Masonic conscience,
the Masonic heart would find satisfaction in such a Lodge which
would, as a unit, stand in its community as an exemplification of what
Freemasonry is intended to mean in the lives of its votaries.
North Carolina (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Grand Master Wood, of
New Mexico, takes a crack at another peculiar dilemma which
Masonry faces, as follows:
When candidates are plentiful, our Lodges become "Degree
Mills" grinding out new material. While this commands the interest
of the officers of the Lodge, it becomes monotonous to many of the
brethren on the side lines. When new material becomes scarce, there
is, as a rule, only routine business to be taken care of; which also
seems to become tiresome to many of the brethren who have the
courage to attend.
If there are plenty of candidates, Lodges become degree mills;
if there are not enough, Lodges become petition chasers. Men don't
want to sit through endless successions of degrees; men don't want
to go to Lodge when there is nothing to do; men don't want to
go to Lodge and there listen to much speechmaking under the
guise of Masonic Ed ucation. What is the poor man labeled Wor-

shipful Master to do? The riddle would tax King Solomon, patron
saint of things Masonic, so to speak. We do not know what to do.
We can only suggest variety as the source of sustained interest. We
must work out a program of Lodge work, injecting variety, and_ put
a new sort of interest in each meeting. It can be done. If other
programs of meetings, like those of Rotary and Kiwanis clubs, were
as badly neglected as the agenda of the L odge, nobody would attend
these, either. We have never seen anything of this sort that would
run itself.

We are glad to note that the Brethren of Queensland uphold
customs which call to mind the old country, and while we believe in
the maintenance of the utmost dignity of the Craft, yet in moments
of relaxation, the continuance of an old national custom, if it appeal
to a Lodge, should not be abrogated if it is not inconsistent with the
teachings of Freemasonry. "A little nonsense now and then is relished by the wisest men," and from the Report of the Proceedings,
it seems to us that the Grand Lodge did the right thing in allowing
the continuance of an old custom.
We have enquired just what a "MacDuff" was and the following
information has been secured. Brother McKean says of the "MacDuff Firing" and also speaks of the "Dumbarton" of the West
Country:
"It is done by hand clap three times and then stamp with the right
foot, at the same time shaking the right first forward in unison with
each stamp. These exercises are repeated three times each, and the
salute is ended with the thrbat cutting and Zea Zea Zea of our ordinary salute.

Western Australia (1928):
(Gra1ui Master): From Ancient times there has been the recognized adjournment from labor' to refreshment, and today the practice is ranged among the usages and established customs of the
Order. I have often expressed my own belief in the value of the
Festive Board when properly conducted, and I hope that these
pleasant social functions will long continue to be associated with the
Craft, as they provide the opportunity of extending hdspitality to
visitors and forming and cementing friendships among the members
themselves. As the Master is responsible for the conduct of the
Festive Board, just as he is responsible for the affairs of the Lodge
in the Lodge Room, he should be particularly careful to see that
nothing occurs which might be considered derogatory to the dignity
of the Institution or unworthy of its glorious traditions. There is no
place at the Festive Board of the Craft for any suggestive song or
story or anything that is calculated to lower ·the dignity of Freemasonry, so I trust Masters will be watchful and do everything in
their power to elevate the proceedings of the Social Board.

MEMBERSHIP
Statistics collected by the Librarian of the Grand Lodge of
Iowa show that 18 Jurisdictions during the year 1929 show a net
loss, as against 12 for the year 1928. The net increase for 1929

60

REPORT ON CORHESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

dropped to 676, as against 30,000 for 1928. We cannot help but
think that this will be for the betterment of Masonry. ·
This reduction may not be as serious as the figures would
indicate. General conditions may produce in the future candidates
of quality rather than quantity, which should be the aim of every
Lodge.
As a remedy for this loss the establishment of a rule requiring
a waiting period between the various degrees might work for great
good. Some of the Jurisdictions require this, varying from two
weeks to one month between each degree, while one Jurisdiction
allows the subordinate Lodge to fix the period by their laws. We
believe that if a month should elapse between the time a petitioner
is elected and he receives his first degree, three months between the
first and second, and third, making six months in all, it would
produce a satisfactory result.
In these periods there would be ample time for education of the
individual. "That which is easily gained is lightly held." The
Jurisdictions which have established a waiting period of six months
or more before a member could petition one of the co-ordinate
Masonic Bodies seeking the so-called "Higher Degrees" we believed
raised the standard of membership in those organizations.
This interval, while it might have resulted in a decrease in
membership, had the advantage of attracting those who seriously
considered the proposition. It would undoubtedly have the same
effect on petitions to the Blue Lodge.

individual soon finds himself so heavily involved with his various
obligations that he has little or no money to invest for Lodge purposes. In agricultural districts it has been quite the vogue to charge
the small number of petitions received by Lodges to agricultural depression and the fact that the farmers haven't any money and in the
big manufacturing centers the charge is made that the mills and factories are only working on half time with the result that wages are
scant and men are lacking in material prosperity. All of these are
merely superficial excuses. The real reason why more men are not
petitioning for the honors of Masonry must be sought elsewhere. It
used to be thought necessary in every man's life that he should belong to some fraternal organization. If he wasn't a Mason he usually
selected the Odd Fellows, or the Knights of Pythias or the Red Men,
but at any rate in his ir,iventory of valued holdings a lodge membership somewhere was thought vitally necessary, but our manner of
living has changed all this and membership in a lodge nowadays is
looked upon as a very trifling matter. There is, however, in Freemasonry an appeal to the intellectual and cultured man. The problem
before the Fraternity is to how best present that appeal.

Pennsylvania (1929):
(Grand Master) : For some years the number of initiates has been
decreasing. This is true not only ·in our own Jurisdiction, but in all
Jurisdictions in the United States, and in some states to a far greater
extent than in our own. For the last year twelve Jurisdictions in the

not satisfied that such is the case, although it is not safe to prophesy
in a matter of this kind. During the years immediately following the
war the number of petitioners increased greatly. In the year 1920,
we reached the peak in this state when there were more than 19,000
initiates. From that time the decrease has been gradual, nntil at the
present time the number of initiates is about the number before the
war. There are many who believe that the number of available candidates in this Jurisdiction is from six to eight thousand per year.
Undoubtedly one of the reasons for the decrease is that in the abnormal years following the war many who had any thought of at
any time going into Masonry acted and were admitted. As a result
many were admitted during the first few years following the war
that otherwise would have come into Masonry in a much longer
period of years. If this theory be correct, we must expect decreased
numbers for some few years yet. The condition, however, should

shortly right itself, and the decrease in the number of pet1t10ners

should be, we need have no concern as to ou·r numerical future.

GEORGE WASHINGTON MEMORIAL
When the George Washington Memorial was planned the idea,
as we remember it, was to erect a temple for Washington Alexandria
Lodge and a safe place for the keeping of the Masonic records and
mementoes of Washington's Masonic activities. The cost was set at
$100,000. In 1916 this was advanced to $500·, 000: in 1920 to $1,000,000; in 1922 to $1,500,000, and as times goes on the figures have increased until now it has reached nearly $4,000,000, without providing
for an Endowment Fund to maintain it. Various Grand Lodges
have taken a different viewpoint as to their responsibility. Some
formally joined the Association established to erect the Memorial,
and as members have constantly contributed the $1.00 per member
from the inception of the plan. Others, while not joining the Association. have paid their pro-rata along the original plan. Some have
made voluntary contributions of various amounts, without becoming
members of the Association or adopting any fixed policy. One Jurisdiction felt itself obligated to pay one for the actual number of members at the time the project was launched.

63

One of the redeeming features of this activity is the fact that
those having it in charge have limited their expenditures only to the
money actually collected. The present decrease in new members,
growing financial burdens that must and are being assumed by various Jurlsdictions, and the attitude of some ·o f the Grand Lodges who
are not members of the Association and believe they have voluntarily
paid all they should will, we believe, require considerable time and
ability to raise the balance to complete the building now set at a
total cor.t of $4,000,000. This figure we understand does not include
a maintainance fund which is suggested must be a million dollars or
more.

Western Australia (1929):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Our United States
Brethren are laboring strenuously to insure that the George Washington National Memorial will be ready for opening on Washington's
birthday in 1932, the date assigned. The wisdom may be questioned
of proposing a scheme to cost some £20,000, and afterwards developing it into one to cost fifty times that amount. But the point today
is not a question of wisdom. It is that the honor of Freemasonry in
the United States has been pledged by the Jurisdiction to the more
costly scheme, and indirectly such a pledge affects the Craft the world
over in the eyes of those outside our pale. The Brethren in the
U ni;ed States recognize this, and deserve commendation for their
determination to see the work through.
PROHIBITION
This occupies a place in the Proceedings of a number of the
different Jurisdictions, due mainly to the failure of Lodges to
discipline their members for violation of the law.
As Masons we are enjoined to obey the moral and civil law,
and this must be the attitude of the Craft towards the 18th Amendment and all laws passed in connection therewith.

Indiana (1930):
(Grand Master) : I was invited to a meeting of the committee appointed by the Governor of the tsate to consider crimes and the
enforcement of the law. While I was present at this meeting I was
called upon to make some remarks and I assured the committee that
Masonry was in · sympathy with their efforts. At that time I called
their attention to our law in regard to the matter under consideration, which is as follows:
"Whatever is a breach of good morals, contrary to the precepts
of the Holy Scriptures or a violation of the laws of the State or of
the United States is an offense against the principles of Masonry
and must be promptly dealt with."
This committee was very much pleased to learn that we had a
law like this. I find there are a few Masons who evidently do not
know of this law or have forgotten it.
New Jersey (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master
(Colorado, 1929) had few decisions to make, but in one he was asked

and gambling and the Grand Master ruled that the burial of a Mason
from another Lodge might be refused on evidence that the deceased
Brother was notoriously un-Masonic in his conduct. We think the
last few words were the gist of the whole matter, but we have never
heard of any decision before on this particular question. Personally
we are glad to see that the Grand Master upheld the Master.

One ruling by the Grand Master would hardly pass the Jµrisprudence Committee in Utah. In effect, but indirectly, he appeared

was then serving a sentence of from two to three years at hard labor
on the county roads. The Master, reporting the case, stated that the
offending member was a "member of the Shrine" I What has such
membership to do with the case? The Master urged that the Masons
should do something, out of respect to the offender's father and in
keeping with the teachings of Masonry. There is nothing in the teaching of Masonry known to us that requires, or suggests, that Masons
should put forth ·"some effort," or any effort to relieve a convicted
law-breaker of the fruits of his deliberate wrong doing. It is our understanding that Masons should be law-abiding citizens. We do not
find in the Grand Master's ruling anything concerning a Masonic
trial and expulsion of the young man. Is this young man retained
in good standing by his Lodge, while doing time on the highways,
as a convict?· This was only one of several cases in which members
of the Craft had been convicted of crime and sentenced to jail or to
the penitentiary, and friends stated or implied by their statements
that Masons, as such "ought to do something!" We think something
should be done-the rosters of the Lodges should be purged of such
material.

READING-INTERESTING

RITUAL

The attention of' those who are interested, and have access to the
Prnceedin,gs of the various Grand Lodges, is called to the following
Orations, Papers and Reports from the Proceedings reviewed. They
are entertaining, worthy of examination and valuable for reference.

A Canadian Past Master, after visiting Lodges in many sections
of the United States, summarizes the place ritualism assumes in
our organization, as follows: "First-Ritualists have been placed
upon a pedestal and the social features of Freemasonry almost
eliminated. Second-The charity lecture to candidates has been
nullified, the benevolence of The Craft commercialized and dispensed by bureaus. Third-Large Lodges and large classes 'a re a
menace to the existence of Freemasonry, a departure from the
original plan. Fourth-Lodges are rapidly becoming 'Degree Mills,'
grinding out Masons with merely a superficial knowledge of the
ceremonies. What _so_rt_ .of Masonic ideals can 'Degree Mills' produce?" We believe that ritualism is largely productive of nonattendance. Some tim-e ago this Jurisdiction reduced the lecture of
the First Degree. It does not appear that it worked any great
hardship.
A thorough study of our present ritual with a view of amending
it so as to conform to the present condition of living, we believe
would be worth while. One Grand Master stated it in the following language: "Antiquated ceremonies and usual repetitions are
working great injury to the cause of Freemasonry."

Alberta (1929):
(Grand Master): I ruled, in the case of an elderly brother of
Scandinavian origin who could not memorize the series of questions
and answers required by the York working, that a "satisfactory
examination as to his proficiency" would be the satisfaction of his
examiners that he could identify himself as a Mason for admission
to a strange Lodge.
Repeated complaints that the ritual of the York working is
topheavy have been received at frequently recurring intervals. · Complaints regarding the length of the opening and closing ceremonies
in the Canadian ritual are likewise common. I~ my own opinion the
York ritual contains much extraneous matter which could be very ·
well demonstrated on set occasions during the year or dropped altogether, and so - eliminated from the exemplification of the degrees
themselves.
Long-drawn-out ceremonies find "little favor in this swift moving
age, and where the work can be readily reduced to the essentials .
required by time-honored exemplification I believe this should be
done.

Arizona (1930):
(Grand Master) : I am not a fanatical ritualist as I ' attempted to
make clear on various occasions during my official visitations. Of
course, I believe that a reasonable degree of word and action accuracy
must be insisted upon, and the more nearly letter perfect the work
may be, if intelligently and. effectively rendered, the better. But, as
between practically letter perfect ritualistic work, listlessly and colorlessly given, and work slightly less accurate in its rigid adherence
to the absolute text, but earnestly arid impressively delivered, I admit
decided preferei:ice for the latter.

Florida (1929):
. (Grand Master) : The first class of tools or implements are what
might be termed the tools of preparation which we use to prepare the
materials to fit them for the builder's use. The second class of tools
are what might be termed testing tools by which we try and test the
quality of the work upon which the preparation tools have been used.
Th~ third class of tools are the construction tools or the tools which
are used in placing the materials which have been shaped, tested
and tried, in the super-structure of the temple. Unless we have
been able to correctly read and interpret the designs which have
been on our · trestle boaJ;"d, much of the material will be so crudely
pre.p ared that it may not pass the inspection of the Master's square.

Georgia (1930):
(Grand Master): The official Masonic code of the Grand Lodge
of Georgia requires that some form of lecture be given in each of
the symbolic degrees. Substantially the same lectures as are printed
in Simon's Monitor are printed in our code, but our laws do not
require that these lectures be given either in full or in part, but leave
to the option of the Master the privilege of substituting other appropriate lectures.
During the twelve years in which I have engaged in instructing
our Lodges ·in the ritualistic work, I have made it a practice to
recommend that all ·officers prepare their own lectures instead of
in following verbatim the regular lectures printed in the code. My
idea is to encourage original research and to provide instruction and
entertainment for the class as well as to make some departure from
constant, monotonous repetition of the same old lecture with which
all are familiar.
I nave found that this procedure has resulted in bringing about
better attendance in our Lodges and has already served very effettively to discontinue the practice o·f which you. complain, that is, a

Nova Scotia (1929):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Somewhat of an interesting subject came before the Grand Master · of Oregon in the form
of the question, "When is a ·m an a Mason?" In the U nited Grand
Lodge of England, if we remember correctly, a candidate is recognized as a Mason when he takes his first or Entered Apprentice
Degree. In Oregon, however, it appears that not only must the
candidate take all the three degrees, but after that must pass an
examination on the candidate's third lecture before he is a Mason.
In justice to Grand Master Eakin it should be noted he did not
altogether agree with the above, but felt that, even against his own
wishes and contrary to his honest opinion, he considered himself
bound by previous decisions of Grand Lodge. In our humble opinion
no Grand Master is bound by previous decisions if he is honestly
of opinion they were wrong. It strikes us that the proper course
for a Grand Master, under such circumstances, to take is to give
his ruling or decision and the grounds upon which it is based, inform
Grand Lodge of contrar.y decisions and then let that Grand Body
decide what is right and which is wrong.

Washington (1929):
(Grand Master): At the December meeting of the Board of Custodians the matter of "degree teams" of two types was under discussion.
The first type is not under the direction of any constituted Lodge,
but seeks engagements in any Lodge that will invite them. It was
the expressed opinion that such teams served no good purpose and
prostituted our ritualistic ceremony, which is the property and prerogative of constituted Lodges, to the purposes of other organizations.
The second type of "team" is composed of officers and members
of a constituted Lodge; but also seeks engagements to fill the stations
and places of other Lodges. This type does serve some good purpose,
as they are usually accompanied on their engagements by members
of the Lodge, and the exchanges of fraternal visits which result are
to be commended. Only where the desire for individual or collective
notoriety is the impelling motive is this type of "team" greatly to
be condemned. Nevertheless, "team" is not a Masonic term, and the
practice is largely aped from other organizations. It would be an
interesting experiment to see an exchange of fraternal visits between
Lodges when the officers of the host Lodge retained their stations
and places and conferred work themselves.

of the Correspondence Co~mittee of Vermont stated: "Many Secretarys, being human, are careless, but the percentage of this type
is evidently in the minority."
One of the Jurisdictions considered _a resolution to allow the
Secretary to participate in the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, the
same as the other elective officers and Past Masters, but the proposition failed of approval. While this thought was drastic departure
from custom, still the idea is being developed in some Jurisdictions
by combining the Secretaries in some organization so that their
experience and ideas may be available to each other and themselves.

in old rituals, spurious and genuine, of the early days of last century~
but outside America, and especially in British countries, is not conferred. British and Australian Masonry adopts what does seem to
be the more logical practice of the Installed Master's Degree, conferred upon the Worshipful Master-elect, on the night of his installation into the chair, and performed only by a Board of Installed
Masters, of whom there are often more than 100 present, constituting
the board. The ceremony is one of the most impressive and dignified
in Masonry, and vastly superior to that of the Past Master's Degree.

upon the efficiency of the Secretary. He generally continues from
year to year, while the Master emerges from the ranks only for a
brief time. This Secretary of the Lodge not only has a great
responsibility but also acts as a "shock absorber." As Chairman

SUSPENSIONS
Suspensions for non-payment of dues have been responsible for
reducing the net gain in a number of the Grand Lodge Jurisdictions. While this may be due in part to present financial conditions, still we believe the· chief reason is that the Lodge has lost
its appeal to the Member.
We do not think as some Grand Masters charge, that suspensions are due to the failure of the Secretary to perform his duties
in so far as the collection of dues are concerned. If a member
refuses or neglects to pay his dues alter the usual Lodge procedure
is followed of rendering bills, notifying him of the result of the
failure to pay the same, and no reply is had, it is presumptive
evidence that the Brother is not enough interested to keep himself
in good standing. We hardly believe it is the province of a Secretary to constitute himself a Collection Agency where the ordinary
methods have proved futile.
Connecticut (1930):
(Chairman C orresponaence Committee) : A few reviewers argue
that a Brother dropped N. P. D ., who fails of reinstatement, should
have the money which he paid to restore his standing refunded. We
dissent. •The sum paid as a preliminary to petition for restoration is
simply rightful payment of a legal and moral debt incurred while his
standing remained unimpaired, and is the price he pays for becoming
a non-affiliate in renewed good standing. But to again become a
member of either his old l.,.odge or a nother requires further and separate. procedure.
There is a technical difference between suspension and striking
from the roll of membership. In Connecticut, the latter is the sole
penalty for non-payment of dues. Its only effect is to make the delinquent a non-affiliate, but his accrued debt impairs his standing as
such. According to our law, he must as a prerequisite t o petition for
reinstatement (which 'is r eally for r eaffiliation) pay the debt incurred
whil.e he was yet maintained in fult standing. As he had continually

HEPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

83

the benefit of good standing, there is no logic in a refund. He must
then file a regular petition for affiliation, which must take the same
course as any other such petition. Should his petition fail .of a unanim ous ballot and so be rejected, he can claim a certificate of good
standing as 'a non-affiliate, which with us answers all purposes of a
demit. Payment of his debt restores his standing, ·but leaves him
, a non-affiliate, and free to affiliate with any Lodge which will accept
him by a clear ballot.
There is some merit in the contention that refusal to pay dues
by a member clearly able to pay constitutes a Masonic offense, punishable by indefinite suspension. In such cases, reinstatement becomes a different and much simplier matter.

the society. Men who care nothing about the institution have no
business holding membership in it and the sooner the fraternity
eliminates this class of material t he better off it is going to be.

North Carolina (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Grand Master Hanson
Peterson of Vermont reports that at some time before 1 :00 p. m. on
January 9, 1928, one Mrs. Daisy C. W hite bought a money order at
a California post office to pay the dues of her husban d, James G.
White. Brother White had been notified during the previous year
to pay dues or lie would be suspended; and since his dues were not
paid before the date mentioned in that notice, he w as suspended on
the date mentioned in the notice. Mrs. White mailed the money
order immediately after purchasing it, as shown by her affidavit and
the statement of the postmaster from whom it was bought. Between
2:45 and 3 :00 on the same day, January 9, 1928, Brother White died
while driving his automobile, a hundred or more m iles away from
the place at which his w ife bought the m oney order. Under the
Kentucky law, h e is restored automatically if member pays what he
owes to the Lodge within two years after suspension ; but the L odge,
having received notice of his death prior to the receipt of the money
order, refused to accept the payment of dues, and placed it upon
record that at his death he was not in good standing. The family of
the deceased appealed to the Grand Master for a decision. The
Grand Master decided that the placing of the remittance in the post
office, properly stamped and addressed, is a constructive delivery
thereof to the Secretary at that moment. The Grand Master therefore
rules that James G. White died in good standing and that the Lodge
must accept the money order in payment of his dues.

TEMPLES
The regulation adopted by a number of Jurisdictions, as well as
our own, requiring either the direct approval of the Grand Lodge before a Temple can be erected or at least consideration by a Grand
Lodge Advisory Council, has undoubtedly prevented Lodges from
assuming a financial burden that they could never meet. Other
Grand Lodges are considering the adoption of like regulations. The
well-known railroad sign, "Stop, Look and Listen," is particularly
applicable to ventures of this kind. A number of ·the existing edifices
are evidence of the fact that you cannot mix fraternalism and business, and also that it is a wise man, Committee or Lodge that can
tell what the future will bring forth.
As usual, in the various Jurisdictions there are rules regarding
the purposes for which a Temple may be used. Some exclude all
organizations except the Lod!'re itself, and even limit the occupancy
to Masonic meetings only, frowning upon the use of the Temple f~r
dancing, card parties or other social activities, eve? under Masomc
auspices. Personally we believe that our factories, schools and
churches, like an industrial plant, should be in continuous operation,
rather than operating on part time only.

Ohio (1930):
(Grand Master): It is most laudable when an enthusiastic membership desire a new home and in ·a lmost every case where a new Temple
has been erected, the interest has always increased.
However, high-powered salesmanship for new Temples' has entered the field of Masonry. These campaigns are generally conducted
by ~ompanies or individuals for profit to themselves. They are usually
entirely unaware of local conditions and no further interested than
that th~ campaign goes over the top. Then the aftermath: pledge
cards signed under more or less pressure, carrying a legal obligation
to pay, neglect of which is followed by court action. Consult the legal
records of one of Ohio's largest cities. At least ten to fifteen Masons
b.efore a court, sued for non-payment of pledges. In some cases, possibly, they were able to pay. In others, positively unable to pay.
I have made a personal investigation of this situation and am well
aware of the facts.
In a number of cases where correspondence took place relative to
charity work or a request by the Grand Master that a Lodge assist
in performing its obligation to a sick member in care of a Sister Jurisdiction, the answer was, "We have built a Temple and are so financially embarrassed that we have been unable to render further assistance." Another Lodge doubted their ability to pay the Grand Lodge
tax for the same reason.
Before a Lodge proceeds by the "Intensive Campaign Method,"
led by strangers to the community, permission should first be obtained from the Grand Lodge. There are enough able business men'
in every community who are Masons to conduct their own campaign
without embarrassing a single member of the Fraternity.
Every Lodge could, without harm to anyone, establish a building
fund , constantly adding a m ite at regular intervals; then, in the
smaller hamlets, where fire is a constant hazard, where the Lodge is
in rented quarters, should a fire occur, the fund with its interest accumulation through the years would be instantly available, and far better quarters be secured with no hardship on the membership. The
same idea would apply in the cities where a number of Lodges are
located.

Maryland:
Grand Master Jones condemns the injection of politics into
Masonry in the strongest terms and says that the ·old Charges of
1722, which resolved against all politics, is as good law today as
when adopted.
The 1927 Report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence
by Brother Jesse M. Whited is a valuable compendium in the nature
of a topical review of what the Committee thinks are the outstanding
actions of other Grand Jurisd.i ctions and expressions of opinions of
leading Masons. It is accompanied by the opinions of the Committee
with some of which we cannot agree.
We must, however, congratulate Bro. Whited upon giving to
the Craft a splendid presentation of the Masonic thought of the
country at large and thank him for the condensed information in
the Appendices.

The experience of the present writer as a reviewer is only a
few weeks old and the number of proceedings is about a dozen at
this writing. An opinion from me would be worth very little, but,
I venture to say that the report on Foreign Correspondence written
by Brother Jesse M. Whited is one of the best to be found in any
of the Proceedings. He writes a topical review touching upon all
the important things in the various proceedings. The last subject,
which he calls "Olla Podrida," he tells us is "a Spanish term, meaning
a dish of stewed meat," hence a mixture, and Brother Whited has a
variety of interesting items under this head. He quotes the Grand
Secretary of Nevada as saying "A wise borrower hath more wisdom
than a poor composer, and whomsoever has not made this discovery
is not wise." Believing the truth of this quotation I submit the
clippings from Brother Whited' s report and wish I had room for
more.

The Report of the Correspondence Committee of ISO pages is
by Jesse M. Whited, Past Master of California Lodge No. l. The
old preachers used to divide sermons into two classes, "Textual" and
"Topical." Correspondents generally follow the textual plan; so a
correspondent who wishes to know what another correspondent said
about his Grand Lodge had only to turn to the comment on that
Grand Lodge and could skip all the rest of the report. But W. Bro.
Whited adopts the topical plan. He gives a hundred pages to topics
from "Advertising" to the "Washington Memorial." Then we have
fourteen pages devoted to "Bouquets and Brickbats," in which he
refers briefly to the Proceedings of many Grand Lodges. Then follows a heading, "Olla-Podrida," which is defined as "a Spanish term
meaning a dish of stewed meat." His "mixture" makes good eatinl('
and this Scribe looked over all pages of his report but found nothing
that would harm Missouri.

O regon:
The Grand Master, William Howard Fischer, is well known in
California for his constructive work in civic, business and Masonic
circles. To his constructive work this Grand Lodge is indebted for
the certificate system of vouching for and admitting members to
Grand Lodge.
An important historical observance took place at Coloma June
2 and 3, 1928. This was planned and held in recognition of the 75th
anniversary of nine Lodges chartered in 1853. A special train ran
from Los Angeles to Coloma. By train and automobile many brethren
from San Francisco joined the pilgrimage to the historic site where,
on January 19, 1848, gold was discovered at the old Sutter Mill by
James W. Marshall. The brethren arrayed themselves in the costume
of mining days. Some of the Grand officers arrived in a stage coach
once used between Placerville and Carson City in the days of the
gold excitement.
Brother Howell B. Murphy of Placerville, impersonating a pony
express rider, arrived and swam his horse across the river to deliver
"!\•hat purported to be the first Masonic charter.
An historical play, "Men of Destiny," was presented in a natural
stadium. In the play the story of the participation of Masons in the
controlling events of the early days was developed. There was an
uplifting Sunday morning service, following which the brethren
began journeying toward home, taki ng with them the lasting impression of the living past.
Masons in California are rendering service to their brethren
who are World War veterans in the Government hospita ls at San
Fernando, Livermore, anci Palo Alto.
Worshipful Brother Rufus B. Van KleinSmid, Grand Orator,
delivered an eloquent oration which was received with deserved
applause.

South Carolina:
The book of Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of California iS

In the matter of building Masonic Temples without the assurance of adequate plans for financing, Grand Master Fischer states
that the brethren have been betrayed by their enthusiasm. This is
a serious problem confronting many Grand Lodges and California
is not an exception.

Western Australia:
The Grand Master held it to be no impropriety for the Brethren
of a Lodge to participate in a simple picnic on Sunday, provided it
was private, restricted to members and their families, with no advertising, sale of tickets, or "commercfal features," whatever that may
mean. Well, in Sunny California, the Brethren seem to have time on
any old week7day for a festive jaunt, and why Sunday should be
roped in to provide a seventh opportunity is, as Lord Dundreary said,
"one of those things no fellah can find out."
A recommendation of the Grand Master, adopted by Grand
Lodge, was the provision of buttons, "made from the pure gold of
California's hills, for presentation to veterans of not less than fifty
years' standing." This is the adoption of a charming custom in many
American Jurisdictions, and probably the adoption will be all the
more charming by the recognition that the hills of California produce
gold which is so wonderfully pure.

Under this topic we have endeavored to collect the activities of

Jurisdictions, where the events of the Masonic World are set forth

Alabama :
By invitation of the Governor, the State Superintendent of E<lucation, the State Commander of the Ame~ican Legion, and the
President of the Alabama Education Association. the Grand Lodge
was represented at a meeting called to consider plans for improving
the public schools of the state.
The Masonic Home shelters 340 children and sixty-five older
people, " the largest number in the history of the institution." Ninetyone of the children attend high school, and 162 arc in the grammar
school. The latter are being taught in a building located on the
Home grounds and owned by the Craft.

Tw.o hundred <J.nd eighty-eight children, boys and girls, have had the

attended Masonic Tuberculosis Children's School at the Sanatorium

Two Negro " Grand Lodges" operating in Colorado were enjoined by court decree, obtained by Grand Lodge, from including in

Connecticut:
Attention is called to the disadvantages to Grand Lodge of a
resolution adopted in 1879, exempting from Lodge and Grand Lodge
dues any Brethren who have been in good standing for thirty years.
He shows that, as a result, more than ten per cent of the
Craft's entire membership neither pay the per capita tax for the
support of Grand Lodge nor do they contribute to the support of the
Masonic Home.
.
The membership in the Masonic Home and Hospital numbered

Charity Foundation has been fifty-six during the year . The average
per capita cost was $501.10. The Endowment Fund of the Charity
Foundation now is $341,227.70. Several new legacies were added
during the year.

Grand Master decided to try an experiment. It was announced in
the form of an edict issued to all the Lodges. In substance it transferred the actual presentation of a leather apron from the first degree
to the time when the new Brother shall have received the Master
Mason degree and passed an examination in open Lodge proving his
proficiency in the work. The "presentation" in the first degree is to
be a symbolical act only.
Another edict ordered and directed that no Brother may become
a member of any organization predicating its membership upon good
standing in the Lodge, unless such organization shall first have
secured the approval of the Grand Lodge of Florida.
Brethren who already had joined organizations not previously
approved by Grand Lodge, are ordered to withdraw or become "subject to trial and expulsion from the Lodge."
