Iowa:
The Grand Master finds that some Lodges are too ready to turn
over to the Trustees of the Charity Fund calls which come to them
for help. He believes that every Lodge should pay at least a portion
of the amount necessary for the relief of any needy one who has a
claim upon the Lodge. One point he mentions in connection with
this subject deserves wider recognition as a caution 'to be observed
by Lodges everywhere. He points out that often there is carelessness in the manner of reinstating Brethren who have been suspended
for a number of years. The same censure applies to the election to
membership of Brethren who have carried their demits for extended
periods of time. Often such Brethren have not contributed anything
to ·the cause of Masonry during the best earning period of their
lives and then, when doubts arise as to their condition in approaching
old age, they hasten to regain a standing in the Craft, usually with
the thought in mind that in case of misfortune assistance will be
forthcoming, or at least that they will be assured a fraternal burial.
The Grand Master cites one case where reinstatement was effected
after the Brother for whom the application was made had been dead
for six months. Back of the latter act was the intention to foist upon
Grand Lodge through the Lodge, the "care of a needy and really
deserving family, a widow and three children." Such experiences are
not confined to Iowa. This is the first time we have seen the matter
referred to by a Grand Master in his Annual Address.
What is referred to as the "Iowa plan" is the contributing from
the Grand Charity F und toward the maintenance in their home

Massachusetts:·
. Grand Master Walker of Connecticut, when called upon, gave a
brief sketch of Masonry in the early days of Connecticut, showing
how in Colonial times Massachusetts and Connecticut were bound
together by many ties. When the news of the battle of Concord and
Lexington reached New Haven, he related, the Second Company of
the Governor's Foot Guard demanded powder and ball to take with
them to Cambridge. Their request being refused by the Selectmen,
the determined Guardsmen, by a show of force, got posse~sion of the
keys and ammunition. Since then, once a year the present members
of the old military company, of which M.'.W.'.Brother Walker is
the Captain, march from the Armory to the Green in New Haven
and, after attending church service, proceed to the city Hall and
rehearse what took place in 1776. Demand is made for the keys of
the powder house, it js refused, the Guardsmen declare . they will
seize the powder if the keys are not forthcoming, and all they ask is
produced. Many of the Guard of 1776 were members of Hiram Lodge
No. 1 of New Haven. That Lodge received its charter from the
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts in 1759. With the old military company marched Brother Israel Putnam to Cambridge and afterward
became a Major General in the Continent:! Army.
"We are a modest group, we Past Grand Masters, but even we
find the limit of humility. We can stand it when a man takes out his
watch and looks at it while we are speaking, but we do object when
after looking at it, he puts it to his ear to see if it is going."

New .York:
A Permanent War Memorial Building to the American Expeditionary Forces is being constructed in the heart of Paris, France,
by the American Legion. It will be named "Pershing Hall" · after
General John J. Pershing, who commanded our forces in the World
War. A large dwelling house has been purchased, and the moneys
required for its con~ersion into a memorial have been raised as well
as a considerable portion of an endowment fund for its maintenance.
To complete this fund invitations .have been extended to the Young
Men's Christian Associations, the Knights of Columbus, the Salvation Army, the Jewish Welfare Board, the American Red Cross and
the Masonic Fraternities to establish particular memorials in the
building. Each memorial will consist of a room which will take the
name of the donor and in which will be perpetuated in sculpture or
bronze tablets or other forms, the services and sacrifices of the men
of each particular organization.
All of the other organizations receiving the invitation, with perhaps one exception, have accepted.

Many valuable additions have been made to the Masonic Libracy.
The government of the Republic has conceded to Grand Lodge a
· valuable piece of property in the city of Havana, in recognition of its
help in providing a ·school for children and a public library. The grant
was voted by the Cuban Congress with the hearty endorsement of
President General Gerardo Machado, Past Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of Cuba, who ~igned the bill conveying the property.
Aside from the school and library, a Masonic Temple will be built on
the property, a Palacio de la Masoneria, which will be headquarters of
Grand Lodge. The grant also partakes of the nature of an official
recognition by the Republic of Cuba of the National Masonry for the
latter's services in the promotion of the principles of the Cuban Constitution and the education of the people. "The author of the law by
which Grand Lodge obtained the land, is Dr. Antonio Bosch who is
not a Mason. Many other distinguished members of both Q.ouses of
Congress gave enthusiastic help to the project from a high regard for
the Fraternity, though they are not affiliated with it themselves.
One Lodge, with the cooperation of Grand Lodge, helps to maintain a Dental Dispensary for Children in the city of Camagiiey.
Another gave an ambulance to a Hospital.
La Misericordia is the outstanding benevolent institution maintained by Grand Lodge. It is the National Masonic Home and at
present has 180 residents. The property and equipment has b.e en
improved progressively. New pavilions have been erected from time
to time. The investment is estimated at $400,000.00. . A new small
edifice is under construction, which will be used as a Masonic Temple
where Masons of the city may hold meetings and where sessions may
be held to bring comfort and joy to the Brethren in the Home.

New Brunswick:
The Grand Master reports that on Jan1,1ary 26, 1929, the beautiful Masonic Temple, at St. John, which served as headquarters of
Grand Lodge, was totally destroyed by fire. The structure was erected
in 1879 and contained a valuable irreplaceable collection of portraits,
dress regalia, and other cherished possessions. Steps were taken to
provide for the erection of a new Masonic Temple.
Norway :
For over ninety years Norway was united with Sweden until she
became an independent Kingdom in 1905. During the greater part of
this time the Norwegian Lodges worked under the Grand Lodge of
Sweden, as a Provincial Grand Lodge which on May 10, 1891, transformed itself into an independent autonomous National Grand Lodge.
Only one Stated Communication is held each year, on March
22nd, and is known as the Great Feast of the Order.
The Norwegian Brethren are not permitted to be identified with
any other Masonic or soi-disant Masonic body. Candidates belonging
to any Secret Society known to be of a Masonic type, are not admitted.
Fuller accounts of the history, organization and operation of the
National Grand Lodge of Norway were given in the New York
Foreign Correspondence reports of 1928 (page 225) and 1929 (page
146).

Worship, a sacriligeous Satanic cult, pictured in lurid colors as a
practice of weird gory rites and laboring frantically to place Satan on
the throne of Jehovah. The ·reverend Christian father spits venom
at every turn and has the wild fabrications of the notorious Leon
Taxi! of sixty years ago beaten by about that number of miles. It may
appear impossible that such silly stuff can be believed by anyone. But
prejudice is a blind voracious thing and swallows anything · that is
thrown into its trough. All in all the Swiss Craft appears to have
had as rough a time of it as did the Germari Craft under the ceaseless
firing from the General Ludendorff batteries. Silence seemingly
having ceased to be a virtue, the Grand Lodge Alpina encouraged a
literary campaign of defense, believing that at least the intelligent
reading public ought to be set right. It offered prizes for effective
expositions of the true principles and activities of Freemasonry.
Many essays were received and referred to a competent ·jury. which
reported that the first prize has been reserved for a possible future
award, and that three prizes of 500, 400 and 300 Swiss francs, respectively, were .accorded for one French and two German contributions.
In Zurich there is a Brockcnhaus ( House of Crumbs) which ·was
called into existence through the init:iative of Modestia Lodge, but is
not maintained under Masonic auspices, a separate society having
charge of the institution. Used household articles, wearing apparel
· and other useful objects are contributed by residents of the City,
which are then offered for sale at a nominal cost, for the benefit of
self-respecting .poor among the population. Whatever money balance
is left at the end of each year is distributed among the benevolent
institutions of the City.
Among the many valuable additions made · to the Grand Lodge
Library and Museum, reported for the Quarter ended March 1, 1930,
is a photograph of a Lodge Certific.a te, dated 1763, of "Lodge No.. 2
on the Registry of England" (Provincial), now St. John's Lodge No.
1 of New York City, to Edmund Leslie, M:.M:.

ity was given to the Lodges to use appropriate music in the Ceremonies. The W:.M:. of a Lodge is made responsible that no part
of the Ritual be left out and that no additions or alterations are
introduced.
Grand Lodge voted the establishment of a Centenary Fund for
the fitting celebration of the hundredth anniversary of the constitution of Tasmanian Freemasonry in 1935_. A "Special Levy" of four
shillings a year per member was authorized. I.t is estimated t4at this
Levy will realize, w ith interest, approximately £6,000, in 1935.
Recommendations of the Third Australian Masonic Conference,
held at Sydney, in July, 1928, were adopted. One assumes uniformity
of Signs, Tokens, a~d Words for all Australian Grand Jurisdictions.
Another provides that a Brother who ceases to be an affiliated member of a Lodge for a period of more than one year shall not be permitted to visit any Lodge unless by dispensation from the Grand
Master. A third prohibits membership in and the attendance of any
meeting of the Order of the Eastern Star; it also excludes the Eastern
Star from holding ·meetings in any Lodge room. A fourth declares
that "it is not desirable that Lodges should become so large in numbers as to prejudice members from engaging in and enjoying fraternal
intercourse with one another," a nd that the membership of a Lodge
should not exceed 150. A fifth wants each Lodge to appoint a Committee to visit sick or afflicted members, and to renew an interest in
their Lodge in members who absent themselves from Lodge meetings. It also recommends that the delivery of short talks upon the
symbolical meaning of the several parts of each ceremony in each
degree be encouraged, and that the Grand Lodges institute circulating libraries and arrange for the delivery of lectures.

Tasmania:
A new Ritual adhering as closely as practicable to the Emulation
Workings was adopted. Also a "Drill Book of Craft Masonry" giving
the Master's instructions as to a correct working of Degrees. Author-

Turkey:
The newspaper men among the membership, the physicians, the
artists, those ·interested in child welfare, and others held profitable
group meetings. The outstanding undertaking probably is the organization of a commission for the study of ways and means of how
Masons may h elp boys and adolescent young men to adhere to the
moral law and to share in the spirit of brotherhood and other inspirations cultivated by the Craft. Brother Andreas Somlo, Elizabethstrasse 2, Vienna, was made the Chairman. Under his leadership
many new Societies of young men have been formed in many centers.
In Holland and Switzerland such Societies have been fostere d by the
Masons for some years. In Vienna a splendid start was made. In
Prague, too, much practical good has been accomplished through the
zeal of the Brethren there.

136

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Other useful departments of work were formed under the chairmanship of outstanding specialists.
There is no intention of encroaching upon the field of Lodges or
Grand Lodges. The idea merely is to bring together Brethren Of
many Jurisdictions in an informal manner to enjoy the pleasures of
meeting with .one another, once a year, exchange experiences, and
be inspired to unite more closely, as the years go on, by ties of friendship and the profit gained by such intercourse, to be of service to
their time and generation.
The membership fee is only One Dollar a year. Members are not
bound to any embarrassing Declaration of Principles. It is just a
good-will get-together of Masons under fraternal auspices.
Victoria:
The Grand Master reported that "the outstanding feature" of
1927 was the purchase of twenty-five acres of land for the establishment of a future Masonic Institution comprising a Hospital for
Brethren and their dependents, a Convalescent Home for those not
yet able to resume their usual tasks, and a Hostel for the aged and
infirm, who by reason of their affliction can not be cared for in the
Freemasons' Homes.
Active interest in the Boy Scout and the Big Brother movement
is commended to the Brethren. They are also asked to support the
National War Memorial of Victoria for the Shrine of Remembrance.
Western Australia:
Grand Lodge joined the other Australian Jurisdictions in sending
an invitation to the Grand Lodge of England to have a Delegation
visit them.
For the twenty-eighth year in succession the books of Grand
Lodge have closed without there being one single Lodge in arrears.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as t he York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be t.e rmed the American Rite and the Scottish
Rite,' for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized
proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic beca use t heir prominent mode of inst ruction is
by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are t he
Mark Master, · the Past Master, the Most Excellent Mast er and the
Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests upon those who have
been regularly elected to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a
Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are confer~ed in a Council. They .are the
Royal Mas ter, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or unde.i ;ground passage.
The T emplar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the
temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them, are: L odge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °,
inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15 ° to 18 ° ; Council of Kad<>sh, 19 ° ·
to 30° Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States north of
the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River); the degrees conferred are : Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council Princes
of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Crnix, 17° and 18°; C<>nsistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33•.

Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple

Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.

JOHN STEWART ROSS
Grand Master
1930

John Stewart Ross
Grand Master 1930-1931

John Stewart Ross, sixty-fourth Grand Master of Masons in the
jurisdiction of California, was born May 21, 1879, at Osceola, Nebraska.
The. family removed to California shortly thereafter, and he received his
early education in the public schools of Pomona, San Diego and Los
Angeles, graduating from the Los Angeles High School in 1897; he
received his A.B. degree at the University of .California in 1902, and the
degree of LL.B. from Harvard Law School in the year 1905.
On May 5, 1906, he was married to the charming Dora Bramlett of
Fresno and to them were born two daughters, Isabella and Anna Head,
and two sons, Neil and John Gordon. The family made their home at
Los Angeles where he practiced law ~rom 1906 until 1910, in which year
he took up his residence at El Centro in the Imperial Valley, where he
lived and continu<!d to practice until 1927. Upon his election and installation as Junio_r Grand Warden he removed his family to Los Angeles and
closed his once busy law office at El Centro.
During the period of his residence in Imperial Valley he was the legal
representative of some of the largest concerns operating there, including
the Imperial Irrigation District, and was active in all fraternal and civic
affairs. He served as member and President of the Board of Directors of
the Central Union High School District; President of the El Centro
Rotary Club; representative of the District Governor in the organization
of Rotary Clubs at Calipatria, Brawley and Holtville; and President of
the Imperial Valley Scottish Rite Club.
John Stewart Ross was raised a Master Mason in Highland Park
Lodge, No. 382, on June 9, 1910, and thereupon began a long, busy career
in the Masonic vineyard. He received his Chapter Degrees in Los Angeles
Chapter No. 33, R. A. M., in September, 1910, and the 'Council in Los ·
Angeles Council No. 11, in November, 1910; he was knighted in Imperial
Valley Commandery No. 24, March 14, 1916. He received the Scottish Rite
Degrees from the 4th to the 32nd concluding on October 6, 1911, in the

•• >.

•

Los Angeles Bodies; he was coroneted K. C. C. H. in October, 1919, and
was elected to the 33rd Degree in October, 1927.
During the years of his activities he served as Worshipful Master of
El Centro Lodge No. 384, Inspector of his Masonic District, member of
the Grievance Committee of Grand Lodge, member of the Board of
Trustees of the Masonic Hom~s, High Priest of El Centro Chapter
No. 109, Commander of Imperial Valley Commandery No. 24, Inspector
of the Grand Commandery, Potentate of Al Bahr Temple, San Die~o, and
its representative to the Imperial Council. He was elected Junior ~rand
Warden of the Grand Lodge in October, 1927, and has devoted hiplself
to Masonry from that time forward, being elected Grand Master in 1930.
His frank and outspoken stand for the right as he sees it ~as won
for him the respect and admiration of .his fellow citizens as well as his
brethren in Masonry.

MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
·. Brethre11 of the Gran.d Lodge:

Today we assemble for the eighty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the · jurisdiction of California. One year
ago, when you installed me as Grand Master, I faced the responsibilities and duties you bade me assume, as a challenge. I am before
you at this hour to present an account of my official acts during the .
year, to exhibit the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and to recommend such legislation as I deem expedient for the
welfare of the craft. I fully realize that I have not measured up to
the full standard set by the honor, dignity, and importance of. the,
office, but I have done my best.

The ceremonies of laying t)le cornerstones of the Masonic Temple
at Santa Paula and of the Federal Building at Pomona were performed at night under the electric lights. I know of no previous
occasion on which such a ceremony has been performed at night, but
I believe that in each instance the change in hour added to the attendance and the beauty of the ceremony in every way.

The time came, however, when prudence and wisdom suggested
the consideration of other arrangements. A committ ee was therefore
appointed by the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles to consider
the abandoning of the Masonic cemetery and the removal of the
bodies theretofore interred, to another cemetery. Thus t he Masonic
section of Fo1>est Lawn came into being.
The contract for the purchase of the plot was entered into in
the fall of 1917. The contract with Forest Lawn set forth the expressed desire on the part of the Masons to have a plot adequate for
all the reasonable needs of memb ers of the fratern ity and for the
erection in t his plot of a memorial appropriately representative of
Masonry. This memorial is distinctive for many reasons: its very
hugeness makes it impressive; it is situated on a lot 43 73 feet by 54
feet; the size of the memorial itself is 39 feet by 44 feet 10 inches.
Into its design have been woven many of the cardinal principles of
Masonry·: the three, five, and seven steps; the two columns, one with
the terrestrial and the other wit h the celestial sphere, and the altar
with the Bible opened whereat is t he Divine command, "Let there be
Light." Around the altar there have been inscribed those virtues
which form the foundation of Masonry-"Brotherly Love, Relief,
Truth."
The Grand Lodge of the jurisdiction of California having been
invited by the Masons of Los Angeles to dedicate this beautiful
monument, it was by me convened at Glendale, California, on the
26th day of September, 1931; and at 3 :30 p. m. the Maso nic Memorial
Monument was dedicated accord ing to the ancient form and usage to
the cardinal principles of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth. A tablet
appropriately and symbolically ties in the dale of its dedieation with
that of the founding of Masonry.
The Masons of Los Angeles are to be congratulated not only on
this beautiful monument, but as well on the Masonic section of Forest
Lawn Memorial Park.

Aahmes Temple Widows and Orphans Fund
At our last annual communication, the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommended that the controversy over a death
benefit of $1500.00 claimed by the Masonic Homes of California from
the Widows and Orphans Fund of Aahmes Temple "should be adjusted by Masons in a spirit of kindness, and on a basis of equity,"
and that a special committee of three be appointed with fu ll power to
adjust. While Grand Lodge concurred in this recommendation, I felt
that the Masonic attitude of the brethren who administer and compose
the Fund on the one hand, and the brethren who are the Trustees of

44<:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

our Homes on the other, was such that the matter could be adjusted
without the necessity of a formally appointed committee.
The committee's report erroneously referred to the claim as one
against Aahmes Temple. The Temple, as such, has no control over
the Fund, and the fund consists of only a portion. of the members
of the Temple who voluntarily join.
Believing that all differenC!!S of opinion should be reconciled in
a spirit of Masonic brotherhood, rather than on any basis of technical
legal rights, I discussed the situation at length with Brother Herbert
L. Breed, the chairman of the Fund, and found him more than willing .
to meet me in this spirit. Both he and his committee whom he specially
called together, agreed that under the circumstances existing in this
unfortunate case, where the beneficiary was a resident of the Decato
Home at the time of his death, and also at the time he became delinquent to Aahmes Temple, it would be a most graceful Masonic act
for the Fund to pay the amount to the Homes.
Brother Breed called a largely attended general meeting of the
Fund to consider the situation, at which I was present. After fully
and fairly stating the situation, he recommended· that, without regard
to its legal rights, the F.und voluntarily make the payment as an exemplification of Masonic charity. His recommendation was unanimously
approved, and the amount has been paid to the Trustees of the Homes.
I am glad to be able to report that because of this voluntary payment by the Fund, any discussion of legal rights in the premises
becomes unnecessary. However, Grand Lodge should understand
that the committee in charge of the Fund is bound to administer it in
accordance with its by-laws; of this there can be no ·doubt; equally,
there can be and is no question in the mind of anyone that when payment was refused, the administrative officers of the Fund acted in
accordance with what they were and still are convinced is a proper
construction of the by-laws of the Fund, and their legal obligations
to th~ Fund and its membership.
It is true that Brother Alexander was in suspension in the Fund
by reason of not having paid his dues to Aahmes Temple, though he
was not in arrears in the payment of his assessments to the Fund.
I commend Brother Breed and his committee for the truly
Masonic spirit which they have exemplified in recommending that the
amount be voluntarily and willingly paid to our Masonic Homes,
·n otwithstanding their conviction a·s to the lack of legal responsibility.
I also express to the membership of the Fund the appreciation of
Grand Lodge for concurring in the recommendation of the Administrative Committee.

Suspension of a Master
At our last annual communication, the Board of Control reported
(1930 Proc. p. 255) facts which it termed "A striking case" and on
the recommendation of the Board of Control, Grand Lodge ordered
the Lodge in question to reimburse the Los Angeles Board of Relief
for funds amounting to $197.00 in the relief of one of its members.
On a demand for the funds by the Board of Relief after the November
stated meeting of said Lodge, the Master replied that the matter was
continued to the December stated meeting. After the December stated
meeting the Board of Relief was again informed by the Master that
he had postponed action until the January meeting. It appearing that
his successor had been elected and would be installed before the
January stated meeting, I suspended the Master from office just
before his successor was installed, because of his ·continued defiance
of constituted authority as evidenced by his refusal to comply with
the mandate of Grand Lodge and because of his previous actions as
fully set forth by the Board of Control. This action .deprived him of
the rank of Past Master.
His successor in office immediately caused the reimbursement
of the Los Angeles Board of Relief. The Lodge has since then, with
the co-operation of the Board of Relief of Los Angeles, been doing
its full duty toward its member in distress and his wife and daughter.

Public Schools Week
Public Schools Week has become an institution in California. It
was started by Grand Master Adams and this year we had the twelfth
annual observance. Each year the observance has been under the
direct leadership of Brother Adams and his committee. Through his
painstaking and intelligent study of the reports from each of the
Lodges during the years since he was Grand Master in 1919 he has
been able to develop the Public Schools Week from what at its inception was a Masonic event to the community institution it now is. The
purpose of the observance has gradually enlarged and might now be
stated as follows: To afford an opportunity for the people to be kept
thoroughly informed of California's program of public education, to
combat destructive criticism, to aid in correcting errors which may
creep into the system, and to insure the close contact between the
public and its schools so essential to a continuance of the friendship,
faith and confidence upon which they necessarily depend.
Th~ value of this obs.ervance cannot be judged from experiences
in any one community, in any one year and under any one leadership.
Conditions may be such i~ a community that its necessity may not be
apparent, but if permitted to lapse, its value may become apparent
only when it is too late, for destructive forces work the more effectively when other forces are asleep. In this as in all other things,
leadership is all important.
I desire now to express the sincere thanks of Grand Lodge to
Brother Adams and his committees and to those Masters, Inspectors
and other brethren whose efforts have made the twelfth annual
observance of Public Schools Week so great a success. Brother
Adams; I am sure will give you an interesting account of it.

Masonic Education
The necessity of our membership µnderstanding the nature of
the art of Freemasonry, what it means, what its ideals are, what its
purposes are and what its possibilities are in the human soul and in
society as well is realized by all Grand Lodges today. For some years
many Grand Lodges have been experimenting with the hopes of
finding some method of filling this necessity.
Grand Master Bledsoe in 1915 appointed the first Committee on
Masonic Education in this jurisdiction. One year ago I found that a
committee under the chairmanship of Brother Irving Magnes, with
very little change of personnel, had been studying methods and administering this important Grand Lodge activity since 1925. I did not
then know, nor do I now know of any group of men better qualified
to carry on this enterprise. Because of their experience in this work,
I regarded them the best qualified and so re-appointed them as the
Masonic Educatio~al Committee. Realizing tha-t I ·had not sufficient
knowledge of the subject to assist or direct them, I delegated to them
full power and authority to conduct the activity with which they were
charged. The committee will make its report for your consideration.
The place that Massachusetts has reached in its program of
Masonic Education, as reported at the Grand Masters' Conference,
by Grand Master Dean, may i~terest you. H~ said:
·
"Briefly what we are doing is giving up the primary idea of the
education of the whole fraternity, which we found almost impossible
to accomplish, and reaching those . over whom we do have control,
namely, the candidates. We form groups of Lodges running from
3. to 15 which are conveniently located. They agreed to send their
candidates to the school of instruction,. which is instructi.o n not in
the ritual, but in the practical things of Masonry, what Masonry is,
what it is designed to do, the history of Freemasonry, some things
about our charitable enterprises-the Home, the. Hospital, and the
Board of Relief; we tell them what the collateral bodies, so-called,
are which we recognize and we also state very plainly those organizations which are not Masonic and which have no connection with

Masonry as far as we are concerned .. Our idea being to have the
candidates, when they complete the third degree, know ~ore about
Masonry than any of us did when we had COI?pleted our third degree.
We are building for the future, inasmuch as if we proceed at the rate
we are going, with 3500 candidates \!. year, we ~gure that .at the e!ld of
ten years we will have 35,000 Masons who will be running affairs. at
that time and who have the ground work of Freemasons, who reahze
the things that Masonry can do and the things it cannot do.
"These ·Lodges of Instruction
1 while being primarily for candi0
dates are open to all Ma ster Ma sons. We find in many of t~ese
Lodies of Instruction that we are getting 200 to 300 present besides
candidates."
Decisions and Recommendations
The Grand Lodge of the jurisdiction of California is bound to a
"strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks of the Order, and by the
provisions of its own Constitution and Regulations." (Constitution,
section 7.)
"By a regulation of 'the Grand Lodge is meant any resolutio~,
edict law or ordinance of any kind whatever, other than the Constltutio~, which it may adopt." (Constitution, section 228.)
"The ritual itself constitutes binding law regarding th~ matters
contained in the written law, and as to these matters, the office !Jf the
Constitution and Regulations is substantially to construe the ritual."
(Macka:y's Masonic Jurisprudence.)
The law that binds every Mason in this jurisdiction is to be
found in the Ancient Landmarks of the Order, our Ritual, the Constitution or the Regulations. I have found officers of Lodges attempting to justify illegal actions on their part by asserting that at some
time or other some Grand Lodge officer had advised them to proceed
in the way they were doing. Inasmuch as it is only the decisions of
the Grand Master · that are submitted to Grand Lodge for adoption,
and become Regulations, not necessarily in the form submitted, but
in the form adopted by Grand Lodge, .I have welcomed questions by
Masters on the construction of our laws. I have answered many
questions by a reference to our Constitution or Regulations. In those
instances if the Master had taken the trouble to consult the written
law or even to have asked his Inspector, who could have referred
him' to the written law as well as I, he would have had his answer
when he wanted it, instead of having to wait until the Grand Master
had had time to hunt the answer up for him and communicate it to
him. Those decisions I have rendered are here reported for your
consideration.
Decision 1. At various times Inspectors have asked for an interpretation of the law as to their powers and duties.
The Inspector is appointed by the Grand Master, is the representative of the Grand Master in the district, and as such shall be
received with grand honors on official visits. He, as representa:tive of

the Grand Master, should take such steps as are necessary to require
the officers of the Lodges of his district to comply with the laws of
Grand Lodge, and, if necessary, report infractions of law to the Grand
Master.
He is also the representative of the Grand Lecturer in matters
pertaining to the ritual.

It is his duty to instruct and 1qualify the officers of the Lodges
of his district, and to issue certificates to such as are qualified where
required by sections 136 and 137 of the Constitution. In order that
he may so instru.c t the officers and determine whether or not they
are entitled to receive certificates, he may require attendance of the
officers of his district in one or more groups as may be most convenient in his district, at such times as he or the Grand Lecturer
may direct.
All Masters-elect and Senior and Junior Wardens-elect are
.required by the Constitution to be thoroughly proficient in those
portions of the Constitution and General Regulations of the Grand
Lodge which relate to the government of a Lodge, as well as in
ritual. An Inspector should not give a certificate unless he has knowl~dge that the one receiving it is thoroughly proficient.
Decision 2. My attention has been called to the declaration hv
this Grand Lodge in 1888 (Proc. pp. 464, 678) that "the indispensable
Qualification of a candidate for initiation is that he must have faitli
in the true God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob," and I have been asked
if such a belief is still indispensable.
I answered that in 1857 (Proc. p. 105) this Grand Lodge declared
that Masonry is not a religious order "except insofar as it requires a
helief in the existence and omnipotence of a Supreme Being."
That in 1894 (Proc. pp. 541, 771) Grand Master Orme ruled and
·
his decision was adopted by Grand Lodge, that
'.'0th.er than a belief i.n '.'- Supreme Being, there is ~o religious
qualification for membership m the Masonic order."
In view. of this later decision at variance with the decision of
1888, I held that a belief in God defined as the true God of Abraham,
Isaac and Jacob if ever indispensable, can no longer be regarded as
such.
Furthermore, the Jurisprudence Committee points out in app~ov­
ing the decision in 1894, "That law (referring to its statement in the
decision) is older than Grand Lodg.e, and is ·a landmark which no
man or body of men has power to change."
·
In 1913 (Proc. p. 162) this Grand Lodge sets forth " Belief in
God" as one. of the Ancient Landmarks that must be recognized and
supported by a grand body of an English speaking country seeking
recognition by this Grand Lodge.

451

"Landmark Nineteenth" as expressed in "Foundations of Masonic
Law," authorized by this Grand Lodge to be published with the Constitution, is as follows:
"A belief in the existence of God as the Great Architect of the
Universe."
There never was a. time when this belief did not form an essential
part of the Masonic system. Beyond this Masonry offers no definition
of the Supreme Being.
Decision 3. Questions continue to come as to physical qualifications of applicants for the degrees.
I have held:
That our ritual determines this .question and that section 94 of the
Constitution must be read in connection with the ritual and as a
construction thereof.
The amendment to section 94 of the Constitution in 1928 in no
way changed our law as to physical requirements; that the question
involved is a question of fact, rather than a question of law, and those
asking such questions, being in possession of the evidence» were the
best qualified to answer them.
That the 1928 amendment simply permitted the Lodge, after the
Master had stated the nature and extent of the disabilities of the candidate, to determine the fact as to whether or not the maim or defect
in his body would rend~r him incapable of learning the art, and
whether or not he was physically able to conform substantially to
what the several degrees respectively require of him.
That the Lodge may determine this fact by ballot previous to the
voting upon the ballot for th e degrees of Masonry, and if by this
preliminary ballot the applicant is found disqualified because of physical disability the Master may direct the withdrawal of the application
without further action, and such direction shall be entered upon the
record as provided in section 104 of the Constitution.
It is, however, the question of fact of the physical sufficiency of
the candidate that is to be determined and not the question as tu
whether or not the Lodge is willing to admit him in spite of the fact
that he is physically ·insufficient. The latter misconception of the law
is found among many of the Lodges and has led to the admission of
applicants physically insufficient.
I have held that the fact for a Lodge to determine is whether or
not the applicant is physically able to conform substantially to what
the several degrees respectively require of him without the aid of an
artificially substituted hand or leg.

Decision 4. If a Mason h;i.iling from the Grand Lodge Vallee de
Mexico (said Grand Lodge being recognized by the Grand Lodge of
Arizona but not by the Grand Lodge of California) should affiliate
with a Lodge holding obedience to the Grand Lodge of Arizona and
then withdraw from such Lodge, he could without question lawfully
affiliate with a Lodge of our obedience . .
Query: Could such a Mason lawfully affiliate with one of our
Lodges direct from the Lodge Vallee de Mexico? And if so, should
such Mason be "healed" after election?
My answer: Constitution, section 124, provides "No Lodge shall
. . . admit or hold Masonic intercourse . . . with any Mason not
acknowledged as such by this Grand Lodge." Hence no Lodge of this
jurisdiction can lawfully receive an application for affiliation from a
Master Mason holding a <limit from a regular Lodge of a jurisdiction
not formally recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
"Healing" is reobligating. A Lodge can not reobligate a Mason
with whom it cannot hold Masonic intercourse. Reobligating is not
necessary under said section 124, and nowhere in our Constitution
is there a provision for healing.

Decision 5. I was asked for a decision by the Master of Turlock

Under date of August 11, 1924,. an applicant presented an application dated August 1, 1924, for degrees to Seattle Lodge No. 164,

My answer was as follows:
Applicant received the degrees of Masonry in Seattle Lodge No.
164. Seattle Lodge is a subordinate of the Grand Lodge of Washington, therefore its work was regular. Applicant was expelled by
that Lodge for cause in a trial had upon charges based upon hi11

tion among the Lodges, convinces me that the result hoped for by the
amendment to the Constitution, section 94, in 1928, has not been
attained. But on the contrary in an attempt to comply with the law
Masters have repeatedly submitted to a vote of the Lodges the question as to the physical sufficiency of a candidate having disabilities
that they well knew would prevent him from conforming substantially
or at all to what the several degrees respectively required of him. This
has resulted in flagrant violation of the Constitution by Masters and
Lodges.
The word "substantially" in the Constitution, section 94, also
gives rise to confusion. If an applicant "substantially conforms," he
conforms. There is no force to the word "substantially." The applicant either conforms or does not conform. If a Lodge admits an
applicant who cannot conform as required, it violates Landmark First
as authorized by this Grand Lodge to be published in the Blue Book.
. I recommend that the Constitution, section 94, be amended by
striking out the word "substantially" and the last two sentences of
the section.

library and as a joint owner to contribute to the said association.

Decision 6. A ruling was asked on the right of Lodges to support the Masonic Library Association of Los Angeles.
Past Grand Master Wollenberg reported in regard to this subject
as follows:
"In April I received a communication from the Secretary of
East San Diego Lodge No. 561 calling attention to a circular of the
'Masonic Library of Southern California, Inc.' suggesting by way of
financial assistance a 'contribution could be made by the Lodge.'
"My reply was that such a contribution by a Lodge would be in
contravention of the provisions of section 88 of the Constitution and
could not be permitted.
"This led to a considerable correspondence with the President
of the library, and finally a meeting at the library in Los Angeles.
"There is no question that a Lodge could spend its funds for the
purchase of books and maintenance of a library for the benefit of its
members, and that likewise several Lodges could unite in such an
activity. This library, however, is a private corporation, and although
organized by the Lodges of Southern California, it is no longer under
their control. The Masonic Library of Los Angeles is a necessary
institution, and should be of great value to the brethren of the southern
part of the State, and the programme of the directors of the corporation is one that deserves support of the Lodges. . They recognize that
the value of a Masonic library consists in a great degree upon its
accessibility to those who have the desire or the necessity to consult
its volumes. Their present financial set-up does not make this, the
largest collection of books on Masonic subjects in our State, as accessible as they should be."

Decision 7. From one Lodge I received a petition for a dispensation to open Lodge and confer a degree in a Lodge room located in
the same building in which was located the Lodge room in which it
regularly met.
I held that under our Constitution it could properly do as prayed
for in its petition and that a dispensation was not necessary.
From another Lodge I received a petition for a dispensation to
open Lodge and confer a degree in a Lodge room located in a building
other than that in which it regularly met.
I held that under our Constitution this could not be done, and
consequently I had no power to grant the dispensation prayed for.
These decision~ involve the interpretation of several sections of
the Constitution.
The dispensation to form a Lodge and the charter following it,
name only the town or city in which the Lodge is to meet. However,
section 73 requires th e proposed Lodge to name " the location of the
Lodgeroom or hall." Thus its "place of meeting" is fixed and can . be
removed only as provided in section 93. If that "place of meeting" is a
building having more than one Lodge room, the Lodge may meet in
any of the Lodge rooms therein or in ·different ones at different times;
but under section 78 the Lodge room in which it opens becomes the
appointed Lodge room therein, "there can be no adjourned meeting
and each meeting of a Lodge must be closed when the business which
it is proposed to transact at that meeting has been concluded."
, Hence a Lodge can c_o nfer a degree only in a Lodge room in the
building it has fixed as its place of meeting, and when opened in one

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

room it must close in the same room with no adjournment between
opening and closing.

Decision 8. During the year I have. received a number of requests
made to me by Lodges by a unanimous vote by ballot for the issuance
of dispensations to reballot within a year on rejected applicants. I
have in every instance refused such requests on the ground that the
Constitution does not grant the power to the Grand Master to issue
such a dispensation. Section 43, subd. 4th does grant power to grant
dispensations to receive and act upon the petitions of rejected applicants, which means to permit the Lodge to receive new petitions, but
it does not mean to reballot on the petition on which an applicant has
been rejected, so that the Lodge may avoid breaking the unpleasant
news of his rejection to the applicant.
·
In this connection I have had occasion to reprimand Secretaries
as severely as I was capable of doing, for not notifying applicants in
clear and concise language of their rejection when they were rejected.
It too often happens that Secretaries, in order to save the feelings of a
rejected applicant, notify him in such a way that he at least claims
that he didn't know he was rejected. I have held such action on the
part of Lodge officers to be a gross violation of their duty, and had I
not been convinced of the best of motives on the part of Secretaries,
though inexcusable in fact, I would have ordered charges of unmasonic
conduct to be preferred against them. I am satisfied that the same
Secretaries will not commit this error again and I trust others will
take notice.
I have also refused to grant dispensations to receive and act upon
the petitions of rejected applicants as provided for, except where the
individual who had cast a cube admitted that he did it, and gave assurance that he did it either through mistake or inadvertence which he
desired to rectify, or because of some reason that was no longer
operative with him. I have made such refusals not in the exercise of
discretion but because I felt bound by the law of this Grand Lodge
adopted in 1853 (Proc., p. 262; Digest, 223) as follows:
"The Con~titl!tion of our Grand Lodge says, Article X Section
14: · 'On the reJect10n of any applicant for initiation or memb~rship by
any ~odge under the juris.diction. of this Grand Lodge, the Secretary
of said Lodge shall forthwith notify all the Lodges in said jurisdiction
thereof, and no . Lodge shall be allowed to receive his petition short
of one year from such rejection.' This law is imperatively binding
not only on each · of. the subordinat~ Lodges, but also on the Grand
Lodge? o,r any occa~10nal L<?dge which may be convened by virtue of
the ex1~tmg Masomc authority, as regularly constituted and acknowledged .m the Grand Lodge of California. Nor will it admit of a dispensation, while the cause remains which induced the rejection.

Decision 9. In the case where the Senior Warden had succeeded
to the office and duties of Master, upon the death or disability of the
Master of the Lodge, as provided in Constitution,. section 148, and
interpreted by this Grand Lodge 1894, (Proceedings, p. 765; Digest, .
113), I was asked if the Senior Warden automatically assumes the
title of Master? If so, what happens to the office of Senior Warden?
My answer was that the Senior Warden, succeeding to the powers
and duties of Master, assumed that title. There is, however, no
vacancy in the 9ffice of Senior Warden. He not being able to physically fill the stations of Master and Senior Warden at one and the
same time, the station of Senior W;tr.den must be filled by appointment for each meeting. Not having been elected as Master he will
· not become a Past Master at the expiration of the term of the Master
whose powers and duties he had assumed.
The foregoing decision was made reluctantly, although it is the
law of this jurisdiction. The rule in my judgment rests upon no
proper foundation of reason or logic and is not a proper construction
of section 148 of the Constitution.
In construing sections 138 and 148 of the Constitution, it is my
opinion that the office of Master becomes vacant by reason of the
death or resignation of the Master and that such vacancy can be filled
only by an election. During the time of such vacancy the Senior
Warden (or in his absence the Junior Warden) succeeds to the powers
and duties of the Master and acts as Master pro tempore. If the
Senior Warden automatically and ipso facto succeeded to the office
and title of Master, then there would be no vacancy and therefore
there could be nb dispensation to elect a Master as provided for by

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

section 138. There would be no vacancy in the office of a Warden
who was acting as Master pro tempore, because his very right to act
as such is based upon the fact that he is such a Warden, authorized
by the Constitution to exercise the functions of a 'Master in case of a
vacancy, until the election by the Lodge of a Master.
Because of the confusion that l'tas arisen by re~son of said decision
of 1894, I recommend that said decision be abrogated. If said decision
is abrogated, -then my ruling would fall with said decision and the
law would be clear that a vacancy in the office of Master could be
filled only by an election,' and that a Warden succeeding to the powers
and duties of such office would act as such only pro tempore, and
would have neither the office nor the title of the Master.

Decision 10. The question as to whether or not the right to
apply for membership in a Lodge is a right, privilege, or benefit of
Masonry, which may be lost by a Master Mason under the . terms of
Constitution, section 165, has caused much· confusion among officers
of Lodges since the amendment of that section _a t the last communication of Grand Lodge.
I have held that the right to apply for membership in a Lodge
is not a Masonic right but a right possessed by any one. Our Constitution does not say who can or cannot apply, but section 122 does
state the requisites of an application before a Lodge can receive it.
Section 98 requires that only· an application for affiliation in the
form prescribed in section 247 can be received by a Lodge. None but
dimitted Master Masons in good standing and applicants for dual
membership can comply with the form prescribed.
Hence applications for affiliation.
1st. From a member of a Lodge in this jurisdiction accompanied
by a receipt for dues and demand for a dimit as provided by section
161, or
2d. From a member of 1 a Lodge in another jurisdicti9n, accompanied by a certificate from his Lodge that a dimit will be issued on
notice of his election to membership in a Lodge of this jurisdiction; or
3d. From a Master Mason accompanied by a proper dimit dated
more than one year previous to the reception of his application by a
Lodge, any of which applications a Lodge is permitted to. receive
under section 122 of the Constitution, cannot be. received because the
form prescribed in section 247 does not provide fo~ them.
I have held that the substantive law as set forth in section 122
governs, and that when the form prescribed does not apply, a form
not prescribed but conforming to section 122 may be received, and ·
that an application for affiliation from a non-affiliated Master Mason

Decision 11. I have been asked if the Secretary of a Lodge can

from one applicant, and that when that application' is received by the
Lodge, as provided in section 101, it is the duty of the Secretary to
keep that application in the archives of the Lodge so that it shall not
be altered; that neither the Secretary nor any one else has the .right
to require an applicant to fill the form prescribed except for the purpose of its being received by the Lodge; that the so-called filling out
of the form in quadruplicate is in truth and in ·fact the presentation of .
four separate applications, which is not required and should not be
permitted.

Decision 14. Question: Referring to the Constitution, sections
99, 101, 104; First : Can the Master of a Lodge appoint an investigating committee which shall be known only unto himself?
My answer was yes.
Second: Shall the report of the investigating committee be
known only to the Master of the Lodge?
My answer was yes. The fact of the appointment of the committee and . the character of the report (favorable or unfavorable)
should appear in the minutes and be made known to the Lodge.
Third: What is the Secretary's position with reference to the
above two questions?
I answered as follows: To obey the will and pleasure of the
Master. In order that the Secretary may mail requests for reports
to the committeemen, the Master may make the names of the committeemen known to the Secretary. It is not within the rights of the
Master to delegate that appointment of the committees to the Secretary, or to permit him to read the reports.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

463

Fourth: Referring to the Constitution, sections 150, 151, 152,
Digest, sections 21, 22, etc. The general understanding is that all
books · and records of a Lodge are confidential. If this is correct, by
what authority can a Lodge publish a roster of its membership for
distribution ?
I answered as follows: Our law does not prohibit a Lodge furnishing a roster of its membership to its members for proper use.
Though not prohibited, it is appropriate that a warning be given to
the membership respecting the unauthorized and unwarranted publication or use of rosters of members. The sole purpose of publishing
such a roster should be for Masonic uses and for the benefit of the
1hembers. It should never be used for advertising or as a "sucker
list," or for the commercial exploitation of Masonry or of the members. The publication of such rosters opens the door to serious abuses
and Masters of Lodges are charged with an obligation, if not a requirement of the Constitution, t.o prevent any unauthorized or unwarranted
use of such a list.
·
My answers to the first three of the above questions are based
upon m)9 interpretation of sections 99 and 100 of the Constitution,
together with sections 142 and 150 thereof.
Section 99 prescribes that the investigating committee shall report
to the Master; section 100 that "the names of the members of the
committee shall not be made known except to the Master and. the
Secretary." However, section 142 provides that "the Master shall
have the power" (and it is certainly his duty) "3d to discharge all the
executive functions of his Lodge." No such powers or duties are
assigned to the Secretary in section 150 or elsewhere.
The most important executive function that a Master is called
upon to discharge is the selection of members and that he does
through committees, which, to work efficiently, must be directed by
him. In the last analysis the quality of our members is going to
determine the future of our Institution and the mere aggregation of
individuals is a liability. Because of the financial responsibilities w hich
are bound to be entailed in the growth in numbers, he must consider
the financial responsibility and the social aspect of those his Lodge
takes in. He must see that his committees get the facts necessary to
determine whether the applicants have the necessary moral, mental,
physical and other ?roper qualifications. Applicants not possessing
such qualifications usually are potential financial liabilities who will
in time make it necessary for the Lodge to draw on the fees from
candidates for the payment of necessary expenses of the Lodge. Those
fees .s hould constitute a sacred trust fund to meet special calls for
charity for which the Lodge was instituted.

No man should be made a Mason unless he have "an estate,
office, trade, occupation, or some visible way of acquiring an honest
livelihood, as becomes the members of this most ancient and honorable fraternity; who ought not only earn a sufficiency for themselves
and families, but likewise have something to spare for works of
charity and mercy." (I quote from Hardies old Manual, and believe
it to be good doctrine now.)
In the exercise of this most important executive function, the
Master should not only direct his committees but should see to it that
the members that he appoints on his committees are instructed so
that they will be qualified to discharge the important functions with
which they are charged. It is most certainly, in my opinion, the
Master's duty to appoint the investigating committees.

Recommendation p: Constitution, section 87, provides "It (a
Lodge) may, through trustees provided for in a standing resolution,
who shall always be under its control, hold, mortgage, sell and otherwis~ dispose of its property and funds, which may be invested and
reinvested as the Lodge shall direct."
In 1914 {pp. 21, 129-Digest, 429) Grand Lodge adopted Grand
Master Murphey's decision that the statute of the State of California
(Statutes 1911, p. 1093) "does away with the necessity for conveying
to trustees and the corresponding difficulty of keeping track of their

The statute referred to qualifies such power as is given to the
branch of the fraternal association as follows: "Subject to the laws
and regulations of said society or association."
The question is often raised by counsel for title companies as
to whether or not Constitution, section 87, gives a Masonic Lodge
power to borrow money and to secure such borrowing by pledge of
real property belonging to the Lodge, or by conveyance of such real
property as security for a note of the Lo~ge, s~ch conveyance to be
in trust in the usual familiar form of a · trust deed.
In order to clarify this question, I recommend that Constitution,
section .87, be amended by inserting after the words " It may," and
befo~e the words "through trustees," the words "either in its own
name or."

Decision 24. During my absence from the State, R.".W.".Brother
Gaylord, Deputy Grand Master, acting under authority of Constitution, section 45, in response to questions from San Fernando Lodge
No. 343, gave an accurate and concise statement of the law pertaining
to the questions asked. I quote his decision so that Grand Lodge may
review it:
"You ask the general .question whether a person residing within
a normal jurisdiction may petition a Lodge in a neighboring jurisdiction, provided the distance between the 'two jurisdictions' is less
than ten miles, without a waiver. The answer to this question in the
form in which it is presented is 'No.' Section 82a of the Constitution provides that a person may petition any Lodge whose Lodge
room is within ten miles of his residence, notwithstanding ·the normal rules of jurisdiction. The distance between jurisdictions is immaterial. The determining factor is the Lodge room and the place
of residence. A person residing within a normal jurisdiction· may
petition a Lodge in a neighboring jurisdiction without a waiver, provided the distance between his place of residence and the location of
the Lodge room does not exceed ten miles.
"Your next question concerns contiguous jurisdictions, and the
question is whether a person living within ten miles 1of the 'boundary
line' between the two jurisdictions may, without a waiver, apply to
a Lodge in the jurisdiction across the line from his residence. The
above comments equally apoly to this question. The fact that the
person lives within ten miles of the boundary line does not of itself
permit him to apply to a Lodge across the line. On the other }land,
if there are two contiguous jurisdictions, a person living in one jurisdiction may, without a waiver, apply to a Lodge in the other jurisdiction, provided the distance between his place of residence and the
location of the Lodge room does not exceed ten miles.
.."Your final question is whether the answers apply to San Fernandb Lodge. By the resolution appearing in Decision 286, San
Fernartdo Lodge is' given exclusive jurisdiction in San Fernando and
also in the territory outside of San Fernando over which it had
jurisdiction immediately prior to annexation by the city of Los Angeles. This resolution was adopted in 1919 under section 92a of the
Constitution, which was adopted in 1912. Section 82a was adopted
at a still later date (1926). It permits application without waiver in
a jurisdiction outside the residence of the petitioner, provided the
distance between residence and Lodge room does not exceed ten miles,
'anything in this Constitution to the contrary notwithstanding.' Notwithstanding the definite language of section 92a regarding allotment
of exclusive jurisdiction to Lodges, I am of the opinion that section
82a controls section 92a, because of the chronology of adoption, and
the language of section 82a. It follows that it is my conclusion that
the above answers apply to San Fernando Lodge, and that a resident

Decision 25. I have been asked the following question:
What proceedings must be had to qualify an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft to advancement in the degrees of Masonry after
suspension for cause?
Answer; 1. If the suspension was by a trial commission in his
own Lodge, his Lodge may, after the record of suspension has been
reviewed and approved by· Grand Lodge (1925 p. 635-Digest, 461)
restore him under the provisions of Section 210 of the Constitution.
He would again "be an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft of his
own Lodge. He may then be advanced by his Lodge or by another
Lodge on a waiver of jurisdiction by his own Lodge the same as if no
suspension had occurred.
2. If the suspension was by a trial commission in another Lodge
he must apply for restoration to the Lodge which suspended him
(1905 pp. 17, 112-Digest, 463). Restoration by the Lodge that suspended him would not operate in and of itself to restore him as an
Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft in his own Lodge. That statt¥>
ceased upon his suspension by the trial Lodge affirmed by the Grand
Lodge, and that connection, having been thus completely extinguished, could only be revived by a new election on a new petition
for the remaining degree or degrees ( 1880, p. 563-Digest, 467) in his
own Lodge, or in another Lodge, on a waiver of jurisdiction by his
own Lodge and an election in the other Lodge.
3. If the suspension was by Grand Lodge on an appeal from
an acquittal or sentence or reprimand by a Lodge, the Lodge cannot restore -him under the provisions of Section 210 of the Constitution for it was Grand Lodge that suspended him (1868, p. 381-Digest,
366; 1878, p. 576-Digest, 367). He can only be restored by Grand
Lodge under provisions of secs. 211 and 212 of the Constitution. It is
not in the power of Grand Lodge to restore him as an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft of his own Lodge. Hence he can only
regain his status as an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft of his
own Lodge and be entitled to advancement after petition for the remaining degree or degrees in his own Lodge, or in another Lodge
on a waiver of jurisdiction by his own Lodge and an election in the
either Lodge (1880, p. 563-Digest, 467).

I report this case because. there seems to be a general. misconception that our law on automatic expulsion relieves !he _Jun~or Warden of his duty set forth in section 189 of the Constitution m a case

forth in section 189. The procedure is precisely as set forth m
section 192 in the case of a member imprisoned in pursuance of a final
judgment of conviction who has elected to have a trial in the Lodge.

D"ecision 28. A case was stated. where in open Lodge a member
moved that the Junior Warden be directed to prefer charges of
unmasonic conduct against a named brother. Another brother sought
to r!ebate the question and was ruled out of order by the Master on
the ground that such debate would be unfair to the accused, he not
being present. The motion was put and carried.

475

I held that the Master was right in his ruling debate out of order
but wrong in entertaining the motion. In no instance can a Lodge
prefer, dismiss or otherwise control charges.
Prior to 1928, Decisions and Regulations 410 had contained the
·syllabus, "The Lodge or Master may be accuser." An examination
of the citations under that syllabus reveals the fact that in no case
had the Lodge directed charges as in the above case attempted, but
that in one instance where the Mast er had directed charges it was
held the same as the Lodge directing them. However, in 1928 Grand
Lodge repealed 410 of Digest and Regulations. (Digest, 520.)
Under Constitution, section 189, it is the official duty of the
Junior Warden to prefer· charges within a certain time after the
facts are brought to his knowledge, and the Master may direct him
to do so. This makes sufficient provision, and a motion of this character should not be entertained.
Recommendation q: I recommend that Constitution, section 251,
be amended by striking out the words "the direction of the Lodge
or Master" in the second line ori page 233 and inserting in lieu thereof
the words " Constitution, section 189."
Also by striking out the words ."by direction of that Lodge (or
of the Master thereof)", as appear in the form following.
Then add after the last paragraph of the form direction as follows :
Should the charge be preferred by the Junior W arden under
the direction of the Master, the words "by direction of the Master
thereof" should be inserted in the foregoing paragraph after the
words " does hereby."
Our substantive law has been amended since this form was
adopted. It should .be amended to conform. with our present law.

Visitations
At the time I assumed the office of Grand Master I appreciated
that. my duties were executive, and I believed that in order for an
executive to administer the affairs of the Institution over which he is
called to preside with any degree of effi.ciency, it is necessary that he
inform himself on its conditions and its problems. With this in
view, I set out to visit each Inspectorial district in the jurisdiction.
I can now report that I have visited .e ach district at least once and
some districts more than once. To do that I have traveled in the
State of California in my own automobile, in excess of twenty-four
thousand miles. I found this method of travel to be a recreation, and
it enabled me to arrive at the place of my meeting at the hour the
brethren had fixed for it. It also permitted me to pass through the
county seat of every county in California and to appreciate the extent
and beauties of our State in a manner that I might not otherwise
have been- privileged to <lo.
Before making my visitations I advised each Inspector that if
any of the officers of the Lodges in his district desired to meet with
me informally, I would be very glad to meet with them. In response
to that suggestion I have been given the opportunity and privilege
of hearing their problems and methods of handling them from the

officers of practically every Lodge in this jurisdiction. From them I
have learned much of Masonry. It is they who are in touch with· the
individual members of our Lodges. Masonry is concerned with the
assistance and development of the individual. It is the individual
that does or does not practice outside of the Lodge those things that
he has been taught in it. It is for the Masters who have been intrusted
with leadership, to see that no Master Mason shall be led to believe
that our obligations are only a part of the ritual. I find that many
Masters are alive to their opportunities and personally or through
properly organized committees, make those personal contacts with
the members of the Lodge that are necessary to fulfill properly the
obligations of Masonry.
The recommendations to Grand Lodge that I have heretofore
made, in most instances are the results of one or more of these meetings with officers wherein we considered the questions involved as
if we had been acting as a committee of the whoie.
I trust that these meetings have likewise been of value to the
officers for I have endeavored to carry to each district those constructive suggestions that I had received in previous meetings.
This year with financial conditions as they are, the question of
the utilization of Masonic Charity Funds has been of frequent discussion,
The Best Utilization of Masonic Charity Funds
Relief is a basic principle in Masonry. It is the duty of a Mason
to contribute from his means to aid a worthy distressed brother and
his family. As a practical matter, however, Masonic relief of a material nature can never be sufficient in amount to take care of all the
needs of all the Masons whose misfortunes are such that they are
suffering.
This being the case, it is the part of wisdom to administer available relief funds in such a way as to make them go as far as possible.
The question may well be raised as to whether Masonry should undertake the entire burden of material relief for its distressed members
in those cases where other agencies can be utilized to carry part of
it. In many cases the best service the Masonic relief can render is to
bring to the aid of the distressed brother those non-Masonic sources
of help which are applicable to his condition, but which through lack
of information or inability to act he may not have been able to enlist
for himself. These include first of all, his own relatives, who may be
able to help but who for one reason or another have failed to ·do so.
For certain cases of need, State aid is available, both for children and
for the aged. It is my belief that the desire to make the proud boast
that "Masonry takes care of its own" should not deter Masonic relief

477

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

478

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

agencies from seeking and getting such aid. Public health service
agencies can often be called upon for needed medical or surgical
treatment.
Masons contribute, through taxes, to all the gove.rnment agencies
that extend relief and need have no hesitancy in calling on these·
agencies for aid. They also contribute a large part of the public donations given to our charities, and are entitled to the benefits from them.
Helping needy brothers to secure employment has long been
recognized as a constructive measure of relief, much better than giving
money. The extension of the same principle indicates the wisdom of
expending effort and time on repairing and reconstituting broken
family structures when this is possible. In many cases the condition
which produces misery and suffering r~sults from a repairable breakdown in family life. It is coming to be recognized that in the past
too much of our relief work, by taking individuals away from their
relatives and putting them into institutions, has separated families
and broken them up, whereas in many cases the same or less expenditure would have kept them together and put them back into successful
functioning. The fact that there. has seemed to exist the need for the
institutional method of relief has caused us to create institutions· once
we have them there is the tendency to use them in cases that' could
better be handled in other ways. A good doctor does not perform an
operation when a lesser measure will suffice.
Oftentimes the Masonic family in distress does not know w"hat
it needs. It may think it needs money or needs to get some of its
members into one of our Homes, when in fact fifty per cent or possibly seventy-five per cent of what it needs is intelligent planning to
show it how to put its own resources into effective operation, and
thereby work out its own problems.
Any given sum of money, whether $1000 or $100,000, available
for Masonic relief, can be made to go farther and produce more and
better results, if in conjunction with its use all other available agencies
and means, public or private, are called on alld induced to help.
A Master should not wait until calls come to him, for many are
too proud to ask. The 'Master, by personal investigation through a
committee, should acquaint himself with conditio~s of his members
that might entitle them to assistance.
. In many Lodges the Committee on Delinquent Members, prescribed by Regulation 121, procures this information. That committee,
if it does its work efficiently, should have members that continue over
from year to year· in order that the committee may have a continuity
that will enable it to know whether or not a member, when he becomes
t.welve months delinquent in his dues, is entitled to remission of dues,

479

or whether the Master should do that which the Constitution requires
him to do if the man is not entitled to such remission. The committee
should be in a position at the time he is delinquent in his dues for a
period of twelve months, to advise whether or not a member is ~n­
titled to relief to the extent of his Lodge paying his dues for the period
of· delinquency. If he is entitled to that relief it should be given him
and a receipt issued to him to date, charging the same to the Lodge.
This should be done whether he requests it or not; otherwise his dues
will accumulate and be still more impossible for him to pay.
Service Committee
The Committee on Delinquent Members could well be called a
"Service Committee," for the information it should have would be
such that could be used to determine whether the Lodge should
expend its funds for relief 9f a member, either in paying his dues or
in otherwise assisting him.
We may well profit by the experience of Massachusetts in this
work. Grand Master Dean told us at the Grand Masters' conference
that
"The Service Committee was organized to take care .of things
that did not involve any expenditure of money, but simply a helping
.hand, or advice, or something of that kind.
"It did not progress as we wanted it to, and we tried to find out
what was the trouble, and · finally we decided it was because. ~he
Service Committee did not have enough to do. They sat there wa1tmg
for a service case to come along; and when it did not come along .t hey
made up their minds that the service was not needed. So we added
the idea of hitching it up with the welfare work of the Lodge.
"Among the ·suggestions that were made for the Service Committee was, first of all, to go to the widow of every ~faster M~son after
the funeral was over and inform her of the Service Committee. We
had on the Service Committee a lawyer and a banker, and the name of
the banker was given to her particularly. J:Iere was. a member of the
Lodge who felt it was his privilege to advise th~ widow of ~ brother
Master Mason. The lawyer would do the same with legal advice.
"We have found many cases where widows have been saved the
amount of their inheritance.
"I think that the great trouble is that we bury a Master Mason, go
through our program at the grave, and then. forge! all about t~e
widows and orphans unless they need financial assistance; and m
many cases the advice and help of the brothers are more valuable than
financial assistance .

A member who is not able to pay his dues may very likely be in
such condition that he will require more than the remission of his dues,
and this the Lodge should know through investigation.
In my visits to the Lodges this year I have stressed this important
work to be done by Masters. Too many Masters in the past have
known nothing but ritual and left everything to the Secretaries. Many
Lodges elect men as Secretaries, not for their qualifications, but because they need the job. It would pay such Lodges to give such men
charity and employ competent men. Big industrial concerns find it
profitable to pension old employes rather than keep them in responsible positions.

policy. If and when a member fails or refuses to pay his just dues
for a period of twelve months, the Committee on Delinquent Members should report defir.itely and promptly to the Lodge the financial
situation of all such delinquents, and immediate action for suspension
or remission of dues should follow. Generally it is good business to
order the Secretary to issue receipt for dues to date, charging the
same to the Lodge. But if the Lodge ascertains, either by the efforts
of the Committee or otherwise, that certain delinquent members are
in fact able but not willing to pay, suspension should not be delayed.
In no instance should further time be granted except for a definite
period. If entitled to further time he should have his dues remitted,
unless he can show definite ability to pay at the end of the period.
"Sections 117 and 118 of the Constitution are mandatory and must
be obeyed. The present financial stringency of course s hould be considered. If Lodges can save a delinquent member by remitting his
dues, sound business judgment would indicate that such action would
best subserve the interests of the Lodge. Wholesale suspensions are
not wise. A small percentage of suspended members ever return to
active membership. Lodges frequently are to blame for loss of interest.
But after due effort to enlist interest has failed, leniency is idle.
"It is my order that each Lodge report to the Grand Secretary
immediately after the July stated meeting any members delinquent

action may be taken at the August stated meeting. Any Lodge that
has failed to report full compliance with Constitution, Sections 117
and 118, either immediately after the July or August stated meetings
will be subject to discipline. See to it that a report is in immediately
after the July stated meeting and if necessary a fur ther report immediately after the August stated meeting.

These organizations, the prerequisite of membership wherein is
