Conditions that Contribute to Suspensions
During the year l have made a study of the conditions that contribute to the suspension of members for non-payment of dues.
In the first place, the majority of our suspensions. are of members
who have left their Lodge localities. When we realize that all who
knock on our doors for admission select themselves as our candidates,
without solicitation on our part, and are required to wait until they
receive our <iegrees before they learn anything in regard to our Institution, it is not surprising that some take little interest in our fraternity
which they have thus joined. The natural thing for them to do is to
drop out when they get away from home, if they have not done so
before. Unless we develop Masonic interest in ·our members before
they move from the locality of their Lodges, and thus keep their
Masonic enthusiasm alive, .we will continue to lose those who may
constitute a valuable asset to the fraternity.
Another condition that contributes largely t~ our losses results
from too .much pursuasion exerted upon our membership, especially
our new members, to join some body or organization the prerequisite
of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason. Reports
have been made to me that members of these bodies or organizations
have solicited and persuaded Master Masons who were not financially
able to pay the initiation fees into these organizations (and thus
present their applications direct) to enter into a contract under the
guise of a "club," under the terms of which contract these Master

Throughout this advertisement the emblems and terms of Craft

In other advertisements Pyramids of the Sciots publish in alphabetical order, a list of the business or professions their members are
engaged in, and opposite each businss or profession, the names of their
members engaged therein, and further publish an additional list of the
members in alphabetical order, and opposite each name, the business
or profession in which the Master Mason, who is also a Sciot, is engaged. Then when the Pyramid says "Boost One Another" its members may easily distinguish which of the Master Masons in any

particular community are Sciots, entitled to have their business
"boosted" and not mere Master Masons who are not entitled to support
in their business by brethren who belong to that "Business Pyramid"
composed of Master Masons in good standing who are pledged to the

In addition to newspaper advertising and the publication of lists
as above set forth, this organization propagates this unmasonic
doctrine of preferring one Master Mason who joins its organizatio~,
to another who fails· or refuses to join, by use of placards posted m
public places and by canvas streamers stretched across public streets.
On these are used the square and compass, the letter G, and the
term Master Mason, used of course to place its members before the
public as Master Masons.
The business inducements offered, and the threats made . by
Sciots to induce and compel Master Masons to join their organization,
as reported to me by Master Masons, amount to a "racket."
Master Masons in the various localities where this organization
has held its ceremonials have reported actions of Sciots that are clear
examples of unmasonic conduct. In such cases the Ju~ior Warden
should prefer charges in compliance with his duty as plamly set forth
in section 189 of the Constitution.
Brethren, the Sciots is not only NOT a Masonic organization, but
is an unmasonic organization. I base this opinion on its doctrine as
advertised to the public and on its practices as reported to. me by
Master Masons, both within and without its organization.
I have the highest regard for the York and Scottish Rite bodi:s
and for the Shrine. The Shrine in no way claims to be a Masomc
organization. Unfortunately there are members of these organiz~tions,
as there are of our Lodges, who commit acts that are unmasomc, and
in those instances the duty of Master Masons or Junior Wardens of
Lodges is clear. But this is not a criticism of the organizatio~ or
organizations to which they belong. A Master Mason wh~ receive~
honors from any of these organizations should either appreciate them
or get out of the organization. I know that I a~preciate honor.s I
have received from the Scottish Rite, the York Rite and the Shrme.
I believe that any man who can afford to take the degrees in e!ther ~r
both of these Rites of Freemasonry will the better appreciate his
Masonry.
I wish here to express my appreciation of a courtesy paid your
Grand Master at a \eccption tendered to him by the 97th and 98th
Masonic Districts at Long Beach.
It happened that Long Beach Commandery, of which the present
Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of California is a

486

member, was tendering to him a reception. The conflict of the two
meetings was not realized until too late to change either reception.
There were present at the reception to the Grand Commander nearly
all of the officers of the Grand Commandery, severa1 of whom were
officers, past officers, committeemen and members of the Grand
Lodge, and none of whom would have traveled from their Masonic
districts to attend the local reception tendered to me as Grand Master
by the 97th .and 98th Masonic Districts.
Interrupting the progress of the reception which occasioned their
presence, these brethren changed from their Knight Templar uniforms
to business suits and, headed by the Grand Commander, appeared as
Master Masons before the altar of the tiled Lodge in which the reception to the Grand Master was being held and expressed their first
allegiance to the Grand Lodge of California.
I have already expressed my appreciation of the truly Masonic
spirit which actuated those Master Masons who compose the membership of the Widows and Orphans Fund of Aahmes Temple of the
Shrine in taking the action hereinbefore reported.
But the fact remains that no matter whether or not it may be
desirable for a Master. Mason to join any body, order, or organization
the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master
Mason, he should realize that his Lodge bears the same relationship
to the organization that he may later join as the necessaries of life
bear to those luxuries which are but comforts.
This is what often happens: A man may join a Lodge. He can·
afford that. He can also afford to pay nine, twelve or fifteen dollars
as dues per year to his Lodge. Then some enthusiastic member of
another organization persuades him to join that other organization
and, so influenced by the solicitation of members oi various organizations, he proceeds to pyramid memberships that he cannot afford. He
faces an obligation of forty or fifty dollars or more pe·r year in dues.
Even though he may have been financially able to afford the fees
required by other organizations at the time he joined them, financial
difficulties may arise which make it impossible for him to meet his
dues in all the organizations that he has joined.
Since no one has explained to him that he may drop out of all of
those other organizations and still be a Master Mason in good standing, if he pays his Lodge dues only, he drops all.
A very large portion of the Master Masons who are suspended
from our Lodges for non-payment of dues are members of one or more
of these other organizations. Oftentimes these other organizations, I
suppose because they need the money, continue to collect dues from
these suspended Master Masons and retain them as members in good

Our Lodges should give their newly raised Master Masons a full
appreciation of the relative positions of Lodges and these ot_her. organizations. If this were done before they join other organt~ation~
than the Lodge we would save many members who are lost t roug
lack of this kn~wledge. Every member should kno'; that t?e Lodge
is the Masonic body in which he should keep good his standing.

Digest
At our last communication Grand Master Wollenberg recommended that Grand Lodge publish a Digest and Compilation of Approved Decisions and Regulations, so that the same might be
accessible to all officers in the jurisdiction.
A Digest has been compiled in which an attempt has been made
to set forth those decisions and regulations that have been adopted
by Grand Lodge since its organization that are still in force as Regulations. In some cases decisions have been added that are now superceded by provisions enacted as parts of the Constitution or by
Regulations, with the view of explaining the purposes and the history
of. our present written law.
Grand Lodge is indebted to our Very Worshipful Grand Secretary
for the attractive form in which this Digest is presented to you.
General Condition of Masonry
I believe the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction
is better than it has ever been, at least in recent years. Although depressed business conditions have sorely affected members of our
Lodges, Lodges through Delinquent Members Committees have given
them just consideration in most cases. If in any instances the committees have not acquainted themselves sufficiently with the reasons
for which members were suspended, they can and should make further
investigation and correct any errors that may have been made.
Through intelligent study in ·our Officers Associations our Lodges
are not only continuing in high standing in our ritual but are paying
attention to things Masonic outside the ritual. An awakened sense

Appreciation
I wish to express my appreciation to those officers of Lodges who
have done so much to improve conditions in their respective Lodges
during this year; to the Inspectors who have so efficiently discharged
their important duties, and in many instances done much more than
might be said to be their duties; to our Grand Lecturer, with whom
I have been in close association since 1911, who has given me all the
assistance and co-operation that his office could afford; to our Grand
Secretary for his counsel and assistance that he is so well qualified to
render; to the Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens for their co-operation and assistance; to all Grand Lodge
officers and committeemen for services rendered; and last but by no
means least for the opportunity and privilege of becoming better
acquainted with not only those with whom I was frequently in contact
but with those good brethren and their families whom I met throughout the jurisdiction. The memory of the courtesies and reception accorded me and members of my family that chanced to be with me at
times will be ever cherished by my family and me. Those courtesies
are too numerous to mention, and to mention one without mentioning
all, would be unfair. I therefore request that all those present take
back to the good brethren and friends at home, both in California and
the Hawaiian Islands, this expression of my deepest gratitude for their
kindnesses to my family and me.
Conclusion
In bringing to a close the year I have been privileged to serve as
your Grand Master, I trust that my labors may have accomplished
something at least, for the upbuilding and advancement of Masonry.
In relinquishing my high office I pledge continued support of the
principles of our Institution.

The Deputy Grand Master referred the message to William B. Ogden, Joel S. Conklin and Clarence L. Fraser, for
segregation and distribution to appropriate committees.

Growth During Twenty Years

Conference of Grand Secretaries
In accordance with the action of Grand Lodge at its last annual
communication, I attended the annual conference of Grand Secretaries held at Washington, D. C., February 24, 1931. Twenty-seven
jurisdictions were represented by their Grand Secretaries. Three
main subjects were discussed: the matter of uniform blanks, the
administration of interjurisdictional matters affecting d ual memberships; and uniform receipts for due~-all pertinent subjects. The
conference of course had no power to enact any legislation, but the
interchange of ideas was worth w hile, and I returned home in the
belief that in general the laws and procedure of the Grand Lodge of
California were better than many other jurisdictions. Probably the
most illuminating report was presented by the Grand Secretary of
Virginia, relating to dual membershi p. That jurisdiction has always
permitted its members to affiliate with other Lodges, in and out of
the State, without requiring them to withdraw from the mother
Lodge. It now has twelve hundred who are members of two or more
Lodges, and not one of them has ever been suspended fo~ n.o~­
payment of dues or because of unmasonic conduct.- Our V1rgm1a
brethren are heartily in favor of continuing the permission of dual
membetship, largely because such members are thereby kept in active
Masonic work, and incidentally because it increases the revenues of
the Lodges.
,
I enjoyed the personal contact with my fellow Grand Secretaries,
and believe the conference was worth the time and expense.
Unfinished Business
The petitions of Maricopa Lodge No. 434 and Temblor Lodge
No. 477 to grant each of said Lodges exclusive jurisdiction over territory adjacent to and surrounding such Lodges, presented 1ast year
and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, were by . recommendation of said committee, laid over for consideration until the
1931 communication.
The Committee on Jurisprudence also requested further time in
which to consider and prepare legislation to carry out the recommendation of Grand Master Wollenberg with respect to the conferring of degrees by foreign language Lodges; and the matter wa'.
continued until this communication.

Report of Audi~ors
Finance Committee, Grand Lodge, F. & A, M. of California:
In accordance with your authotization, we have audited the accounts
of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1931 and submit herewith certain financial statements as follows:
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash · Receipts and Disbursements--General Fund.
Exhibit B: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash Received for Account
of Masonic Homes.
Exhibit C: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash Receipts and Disbursements--Emergency Relief Fund.
Exhibit D: Grand Treasurer's Report of Cash Receipts and Disbursements.
Exhibit E: Grand Treasurer's Report of Assets on Hand July 31,
1931.
This audit covered the cash funds received during the year ended
July 31, 1931 from the annual returns for the fiscal year ended July 31,
1930. Funds received and on hand at the date of our audit from annual
returns for the fiscal year 1931 were not included in our examination.
We certify that the attached statements, with exception as to the
stated value of the securities on hand, set forth the condition of the
Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California at July 31, 1931, and that a
proper accounting has been made of all receipts and disbursements.
Respectfully submitted,
RucKsTELL & LAND, Certified Public Accountants.

AFTERNOON SESSION
Tuesday, October 13, 1931
Grand Lodge was called on at 2 :30 o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.
Distinguished Visitor
M.".W.".George R. Harvey, Past Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, was introduced and
received with the honors due to his rank.
Report of the Committee on Segregation
To theM.'.W.'.Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee to which was referred the message of the Grand
Master, begs leave to report as follows:
An attentive reading of the message of the M.'.W.".Grand Master
discloses care in its treatment, and doubtless many hours of thoughtful labor in its preparation. Moreover, it discloses an industrious performance of his official duties, not merely a perfunctory performance
of those duties, or even a faithful performance thereof, but rather a
performance that entailed an added bit here, and an added bit there,
whenever in his judgment such added labor contributed in anywise to
the good of Masonry. It discloses a lively interest in the affairs of
Masonry, in his duties as the head of Masonry in California, and in
the welfare of the fraternity throughout this grand jurisdiction seldom
displayed .by one so honored by his brethren. His virility and honest,
straightforward dealing with his brethren is recognized by all who ·
have been so favored as to have known him, and has earned the respect and admiration of his brethren. His incumbency will long be
recognized as the work of a great administrator. His message is replete with recommendations, some vital to the welfare of Masonry in
our jurisdiction, and others such as will conduce to regularity in the
transaction of our affairs, and tend to smooth the way of those who
come after.
Your committee recommends that the following portions of the
Grand Master's message be referred to the following committees:
Suspension of a Master: To Jurisprudence Committee.
·George Washfogto11 Memorial: Policy and Purposes, and Finance.
Grand 1'.foster's Confere1ice: Policy and Purposes, and Finance.
Masonic History: Policy and Purposes, and Finance.

ANNUAL ORATION
By LESLIE E. LF.ARNED, Grand Orator

Brethren of the Grand. Lodge:
I am deeply sensible of the responsibility devolving upon the speaker
who is commissioned by the Grand Master of any jurisdiction to deliver
the annual oration to a representative body of Free and Accepted Masons.
It is required of such an officer that he shall be well informed in the
ceremonial of the Fraternity, and also that, from a wide and thoughtful
acquaintance with mankind, he shall be able' to interpret the ancient and
profound principles of the Rite.
I do not stand here,. therefore, merely to utter in sonorous English
a succession of bombastic syllables, the sound of which shall be agreeable
to your ears, but to speak as simply as I may to my brother Masons
concerning the imponderable and eternal significance of our degrees.
Most, if not all of you, are very familiar with the phraseology and the
work of the Lodge room. Many of you have dwelt at length ~pon the
inner meaning of our ritual. But it has been given to few of those who
pass through the ascending series of our official positions until they
occupy the exalted place in the East, to pursue studies and to travel widely
in order that an adequate comprehension . of Masonic truth is in their
possession.
Indeed, no living man would dare to make that claim. Yet, I am
here to act as your spokesman and to interpret your inner emotions, your
sincere reactions and your high resolves, which in greater or less degree,
Masonry has created in· your minds and hearts.
Humbly, earnestly, faithfully, and with enthusiasm I now address
myself to this task.
It baffles the imagination to visualize the far-flung scope and history
of Free Masonry. Its ritual discovers its origin in the ancient kingdom
of Judea over three thousand years ago, and who can say how long before. Mystic symbols are discernible by the initiate in many lands and
under varied skies. When our own era dawns and those mighty movements of the new age gather momentum, history shows the active influence of our Institution in the Crusades for the recovery of the Holy
Land. It is not easy to pick up the threads of an organization which has
always treasured its secrets and maintained inviolable its high principles
of faith and conduct. But ever and again an operative Mason leaves his
mark upon the enduring granite or marble and we, of a later age, stand
in silence before the relic. Only this summer I thus stood in the Temple
Church only a few feet from the busy traffic of Fleet street in the very
heart of London and conjured up the scenes which the sculptured forms

SIE

of the Knights brought vividly to mind, their weary marches, the burning
noontides, the desert nights with the cool stars overhead, and dreams of
the clash of arms on the morrow.
If only we could gather. together the secrets of.. thos~e ?1yriads of. our
brethren in the storied past, how our hearts would thrill at the recital I
It is well to interpret this' august past to each either, meager th9ugh
our kriowledrre be. Think of what it means that each new brother who
is made a M~ster Mason, is introduced into so noble and anci~nt a h~ri-..
tage ! He is · lifted out of petty and narrow env~ronment into th~ . 1~­
ponderable antiquity of human life at its best. _He 1s no longer a ch1l~ of
the present; engaged in buy'ing and' selling; in building and transporta~1on:
He is ·maae a companion o'f the multitude · of brethren of many nations,
and he views the pageant of the long history of those who have passed
from step to step in the identical symbolism to which he ha~ just be~n
introduced. It is as if a gigantic panorama had been passed before his
eyes as blindfolded he has been' led through" the mystic wonder of the
Mas~er'~ degree and' by some most modern touch of' movietone, has hear.d
the voices of the far past sounding in his ears, ·saying, "We ·pa'Ssed this
way centuries ago, my brother: We ·have seen and you will see. Years
came · and went before we understood, but by patience and fortitude you,
too, will. grasp in part the age-long, world-wide meaning of Masonic
mysteries."
Masonry, therefore, paints a picture. On its canvas move vast n~m­
bers of men; Leaders of great movements are there. Founders of nations
loom high in the great throng, Godfrey de -Bouillon, the Crusader; Jacques de M alay, the Templar; Washington, the first figure of our beginning history. as .a nation, are a trinity of fame ~mo~g ma~y. others.
Our In,stitution· summons every Master Mason to this high privilege of
partnership with these great men. They, t~, drank deep of. the fountains . of wisdom. -in our .unchanging ceremonial. They, also, mterpreted ·
the mystic symbolism of the Rite. And they knew the august ins~iration
of words which have .meaning so profound that secrecy must wrap its c?ncealing folds ·about the mystery which runs on in the hearts of men hke
the underground rivers of California.

High-poised example of great duties done .

It 1s logical, from this great delineator of the character of our foremost .American Mason, to pass to a brief consideration of the scope and
meaning of our Institution in this country where the majority of us had
our birth.
. Have you ever studied our own inviolable and unchanging obligations as Master Masons, in relation to the principles which underlie our
Constitution? Have you, as American citizens, ever sought to connect the
two roles which you play in public, that of a free voter, and that of a
Free and Accepted Mason? Or have you rested complacently in your
election to some Lodge in the Craft and wholly or partially treated your
duties as a citizen with scant respect? .
Alas ! How many Masons are poor citizens ! How many are ei~her
slaves of their prejudices or blind to their country's dire needs! How
many follow the perilous fires of the pursuit of wealth or the gratification of their lowest appetites with no thought of the enormous evil
which accrues to the country they profess to love !
Every member of the Lodge, to say nothing of those who have taken
the higher degrees, cannot thus neglect his duty to the nation without
violating certain deep and fundamental responsibilities to this great Institution which is here assembled in Grand Lodge.
.F or Masonry stands today as it always. stood, for freedom for the .
possibility of the greatest good and the highest place for e;ery man
despite any conditions of birth, occupation, or fortune. Masonry is the
bulwark of true democracy. Note, my brethren, certain familiar facts
too often left out of consideration when one rejoices in his Masonic
fellowship. First, that there is no caste in a Masonic Lodge. The chairs
are not reserved for the rich or for the highly educated, or for the
lawyer, doctor or clergyman. The poorest Mason may hold and often
does hold the highest position the Lodge offers in the sacred East, but
none has a monopoly of the opportunity.
But why use up our time by reiterating such a commonplace fact in
the life and experience of a Mason? Because, my brethren, only a few,
and those who are widely read in the long and devious history of mankind, realize the incessant struggle mankind has waged to reach such a
happy principle, and how equally difficult it is to maintain this principle
which lies at the very foundation of democratic institutions.

Corruption stalks openly abroad in our cities at the expense of honest
merchants and innocent babies' lives. There is no great city which can
hold its head erect as a guarantor of .the inalienable rights of a man to
run his business as he pleases without tribute. Such a condition is not
freedom. It is slavery of the deepest dye and it should bring the blush of
shame to the cheek of every Mason, that such conditions are permitted
to continue. Imagine, my brothers, a secret organization within the
Grand Lodge, which permitted no man to occupy the position of Worshipful Master, without an enforced tribute to this cabal of hidden
Masonic robbers and thieves I Why ! The thought is absurd. Masonry
would not last a decade under such conditions. What sane man, of his
own free will and accord, would become a member of such a corrupt
order?
Why, then, do we find it in our political life? Because millions of
Masonic brethren throughout our land are indifferent and apathetic, or
worst of all, absentees at the polls.
I realize that Masonry, as such, must never organize for political
results. Th_ere must never be in any nation, a Masonic political party.
That, too, is written large in the tenets of our Free Masonry. But that is
not to say that we must carry our Masonry in our hearts and our citizenship in the tough soles of our feet.
The undying flame of the light which every brother has seen, as he
emerges from darkness, symbolizes liberty, freedom, equality of opportunity ·for every man, always and everywhere. Masonry can never tolerate a dictator who rides rough-shod over popular rights. Masonry can
never permit an oligarchy of the favored classes to decide the doctrines
of a nation. Masonry operates, as Almighty God operates, through the
wills of men, inoculated with its enduring principles, and we must see
to it that increasingly the vast impact of our purposes and ideals shall
destroy the corruption and debasement of our American cities and institutions. Quietly but powerfully, we must work and vote for men who
will be strong for the right and yet never seekers for their own autocratic place and power.
The work of the Lodge is not therefore, a vain repetition of timehonored syllables. A Mason is supposed to conceal within the secret
places of his mind a considerable number of words and phrases. But
our Fraternity will cease to attract men of the calibre we desire, unless
the mystic symbols are deeply interpreted and adequately applied to the
morals and government of the land in which we live. Patriotism is more
than proud self-congratulation that America is a country of broad rivers
and fertile and lofty mountains. No country ever has, or ever can maintain its vitality by enjoying its scenery. The foundation stone of Masonry
is mystic brotherhood and its degrees insist in unequivocal and emphatic
terms, that such fraternal obligations are concerned, not merely with the
craft, but with the whole human race.

This is not a seTmon, rny brethren, but a plain talk in- blunt language
about Masonic obligations which shall send Master Masons out to ·the
busy marts of trade imbued with moral enthusiasm. We shall coine, in
a moment, to the two highest revelations to men, who travel ever toward
the truth of the sunrise. I am reserving them for the final paragraphs
of this oration. Just now I am concerned with the reputation of men
who call themselves Masons, with their reputation among those with
whom they are associated in the home, in the mill, in our great buildings,
and in their hours of leisure by night and in the day: ·
Does your wife look upon ·you· as a man who exemplifies .truth and
loyalty for her, whom you have pledged yourself to love and to cherish
until death do us part? Does your family discover in you strength and
honor and patience and tenderness the morning after you have been to
.Lodge. Is there no suspicion of your untrustworthiness in the minds of
your business acquaintances? Is your word as good as your bond? Have
you ever made money, knowing that another man or woman would surely
,los.e in .the transaction?
These are the questions for us to face today, and they are all con-Cerrie'd with homes and with our country. Politics too often degenerate
into . not too honorable methods to keep a given party in power, but a
country prospers only when good and true men are at the helm to insure
common honesty and sweet purity and so, enduring safety to the little
children, their · mothers- and their fathers.
If you and I have travelled Masonic ways and on our knees have
taken its solemn oaths without making a stern resolution thus to fulfill in
public what has be~n secretly conferre.d upon us, then we have miserably
failed to reach the lofty goal of Masonic purpose.
It is not an idle act to remember the great word which calls each and
every one here present a Free Mason. It is just that rich possession . for
humanity which Masonry strives to keep in our hands. Whatever comes,
we will not be enslaved by despot or tyrant. We will exercise the heavenborn rights of freemen at the polls. We will not suffer our liberties _to be
stolen from us by specious promises of ease or money .. We will suffer
hardship in freedom's name. We will never lower the standard of our
- integrity. On our banners will be emblazoned right, truth, justice, until
Free Masons shall by their heroic struggle make this earth a dwelling
place .for free men everywhere.
Listen to a California poet: .
"No, not as in that elder day

And now, my Brethren, a little time remains for me to bring your
minds and emotions face to face with the two holy articles of our Masonic
faith.
The laynian is modest in giving expression to his feelings on the
themes I am now about to discuss. He feels that they are too high for
him to describe, and he contents himself with a brief allusion. But the
profession of your Grand Orator makes him more courageous, and perhaps fits him to speak simply, but emphatically, about Masonry and
religion.
Let me repeat what I have often said before to many Masons, that
an enduring bulwark against skepticism and the moral anarchy which
invariably-goes along with atheism, is found in Masonry.
No skeptic has a right to be a Mason. He perjures himself if he takes
our vo~s, while scoffing in his heart at Almighty God. Here, the Lodge
goes hand in hand with the church and synagogue and mosque. In unmistakable terms it confesses a faith in God, which is symbolized by the
shining letter in the East, emblematic of the eternal Being Who sits upon
the circle of the heavens and takes up the islands of the sea as very
little things.
It is well that Masonry does not indulge in long-winded and sanctimonious cant. It treats religion with dignity and reserve, but always
insists upon its foremost place in the unchanging 'principles of the Rite.
These· easy 'purveyors ' of· doubt, who write so brilliantly about the decay
of religion, do not know what is taught behind the tiled doors of .Masonry.
Those new rulers in Russia are convinced that they can build a lasting
republic upon five year plans and the embalmed body of a successful
revolutionist. · But neither do they know that perse~ution through the
long centuries has not availed to crush out the deep faith of Masons.
Nor is it like the religion of the ~ncient Ro~an Empire, a sop thrown
to the ordinary man while the chosen few discard it. The higher you
go in Masonry, the more light shines upon our faith in the Almighty
Being Who has created the universe and maintains it by His Divine
Power.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Yet it is all to be found around a lonely grave under the green acacia,
where the climax of all the lectures and obligations is reached by the one
who impersonates the ancient Master. I make no disclosure of our secrets;
I only remind you, who are qualified to understand the reference, that
when all human power failed, the appeal is made to the Almighty and
the prayer is answered. Many of us have received the higher degrees
and seen noble ceremonials, b~t they all hark back to that spot, sacred
to every Mason, where prayer to God is made and that petition is fulfilled.

In my own heart I am wondering how you are following the words
your spokesman has been uttering. Perhaps some of you have thought
that Masonry has been made too idealistic and that it would have been
saner to' build Masonry frankly upon human fellowship and claim no
more for it than the most thoughtless find within the Lodge, merely calling attention to the distinguished men of all nations, who have been proud
to call themselves Master Masons. Perhaps others have made charitable ·
allowance for the tenor of my thoughts by saying that he cannot avoid
a preachment, seeing he is himself a preacher.
My brothers, we have been blind and deaf, if we have failed to
perceive the profound teaching embodied in the ceremonial of the Lodge.
Surely it is true that the higher degrees throw a bright light on the first
three. But I have not assumed that all of you have had that privilege.
Purposely I have confined myself to the deep significance of the original
degrees.
Again I quote from the great Masonic teacher:
"Masonry teaches that God is good and merciful and loves and
~ympathizes with the creatures He has made; that His' finger is visible
m all the movements of the moral, intellectual and material universe·
that we are His children, the objects of His p~ternal care and regard;
that all me!! are.• ~rothers, whose wan.ts .w!! a.re to supply, their errors to
par~on,. their opm1ons to to.lerate, .their miunes to forgive; that man has
an immortal soul, a free will, a right to freedom of thought and action·
that all men are equal ii;i God's sight; that we ~est serve God by humility'.
meekness, gentleness. kmdness and the other virtues which the lowly can
practice as well as the lofty; this is 'the new Law ' the 'Word ' for which
the world has waited and pined so long."
'
'
One great interpretation I have left for the closing words of this
oration. Most of us bear our initiate's part in the tragic events of the
Master's degree without perceiving the full meaning of our being raised
to that exalted degree. We are keenly alive to our prostrate form and
to the simple but majestic words by which we are made to assume the
normal posture of a man. But we do not delve below the obvious significance of those acts and words which describe an event of the most ancient
Masonic history, but which really embody a profound article of faith
in the imperishable soul of every man.
Along with the belief in God, Masons must carry from that lonely
grave out from which by a mysterious grip we are raised, a confidence
sure and certain in another life beyond and above the present. If modernism should laugh to scorn such a belief, as a few of its apostles have
and do, if the cold conclusions of science leave man to the cold oblivion
of the tomb, Masonry will still keep alive in the hearts of men a faith
in the immortal existence of the soul.
The Mason is not indifferent to the fate of the soul after its present
life, as to its continued and eternal being, and the chara~ter of the scenes
in which that being will be fully developed. These are to him topics of

520

The modern movements of thought are slowly demolishing the materialism which has been a popular doctrine among many scientists during
the last century, and the trend of opinion is toward the ancient faith in
a Supreme Being to which synagogue and mosque and church have clung
and to the 'essential elements of which the principles of Free Masonry
have always been loyal.
I have said on many occasions to my Masonic Brethren that the
world can never lose its religion while Masonry lasts. Enshrined in our
ceremonial there is a Holy Book and an Almighty God. Centuries come
and go, history plays upon the stupendous keys of the world instrument,
nations rise and fall, races vanish or are absorbed by the stronger,
civilization alters the methods and appearances of life, but Masonry does
not change. It is the most conservative force in the world. It is international. It is inter-racial. It is inter-religious. Mohammedan and Jew
and Christian can be and are believers together in the one God, Who has
been described in the classic commentary on Free Masonry.
Listen to these words written decades ago by the facile pen of
Albert Pike :
"Masonry teaches that God is a Paternal Being, and has an interest
in His creatures, such as is expressed in the title 'Father'; an interest
unknown to all the systems of Paganism, untaught in all the theories of
philosophy; an interest not only in the glorious beings of other spheres,
the Sons of Light, the dwellers in Heavenly worlds, but in us, poor,
ignorant, and unworthy; that He has pity for the erring, pardon for the
guilty, love for the pure, knowledge for the humble, and promises of
immortal life for those who trust in and obey Him.
"Without a belief in Him, life is miserable, the world is dark, the
Universe disrobed of its splendors, the intellectual tie to nature broken,
the charm of existence dissolved, the great hope of being lost; and the
mind, like a star struck from its sphere, wanders through the infinite
desert of its conceptions, without attraction, tendency, destiny, or end.
"Masonry teaches that, of all the events and actions that take place
in the universe of worlds and the eternal succession of ages, there is not
one, even the minutest, which God did not forever foresee, with all the
distinctness of immediate vision, combining all, so that man's free will
should be His instrument, like all the other forces of nature."

There is an altar in every Masonic Lodge room, no less than in
lofty cathedrals. On that altar is always to be found the Holy Volume
which contains our faith. Undeviatingly, from century to century, we
promulgate our ancient truth. New fashions of speech and thought come
and go . . New inventions are created and fascinate by alluring sound and
motion the sensitive minds and imaginations. New theories of the univer!!e
are formulated and, 'in their turn, are succeeded by still newer scientific
conclusions. But Masonry knows the unchanging content of hu·m an nature:
Our ritual has eliminated the unnecessary and the non-esset)tial. It builds
its house on the solid rock of human hope and human need.
It is in· close touch With human experience, that great mass of sorrow
~~d joy, of success and failure, of struggle and defeat. It sings· the hymn
of "human history ·and links together differing climes and peoples under
the inclusive harmony of its fraternity and fellowship. ·
·It kn~ws too much to be merely hum~n, for"it is .convinced th.a t only
an Infinite Mind could make so delicate an organ as the human intellect..
it sees too far to be content with the narrow bounds of· this visible
earthly life, and commands us to lift our eyes to a house eternal in the
heavens.
· So it makes us free. So we are accepted by the great God on high as
the ancient w,ords gain ever greater power over our every thought and deed.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M:.w:.Grand Lodge of California: .
I herewith submit to the Grand Lodge my twenty-fourth annual
report of my stewardship as Grand Lecturer. I have at ;i.11 times to
the best of my ·ability endeavored to merit your confidence. Masonry,
as well as everything else,- is feeling the depression that now exists,
yet the fraternity has made a substantial gain. ·Many of the newer
Lodges have felt the slowing. up of petitions, some of them having a
hard time to exist. This, however, is somewhat compensated by the
fact that more time is had fo r other activities.
The Officers' Associations that have been formed in the different
Inspectorial districts have proven to be successes. The officers are
getting much out of the meetings. T hese were formed at the suggestion of the Grand Master. ·
I have-visited every dist_rict in · the jurisdiction. I find the Lodges
generally in good condition financially, most of them doing a little
work, and all striving to perfect themselves in the ritual. I notice
a marked improvement in this respect, which is very gratifying.
I have accompanied the Most Worshipful Grand Master on many
of his visits. The messages which he left with the brethren were both
instructive and beneficial. I believe all the brethren get a great deal
out of his explanations and comments on the condition of the fraternity. He has covered the entire jurisdiction in these visits. Th~
visitation of Lodges is most highly commended. I believe much good
is accomplished by such visits. The Lodge that is visiting, if they
are to confer a degree, should go over the work carefully and endeavor to put it on in as perfect a manner as is -possible. The ritual
is a compact and carefully worded fab ric ; there is little in it that is
redundant and without significance. It is all purposeful and definite.
I have at all times been anxious and willing to assist and instruct
the officers and brethren in the ritual. Many have availed themselves
of this opportunity in my office and at various other places, or whenever o r wherever they happened to contact me.
I suggest that section 115 of the Constitution be amended so
that a Lodge can only confer three firsts, three seconds and one third
on a candidate at one time and in one day. This will give the Lodges
more time for educational and social purposes and will not tire the
officers or the members in hearing the repetition of the degrees.
This will, I believe, greatly increase the attendance. The brethren
will not remain in Lodge and witness four or five degrees conferred
in one evening. You cannot blame them.

524

GRAND LODG~ OF CALI~ORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Many of the newer and smaller Lodges are having a hard time
to exist, many of them doing very little or no work, some of them
not having had a candidate for a year or more. It would be far
better for some of these Lodges to consolidate. Their burden of
expense goes along the same when they have no candidates as when
they are plentiful.
.
I have received rep~rts from all the Inspectors. They report the
Lodges in their respective districts to be in good co~dition with but
few exceptions, this being largely due to lack of candidates.
.
I desire to thank the V. W. Grand Secretary and his assistant,
Brother Hobbs, for many courtesies extended to me in his office
during the year just closed.
.
The Inspectors of San Francisco will confer the first degree. on
Thursday evening, October 15th, at 7 :30 P . M., under the ausp1c~s
of Presidio Lodge No. 354 ·of this city. Justice Lodge No. 549 will
furnish the candidate.
Thanking the Grand Lodge for the honor ·conferred upon me
during the years that I have been Grand Lecturer, which I have at
all times endeavored to appreciate.
THOMAS JOHN BAKER,

Grand Lecturer.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES MASONIC HOMES
To the M.' . w: . Grand Lodge of California:
Y c;mr Board of frustees of the Masonic Homes of California
herewith submits for your consideration its annual report for the
fiscal year ended July 31, 1931, together with a roster of residents to
Aqgust 31, and a statement of r~venues received since the close of
the fiscal year, to September 30.
Immediately after the close of Grand Lodge, October 17, 1930,
the Trustees met as required by the Constitution and organized as
follows :
President, Charles M. Wollenberg, term expires 1934;
Vice-President, James B. Gist, Junior Grand Warden;
Chas. Albert Adams, term to October, 1933;
Samuel E. Burke, term to October, 1932;
Dana R. Weller, term to Octol;>er, 1931;
Robert B. Gaylord, Deputy Grand Master;
Frank W. Mixter, Senior Grand Warden;
Treasurer ex-officio, William P. Filmer;
Secretary ex-officio, John W hicher.
In addition to the annual meeting the Board met at Los Angeles
and Covina in November, 1930 and at San Francisco and Decoto in
April, 1931. ·Weekly meetings, as usual, for the transaction of routine
business, were held at Los Angeles and San Francisco, local members
attending.
The past year has been one of severe trial, not only to the Lodges
of the jurisdiction, but as ·well to the members of your Board of
Trustees and
executive officers of the Homes. The depression in
business, the increasing numbers of men and women out of gainful
employment, the decreased number of accessions to the meinbership
of our Lodges, the remission of dues of nearly three thousand
member~, the unusual calls for relief, have affected the Homes as well
as the Lodges. Thi~ general stagnation is undoubtedly reflected in a
condition of pessimism, mental and spiritual. Bu·t other years now
gone have shown even darker days, more trying times, more stringency in business, more lowering of the ·morale which should actuate
thinking, courageous men and Masons-and we have lat er enjoyed
the prosperity that followed the fru its of th.- fortitude, t he prudence
and the resourcefulness of our forebears. We may well take heart
from the history of past years of depression, of past years ,of happy
recovery, and hold fast to the faith that the sun of better days will

all

526

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

surely shine upon us. "Be ye strong, therefore, and let not your hands
be weak; for your 'work shall be rewarded."
The Covina Home
At the annual communication of Grand Lodge in 1929, you
approved of our policy of restricting admissions of childr~n to the
Home to those for whom private homes could not be provided. We
said to you then, and repeat it now, that "The welfare. of the child
should be the first consideration of the Lodge. No child should be
sent to the Home until every effort has failed to find a place in a
private home. The Trustees w:II co-operate with Lodges in ende~v­
oring to maintain the relationship and contact of parent or guardian
and child, even to the extent .of a reasonable allowance from the funds
of the Homes."
In accordance with this policy, the number of children maintained in the Home at Covina has been steadily decreased until on
August 31, 1931, there are only 152 b?ys and girls d?mi~iled there, as
against 177 last year. Fifty-seven children were ~amtamed ~ast ye~r
outside and this year the Homes ;tre caring for sixty-one children m
private homes, at an expense of $1,275.00 a month.
It will be noted by reference to the Secretary's report, attached
hereto that the per capita cost of maintaining the children is considerably' in excess of the per capita cost of caring for the old people,
residents of the Decoto Home: To those of you who have had practical and personal experience in the management and maintenance of
children, · this will be understandable. To others it may appear that
the cost of conducting the Home for children is beyond a reasonable
expense. But we who are intrusted with the management of the
business of the Homes earnestly assure you that your Trustees have
always kept in mind that responsibility, have constantly urged the
strictest economy, and are pleased to report that our efforts have
met with a sympathetic and intelligent response on the part of the
Superintendents. The proper demands for the care and education of
the children are necessarily greater than for the care of those who
are far advanced in life as are the residents at the Decato Home,
who do not require house mothers, nor teachers, neither do they wear
out their shoes and clothing as do the little folk. Every effort has
been made to conserve the funds of the Homes, and we have succeeded in reducing the per capita cost to $46.71 a month for each
child, · as against $49.18 last year. Each child is fairly ent.itle~ .to
intelligent, conscientious supervision and care, and to acc~mphsh this,
funds must be provided. We are sure that no Mason will begrudge
the expense necessary to so conduct the Ho~e ~hat its ~adua!es
may go out from the sheltering care of that institution and pomt with
pride to its fostering influence.

We refer you to the report of Brother Downen, Superintendent
of the Covina Home, attached hereto, who succintly sets forth the
problems daily confronting him and his associates in the management
of our large group of children-problems worthy of at tempted solution which would tax the ingenuity and intelligence of the wisest
of men.
The Decato Home
The life and activities of the Decoto Home are detailed in the
report of Superintendent Hartman. There we have no problems
incident to child life. The lives of the children are in the future and
proper mental expansion, correct habits, the making so far as po~sible
of self-sustaining, independent, respectable members of society, are
the paramount endeavors· of those who have charge of the growing
boys and girls. At Decoto are domiciled men and women whose•race .
is run, whose habits are fixed, who need only food, and clothing, and
medical attention, and sufficient diversion and light labor to make
and keep them contented, even happy. A few of these aged residents
are not happy-they are of that unfortunate type who never knew or
have forgotten the pleasure of trying to make their fellows happy,
who demand undue attention; and in some instances some of these
few believe they could conduct the Home better than. the management. The major number of these aged wards, however, tomport
themselves· as becomes kindly-disposed men and women, and they
have naught but words of cordial commendation and are contented,
thankful for the haven provided for them by their brethren of our
great Fraternity.
Forty-seven men (average age 69.76) and twenty-two women
(average age 70.54) have been admitted since our last report. Nine
have departed, and 34 have died; average age 77.79 years. Number
of residents August 31, 326.
Concerning Revenues
We cannot too strongly emphasize the fact that except as endowment is increased through testamentary and other gifts, the sole
source of revenue for the Homes is the Lodges of California. Present
current revenues are insufficient to maintain the expenses of the
Homes, and care for the building program. Grand Lodge cannot
maintain the present standard at the Homes without additional funds·
the substantial source for the funds necessarily must be either a~
increased per capita, or participation by the Lodges in some other
form in the maintenance of the Homes. The majority of our Lodges
are conservative in the admission of candidates, and in the presentation of applicants for admission to the Homes. Some Lodges, however, must be reminded that every applicant admitted to the Homes
means an additional burden, not only upon the Lodges of California

528

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

at large, but proportionately upon the Lodge itself; that every candidate for admission to the Lodge, whether by affiliation or initiation,
whose advanced years, or other causes, may possibly make him or his
family a charge upon the Fraternity, should be most carefully considered, lest our already too great burde.n be still further increased;
that no application for admission of either adults or children to the
Homes should be presented except under circumstances where the
Lodge itself would feel obligated to bear the expense. of support if
the Homes were not in existence; that the Homes are merely an
agency for the expenditure of Lodge funds, and that in effect, and in
the general average, each time an applicant is admitted at the request
of a Lodge, the Homes as an agency of that Lodge are expending for
that Lodge the amount represented by the maintenance of the applicant. While we do not at this time recommend increased per capita
.o r other legislation for the direct increase of income, we believe the
problem must be solved in the near future, and that it deserves serious
consideration by every Loi;lge.
Endowment Fund
Donations to the Endowment Fund in the year amounted to
$52,147.95, nea,rly all from bequests of deceased friends of the Homes.
The largest gift to this fund came from the estate of the late Christine
Breon, a woman who left a legacy of good deeds to many friends and
charities. The total amount of her bequest has not yet been delivered,
but so far the Fund has received the tidy sum in stocks and money
amounting to $45,374.82. The detail of receipts for the benefit of this
Fund will be reported by the Committee on Endowment. The gross
amount in the Fund is now $694,852.58.
Luckenbach Bequest
By the last will and testament of Lena Luckenbach, deceased,
the Grand . Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California, was
bequeathed the sum of $60,000, to be known as the "John and Lena
Luckenbach Fund," requesting "that the principal there'o f shall never
be expended by the legatee, but that the interest shall be used for
the care of orphans or the aged in the Masonic Homes conducted by
said Grand Lodge." The estate was largely in real estate, but partial
distribution has been made, and the sum of $26,361.36---$24,000 of it
account principal-has been received from the executors.

Commetits
Construction of the new administration building at Decoto was completed in September of 1930 and the total cost amounted to $303,234.19, as
evidenced by the various construction contracts including architect's fees . .
All contracts were properly paid in full.
We have written off against the capital account (Exhibit C) certain
items of the fixed properties accounts, in amount $9,414.22. The5e accounts
were of doubtful origin and value.
· No accrued interest has been taken into account in the attached balance sheet.
An examination of the life insurance policies on the lives of H. J.
Clossen and Emil Cohn reveals that the cash surrender value of the former
is $202.00 and the latter $673.48. These policies are carried at full face
value of $3,000.00 in the Special Rule No. 16, Securities Account.

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
To the Board of Tr11stees:
I herewith present for your consideration the following report
for the year ending August 31, 1931.
The management of the Home has been substantially the same
as in former years. We have endeavored to create and maintain a
social atmosphere in keeping with the ideals of our fraternity and
bring as large a measure of contentment as possible into the daily
life of all who are enjoying the many comforts of our Home.
During the past year, on the final completion of the new Administration building, the first floor is occupied by the offices, library,
reception room, etc. The ·four other floors by single women who
formerly roomed in · the East building. The first and second. floors
of the East building are now occupied by men residents. The third
and fourth floors are now available for new accessions to the membership of the Home.
Owing to the building program for several years past, the
grounds near the main buildings have received little care. The roads
have now been graded, the lawns renewed and a variety of shrubs,
climbing vines and ornamental trees have been planted in various
places, and a good beginning has been made to enhance the beauty
of the grounds.
A few minor improvements have been made, and among those
worthy of mention are the erection of a flag staff in front of the
main buildings, where the American flag is daily raised at sunrise
and lowered at sunset. A new croquet court is being prepared, regulation size, in front of the South wing and will soon be ready for
use by the members of the family.
Health-There are at present 40 persons being cared for in our
hospital department, where to those who are ill every care and attention is given. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance. The
general health of the Home has been normal with the exception of
those who are infirm and feeble. owing to advancing years.
Members.-There are at the Home 326 residents-176 men and
150 women. During the year there have been admitted 47 men and·
22 women. The number of departures has been 9, and 34 have passed
away.
Industrial-All the members of the Home are encouraged to
render some service in keeping with their strength, and in their
leisure hours interest themselves in healthful and wholesome diversions for their general well-being. A number of the brethren have
contributed by their labor to the welfare of the Home by their
services in the carpenter and paint ~hops, care of the garage, mail,

550

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

passenger and ·auto service, kitchen, pantry, hospital, vegetablC room,
laundry, store room, chiropodist, poultry yards, roads, care of flower
beds, lawns, clerical work and messenger service, attending telephone
calls and light work in a general. way. During the year all minor
repairs have been attended to by brethren of the Home.
· .
All making, marking and mending of linen, sheets, pillow slips,
table cloths, preserving fruit, etc., is attended to by the women of
the Home. They also assist in preparing fruit, vegetables work in
the kitchen and dining room, and take care of their rooms, ' halls and
laupdry and general household duties.
Water-At this season of the year the natural supply of water is
low, and there has been a marked decrease in service given by our
dee,p well pump. When necessary we are enabled by means of our
auxiliary pump to connect with the Niles water supply and keep our
reservoirs full at all times and equal to any demand made upon them.
Library and Club Rooms-There are now 5500 books on the
library shelves of our main library and branches located in the ·c1ub
rooms and hospital department. The Masonic Hill branch of the
Alaineda County Free Library continues to be well patronized and
we are the recipients, through members of the fraternity, of daily
papers, magazines and pe'r iodicals which are placed on the tables of
the men's club rooms and the women's reading and social rooms.
A reading class for those with impaired eyesight or entirely
?.1ind, meets daily. At that time the daily papers and subjects of
mterest are read to them by good readers selected from the members
of the Home.
Social Life-The members of the Home have during. the past
year enjoyed many splendid programs and stage plays provided by
friends -who are int.erested in our welfare. These evening programs
ohen close with dancing. E:very Tuesday evening many of the family
gather in the library where tables are provided for cards, chess,
checkers, etc. Chorus practice every Friday evening. The usual
servic~s are held every Sunday afternoon. These services are .often
conduc_ted by ministers accompanied by the choirs of their churches,
after which a. few numbers are given by -the Home orchestra.
The Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, at
their annual com_m unication in 1930 appropriated $1,000.00 for the
1>urchasP. of three domestic Persian rugs and a Stromberg-Carlson
ra_dio .a·nd gramophone for the general reception room on the first
ffoor of the Administra_tion building. The above have been added to
the furnishings provided by them for this room several years ago.
The· Remler radio so kindly donated by Mrs. A. E. Selig of San

GRAND LOIDGE OF CALIFORNIA

551

Francisco has been placed in the ' men's club room in the East wing.
A number of the members of the Home have radio sets installed in
their rooms. This privilege is particularly appreciated by those wh.o·
are blind and those who are confi ned to their beds in the hospital
department.
All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The
specials were those which were held on New Year's Eve, Ne~ Year's
Day, Lincoln's and Washington's birthdays, Easter, Memorial Day,
Fourth of July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Farm-There has been no change in the management of the
farm. The greater part of the hill ranch has as in the past been
leased either on shares or cash rental. Our share has been more than
sufficient for the needs of the farm department, the surplus being sold
in the local market. The orchards have supplied plenty of fruit for
table use, the surplus being preserved or sent to the drier and stored
for future use. The garden has supplied a variety of vegetables and
greens. The chicken ranch has supplied all eggs for table and kitchen
use. All over and above our needs have been preserved in water-glass
or sold in the San Francisco market.
Arrangements have been made w hereby members of the family,
a few at a time may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest.
During this yea; many trips were made to Oakland, San Francisco,
San Jose and towns in the vicinity of the Home.
Grand Master John Stewart R oss, officers and members of the
Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the Home during the
year, and a large number of brethren from various L odges have spent
many pleasant hours with us. The number of visitors and donations
received this year indicates an increasing interest in t he welfare of
the Home family.
I wish to extend my appreciation of the loyal · services rendered
by the officers and employees throughout the year,. and to express
to the Board of Trustees my sincere gratitude for the friendly advice
and support they have at all times given me.
FRA N K

B. HARTMAN , Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina
To the Tr11stees of the Masonic Homes:
The past y~ar has been one of stress and trial, of effort to
retrench expenditure without materially reducing the . se~vice rendered
to the children under our care. We realize that funds for the support
of the Home come from those whose incomes have in inany cases
suffered impairment. All members of our staff have willingly co-operated in the effort to reduce expense, among other things accepting
without complaint a reduction in their own salaries.
If' progress in a given year seems slow, one has but to compare
the Home now with what it was ten years ago, when there were but
half as many children and far less in the way of equipment and
facilities, to realize that through all this time and through many years
before tha.t, the steady purpose of California Masonry to provide for
its dependent children has never. faltered, and that what we have
today is the result of tlie unselfish devotion of thousands who have
done their bit and passed on, many of them to their final reward.
During the past yeat we have had abundant evidence, through visitations from Lodges and other Masonic organizations as well as from
thousands of individuals~ and from many generous gifts, that the
welfare and happiness of the children in the Home continues to be
the heartfelt concern of the Craft throughout the jurisdiction.
The health ~f our children has been good during the year. No
outbreak of epidemic illness has occurred. Prompt attention fo minor
ills has proved valuable in preventing the development of more serious conditions. The average number of children in our hospital,
mostly for slight ailments, has been 3.6 per cent of our total number.
It is a fact worthy of remark that since the Home was founded no
child therein has ·died, except one who was killed in an automobile
accident, and one who was seriously ill when admitted.
Our efficient and kindly nurse, Mrs. Susan Burgess, now in her
eighth year of service, has done a notable work in giving skilled and
sympathetic care to those who needed her ministrations. Drs. S. S.
and W. P . Magan have cared most efficiently for our sick during the
past ten years. We are indebted to Dr. Edgar K. Schumaker of Los
Angeles for eye and ear work, which he has done as for many years
past without charge. Dental work has been taken care of satisfactorily by Dr. Donald H. Wilkins.
The swimming pool, gift of Mrs. Almina Runyon, has now bee11
in use for a year, and has proved to be a valuable recreational asset.
The water is kept clear and pure at all times by continuous filtration
and chlorination. Separate times are assigned for its use by boys and
girls, and by larger and smaller children. Located as it is and sur-

575

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

rounded by attractive landscape planting, it is a beauty spot which
adds greatly to the attractiveness of the Home.
Bro. William Hoogendyk has continued with unabated interest
his volunteer work as Scoutmaster, giving much of his time to the
leadership of our splendid troup of Scouts. "Hoogie" is a great favorite with the boys, and justly so, because he has their interest sincerely
at heart.
The employment of a field worker has been continued throughout
the year, investigating applications originating in the Los Angeles
area for .admission to both the Covina and Decato Homes, and also
keeping us in touch with the families of children in the Home. I
regard it as well proved that we are able to do much better work
with the children in our care as a result of the knowledge of home
conditions thus obtained. In a number of instances we have been
able to return children to mothers as a result of such information. In
many cases our handling of the child has b.een guided more intelligently by the data thus obtained.
We favor keeping the child in touch with his surviving parent or
other relatives. The Home will be doing the child a poor service if it
weans him away from his kin. Children are allowed rather liberal
opportunities to visit relatives, and they in turn are allowed to visit
the child in the Home. We find that it is only in the exceptional case
that such contact operates detrimentally; in general we have received
most satisfactory co-operation from mothers, fathers, and other relatives. Most of them have a sincere appreciation for what we are
doing for their children, and we have many evidences of their confidence and gratitude.
The ideal of our institution is that it should not be an institution
but a home-a place where children can live happy lives, surrounded
by security, protection and love, and where their individual needs
will be studied and supplied. I believe that we have succeeded to a
large degree in attaining this ideal. In twenty years of · experience
with institutional groups of children I have never seen so good an
atmosphere of kindliness, cheerfulness, and willingness of each to do
his part, as obtains in our Covina Home at present. A measure of
this is found in the attitude cif ~ome of our older girls. Each summer
some of !hese go into private homes to work as mothers' helpers,
and some of them are always invited to remain throughout the school
year. Almost invariably they have chosen to return to the Covina
Home;. they feel that they do not wish to forego th~ pleasures, joys
and associations which our Covina Home stands for in their minds.
During the past summer a considerable number of the older boys
were employed at Covina, at various duties on the farm and grounds,

at painting and repair work on the buildings, and some in kitchen
and house work. Whatever duties were assigned them, they did their
work excellently and in good spirit, and their behavior was beyond
criticism. It means a great deal when a group of boys fifteen to seventeen years old work and deport themselves as these boys did.
The younger children spent July and August, as usual, at Camp
Tucker, Balboa. There sunshine, sea air, and salt water swimming,
boating and a varied recreational program, through many happy days
built stronger bodies and prepared them for another year of school
work.

More than forty per cent of our children are fourteen years old
or older. While in general older children can perform more useful
work in the Home than can those of younger ages,. it is also true that
in the adolescent period they present peculiar problems which have
been absent up to that time.
One of these problems involves the child's conception of his relation to the institution. When he was small he could receive the
benefits of the Home-food, clothing, and all the necessities of lif~,
without any unwholesome sense of dependency. But when he begins
to attain the adult outlook on life, there is a distinct danger in giving
him those things which he needs without any thought upon his part
of doing something in return. At this stage it is easy for him to take
on an unhealthy attitude of expecting and even demanding uncompensated benefits; and from this it is not a far step to the abyss of
pauperism. If we send our boys and girls into the world at eighteen
habituated to the thought of having their needs provided for without
compensatory effort on their part, they will be ill-prepared to take
their places in the world as self-respecting and self-supporting individuals.
We have sought to meet the very real problem here involved in
two ways. First, for the past several years we have been operating a
system whereby these older children are paid for a certain portion of
the work they perform in the Home, and at the same time required
to buy and pay for certain of their necessities, such as clothing, and

576

all of their luxuries. When a boy needs a pair of shoes or a suit of
clothes, from the standpoint of moral effect it makes a wide difference
whether he asks and receives it as a gift, or whether he buys 'it with
money which he feels he has earned.
The second measure that has been taken to foster in our older
children a more wholesome attitude in their relationship to the Home
was initiated in your resolution adopted in August, 1930, to the effect
that from and after June, 1931, con.tinued membership in the Home
by any boy or girl sixteen years old or more must be authorized
annually by the Trustees in each case. The import of this resolution
was explained to these plder children, so that they understood that
their retention in the Home until the age of eighteen would no longer
occur automatically, regardless of their response to the opportunities
which their membership afforded them. At the. end of the past school
year each ward of the Home who had attained the age of sixteen
and who desired to remain therein another year was required to make
out a written application for reappointment, setting forth therein his
progress and achievement in his studies, his vocational plans for the
future, his conduct record during the past year, the amount of money
he had earned toward self-support, and a statement of what might be
expected of him in general attitude and performance.
Twenty-six boys and girls made such application; of these twentyfour were reappointed unconditionally; one received a probationary
reappointment; and one was denied. One boy whose record had been
unsatisfactory declined to make application, admitting that he could
not reasonably hope to receive reappointment.
The effect of this procedure has been far-reaching. It has caused
these older children to have a new conception of the value of their
opportunities in the Home and to make in many cases a different
kind of effort to de,serve the privilege of continued membership
therein. No longer do they feel, as was too often the case in the past,
that the Masons will as a matter of course take care of them until
they reach the age of eighteen.
We follow with pride the boys and girls who have left the Home,
and in their achievements and their attitude toward the Home we
believe is found evidence of what it has done for them. Often they
return to visit, expressing gratitude for the help it has given them,
and which they can .better appreciate in the light of some experience
in the world.

from' high school, and are occupied as follows:

and entertained, first at the Lyric Theater, then at the
Masonic Temple with a Christmas tree, each child receiving
a gift, followed by refreshments.
23-The Los Angeles Masters' a nd Wardens' Association, as in
previous years, financed and managed the Christmas party at
the Home. The party was held in the gymnasium; of course,
there was a tree and a Santa Claus. The entertainment was
furnished by Bro. Bill Sharples of ·Radio Station KTM, and
a parcy of singers from that station. It was entirely suitable
and was very much enjoyed by the children.
