Referred to Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
T.o the M: .W: .Grmui Lodge of California:
Your· committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the
following report of its activities during the· past y.ear; together with
its recommendations as to f:uture action on the part of this most
worshipful body.
At the last annual communication, you in.structed the committee
to continue the work of gathering and preserving historical information and data contained· in the records and archives of the Lodges,
and appropriated the sum of $3,000 for that purpose. We have carried
out your instructions. During the past year we have earnestly endeayored to cover the whole field and bring our labors to completion.
Bu.t many causes have intervened which have made this objective
impossible of accomplishment. About two, months ago we found that
our funds were practically exhausted, and in order that the work
m,ig:ht be carried forward without interruption, we discussed the entire
matter in all of its ramifications with Brother Wm. P . Jeffries, chail:man of the Finance Committee, and with the Grand Master an'd
r.equested additional funds. After fully considering the rather peculiar

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

599

and unusual conditions which confronted the committee, the Grand
Master made available to us the further sum of $500.00.
For the first time, the committee has devoted a full year of active
effort to research work. The entire State ·has been covered. Brother
Ingram, our investigator, has traveled approximately 25,000 miles in
visiting Lodges from Yreka on the north to San Diego and Calexico
on the south. Due to the wide expanse of territory covered and the
increased average distance between Lodges, .t he traveling expenses
of our investigator were s<>mewhat in excess of last year.
Much valuable time was spent in locating records inadvertently
misplaced. In a number of focalities .it was found that ~he rei::ords
were scattered, many of them in the possession of various past Secretaries whose places of residence were far removed from the Lodge
rooms. While the time spent in reassembling these records .and
placing them in their proper places might be considered constructive
work, yet from the standpoint of historical research it constituted a
decided hindrance, although one that 'could n{)t be avoided, and one
that had not been anticipated by the committee. In a few instances
considerable time was lost through the refusal of certain Masters to
recognize the credentia1s 'of ~he committee's field man, and recourse
was had to the Grand Master, who quickly corrected this conditi<>n.
The records of some of the Lodges were inc<>mplete, w'hrch
necessitated interviewing individual members in order to ·-p iece together in narrative form the ·activities of the Lodges covering lon.g
·periuds of time.
In other cases, the loss of records made it necessary to search
the local newspaper files in order that the Masonic activities in the
community might be preserved and made available.
These are a few of the conditions which were encountered during
the year, wnich greatly ·slowed up the work of our investigator, a:nd
.a:ccount ·for the higher cost per Lodge as compared with ' last )rear.
They explain the need of funds over and above the amount appropriated by Grand Lodge, which need the Grnnd Master saw fit to
meet.
While . the above enumerated ·conditions have at times great1~
discouraged the committee .and have presented "Pl"Obleml; whith ~ried
the patience and tested the ingenuity of our investigator, we still feel
that real progress has been made during the past year. · ·
A review of the year'~ accomplishments clea~ly indicates' that
the .plan adopted of having a full time investigator visit 'the Lodges
and search their records is conduciv·e of quicker arrd better" restdts
than if reliance is pla:ced entirely on rota! comniittees: We ·have
encountered a universal .approval ·of the plan .and purpose· bf' 'Grand

601

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge in gathering and preserving facts and data connected with
Masonic history of California and, with a few notable exceptions, we
found that t.he Lodges prefer that someone t~ained in .~uch work be
sent to search their records: Local members do not have the time
·to. go through .the many pages of minutes in search of material. A
great many honestly and frankly state that they do not k;pow what
to . look for or what to take from their records, notwithstanding the
fact that the committee has from time to time sent out explicit instruction; ··iii· great detail outlining the information sought.
· As the . result of our labors we have now on file in the Grand
Secretary's office complete returns from 280 Lodges. The reports
cover :the histories of all the earliest Lodges, with one or two exceptions. The committee has . concentrated its efforts on the oldest
Lodges for several reasons:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic History was created
for the purpose . of obtaining the histories of the "pioneer Lodges"
of California. While the committee· has attempted to secure the
history of every Lodge in the jurisdiction by the use of local committees, it has not lost 's ight of its major policy. Thus it will be found
that of the complete reports in the Grand Secretary's office, there
are missing only 20 Lodges which were chartered before 1880, or
approximately 50 years ago, In other words, of the 280 reports on
file, 232 of these reports give data on Lodges chartered before 1880.
Another reason why the committee has gone directly to the
older Lodges first is that the oldest records contain the most valuable
facts,. the most romantic stories, and the greatest mass of material.
It is believed that local committees are in a better position to gather
the information in the newer Lodges by reason of association or
personal acquaintance. This latter point · is splendidly illustrated by
our experience in obtaining interviews from the fifty-year members
in the jurisdiction. During the past year we have received the life
stories of about seventy-five of our fifty-year men. The great majority
of these stories have been received from local committees.
Several of the Lodges visited by the investigator have committees
at work on their histories but have not as yet submitted reports to
the. Grand Lodge committee. We respectfully urge all Lodges having
local. committees which have undertaken the task of searching their
own records and which have not sent in their reports, to make an
extra effort to bring the work to completion as soon as possible.
In addition to. the research work carried on, the members of the
committee have been active in other lines. Visits have been made to
a number of Lodges for the purpose of giving talks o.n Masonic history, interviewing Lodge members, gathering information, inspecting

Lodge rooms and their contents .. We found many things of Masonic
interest and have prepared reports of our investigations and filed
same .for future reference. In making these visits members of the
~ommittee 'h ave used no part of their appropriation for traveling or
personal expenses.
.
A brief mention of a few of the Lodge rooms visited may be made
at· this time:
The hall of Table Mountain Lodge at Cherokee has an interior
profusely decorated with beautifully hand-carved emblems, the work
of a brother of the craft. The letter "G" in the east was carved from
a solid block of wood. Occupying a hig.h position in the east is a
representation of the All-Seeing Eye. On the north and south walls
of the room are such emblems as the hour glass, the scythe, the beehive and many others, all hand-carved and artistically .embellished.
, A visit to the Lodge room of Forbes town Lodge No. 50 is well
worth the time and energy necessary in making the trip. This room
is on the ground floor, and the altar, the lights and .the hand~made
rods and emblems which surmount them, and other Lodge paraphernalia, date .back to the early days of Masonry on the Mother Lode .
. Set in the exterior wall of this ancient building is the cornerstone of
the old Fraternal Hall at St. Louis in Sierra county, which was owned
and used jointly by the Odd Fellows and Masons. This huge marble
stone has an interesting history. It is said to be of Italian marble
and was carried on the backs of mules from Oroville. In time, the
townsite of St. . Louis was hydraulicked and the cornerstone ,which
marked the meeting place of St. Louis Lodge No. 86 was washed

Our research through the minutes and records of the Lodges
discloses the fact that many of the Secretaries in the early days were
somewhat lax in properly recording important and interesting actions
taken by the Lodges and the equally important activities of the membership. The extreme brevity with which they at times reported
maios qliestions discussed and decided by their Lodges has necessitated on the part of the eommittee extensive research and the needless
expenditure of valuable time in deciphering and interpreting. their
records. We therefore respectfully urge the Secretaries of the several
Lodges in California to exercise extreme care in recording all matters
which come before the Lodge and which may be record'e d, and to
endeavor to fully and completely St<!-te in their minutes ~11' essential
facts necessary to a proper interpretation of the activities of the
Lodge. Our acts today become history tomorrow, and it is within
the province of the Lodge Secretaries to play a conspicuous part in
the perpetuation of Masonic history in this State.

· ~n th~ rec~rds of \Ypodbridge Lodge No. i31 was fo~nd a statement. and. copy of a letter which .relate .a r~the.r thrilling episode in
the history of Masonry .in this State. Some time during the seventies
a C~lifornia f\fason passed away, leaving a widow and three children
abundantly provided for. Shortly after the death of the father the

a grandmother. In the course of time, the deceased Mason's brother
who lived in Canada, heard reports that all · was not well with th;
children and the estate in California. He came here to investigate
and found the reports ' to be true. The large estate had been dissipated
and squandere·d and the children were ill-kept and in actual want,
and he further learned that it was the intention of the grandmother
to place the oldest child (a girl) in a convent. The Canadian brother
sought legal advice and was told that the only way he could obtain
the children was· to kidnap them. This he proceeded to do. He made
his way from San Francisco to Stockton and there learned that
officers were hot on his trail. Being hard pres·sed for time and money
and realizing the seriousness of the situation, he sought assistance of
the Masters of the two Lodges in that city. These men took him in
charge· and passed him on to the Master of the Lodge at Woodbridge.
This· Master in turn conveyed the fugitive by buggy to Volcano and
placed him in the ha·nds of the Master of Volcano Lodge, who assisted
him in safely reaching Reno, where he boarded a trans-continental
train a.nd in time reached his residence in Canada, where he gave the
children a good home. The sequel to this interesting story is contained in a letter written by the Master of a Lodge in Toronto Canada
to the Master of the Lodge at Woodbridge. The letter expr~sses th;
grateful thanks of the Canadian brethren for the assistance rendered
the fugitive, who was Senior Deacon of the Toronto Lodge.
Further evidence of the recognition of Masonic signs by Indians,
when such signs were given by white emigrants crossing the plains,
was ·found during the past year. Mrs. George Harrison of Susanville
clearly remembers an occasion in 1858 'when the party led by her
grandfather was attacked by Indians. Leader Harrison gave the
Master Mason's signal of distress, which was answered by the Indian
chief. Amicable relations were established and that evening a council
was held, with the white men and Indians alternately seated in a
huge circle around the camp fire smoking the 'pipe of peace. Before
the departure of the emigrant train, the Indian chief presented Brother
Harrison with a war club, with instructions to display it whenever
approached by Indians, and no harm would come to him or his party.
The war club was used on several occasions to prevent trouble, and
never failed to be recognized by the Indians.
We ·also found evidence of the existence of an ·organization
modeled somewhat on Masonic lines among the Indians in the Humboldt · country.
In the archives of Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 is an · ancient
trowel, in connection with which your committee was instrumental
in uncovering a most interesting story. Santa Barbara Lodge was

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

called upon to lay the cornerstone of the first Court House in Santa
Barbara county. Arrangements were made to have the Grand Master
officiate at the ceremony, and a souvenir trowel was procured to be
presented to him on that occasion. At the last minute, however, it
was learned that the Grand Master could not be present and the
Master of the Lodge performed the ceremony and took with him the
trowel. Many years later a member of Santa Barbara Lodge, while
walking along Battery street in San Francisco, saw a trowel in the
window of a pawn shop. He was amazed, on investigation, to find
the name of his own Lodge engraved on the trowel. He immediately
redeemed the tool, later presenting it to his. Lodge, and the souvenir
trowel thus found its way back to its Mother Lodge.
Stories of the struggles of Lodges in the early days to maintain
their organization are not uncommon. Few, however, are as interesting as that of Mariposa Lodge No. 24. In 1856 this. Lodge fell
upon evil days. Owing to a slump in mining, its members moved out
of the jurisdiction in such numbers that but seven were left in the
locality. Jmst at this time a fire swept the town and burned the temple.
All that was saved was an old ark containing a Holy Bible, Square
and Compass~ Determined that Mariposa Lodge should not die, the
seven· remaining members held regular meetings at each others'
homes. On the day of meeting word would be passed around that a
meeting was scheduled for that evening at a certain house. At early
candle light two members would carry the ark containing the Lights
of the Lodge to the appointed place. The ark would be set up as an
altar, the great lights placed upon it, and candles. procured. for the
three lesser lights, and Lodge would be opened in due form, with
seven members· present. This proeedure was carried on for more
than a year, until Mariposa revived as a mining center, and better
facilities were provided.
The committee continues to find instances of unusual and unique
procedure in many of the ea·rly Lodges. Howard Lodge No. 96 of
Yreka had a provision in its first by-laws to the effect that a nomaffiliated brother was privileged to visit the Lodge once without
cha.rge, but thereafter he must pay an admission fee of one dollar
per meeting for each meeting attended until he affiliated with the
Lodge.
Another Lodge, at the conclusion of its regular business, decided
to confer the first degree upon a candidate elected that nigh~ They,
therefore, procured a team, traveled the ten miles to the candidate's
home, brought him back to the Lodge and duly initiated him.
In Texas Lodge No. 46 of San Juan Bautista, the Master at one
time requested that charges be preferred against him. The request

was granted, charges were preferred, a trial held, and the Master
exonerated.
In another Lodge a brother found guilty of unmasonic conduct
and sentenced to be reprimanded, gave notice of appeal to the Grand
Lodge. Later he changed his mind and appealed to the Master of
the Lodge to carry out the sentenced imposed by the trial commission and sought the cooperation of the Lodge in securing a dismissal
of his app~al to the Grand Lodge.
Visalia Lodge in 1868 took steps toward erecting its' own Widows
and Orphans Home, but never completed the project.
In one instance the will of a dying brother charged his Lodge
with the care and custody of his minor child.
In the year 1856, the Lodge at Dutch Flat preferred charges of
unmasonic conduct against a non-al!iliate, held a trial found him guilty,
and expelled him from the rights and privileges of Masonry. The acts
of gu:ilt charged were failure to pay over funds which had been collected from an Entered Apprentice Mason, and the introduction of
certain things Masonic in the ritual of an order know as "E Clampus
Vitus," which was then being formed throughout the Mother Lode.
The records of one Lodge show that for several years the propriety and feasibility of purchasing a hearse was frequently debated.
In 1875 an appropriation of $100 was made for that purpose. Several
years later the minutes indicate that the Lodge was still interested
in a proper showing at funerals, for we find that they · voted to pay
$20 to each member who should make the trip to San Jose to attend
the burial of a Lodge brother. Whether the brethren rode to San
Jose i.n or upon the hearse the record sayeth not.
In Mono County we find a mining district named "Masonic";
within that district is a mountain called "Mount Moriah" and a town
be;iring the name "Masonic." Within the district are mining claims
recorded as "Mount Morfah," "Rough Ashier," "Perfect Ashier,'' and
"Three Ruffians." It . would appear that Masons must have been
somewhat in evidence in that section in the early days..
Many years ago two members of Wilmington Lodge engaged in
a rather spectacu.Jar fist fight; subsequently when meeting' they would
apply rather uncomplimentary epithets to each other. How~ver, they
always attended Lodge and sat together. W·hen asked ·a:bout this
queer performance their answer was that, regardless of their personal opinions, the Lodge room was a place to lay aside all animosities.
The Civil War cast its blight in California, as in other portii:>ns
of the country. Although little can be found in the records of the
Lodges, it is well known that · the bitter feeling existing at the time
was reflected in these groups. There was a marked increase in the
number of trials held by the Lodges · at this time. In some cases

the Lodges were split and new groups were formed as a result. This
occurred particularly at Drytown, on the Mother Lode, and at. Petalu.ma. In the latter place, during the Civil War, two factions grew up
within Peta,luma Lodge No. · 88. To avoid destruction of t4e Masonic
influence in that place, the supporters of the south withdrew and
formed Arcturas Lodge in 1867. Then, for thirty years, although the
war was over, Arcturas and Petaluma Lodges lived in constant
conflict.
In 1898, when most of the Civil War generation ~f Masons had
passed on, their sons and des~endants, being imbued with true Masonic spirit, decided to heal the breach so long 'existing and consolidate the two Lodges. They invited the older members of both Lodges
to a banquet and seated them so they would be compelled 'to renew
the friendship of their younger days. No one was permitted to refer
to the war or any of its consequences. The younger generation talked
in glowing terms of the future and their duty as Masons to work
together in the common cause. A consolidation was effected and
erstwhile enemies joined together that the best interests of Masonry
might be advanced in that community.
·
. Nate Vice, who gave Visalia its name, was probably California's
most '\'ersatile early day Mason. He was a member of the Lodges
at Visalia, Benicia, San Diego and El Monte. Brother Martin, who
knew him well throughout his entire life, says that Vice was a
preacher; a public speaker of note, a gambler, a horse racer, an auctioneer, and a hunter for the markets, and that the rest of the time
he was just a plain dirt farmer.
One of the most unique characters in northern California
Masonry was W. T. C. Elliott, better known as "Rough" Elliott,
who lived near Susanville and was strong in the Masonic faith. In
the fall of 1857, Rough learned that a prominent brother Mason by
the name of Snelling had been ruthlessly murdered in Merced County.
Suspicion point<;d to one Bill Edwards of rather unsavory reputation.
Edwards succeeded in avoiding detection and made good his escape.
Rough decided to bring to justice the murderer of his Masonic brother
and make the · west safe for Masons. He accordingly traveled to the
Carson Valley and in time ingratiated himself into the good graces of
the famous Bill Thorington gang which had for years spread. terror
throughout Western Nevada and .Eastern California. Rough regaled
the gang with fantastic .tales of purely imaginary crimes he claimed
to have committed. This disarmed all suspicion and he was taken into
full fellowship. In the c9urse of time he observed .that one of the
desperadoes seldom left the hangout during the daylight hours when
returning California emigrants were reported in the vicinity. Rough
was particularly friendly with this fellow and at last succeeded in

winning his full confidence; so much so that he confided in Rough
the fact that he was the much sought for Bill Edwards and that he
had murdered Snelling. Rough immediately .sent word to his neighbors and Masonic friends in Plumas County and they in a body raided
the Thorington stronghold, capturing the entire gang. Without delay
they constituted a Vigilance jury, appointed counsel for the prosecution and defense and proceeded to try Bill Thorington.' He w~s duly
convicted of murder and hanged. Then they took Bill Edwards to
Plumas County and tried him for murder before a similarly constituted jury. He was convicted and duly executed for the crime committed in Merced County. And thus did. Rough Elliott the Mason
contribute his mite, as he said, "toward making the ~est a safe;
place for Masons to reside."
Clay Lodge No. 101 at Dutch Flat merits mention at this time.
This old Lodge has shown a fine spirit of cooperation, in the construction of a vault for the safe keeping of current and past records. The
expenditure of $100 in cash and the enthusiastic labor of thirteen
earnest brethren has resulted in a commodious, fire-proof concrete
vault where all Lodge records are safe from destruction or loss. We
bring this accomplishment to the attention of Grand Lodge with the
hope that the older Lodges will herein recognize a project worthy of
emulation.
Our Grand Secretary, Brother John Whicher, has during the past
year performed one of the finest pieces of constructive historical research work undertaken by any member of the Grand Lodge. Brother
Whicher has rewritten his interesting pamphlet published several
years ago bearing the title, "Masonic Beginnings in the State of California." This has involved extensive correspondence covering many
of the grand jurisdictions and has entailed painstaking care in searching records and interpreting facts. He has settled many troublesome
questions with respect to the Lodge affiliations and activities of many
of the distinguished men from other jurisdictions who during the
early days took an active part in the civil and military life of this State.
He has uncovered the hidden history of all the Lodges which have
worked iri this State under charters from foreign jurisdictions and
made available interesting details connected therewith. Brother
Whicher is to be congratulated on this valuable contribution to Masonic history in California.

uneconomical. We have all the facilities in working order necessary

in a frame of mind to willingly assist the committee in making research and collecting material. To hold in abeyance the completion

. impetus, and would further necessitate again going over much of
the ground already covered and would greatly delay making available
to the craft the glorious history of Masonry in this State.

SOUND MOTION PICTURES
The . Masters and Wardens Associ~tion pf Los Angeles. presented
the following which was referred to the Committee .on Policy and
General Purposes :
Grand Lodge of California:
The administration of each Grand Master advances the objects
and objectives of our great fraternity. Each Grand Master, at considerable sacrifice, contributes in large measure to that advancement
and leaves the stamp and imprint of his own character and personality
on the · hearts and in the minds of the craft throughout this great
jurisdiction. Be as diligent and untiring as he may he obviously cannot contact all of our members, but science has provided a means of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

617

not only making the . Grand Master available to all the craft but of
perpetuating the personalities of our Grand Masters, thus rekindling
in the hearts of those who know them the affection and esteem we
have for them and .creating a like feeling on the part of men yet to be
admitted.
We ·refer to sound motion pictures. Through sound pictures our.
Grand ;Masters could speak to us long after the Supreme Grand Master has called them to H is Lodge on high.
Our plan is to take a group picture of all Past Grand Masters,
one serving as Chairman introducing each in turn with a close-up of
each one making a two or three-minute talk; thus we will have these
personalities permanently recorded and available for all of our Lodges.
There can be no question but what this would be a valuable means of
creating and extending interest among the brethren.
Being firmly convinced of the merits of this plan we offer the
following resolution:
•

Whereas this Grand Lodge is not now employing a means of perpetuating the personalities of our Grand Masters, and
Whereas science has provided a suitable and practical means,
Therefore be it resolv ed, That the incoming Grand Master appoint
a special committee for the purpose of investigating the expense of, a:nd
to make arrangements for, securing a sound motion picture of our Past
Grand Masters, and the Grand Master and this committee is hereby authorized to proceed in this matter in collaboration with the Finance Committee of this Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge 'of California:
_Your Committee on Returns herewith .s ubmits its report.
The financial depression continues and it has affected the Ma-·
sopic fraternity in several ways.
Due to the failures of banks four Lodges have failed to pay the
entire amount of their dues to the Grand Lodge.
'. Owing to there beirig a reduction of 1,686 in the number of initia-·
tioris this year there has been a ·serious dimunition in the amount of
in'c ome for the Masonic Homes.
And, for the first time in the· existence 'of the Grand Lodge, there
has been no dispensation for the formation of a new Lodge issued in
a year.
There have been 1,750 fewer candidates raised than' were reported
in !930; 353 fewer Master Masons have affiliated and 33 less were

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

618

restored to membership. Also, let it be said, 63 fewer Master Masons·
withdrew.
The gains do not make cheerful reading. The number suspended
for non-payment of dues increased 868 over· 1930; 9 more were expelled and there is an increase of 129 in the number of deaths over
1930. The number of members having their dues remitted has more
than doubled, showing the Lodges are doing what they can to take
care of their indigent members.
Yet, in spite of all the bad news, the total membership shows a
gain of 360 over the total reported in 1930; Few, if ·any, of the other
Grand Lodges in the United States are able to show a like gain. Our
total membership as of July 31, 1931, is 142,422. ·
· At the last communication of the Grand Lodge dual membership
was authorized. There has been no grand rush to take advantage
of the privilege. We ga·i ned 10 by dual membership.
The serious reduction in the number of candidates ought to give
the Lodges plenty of opportunity to assimilate their new membership, and provide more time for the social amenities.
Whether the number of candidates be more, or less, the main
thing is to see that the quality is maintained and all will be well with
the fraternity.

Adopted as read.

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of Califo,-nia:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows :
Upon the present«.tion of the report of this committee, at the last
communication of Grand Lodge, the continuance of its work was recommended. As but two members of this committee were appointed
this year, the scope of the work was necessarily limited. It was practically impossible to investigate rumors of clandestine activity in
widely dispersed sections of California. Our report, therefore, must
be quite brief.
In the southern part of the State we find most of the clandestine
bodies operating which were specifically located in our last report.
Their activity, however, has not been so intense, their meetings are
irregular and the interest of their members is reported to be' waning.
The Grand Lodge Benito Juarez of Torreon, State of Coahuila,
Mexico, which as. previously report ed had chartered three Lodges in
southern California, to wit, Minerva at Los Angeles, Hiram No. 45 of
San Bernardino and Oriente No. 41 of San Pedro, has withdrawn these
charters and these clandestine bodies are not now operating.
We have made a careful investigation thr~ugh the work of Brother
John Alpers of the San Francisco bay district, and are unable to fin d
any evidence of clandestine activity save that of the negro lodges
organized under the name of "Sovereign Grand Lodge of Ancient Free
and Accepted Masons of California" also known as " Prince Hall
Masons," heretofore reported at our last communication.
The Co-masonic groups still seem to be operating. While we have
no information of new ones starting, there seems to be considerable

interest in the particular group known as Hollywood Lodge at Hollywood boulevard and Serrijlollo &keet in Los Ang~los.
As stated, we havi:. been consider-ably- handk;epped by the size of
our committee. It is maniks,tly impossible to cover so wide a field as
the State of California with but two members.
Your COtllmittee feels t'1aJ this work should not be abandoned.
While there may be at present a decline of interest in these clandestine
bodies, a return to nprmal ecopom.ic copditions will undoubted.ly result
in a revival of activity. Also we feel that we have not exhausted all the
sources of information regarding these bodies nor discovered alt who
are operatipg a$ suc.4 ,
Your committee, therefore, respectfully recommends that a committee of at least five members be constituted, representing all of the
more distant p;ir.ts of the Sta,t.e, that the woi:k of investigation be
continued and that a complete and exhaustive report be rendered at
the next communication of Gr.and Lodge.
W.ILLIAM•A. ScatunDER,
JoHN ALPERS,
Committee.

above rec-0mme:ndation, and t-he report and re(X)mmendation
were adopted.

The fund now amounts, cash and securities, $694,852.58, an increase for the fiscal year ending Ju ly 31, 1931 of $61,828.50.
Time is rapidly approaching when we should manifest our charity
by doing our part toward the unfortunate brethren, bereaved widows
and helpless orphans. They are our dependent wards-a heritage, and
we must not, under our solemn obligation, overlook the blessed privilege of doing them good. Can we not, year by year, spare something
toward the endowment fund until it is sufficient to carry on our great
work, the loving care of our indigent brethren, widows and children ?
This subject is most worthy of you r deliberation and consideration. It
rests entirely with you to determine whethel" future generations shall
point with honorable pride to your unselfish charity.
To give is really a little thing to do where much good is done:
Yet on the ear of Him who thought to die unmourned, that knowledge
of giving will fall like sweet music.

T<J the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California :
At the beginning of the· year our committee consisted of Brothers
William P. Filmer, Grand Treasurer, W. P. Jeffries, Chairman of
Finance Committee, and Robert Greig. On the 9th of April, Brother
Filmer wrote me that Brother Robert Greig had been killed by an
automobile. In the passing of Brother Greig the committee lost the
advice and support of a very loyal member. He was so situated that
he could visit the communities throughout northern and central California, and his genial manner always won the confidence of the
. brethren in the community which he visited. The committee deeply
regrets the passing of Brother Greig as a member of the Grand Lodge
and his services for this committee, on which he had served since its
inception.
During the year ending September 30, 1931, twelve Lodges or
Temple Associations have conducted correspondence with your comm ittee. A few of these were only inquiries as to how to proceed to
raise funds for a building, or to ask the committee their views on
different financial problems.
The committee has reviewed and approved the erection of buildings, or the purchase of real estate, as follows:
Grafton Lodge No. 141, F. & A. M., situated at Knights Landing :
On April 15, 1931, this Lodge was given permission to invest in stock
in the Grafton Masonic Hall Association. The by-law s of the Association provide as follows:
"Stock subscriptions: The right of subscribing to the
capital stock of the corporation shall be confined exclusively
to Grafton Lodge No. 141, F. & A. M. and to its m,embers,
and to Grafton Chapter No. 379, 0. E. S., and its members."
The Association · was incorporated for $20,000 and the par value
of the shares is $10.00 each. The stock was sold with the aim that
· Grafton Lodge No. 141, F. & A. M. should ultimately become the
holder of all of the stock.
The Association purchased a lot, 60 x 120, in the center of the
town of Knights Landing, for which they paid $1,800.00. The estimate
of the cost of their building is $15,000.00. They were given permission
to borrow $7,000.0tl from the Bank of Yolo, at Woodland, on a first
mortgage, cin a twenty-year repayment plan. Under date of September 21, 1931, the Association reported that they had proceeded as
above outlined, and that the build ing was under construction.
Clovis Lodge No. 417, F. & A. M., situated at Clovis: On December 1, 1930, this Lodge was given permission to purchase a property

638

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

100 x 140 on the corner of DeWitt and Fifth streets, in the town of
Clovis, which had formerly been owned by the Presbyterian church,
for the sum of $4000.00, free and clear. The committee was informed
that the building had originally cost in excess of $16,000 to build, but
as the church was no longer using the property, it could be bought at
great sacrifice.
At the time of the purchase, Clovis Lodge had on hand in excess
of $40GO, .and permission was given to the Lodge to pay $3000 cash
and to give back a mortgage for $1000, due on or before five years
at 5%.
Under date of September 12, the Lodge informed your committee
that they had converted the building into a Masonic hall at a very
small expense, all work having been done by members, and that a
recent appraisal had valued the property in excess of $20,000.00.
Pittsburg Lodge No. 429, F. & A. M., situated at Pittsburg: On
January 15, 1931, this Lodge was given permission to purchase a piece
of property 90 x 90, located in the town of Pittsburg, for the sum of
$2,750.00. At that time, the Lodge had cash in the bank in the amount
of $6,200.00. The Lodge contemplated proceeding to raise funds to
build a building to cost from $10,GOO to $15,000, but under date of
October 5, 1931, the Lodge informed your committee that while they
had purchased the lot and paid cash for the same, they did not feel
that they should proceed to build a temple until financial conditions
improved.
Sanger Lodge No. 316, F. & A. M., situated at Sanger: On
December 27, 1930, this Lodge was given permission to purchase a
two-story buiding on the corner of Seventh and "M" streets in the
town of Sanger, for the sum of $11,000.00, the property being 70 x 74.
Qn June 24, 1931, your committee authorized the Lodge to proceed to remodel the building at an estimated cost of $10,000.00. At the
time of giving permission to purchase the property, the Lodge had on
hand in excess of $9,000, since which time they have raised an additional $5,000 from their members. When the remodeling of the· building is completed, they estimate that the entire property will have a
value of $24,G00.00, on which there will be an indebtedness to a private
individual of $10,000, with interest at 7%. This indebtedness is to be
paid at the rate of. $500.00 a year for the first five years, and $1,000
a year thereafter. This Lodge shows a steady financial growth during
the past several years.
Santa Paula Lodge No. 298, F. & A. M., situated at Santa Paula :
Under date of September 18, 1931, this Lodge reported that their
build ing had been entirely completed, and they expected to dedicate
the same on the evening of September 21, 1931. They estimated their
cost as follows:

Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, F. & A. M., situated in San Diego:
On March 4, 1931, permission was given to this Lodge to proceed
with their building. This Lodge at that time had a membership of
approximately 700, and in June, 1930, approximately 450 members
subscribed to beneficial loan certificates, the amount aggregating $73,539. These are .non-interest bearing certificates, the Lodge plec\ging
itself to repay the same on the death of the subscriber.
The chairman of the Finance Committee of Silver Gate Masonic
Temple ·Building Fund reported that on September 1, 1931, there had
been paid in on these subscriptions, $22,053.85, and while some of the
pledges were delinquent, none had been repudiated and they expected
ultimately to collect practically the entire amount. They invested
$12,000 in real estate, and. the.ir contract for building is $55,000, making
a total cost of $67,000.
When the project is completed, they do not expect to owe more
than $25,0CO, which will ultimately be retired by the payment of
pledges, so that their project will be free and clear of debt.
Santa Ana Masonic Temple Association, Ltd., situated at Santa
Ana: On October 2, 1931, Santa Ana Masonic Temple Association,
Ltd., dedicated its new home. This, by far, is .t he largest building
which has been financed under the supervision of your committee
since it . was first organized.
Before Santa Ana started its building project, the temple committee, consisting of Brothers Whitson, Mead, Hill and Hoffman,
consulted with your committee, and the first question asked was how
much they could .borrow towards building their new temple. Your
committee replied that is the wrong question, the right question being
how little could they get along with.
At that time, Santa Ana owned a well situated corner, 90 x 117,
on, which was standing their old temple, and on which they have
erected their new building.
The brethren of Santa Ana, in two campaigns, one for the building and the other for furnishings, received pledges for the sale of stock
and gifts amounting to $210,877, on which, up to. September 30, 1931,
they had collected in cash, $156,764.75, approximately 75%, and they
believe that there will be a . shrinkage of less than 10%.
The total cost of the new Temple in Santa Ana is as follows:
Building ......................................................... ,.... $185,0SR 1I
Land ......................... :........................................ :. 63,000.00
Furniture ....... c..................... i '............................,. 33, 166.49
Total ,... :............................... :.: .... ;...:.. "...... $281,W.60

.,,

641

Their total net liabilities at the present time are $57,501.74. They
still have uncollected pledges amounting to $54, 112.25, on which they
are .sure tha.t they will collect at least $35,000.00.
Pending the collection of these pledges, they borrowed from the
Pacific Mutual Life Ins. Co. $35,000, on a mortgage at 6%. When the
entire financial book is closed they will find that their fixed indebtedness will be from 70% to 10% of the value of the project.
Your committee congratulates the Masonic fraternity of Santa
Ana on the excellent man.ner in which the financing of the new temple
has been handled, and strongly recommend that other communities
endeavor to ·emulate their example.
At this time your committee desires to reiterate that its principal
aim is to be helpful and constructive, keeping in mind the one thought
that the downfall of nations, as well as individuals, is the contracting
of excessive debts. Not "How much can you borrow, but how little
can you get along with" should be our slogan.
WM. P. JEFFRIES,
WILLIAM

P. FILMER,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND
LECTURER'S REPORT
To the M:. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The committee to whom the report of the Grand Lecturer was
referred, herewith submits its report. The report which the Grand
Lecturer presented is his twenty-fourth .annual report. For almost a
quarter ~f a century this sincere and loyal man has faithfully served
the Lodges of this jurisdiction. His efforts in behalf of Masonry in
this jurisdiction have been untiring, and no task has been too difficult
for him to undertake which would promote the welfare of the Lodges.
The high standard of proficiency achieved by the Lodges in their
ritualistic work is visible evidence, not only of the skill and ability of
our Grand Lecturer, but also of the hearty cooperation which the
Lodges count it a privilege to give him.
This committee concurs with that part of his report which recommends that section .115 of the Constitution be amended so that a
Lodge can confer only three first degrees, three second degrees, or
one third degree on candidates at one time and in one day. It is the
recommendation of this committee that this portion of the. Grand Lecturer's report be referred to the Co~mittce on Policy and General

642

· PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAXD LODGE OF CALIFORXIA

Purposes for consideration, and to the· Committee on Jurisprudence
to draft the necessary legislation.
We note with satisfaction that Officers Associations have been
formed in. the different Inspectorial districts .. We heartily concur in
this program initiated by the Grand Master and promoted by the
Grand Lecturer, and we commend it to the officers of the various
Lodges.
We recommend that that ·part of the Gr.and Lecturer's report
refe!'f'ing to the consolidation of certain Lodges which are having a
hard time to e~ist, be referred to the Grand Master with such committee assistance as he .may deem adv.isable, to consult with these
Lodges as opportunity q.ffords and determine if consolidation plans
can be work~d out to the satisfaction of the Lodges concerned.
The healthy and prosperous condition of the Lodges is, we believe,
due in a large measure to the help and advice given by the Grand
Lecturer. We sincerely hope that he may .find it possible to serve the
fraternity for many, many years to come.
DWIGHT W. STEPHENSON,
ARCHIBALD

REPORT OF U. C." L. A. CLUB HOUSE
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Directors of the Masonic Club of the University
of California at Los Angeles fraternally submit their report for the
year ending September 30, 1931. There was received from Grand
Lodge, after our last communication, from the collection of the per·
capita tax for that purpose, the sum of $10,545.45. To this should be
added the sum of $63.22 remaining in the fund from the previous year
~nd the sum of $147.63 interest earned thereon,. making a · total maintenance f.u.nd of $10,756.30. During the same period we expended for
maintenance and general upkeep the sum of $9,078.98. The item of
general upkeep includes equipment and replacements for the year.
During the year outstanding pledges in the sum of $2,013.60 were paid
and interest on campaign funds in the sum of $309.89 was . earned.
The expense connected with this fund amounted to $432.79 making a
total expense for the year of $9,511.77. There remains in the pledge
account, assuming that it shall be realized as explained in a subsequent. par.agraph, $11,369.35 with about $7,000 in unpaid pledges.

643

Your Board had authorized certain improvements to be made and
contracts had been let just previously to the closing of the United
States National Bank, where our funds were on deposit. Fortunately
no work had been done and no materials actually supplied and we
were able to defer their execution until we shall recover these deposits.
In other words, there is impounded in the United States National
Bank funds aggregating $13,046.67. From all the information we can
secure it is probable that we shall lose a very small percentage, if
anything, of this sum, the estimates of shrinkage varying from 10%
to nothing. We were also fortunate in this, that we had invested
$1,000 of the sum of $1,063.22 remaining in the maintenance account
September 30, 1930, in a first mortgage certificate paying us 6% and
were able to borrow sufficient funds to carry us over at the same rate
of interest we were receiving.
Another unfortunate occurrence took place on September 19.
Mrs. Kempton, whom we have had occasion heretofore to commend
for her genial, efficient and motherly supervision of the clubhouse in
her capacity as resident hostess, was stricken with acute appendicitis
necessitating an immed:ate operation. She returned to the clubhouse,
however, on October 7. No interruption of the activities and service,
being rendered to the students, occurred however, due to the fortunate
fact that Mrs. Kempton's sister had just resigned a position of many
years' standing and was able to substitute for her sister during the
enforced absence. We are glad to report at this time that Mrs. Kempton is mending rapidly and will shortly be as vigorous and active as
usual.

Masons of this jurisdiction are rendering through the instrumentality
.of the . clubhouses at Berkeley and at Westwood, n.everthel.e ss some
notice must be given to the great good which is daily being done.
Picture in your minds a home at Westwood, Los Angeles, of 750
young men and women who take advantage of the opportunities
offered, and realize that an average of between 140 and 150 make use
of its accommodations daily, and you begin to realize the contribution
you are making to the welfare of these young people, and to the cause
of education generally. During the year, also, we were able to lay
the foundations of a committee which will function as an employment
bureau for the assistance of Masonically affiliated students and have
been successful in securing part time employment for several young
men and women. Bearing in mind, that it is estimated, that 60% of
the student body must have some part time employment, the importance of this work becomes manifest. We seek the cooperation, in this
regard, of the nearby Lodges and their members. The council · also
has under consider~tion the inauguration of monthly or bi-monthly
meetings to be addressed by various business and professional men,
upon the. subject of ·their vocations as a guide and aid . to. the students
in the selection of their occupations. The importance of this undertaki.ng is obvious.
We recommend that such provision be made for the support
during the year 1933-1934 as will be adequate for that purpo.se.
IRA F. THOMPSON, Chairman.

REPORT OF U. C. BERKELEY CLUB HOUSE
To the M:. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
As Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of California,·
Inc., we submit herewith our report of the affairs of the institution
for the year ending September 30, 1931.
Nothing of more than passing interest has transpired at the clubhouse during the year. Notwithstanding that fact, the facilities offered
by the clubhouse to. the men and women of Masonic affiliation at the
University of California have been used and availed of by an increasing number of students. The usual line of social functions, which
mean so much in the life of young people away from home, have been
held under the direction of the Masonic Council, comprised of the
representatives of the ·various organizations using the clubhouse. The
very efficient manner in which Mrs. J. H. Quinn, hostess of the clubhouse, has supervised all that goes on there has had full and hearty
support by the young people themselves.
As an institution; the clubhouse continues to hold a position as
one of the most prominent organizations for good at the University.
It has .the whole-hearted support and approval of President and Mrs .
Sproul and of the various deans and others charged with welfare
work among students' at the University.
·
Amounts drawn from the reserve for depreciation and insurance
fund, in order to carry on the clubhouse during the year ending
September 30, 1930, have been replaced within the past year, which
will enable the Trustees to have the clubhouse properly painted and
minor items of upkeep cared for before the winter season. Other than
the loss of two small fires, both due to faulty installation of heating
apparatus when the building was constructed; there has been a minimum expenditure for betterments and upkeep during the seven years
of the life of the buildin~. The · faulty installation referred to has been
corrected, and the heating plant now has the full approval of the
Building Inspector and Fire Department officials of the city of Berkeley.

To the M.'.W.'.Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
To convey in a report of this character anything like an adequate
idea of the extraordinary success of the Twelfth Annual Observance
of Public Schools Week is practically impossible. To do this would
necessitate not only mention of scores of particularly notable observanc(;!s, but also specific references to the reports thereof.
The reports this year were not confined to those received from
lodges and from committees in charge of the observance. These
were supplemented by reports received from city and county superintendents of schools in response to a request made by our committee. We regret exceedingly that the limitations of this report
preclude any further reference to them than will be hereafter made.
Some of the communications received from the school people
were restricted to a detailed report of the observance with a statement of their own reactions and that of their teachers 11nd principals. Others included also an account in detail of the arrangements
made in the schools to assist the committee in charge of the Observance. Among the latter was one received from a city superintendent consisting of two volumes in scrapbook form of approximately
one hundred pages. Among other material included there were
copies of form letters sent out by the superintendent and also by
the Chamber of Commerce to industrial, manufacturing and commercial, concerns and to ministers of the Gospel and others from
whom cooperation was sought; also excerpts from the superintendent's bulletins to the staff of the schools giving detailed instructions
for receiving and entertaining visitors, and copies of programs presented at the different schools. And there was an extremely interesting summary of the reports made to the Superintendent at the
conclusion of the observance by principals and teachers giving their

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIF<;>RNIA

personal reactions, with suggestions for the future. It is a very
valuable contribution and will be available to superintendents of
schools in other cities, and to committees .of arrangements, who may
desire to adopt similar plans for future observances.
A special effort was made this year to carryi our observance into
the small rural districts with the little one and two room schools;
and we deem it advisable in this report to stress this phase of our
work. We shall therefore make no special mention of any of the
scores. of particularly nota_b le observances which so well deserve it,
but instead content ourselves wjth a very brief resume of the result
in general throughout the state.
As we have heretofore pointed out, the space devoted by the
newspapers· to any occurrence is . generally in proportion to the interest displayed. Evidence of the increased publicity received this
year over even that last year reported is .found in the report made to
our committee by our Director of Publicity. In this connection it
should be ~oted that his report was based on the clippings received
by him evidencing the result of the state ' publicity campaign up to
and . including April 19; and that clippings attached to the reports
from lodges indicate that there was considerable more publicity
during the week commencing April 20 than had been theretofore
received. This was espcciatly notable with respect to illustrations
and editorials.
The clippings received by the Director of Publicity show a total
of 1605 se.parate editorials and news articles which was an increase
of about 33%% over last year. Furthermore, there was this year a
very noticeable increase in editorial column support by•the state
press. There were 192 editorials including 32 "news editorials" on the
rural school problem which was this year emphasized. In addition
there were 109 editorial articles supplied by the state headquarters
and 41· independently written. In this one factor is best told the
· general spread of interest of the state press in, and recognition of,
the· week and its im:reasing importance. The original news story
covering the proclamation of the Grand Master and the leading article with respect to rural education outlining the situation as set
forth by Dr. Sutton, President of the National Education Association, were handled by practically every paper to which they were
'sent; and the newspaper clippings attached to the reports show fre. quent reference to them in the focal articles appearing in what is
generally known as the "rural press."
As is pointed out by the Director of Publicity, the increase in
. the amount of newspaper publicity was due in great part to the local
publicity co~mittees.' There were this year represented, and contact by state headquarters made with, 92 publicity chairmen as con-

trasted with 42 last year and 7 the year before. In many instances
masters. very properly named a newspaper man of their lodge as
the c~a1rman o~ the publicity committee and they did splendid ·work.
In this connectJon'attention is called by the Director of Publicity to
the fact that while the press in general was most generous with their
space, i.t ':as in the smaller communities that the response was even
mor~ significant. Papers which ordinarily could not well afford any
considerable portion of their limited space devoted columns to the
w~ek, publishing in full the programs of their local schools with detailed accounts of the activities.

received mention in our reports because they were unique. ·And it

?1-ade good use ·of the descriptions of selected observances therein
included. I.n addition to the meetings' held in school auditoriums
thron~ed with pare~ts an~ the public and addressed by noted speakers, with programs in which the pupils participated, there were this

nection, and notwithstanding our determination to avoid reference
to any specific observance, we ·cannot forbear making mention of a
window display showing art actual class in operation with the teacher
and pupils being changed throughout the day after short periods of
time. Needless to say it attracted unusual attention. As a matter
of fact, it created
traffic jam. And in another community where
there was held a· parade preceding a pageant, every store was closed
for three hours; and during that time, as stated in the report, "you
could not buy a penny's worth of anything." Practically everywhere
the schools held "open house" during the week to which parents and
the public generally were invited to witness either the actual work
of the classes, · or special programs presented for the occasion.
So much -for the observance in general. We now pass to a report
of the result of our effort to carry the observance into the little one
and two room schools.
In our report last year reference was made. to the fact that it is
in the remote, sparsely settled community with the little rural school
that the teacher and children need most the encouragement which
is one of the results of the observance of Public Schools Week; and
we referred to the opportunity afforded the fraternity to be of
assistance in the endeavor now being made to equalize the educational opportunities of the country and city child.
No program conceived by educators will be effective without
the sympathetic: aid, support and cooperation of the public. To secure this it is purposed by the National Education Association to
enlist the support of the rural press, and of fraternal and other civic
organizations. The Grand Lodge of Masons in California is peculiarly well adapted to the service to be here performed. Not only
is it state wide in its organization and representation, but it is probably the only institution of any sort represented in practically every
rural community. There may be a Masonic Lodge in a community in
which there is no club, society or other association of any sort or
kind, and where it would be the only organized unit for the dissemination of information; and in the observance of Public Schools
Week the medium is already provided. Furthermore, the membership represents all sorts and classes of people of diverse political,
social and economic views, but all of whom are the avowed and
loyal friends of our public schools.
In pursuance of our plan one entire chapter of our "Handbook"
was devoted to "rural education"; and a copy was sent every city,
county and district superintendent of schools. There was also a per•
sonally signed letter addressed to every county superintendent by
name outlining our purpose and asking his or her cooperation. In
addition to our "Handbook," every county superintendent and rural

supervisor also received a copy of a special "Bulletin" issued by the
State Department of Education. This was prepared by a committee
of rural supervisors under the direction of the Chief of the Division
of Rural Schools and was designed especially for the use of teachers
in the one and two room schools. It contained detailed suggestions
and instructions for holding an observance and was an extremely
valuable adjunct to our "Handbook" and prolific o'f great good.
In this connection, by the way, we are gratified to be able to
report that Public Schools Week has been included among the educational activities with which the State Department of Education
maintains professional contact; and that the member of the staff of
the Superintendent of Public Instruction assigned for that purpose is
the Chief of the Division of Elementary Education and Rural
Schools. Incidentally it may be here said that Public Schools Week
has also received . national recognition. The chairman of our committee received a very cordial invitation to accept a place on the
rural schools conference program of the National Education Association ;i.t their convention held in Los Angeles last July; and to
explain the work being done during Public Schools Week. President Sutton was especially desirous of having a report made to the
Convention of the result of the effort made this year to carry the
observance into the rural districts.

Although some of the reports from the lodges and county superintendents were not received until after the date of the convention
su_fficient information had been obtained to enable your chairma~
to report that our effort had been attended with even unexp.e cted,
indeed unhoped for, success; and that the promise for next year was
exceedingly bright.
We think it is not too much to say that the phenomenal success
of the observance this year is accounted for in great part by the extent to which the very small communities contributed. This was
primarily due to the fine cooperation received from county superint_e ndents, teachers and rural supervisors ; and from others who are
not unmindful of the importance of the little rural schools and who
are ever desirous of assisting in any movement for their improvement. We should like to make special mention of every one of the
observances in these little one room schools, but this is of course
impracticable. Such reference as is made to any of them is only to
indicate the extent of their participation in our observance this year.
There were several counties in which every one of these one and
two room schools either held an observance of its own or participated in one held in an adjoining district. An extremely interesting
report was received from the superintendent of a county in which
there are fifty-two rural elementary, and four rural high, schools. All

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

but one small school held some kind of an observance and that one
was closed by a threatened epidemic of diphtheria.
The programs in these little rural schools were almost as varied
as were those in the larger communities. Very generally they included class demonstrations with exhibits of school work; and in
some there were features not practicable in the urban communities,
such as the playing of simple -games in which the visitors participated. There was thus developed an extremely pleasant relationship
not only between the children and the visitors, but likewise among
the visitors themselves and to which reference will be hereinafter
made. As is now not uncommon in the larger schools, evening sessions were held for the convenience of the parents who were not able
to visit the school during the day. In one school described by the
superintendent as "a tiny one-teacher school in the western end of
the county" the teacher invited the patrons to an evening meeting at
which . a regular school session was held and at the conclusion of
which the visitors partook of refreshments she had provided.
In practically every instance the dominant feature of the observance were the visits by the patrons of the school; and some
extraordinary results were reported. There was one school with an
enrollment of twenty-five children which had a visit to the school
during the week by the father or mother from the home of every
pupil; and an emergency school in a lumber camp having an enrollment of twelve children received twenty visitors during the week.
As an illustration of the willing cooperation received from the
teachers of these little rural schools mention should be made of the.
situation presented in a report from a county superintendent who has
always been exceedingly helpful. It appears that she had arranged
with her teachers throughout the county to hold observances in their
own schools with exhibits of school work, and to urge every parent ·
to visit the school during the week. After all her arrangements had
been made the committee representing the Lodge located at the
county seat urged her to bring all the exhibits to the high school and
have a general exhibit there. This she consented to do; but she very
wisely decided to also have the individual observances as planned if
this could be arranged. The situation was placed before her teachers
who cheerfully agreed to advance the date of the observances in
their own schools and then made their contribution the following
week to the joint exhibit. The result was that through the cooperation of these teachers, in addition . to the joint program and exhibit
held at the high school, each of the twenty-six; districts of the county
held an observance of its own during the preceding week. In passing
we are availing ourselves of the opportunity to suggest that the primary purpose we .have in mind will be best subserved. by having

individual district observances in the communities in which the
schools are located.
For more reasons than one, mention is made of the splendid
cooperation received from the teachers of these one and two room
schools and of the results attained. In the first place it is only fitting
that there should be public recognition of it; secondly, it confirms
the opinion noted in several reports from school superintendents that
one of the benefits of Public Schools Week is thq.t it develops among
the teachers a spirit 0 f cooperation which inures to the benefit of. the
schools; and lastly, it should bring home to everyone the .fact that
there is no Lodge · so small, nor so remotely located, that 1t cannot
participate in an observance of Public Schools Week. The master of
any lodge willing to make the effort may confidently rely on t he
assistance of not only the county superintendent and rural supervisors but in no less d:~gree of the teachers of these little schools.
T~e participation in the observance held in the district school
was not everywhere confined to its patrons and the residents o~ the
district. In compliance with a suggestion made by our committee,
arrangements were .made in the larger centers of some of t~e counties
to include visits to th~ rural schools as a feature of their own observances. In one · county the visitors from the urban centers were
representatives of service clubs and of other civic b~dies . in t~e c?mmuriity who subsequen~ly reported to their respective orgamzations
giving their impressions and reactions. There was thus made a contact which should prove exceedingly valuable. And it was not only
through personal visits that a knowledge of the rural school situation
was brought home to ~he people of the cities. Many of the speakers
made rural education the subject of their addresses and forcefully
reminded their hearers of the fact that the education of every child
in the state is the con~ern of the commonwealth; and that the rural
school problem is one. in which the cities are no less interested than
are the rural districts'.
There is no edu~~tional problem more acute than is that presented by the rural schools. As is pointed out in our "Handbook'' it
is a problem not peculiar to California. It is national in its scope.
There are 170,000 little one room school houses in the United States;
over one-half of all the school children are enrolled. in rural schools
and.' are being taught by approximately one-half of the total number
of public school teachers. In school equipment, in buildings, in
length of sessions, in training of teachers, in supervision, in curriculum and in financial support t he' rural child is denied an even opportunity with the city child. The average city child gets as many school
days in six years as the country child in eight; while in certain sections of the United States a city child gets twice as many school

652

653

654

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

~ays. Even here in California the small rural school, it has been said,
is the predominant type of institution existing for the education of
our children. About seventy-one per cent of all the elementary
schools employ five or fewer teachers; and forty-three per cent employ only one teacher. And there are over seventeen hundred one
room schools. Some of them are as good as a one room school can
be made. There are others, however, which are a disgrace to a state
as educationally progressive as 'is ours.
Many and .varied are the remedies proposed. The adoption of
any however will depend on public opinion. The laity must be made
!o realize the educational handicap under which the rural child starts
m the. race of life, and aroused to the necessity of adopting the
remedial measures born of the knowledge and experience of the
school people. This will require of course a campaign of education·
a?d it must ~e designed to meet not only ignorance, but also preju~
dice and sentiment-and primarily apathy.
It was the apathy of the people it will be remembered that was
responsible for the crisis which confronted the public school system
at the close of the war, and which gave birth to the idea of Public
Schools Week. That apathy in California has been in great part dispelled; and we think it may be modestly claimed that it is due in part
at least to the annual observance of Public Schools Week. Until
now .~owever little work has been done in the very small rural communities; and there, as we have indicated, it is most needed. There
must be created a public sentiment which will not continue to countenance the unequal educational opportunities which now exist between the country and t~e city child; and no inconsiderable part of
th.e work 1:1ust be done m the communities which are still content
with the httle one room school. There are there prejudices to be
overcome, and a spirit of cooperation to be developed.
T?at there does not exist in these little rural districts the cooperation to be found in the progressive urban centers is not strange
There is little opportunity for that personal contact upon which i~
depends. There is no Chamber of Commerce, no service club no
local ne~spaper; and with the radio, mail order catalog, and' the
automobile !o tr~nsport the farmer or rancher with his family to the
n~arest mot10n picture house, there is no incentive to provide a· subsht~t~ for the cross-roads store which was once, for the heads of the
fam1hes at least, a social center where on Saturday night they
gathered around the stove to discuss their common problems.
In many of these little school districts the patrons are widely
separated and fo~ lack of opportunity seldom commingle. The observ~nce of Public Schools Weck will furnish an opportunity and
the httle schoolhouse may well be made the social center of the com-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO~NIA

655

munity. In our observance this year, where only a s tart has been
made, something more was accomplished than merely establishing
the desired contact between the school and its patrons. The teacher
who provided as a part of her program the playing of games in
which the adults participated has builded better than she knew. She
has revitalized a factor of rural life which disappeared with the
"quilting party" and the "candy pull." If she will not confine her
efforts to the fourth week in April of each year, but will afford frequent opportunities for the parents of her children to gather in the
schoolhouse and enjoy a social evening together she will have deserved well of her trustees even though she may not have that
coveted college degree.
We have repeatedly referred to the cooperation we received
from the teachers of these little one and two room schools. That
implies that they worked with us. We regret to say however that in
more than one instance they did all the work and that they did not
receive the cooperation of those of our brethren who might well
have given it. In our correspondence with county superintendents it
appeared that some of them had never received from the masters of
lodges in their counties the request for assistance we had written
them would be made. There were many instances in which the success of the movement to carry the observance into the little rural
school was due solely to the school people-the county superintendent, the rural supervisors and the teachers.
We are hoping that next year there will be nothing left undone
by any master of any lodge to make easier the task the teachers of
these one and two room schools so willingly assume and so successfully perform. Grand Lodge must confine its effort to the annual observance; but the masters of our little rural lodges, and their
brethren, might well continue their efforts throughout the year for
the attainment of the end we have in view. Every one of our brethren should be an unofficial aid and ally of his county superintendent
in every effort to improve the schools of his community.
In line with what has just been said, it is suggested that the
rural school problem might well be one of the subjects discussed as
a part of the lodge Masonic Education program. Speakers may
always be secured through the Division of Rural Schools of the State
Department of Education. Contrary to general belief it is. not a "dry"
subject, but an extremely interesting one, and especially for Masons
it has that appeal which attaches to every question that concerns
human values.
Successful as was our effort in securing the participation in our
Twelfth Annual Observance of the little one and two room schools,
even more is promised for next year. Many of the county superin-

PROCE~DINGS OF THE

tendents are already making their plans; and it might be well for
't hose of our· brethren who will serve their lodges as masters next
year to make immediate contact with them. One of our most successful observances this year was reported by a master who had
started his arrangements immediately after his return from last year's
.communication of Grand Lodge.
Each year we have been gratified to be able to report a success
exceeding that of the preceding year. Never before however has any
report been made with the pleasure and satisfaction with which this
is presented; because the result of the effort made this year gives
promise of the ultimate success of what is :a dmittedly a prodigious
task. Indeed it may be now confessed that it was undertaken with
some trepidation; and only because of the confidence born of a
knowledge of the loyalty and zeal of our brethren in the cause of
public education, and of the sterling worth of those splendid men
and women constituting the school people of the state who are devoting their lives to the service of our children.
In an extraordinarily interesting ad.d ress delivered during the
convocation of the Grand. Chapter of Royal Arch Masons last April
the speaker who has done outstanding work in the cause of rural education referred to herself as a "crusader." That is the spirit which
should animate each one of us. We are enlisted in a crusade in the
cause of childhood; and the motto emblazoned on our banners is,
"Equal Educational Opportunities for All the Children of All the
People."
All of which is fraternally submitted.
