REPORT OF EDUCATIONAL COMMITTEE
To the M:. W.:. Gran.d Lodge of California:
This represents the seventh annual report which your Educational
Committee has had the privilege of presenting to this Grand Lodge.
Some few years back we took occasion to remark that an educational program is not one for a year, or even a few years, but that it is
(like all education itself) a continuous process which will reach a
high point and then in the natural order of progress start toward
still further accomplishment. From the various reports received, it is
the opinion of your committee that the first of the high points in the
course of progress has been attained. This opinion arises from the
fact that there are many, many Lodges who pursue the educational
program as part of their work, as a matter of course, and while the
work itself is not in the category of ritualistic work (being not
required), it, nevertheless, has a similar importance and meaning to
these many Lodges. These Lodges instruct their candidates regularly
in accordance with the pamphlet of information afforded by your
Educational Committee and there are numerous reports which have
been received which testify to the success of this department of in.f ormation afforded the candidates, in addition to that which they receive
through the ritualistic ceremony and lectures. There are now in the
line of officers in many Lodges brethren who, themselves, received
the benefits of the educational program instruction and they report
as to the great value of the additional knowledge which they obtained
through this type of instructi'on. Your committee feels, therefore, that
the pursuit of the program with respect to instruction of candidates
as they receive their degrees is of the highest value, and should under
all circumstances be followed up so that as time goes on all members
of all Lodges will have had the benefit of the type of instruction and
enlightenment afforded by the instruction pamphlet above referred to.
In the matter of publications for general Lodge use your committee is most happy to report that they have been received in general
with enthusiasm and have been likewise generally made use of. Seven
such bulletins were issued this past year, and they were as follows :
In February, "The Intelligent Mason"; in March, "Masonry and Employment," a paper which all agreed was timely and proper; in April,
"The Apron and Working Tools"; in May, "Masonry at Practice"; in
June, July and September, "Questions and Answers." It may be
remarked that the papers containing the questions and answers were
used to very great advantage by an extremely large number of Lodges.
There was also sent to the Lodges, as a matter of information, a
paper on "Free Masonry in Germany," being a reprint of a very
interesting paper appearing in one of our magazines. There was also

659

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sent last year's report of this committee, because of certain conclusions
therein contained which we thought to be of value for the Masters.
The interesting statistics of this year's activities show that there
were 16,500 pieces of literature mailed; that our mailing list contains
1,074 names in the State of California; that there' are 450 Educational
Committees in as many of the respective Lodges; that 3,000 copies of
the pamphlet of instruction to candidates on the three degrees were
mailed; that the Secretary received approximately 1,800 letters of all
kinds from Lodges and members, most of which concerned questions
seeking further information on some of the topics or questions presented; that the Secretary's office mailed approximately 3,200 letters
during the year; that the Executive Secretary has made 78 addresses
on the work, and that other members of the committee have made
approximately as many. This list of activities on the part of the committee thus indicates a year's work, full and complete, and shows the
amount of interest being taken by the Lodges, officers and members.
A very large number of the district officers' meetings have devoted
some time to a consideration of the educational program, and there
have been many meetings in various parts of the State attended by
members of the Educational Committee which have included many
adjoining districts.
The committee at the present time consists of twenty-three members, of whom five are in Los Angeles, four in San Francisco, one in
Fresno, one in Chico, one in Santa Rosa, one in Sacramento, one in
Bakersfield, two in Pasadena, one in Sarr Diego, one in Redding, one
in Santa Barbara, one in Stockton, one in Riverside, one in San Jose
and one in Oakland; each member has a combination of districts
which includes' almost all of the districts in the State. Each committe~
member keeps in touch with the officers of the Lodges in his district
and affords every assistance possible.
From the general appropriation of $5,000.00, the Executive Secretary this last year received $1,625.00, and the balance was utilized in
the maintenance of the committee's office in Los Angeles, and the
expense of publishing the various publications, mailing, and also the
relatively small expense of various members of the committee in
traveling and keeping in touch with the Lodges. It will thus be seen
that the committee has utilized its appropriation in a careful manner
and with the best possible results.
The experience of your committee over this seven year period
once again demonstrates the wisdom of Grand Lodge in originally
adopting an educational program, and our experience dictates the conviction that its unswerving continuance will be for the best welfare
of our institution and its membership.

We reiterate that it is not such a program as can be judged by the
apparent results of any one year, but that its cumulative effect will
go a long way toward advancing the lines of thoug ht of our members
in accordance with the increased information which becomes their
knowledge as the years .g o on.
Your committee, therefore, respectfully recommends:
1. That the program laid down by this Grand L odge in 1925 be
continued ;
2. T hat the Grand Master be authorized to a ppoint a committee
of such number as he may deem advisable for the carrying on of the

658

program;
3. That the sum of $5,GOO.OO be appropriated for the use of the
committee under the direction of the Grand Master for the ensuing
year.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-laws has had under co nsideration amendments of various Lodges to by-laws, changing place and time of
meeting a nd excepting holidays ; increasing and decreasing dues ; fixing
fees for degrees and affiliation, and resolutions fixing fees for life
memberships; petitions for dispensations to hold elections for offi cers;
to receive petitions for membership without r eference to committee,
and dispensations to act on petition of rejected candidates within
twelve months from rejection.
Your committee is satisfied that all Constitutional requirements
have been complied with in these various ma tters, but the records in
many cases are very defective, and your committee believes that if the
Secretaries of all subordinate L odges were admonished to conform to
the provisions of section 250 of the ,Constitution in certifying the
proceedings of their Lodges, much confusion and labor would be
saved.
Your committee recommends approval of the action of the Grand
Master in approving or rejecting the foregoing 'matters, together with
all conditions imposed by him thereon.
RANDOLPH V. WHITING,
V ICTOR MCLU CAS,
FRANKLIN P ADAN,

BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:. W.' . Grand Lodge of Calif ornia:
In accordance with the provisions of Article VIII-a, Part 1, of
the Constitution of Grand Lodge, your Board of Control created thereunder, herewith presents its reports of its activities for the year ending
July 31, 1931.
This Article provides that the Board of Control shall have control
and shall supervise the activities of Boards of Relief and the Employment Service now existing under the authority of Grand Lodge; that
it shall so standardize the work that the operations of the several
Boards of Relief may be conducted economically and efficiently; that
it shall pass upon applications for the formation of Boards of Relief;
and that it shall pass upon and make recommendations on all requests
for reimbursement of funds expended for relief and employment.
Your Board respectfully reports that the work of the Boar.ds of
Relief of California is more systematized and business-like than ever
before in the hist ory of relief work in this jurisdiction; that there is
today more efficiency in operation, with less overhead expense; that
there is not only a uniformity of operation but a better understanding
between the Lodges and the Boards of Relief, and also between the
respective Boards of Relief and Grand L odge and finally that notwithstanding the great increase in membership, notwithstanding the
great influx of dependent and afflicted foreign Masons into this jurisdiction and notwithstanding t·he ·business and employment situation
of the past two or three years, relief work in ·California is cos ting the
Grand Lodge less money than ever before.
The Board of Control was organized principally for the purpose
of bringing about uniformity and coordination in relief work, as well
as economical and efficient administration of Boards of Relief without
overlapping and duplication of effort. That it has succeeded in this
respect is demonstrated by a review of the requests for reimbursement granted by Grand Lodge in the past seven years. These reim-

respective Lodges and Boards of Relief for relief and assista nce

This great reduction has been secured only by the continuous and
insistent demands upon and the fi nal consent of the foreign jurisdie~
tional L odges to reimburse Boards of Relief and L odges for relief
extended to brethren of said jurisdictions.
The grea t problem of the Board of Relief is to secure these reimbursements from the foreig n jurisdictions. Several jurisdiction s have
notified California L odges that they will not make reimbursements for
relief extended where pre-authorization is not sought and/or not
granted. Many foreign jurisdiction Lodges refuse or neglect to reimburse aft er authorization is g iven. N o English L odge nor Scottish
Lodge, few exceptions, will pa y the bills for th e funeral of one of its
deceased brothers. Your Board of Contr ol has sounded t he warning
to the Relief Boards of California and to the respective Lodges not
to ex tend relief in any considerable amount without first notifying the
foreign Lodge and securing the approval and authorization of said
Lodge.
In March ·'of this year by and w ith the consent and a pproval of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master, the Board of Control sent the
following communication to all L odges and Relief B oards in California:
To the Masters and S ecretaries of all L odges:
To all Boards of R elief :
Perhaps never before in the history of Masonry in California have
there been so many demands upon ·our fraternity for relief and assistance by needy brethren fr om other jurisdictions.
<?u.r ~alifo rnia Grand L odge has Ion~ ago established the policy
that 1t 1s incumbent .upon us to render rehef in all worthr cases, and
Grand L odg e has reimbursed L odges and Boards of Relief for relief
extended wher e fo reign jurisdictions have refused to relieve their own
brethren and t he L odg es and Boards of R elief have applied for reimbursement.

662

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

But so great have been the calls for relief and so many requests
for reimbursement are being presented that the Board of Control
believes that it is timely and most important to warn all Lodge and
Board of Relief officers : first-to grant only nominal relief and no
extended nor large amount of relief to any applicant without first
notifying the brother's Lodge and receiving instructions and authorization before said relief is granted; second-to grant no relief to
applicants for the purpose of assisting in meeting payments on real
or personal property; third-to make no loans of Lodge or Board of
Relief funds to any brother; fifth-when an application for relief is
presented, officers should immediately notify, by telegraph, the
brother's Lodge and take no action until authorization is received.
The Board of Control will not approve and in all probability
Grand Lodge will not grant applications for reimbursement where
prior authorization to extend relief has not been asked from nor
granted by the foreign jurisdiction Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
MASONIC BOARD OF CONTROL.
DAVID J. REESE, Chairman.
EUGENE ELKUS,
FRANK M. WISE,

Meetings: Four meetings of the Board of Control have been held
during the year, one at Ventura in March; one at Los Angeles in
May; a third at San Francisco in August, and the fourth at San Francisco during the session of the Grand Lodge. This fourth session has
been devoted mainly to the conduct of hearings in the matter of
reimbursements and has resulted in reduction of the demands upon
Grand Lodge amounting to $3,285.22. At the other meetings, upon
invitation of the Board, delegates of the various Boards of Relief
have attended and conferences have been held which have resulted in
better understanding, as to methods and procedure.
Your Board of Control is pleased to report that Boards of Relief
are more than ever working in entire accord and harmony with the
Board of Control suggestions. Lodges because of constant changes
and lack of familiarity sometimes digress from the established procedure but in general there is efficiency and consequent economy.
During the Masonic year we have had the entire support of our
Most Worshipful Grand Master, who has been most helpful in his
cooperation and endorsement of the work we have had in hand. Our
Worshipful Grand Secretary has given us his assistance and encouragement. For all this we desire to express our appreciation.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Requests for Reimbursements

The requests for reimbursement which we have reported to the
Finance Committee, with the recommendation that payment be made
from the funds of Grand Lodge, are as follows:

Your Board of Control has anticipated that owing to the general
business conditions existing throughout the country, the requests for
reimbursement of funds for relief extended would exceed any previous
period. Fortunately however we are happy to announce that they are
not only not greater, but are a substantial amount less than ever
before.
The results obtained this year were brought about by the excellent cooperation and diligence and business-like methods of the
splendid secretaries of our various Boards of Relief, and the valuable
assistance of our Most Worshipful Grand Master and Very W orshipful Grand Secretary.
We also desire to give special commendation to five of our
Boards of Relief who request NO reimbursement.
Your Board has been able this year to analyze more fully than
ever before the requests for reimbursement with the result that in
several cases the charges have been placed against the individual
Lodge, where they belong, rather than a·g ainst the funds of our
Grand Lodge.
There are still many problems confronting your Board of Control
in the matter of disbursing money for relief.
We also still have with us the matter of duplication of relief and
"repeaters." Two cases stand out as illustrations of this. During the
year a member of an Arkansas Lodge received money from five different Boards of Relief; another member of an Illinois Lodge was
successful in getting money from four different Boards of Relief.
Correspondence in both of these cases would indicate no urgent need
of relief and no disposition on the part of the home Lodge to reimburse. In order that our various Boards of Relief may be better
enabled to guard against duplication and "repeaters," your Board of
Control purposes to send to each Board of Relief an itemized list of
all cases upon which reimbursement has been made.
At the outset your Board of Control had for consideration
requests for reimbursement covering 147 cases. After completing
our findings we have approved requests covering 114 cases, totaling
$6,458.94. This is a decrease over last year of 19 cases and $422.73.
The numbers and amount of the requests approved are:

Totals..................................$9,744.16 $3,285.22 $6,458.94 $6,881.67

Perhaps no phase of Masonic activity is entitled to more attention
or should receive greater emphasis at this time than our Employment
Service. Reports from the established Service Bureaus and Employment Committees throughout the jurisdiction indicate that methods
and procedure are continuing to improve and greater efficiency and
better results are being attained.
A questionnaire sent to the managers of the principal Service
Bureaus resulted in some very interesting information. It was found
that in six cases out of nine the registration of · new applicants is
increasing monthly at this time, as well as showing an increase over
the corresponding period of 1930.
In five out of nine places, more trained men are now applying
for work than formerly, but in only two places, San Francisco and
Los Angeles, are the managers able to place more of these men than
formerly.
It is important to note that inquiries from employers are increasing in the East Bay (Oakland) and Los Angeles districts.
A majority of the managers believe that it is possible and necessary for the Masonic Service to be as efficient and complete as are
the services of the pay agency. They feel that by carefully invest;gating applicants and placing them only when qualified, the employer
gets confidence in our Service and becomes an ardent booster for it.
No attempt is made ordinarily to record the probable value of
our Employment Service, but the Los Angeles Service has submitted
such a report for the months of May, June and July, 1931. This
report shows that the placements made by that office for these three
months would have returned $7,907.32 in fees if the positions secured
had been paid for by the applicant at the same rates charged by the
pay agency.
This "dollar-and-cents" measure of the service rendered by one
office is presented to again urge the importance of the work being
done by the Employment Service.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
Organ Solo, "Traumerei''...................................................................... Schumann
Prayer ..............................................................................................Grand Chaplain
"The Lord is my light and my salvation; Whom shall I fear? The
Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
' 10ne thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I
may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold
the beauty of the Lord, and to inquire in his temple."
Fifty-six members of this Grand Lodge have laid aside their working tools and joined the ever-increasing majority in the Supreme Grand
Lodge of the Universe, since the last report of this committee.
Many of these departed brethren left footprints on the sands of time
in the communities in which they lived, thus adding to the glorious record
of service rendered to this great State by Masons in every walk of life.
Time and space will not permit your committee to go into detail relative to the services rendered by these brethren to their respective communities; however, we find listed the names of four who have rendered
distinguished service to this Grand Lodge. They are: William T. Lucas,
Past Grand Master; Charles E. Glidden, Grand Bible Bearer; William
C. Hassler, Past Grand Orator, and William Kettner, Past Grand
Marshal.
The virtues and accomplishments of these brethren will be given to
you later in more detail by some of the more eloquent members of this
Grand Lodge.
The list of our departed brethren is as follows:

While we mourn the passing of these brethren and extend to their
loved ones our sincere sympathy, we take com fort in the knowledge that
they were so imbued with the teachings of Masonry that they were
"prepared to welcome death, not as a grim tyrant, but as a kind messenger sent to translate them from this imperfect, to that all perfect, glorious and celestial Lodge above, where the Supreme Grand Master of
the Universe forever presides."
"And so we leave them here with happy tears,
Their glorious record on our scrolls to write.
And may their lives of Service through the years
Bring them their great reward, eternal light."
WM. H. PARCELLS,
WM.

M. H OLBROOK,

In Memoriam William T. Lucas
By FRANCIS J. McCoy
William Thomas Lucas was born in Buc.h anan county, near St.
Joseph, Missouri, on March 18, 1850, the son of George J. and Sally
Thomas Lucas. The Lucas family were old Southern stock and traced
their ancestry back to the settlement made by Lord Baltimore in Maryland. The Lucas name is well known in Missouri history, and many of
the family played very important parts in the settlement of the West.
Dr. Lucas grew up as a · boy in Missouri in the stirring times before
the outbreak of the Civil War. His father was an ardent Southerner
and at the outbreak of the war joined the Confederate forces, leaving
the family in charge of this eleven-year-old boy, who gave a good account of himself even that early. While there were many Southerners in
northern Missouri at that time, still the sentiment was very strongly
pro-Union and it was very uncomfortable for the Lucas family, so they
and several of their friends started the westward trek to Montana in
1864, where they located for a time in Deer Valley of that State. They
moved on westward in 1868 and settled at Woodland, California.
His schooling, interrupted in Missouri, was again taken up in Montana by private tutors and the public school, and Dr. Lucas later taught
school in Yolo county, California. His ambition had always been to
become a physician, and he had saved enough money from his school
teaching to defray his expenses in the University of the Pacific in San
Francisco, which he entered in the early 70's. For a short time he practiced in Woodland and then came to Guadalupe, Santa Barbara county,
in 1879, and was continuously in the practice of his profession in the
Santa Maria Valley for more than fifty years.
Under a seemingly gruff exterior at times, Dr. Lucas had a kind
and gentle heart and was most beloved by the thousands of patients that
he had cared for during his long medical practice. I remember an incident that happened in our Guadalupe Lodge many years ago. One of
the brothers came up and spoke to Dr. Lucas and asked him if he remembered who he was, and on Dr. Lucas saying that he did not, the man
said, "You should remember me, as you brought me into the world."
Dr. Lucas jokingly remarked that he had brought many thousands into
the world, and on counting up the members present, there were over
thirty people in the Lodge room that night that Dr. Lucas had helped
bring into the world. He was the most beloved physician that has ever
been in our locality, and many are the stories that are related of his sac-

695

rificing spirit in going at all hours of the day and night, over rough roads
and through winding pathways, on horseback, to relieve the sick and
suffering. His name will ever be a benediction in the Santa Maria Valley.
Dr. Lucas was an ardent Mason. He was made a Mason shortly
after coming to Guadalupe, and served that Lodge for many years as
Master. He was elected again and again to fill the chair in the East. He
was considered the Grand Old Man of our Lodge and some years ago
we gave him a gold card as a life member in our Lodge. He was elected
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California in 1896, and was also
affiliated in the Chapter and Commandery orders. He served the Grand
Lodge for many years on the Committee on Grievances.
Dr. Lucas was a great student of history and had a fine Masonic
library. He was particularly well versed in English history, French
history, and the history of the Popes, and had quite a library on all three
subjects. Indeed, he was quite a student of literature, and Shakespeare
was his favorite poet.
Dr. Lucas was an outstanding citizen of the community, a good man,
and a good Mason. I believe that for the first thirty years of his practice, although it was · a large one, and covered nearly all the northern
end of Santa Barbara county, he had amassed but little money. Indeed
money was never the object of Dr. Lucas' life. He was hardly ever sick
and was strong and rugged to the last, and was ill less than a week.
The day of his death, March 21, 1931, was a sad one in our community,
when we learned that Dr. Lucas had passed, and the community was
plunged in the deepest sorrow, but we all felt that he had lived and done
his duty as a true man and Mason.

In Memoriam of Charles E. Glidden
By Gus A. HuTAFF
Amidst our rejoicing and recounting the blessings we have ·enjoyed
during the. year, we cannot but be saddened by the reflections that the
Grim Reaper-Death- has invaded the ranks of our Grand Lodge.
With the passing of our late Grand Bible Bearer, Charles Edward
Glidden, on December 11, 1930, while acting as Senior Deacon in the
conferring of the Master Mason degree in Howard Lodge No. 37 in
Yreka, California, Masonry has suffered a distinct loss, for Brother
Glidden was always a wise counselor, a faithful and efficient co-operator.
It seemed fitting that, having devoted his life to the best interests of
Masonry, his last moments should be spent within the portals of a
Masonic Lodge. For Brother Glidden was stricken while at the altar of
Freemasonry, facing the East. A most glorious ending to a life consecrated to the high ideals of humanity and of unselfish service.
It is .true that in the life of this Mason there were interests that
to him were infinitely more important than the material things of life,
for, very dear to him were his dear wife and five sons. Upon each of
these boys he had the honor of raising to the sublime degree of Master
Mason, as well as were all movements, objects, and enterprises of educational, cultural and spiritual value. This is shown by his association
with church, fraternal and civic affairs.
He was born in the State of Maine in the year 1856, and while still
a young man adopted California as his home, where the diversity and
variety of the positions he was called upon to fill during his life, indicated at once that he had not only a well developed mind, but a facility
for adaptability that always distinguished him.
Brother Glidden had a keen sense of justice and the right thing to
do, and of that which our fraternity and every member of it, demands
from each individual that enters into its 'makeup, "the very best that is in
one."
Masonically, Brother Glidden filled many offices within the gift of
the brethren of his Lodge, and I know he deeply appreciated the high
honor conferred upon him by our Grand Master in his appointment as
Grand Bible Bearer. He was a Past Master of Sisson Lodge No. 310,
a member of Mount Shasta Commandery, Sacramento Consistory of the
Scottish Rite, and a P ast Patron of the Order of the Eastern Star.
Throughout the years of his association with our fraternity he was
most loyal, fervently devoted to its work, always manifesting a keen,
appreciative understanding of the ideals of our institution, and active
in contributing to their practical application by his personality and service.

Such a life brings no . painful regrets as we approach the end of
our journey here on earth.
Brother Glidden was faithful in the discharge of life's affairs, and
therefore his inspired soul looked with trustful confidence to the Great
Father of us all, "who doeth all things well."
Death, my brethren, is not a descent, but a never ending ascent,
opening up the vast portals of the Celestial City, that building of God,

In Memoriam William C. Hassler
By CHARLES M. Wm.LENBERG
A long and distinguished career was closed when 'William Charles
Hassler died on August 1, after a very short illness.
For thirty years he had been in the public eye as an official of the
Health Department of San' Francisco and as a Mason.
·
Born in Chicago in 1868, he r~moved with his parents to Stockton
in this State at the age of five ye~rs. Graduat~d from the common
schools o_f that city, he went, with his father, a contracting carpenter,
to San Diego, where he helped him build the flume bringing water to that
community.
. Later he went :o New York and entered Columbia University, graduah~g as a pharmacist. Returning to San Francisco, he entered the drug
?usmess, at the same time attending Cooper College (now Stanford Medical School), graduating in 1892.
Married to Carrie Curries in 1896, he left his wife in 1898 to seek
his fortune in the newly discovered gold fields of Alaska and accompanied the Grider Expedition as physician.
'
He returned with a fortune in health and experiences but poorer in
pocket, and again entered into the practice of medicine, first in Stockton
and later in San Francisco.
In 1900 he entered the San Francisco Health Department as Sanitary Inspector and shortly thereafter the bubonic plague first made its
~ppearance. In the fight to control this disease, as well as the recurrence
m 1906-07, he was the chief aid of the Public Health Service and of
Surgeon General Blue.
In 1915 he became the Health Officer of San Francisco, and since
that date his city has made great strides in its health and preventive
activities.
During the World War, when influenza threatened to halt our
i~d~stries, h_e took a .decisive ~te~ when he closed all public places, proh.1b1ted _pub~1c g~thenng~ .and ms1sted on the wearing of masks, a practice which m spite of nd1cule, spread to practically every large city and
undoubtedly shortened the period of the epidemic.
For years he held the foremost place on this coast in the control
of communicable diseases, in infant, maternal and child welfare in mental
hygiene and bringing health knowledge to the people.
'
He was chosen from all the health officers of the United States to
represent this country at the Health Conference of the nations of the
world at London and Geneva in 1926, and at the time of his death was
President-elect of the American Public Health Association.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

699

His Masonry was active and sincere, and he received high honors
from his brethren.
A member of California Lodge No. 1, he was its Master in 1910,
High Priest of California Chapter No. 5, R. A. M.; Illustrious Master
of California Council No. 2, R. & S. M.; Commander of California Commandery No. 1, and Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery,
Knights Templar of the State of California; and finally last year, the
Grand Orator of Grand Lodge of California.
A story . is told of a traveler passing on a road who saw three men
squaring stone, all engaged in exactly the same operation. He stopped
and asked the first man what he was doing and received the reply, squaring stone. The same query to the second man brought forth the answer
"earning $6 a day." The third man on being asked, replied, "I am building
a cathedral."
Dr. Hassler is gone, and we voice our grief for and our appreciation of the man he was, a sincere citizen, a faithful official, a loyal friend.
Nothing was so pressing with him as his sense of devotion to duty.
He gave to the state, city and fraternity invaluable service.
He has gone out of our lives in the full energy of a wonderful'
executive, of a great official, a devoted and loving husband.
More than his memory remains, however, in the work he did in
preventing disease, prolonging life and making his fellow citizens healthier a?d happier.
His city is memorializing his name through the institution he was
building in the hills back of Redwood City where, on 300 acres, institutions were to be created, giving opportunity for restoration to health
of tuberculars, of the convalescent and aenemic child, a preventorium for
children, and convalescent care for mothers after leaving the hospital.
This, in future, will be known as the Hassler Health Home.
In the city itself, the old Buena Vista School, the outdoor school
which Dr. Hassler created some years ago for crippled children, is to
be replaced by a modern building and known as the Hassler School.
William Charles Hassler indeed builded a cathedral.

In Memoriam William Kettner
By CLAUDE H. MORRISON
Sorrow does not last for a friend who has gone. We are proud of
his attainments, we admire the sterling qualities of his character, and
resolve to emulate the worthwhile efforts of his life, but grief for his
passing does not endure. We would not have this different. Only by
facing calmly the fact of death, are we able to prepare ourselves for the
final summons that must come to us all. When the one who has left us
is not only a friend but one who has achieved distinction in public life
as well as in Masonry, it is fitting and proper that we should pause to
pay tribute to his memory and renew our devotion to those principles
which he lived and loved.
William Kettner w.as born in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on November
20, 1864 and died in San Diego, California, on November 11, 1930. His
parents were John F . and Fredericka R. (Lang) Kettner. While he was
still young his parents moved to Galena, Illinois, and then to St. Paul,
Minnesota, and he received his limited education in the public schools of
those cities, leaving at the age of thirteen to earn his own living. When
he was twenty-one he had saved seven hundred dollars with which he
came to California and invested in a mining venture in Julian, near San
Diego. This was not successful, and after he had lost all his money he
went to San Diego, where he took a job driving the horse cars for the
street railway. Prospects were not bright in San Diego in those days,
and in 1888 he went to Santa Ana, engaging in the hotel business until
1892, when he went to Visalia and became the business· manager of the
Visalia Delta and also superintendent of an insurance agency. While
in Visalia he served as a member of the City Council. On August 4,
1905, in Oakland, California, he was married to Marion C. Morgan,
who survives him. In 1907 he and Mrs. Kettner moved to San Diego,
where he engaged in the insurance business, which he built up soon to
be a very successful undertaking. He identified himself with various
civic organizations in San Diego, being particularly active in the Cham. ber of Commerce, with which he worked at all times for the upbuilding
of his community.
He was not active in politics until 1912, when he was asked by
friends in both parties to seek the Democratic nomination for representative in Congress from the Eleventh district. Although that district
was overwhelmingly Republican he was elected for four successive terms.
During his service in Congress he worked unceasingly for the interests of
his district and his State, and many projects of material benefit to the
Pacific coast were due largely to his efforts. During his service also the
World War was started and finished, and his record shows that he was
at all times a loyal supporter of the government and of the administra-

I
I

\

GHAND LOUGE OF CALIFORNIA

701

tion on which fell the responsibility for carrying on the war. He retired
from Congress in 1921 because he could not afford longer to sacrifice his
personal interests, and spent the remainder of his life in rebuilding his
insurance business and working for the community which he loved.
Brother Kettner was raised a Master Mason in Visalia Lodge No.
128 in 1894, and served as Master in 1898. In 1899 he was appointed
as Inspector in the district, then known as the 33rd district, in California. In 1900 he served this Grand Lodge as Grand Pursuivant, was
Junior Grand Deacon in 1901, Grand Marshal in 1902 and 1907, Grand
Standard Bearer in 1908, and Grand Marshal again from 1909 to 1915
inclusive, twelve years of service.
He became a Royal Arch Mason in Visalia Chapter No. 44 in 1896
and a Knight Templar in Visalia Commandery No. 26. in the same year.
He served his Chapter and his Commandery respectively as High Priest
and Eminent Commander. Later he became active in the Grand Chapter
of California and in the Grand Commandery. In 1916-17 he served as
Grand Captain of the Host in the Grand Chapter and Grand Standard
Bearer in the Grand Commandery. At the end of the year he asked to
be relieved from further duties in both grand bodies, stating that his
Congressional duties would keep him in Washington for the duration
of the war and prevent him from performing his Masonic duties. Both
grand bodies, at their meetings in 1917, adopted resolutions of regret
in accepting his resignation but expressing pride in his determination to
consider his service to his country as paramount to all other duties.
Brother Kettner received the Scottish Rite degrees in the Oakland
Bodies, Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, in 1898. Almost immediately
thereafter he demitted from the Lodge of Perfection to become a charter ·
member and the first Venerable Master of Visalia Lodge of Perfection.
He was made a Knight Commander of the Court of Honor in 1901 and
was coroneted an Inspector General .H onorary of the thirty-third degree
in 1909, after he had dimitted to the San Diego Bodies.
Upon his removal to San Diego he dimitted to San Diego Lodge
No .. 35, and affiliated also with the San Diego Chapter No. 61 and San
Diego Corttmandery No. 25. He became a member of San Diego Council
No. 23, Royal and Select Masters at the time it was organized in 19.1-0.
He was a charter member of Al Bahr Temple of the Shrine, having
been originally a member of Islam Temple of San Francisco. He joined
San Diego Pyramid No. 32 of the Sciots in 1923. He was a Past Patron
of Southern Star Chapter, Order of the Eastern Star. In 1927 he joined
with a number of brethren in San Diego and vicinity to form San Diego
Conclave, Red Cross of Constantine, and was an officer and regular attendant at the meetings of that order until the time of his death. During
his residence in San Diego it was his pleasure twice to head executive

702

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

committees for the meetings of the Grand Chapter, Grand Council and
Grand Commandery in San Diego.
Thus reads the record of the life of William Kettner. But mere ·
words of biography are futile. They do not reveal his personality, nor
express the feeling of friendship which he felt for his fellowmen. His
friendly smile, his cordial handclasp and the radiant charm that wa5 ever
in him endeared him to his countless friends. Friendship seems to be
the keynote of the book which he wrote after he had retired from Congress. It is largely a history of his efforts to assist his community and
district, a record of material achievements. But it is permeated with the
spirit of friendship-friendship for those whom he served, for those with
whom he served, for all with whom he came in contact, and that friendship was not one-sided. He printed many letters from his friends from
all walks of life. A former president of the United States, Cabinet members, senators and representatives, leading business men in his district
and in the nation, ranking officers in the army, navy and marine corps
and Past Grand Masters of this Grand Lodge, are represented. Most
of them express appreciation for personal or public service, but few of
the letters are complete without some allusion to the friendship between
the writers and Brother Kettner.
If Masonry means service, he was a good Mason. But his service
carried with it the feeling and expression of friendship and love for
those whom he served. In his love for his fellowmen, translated into
faithful service, William Kettner ably represented a practical ideal of our
institution.

Masonic History
To the M.'.W.'.Gra11d Lodge of California:
Were an irresistible conqueror, animated by a malignant desire
to destroy beyond rehabilitation the unity and spirit of a conquered
race, he would probably begin with the destruction of every vestige
of its history.
From time immemorial marauding and victorious armies have
sought to lay in ruins the libraries and other depositories in which
nations and people assemble the surviving evidence of the traditions,
the struggles and achievements, the habits, faiths and laws, the arts
and cultures, and ideals which, linking them with the past, explain
and dignify and glorify their patriotism and inspire their pursuits of
destiny.
·

Man is the mysterious mirror of a past, leading down the misty
aisles of time to the very advent of Creation. He is history.
As reflected by its report, our Committee on Masonic History
has achieved mightily within the past year. The members of this
committee at grea~ sacrifice of time and energy and with high devotion
and understanding have rendered thus far a service, the value of
which will invite increasing admiration and appreciation with the passing of the years. The work thus so successfully begun should be
prosecuted diligently during the coming year. The committee has
systematized its work, has acquired the services of an exceptionally
satisfactory research worker, and obviously is operating with full
regard for economy in its expenditures.
·
Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:

under an adequate appropriation and that its recommendations Numbers 1 to 6 be approved, subject to such modifications as may be
required by the financial conditions of .Grand Lodge.

George Washington Memorial
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
that section of the M.'. W.'. Grand Master's address dealing with the
George Washington National Masonic Memorial at Alexandria Virginia, and particularly his recommendation· that this Grand Lodge
continue its contributions to the George Washington National Masonic
Memorial Association to meet the terms of the so-called New York
plan, which plan provides for "bringing subscriptions up to $1.70 per
capita, contingent upon those jurisdictions which have not filled their
original quota of one dollar per capita doing their share."
After consultation with the members of other committees and
according with its own convictions, based upon the financial situation
and requirements of this Grand Lodge, your committee must recommend against a present commitment to the so-called New York plan.
At its annual communication in 1927, Grand Lodge approved a
report of its Finance Committee, following the recommendation of
Grand Master Jones, and we quote,
"It also appears that California has so far paid approximately
twenty per cent of its assessment, and as the entire amount should
be P<?-id not later than January 1, 1932, it would mean there still
remaa~s about four years to raise the remaining eighty per cent. Your
committee .therefore recommends that the per capita tax on the
Lodges be increased twenty cents per member yearly for the coming
four years," etc.
The foregoing clearly provided for the acceptance by Grand
Lodge of a commitment of one dollar per capita, although the membership of no particular year was specified. It can of course be argued
that Grand Lodge had in mind the membership of the year in which it
•legislated. As a matter of fact, however, Grand Lodge has annually
levied its . special per capita tax and remitted the proceeds thereof on
the basis of membership shown by the returns of Lodges reflecting
our growth from year to year. This is clearly shown by figures supplied to the committee by the Grand Secretary's office.
The report of the Grand Secretary shows a present Lodge membership of 142,422, which on a per capita basis of one dollar would
require a payment considerably in excess of the total amount thus
far paid to the Memorial Association, but considerably Jess than the

Masonic Education
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has read with
interest that portion of the message of the M:. W: . Grand Master
relating to Masonic Education. This is a subject on which this Grand
Lodge has tried many plans, the success of none of which has yet
been determined. We recommend that the matter of Masonic Education be left to the incoming Grand Master, and respectfully request
that he cause a survey to be made as to the results of the plans which
have been tried and as to the need or desirability of considering other
plans for adoption.

Adopted.
Expenditures for Social Purposes
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
the recommendation of the following amendments by the Most Worshipful Grand Master:
1. That section 88 of the Constitution be amended by striking
out the last clause, to-wit: "Provided that a subordinate Lodge may
in its discretion appropriate from its funds any amount for the purchase of a Past Master's jewel for its retiring Master and for floral
pieces for a deceased brother."
2. Section 89 be amended bv striking out all after the word
"expend" and insert in lieu thereof:
·
"In each Masonic year 20 per cent of its annual receipts of dues
from its members as computed from the last previous annual report
to Grand Lodge and income from its life membership fund, for
refreshments and the promotion of fraternal feelings among the
brethren."
As the Grand Master has stated, much confusion has resulted
from the interpretations of these sections, and your committee feels
that he has arrived at a satisfactory solution of the difficulty.
We believe that under the proposed amendment, the Lodges will
have more latitude as to those expenditures which may be charged to
the social fund, and consequently fewer questions will arise for the
Grand Master to decide. Furthermore, the present method providing
for the inclusion of all income results in an unequality between Lodges.
The Lodge which has investments of its own or sub-leases its own
lodge room or other rooms in its building may compute its 20 per cent
on all" of its revenue, while other Lodges may not have investments or
other income, with a resulting handicap on these Lodges. Dues are
paid primarily for operating expenses and constitute a more stable
form of income for the ·Lodge than rentals, interest or fees which
may fluctuate from year to year. It seems just and wise that the total
amount of dues with the income from life membership fund (if the
Lodge has such a fund) should be the basis for computing the 20
per cent to be used for social purposes.

We therefore concur in the recommendation of the Grand Master
with the reference to the amendment of sections 88 and 89, and move
that they be adopted.

which combined themselves to form the Symbolic Grand L odge of

is excluded, not only for the present but also for the future. Their

German Freemasonry. .According to Masonic law and Masonic usage,

.Much. trouble. has been brought upon the craft in Germany by

Grand Lodges in Germany with which we are in amity and we are
of the opinion that the request for recognition should not be granted.

Italy: An application for recognition has been received from the
Grand Orient of Italy, formerly seated at the Guistiniani Palace in
Rome and now temporarily seated in London, England.
We have not been in fraternal relations with the Grand Orient of
Italy for many years, except that in October, 1917, while our country
was an ally of the Kingdom of Italy in the Great War, permission
was granted to our members to visit Lodges of the Grand Orient and
t? fraternize with its members. Consideration was also given at that
time to the matter of the recognition of the Grand Orient on condition
that it ceased to invade the territorial jurisdiction of Arr:erican Grand
Lodges; but no conclusion was reached on the subject. This condition
was not met and since the war we have had no fraternal relations with
the Grand Orient.
After the advent of the Mussolini government in Italy the Grand
Orient and its subordinate Lodges was dissolved and ceased to exist
in Italian territory. This compulsory measure was not extended to a
number of Lodges of the Grand Orient working abroad out of reach
of the rules of the Fascisti regime. Such Lodges are continuing to
carry on their activities, although the power to which they owed
obedience has been dissolved.
In ?rder to per~etuate if possible the Grand Orient of Italy and
to p~ov1de a go~e~nmg power for the still existing Lodges situated
outside the domm1ons of the Kingdom of Italy, certain members of
the defunct Grand Orient held an assembly and organized a new
Grand Orient of Italy and declared th e same to be a continuation of
the old organization of the Guistiniani Palace and adopted for its
government the constitution, rules and by-laws of the defunct Grand

Grand Lodge of the Pacific, Mexico: For several years your committee has had under consideration the request for recognition made,
and renewed from time to time, by the "Grand Lodge of the Pacific"
(Gran Logia del Pacifico) . In the report of your committee made in
1930 it was stated that the chairman of your committee would visit
Mexico and make a personal examination of some of the matters
which were not clear to your committee.
The chairman made a trip to Mexico for the pa.rticular purpose
of examining into the merits -o f the application for recognition of the
Grand Lodge of the Pacific and visited several of the cities whereat
are located subordinate Lodges of that Grand Lodge. He had the
privilege of inspecting several Lodge rooms and of meeting officers
and members of a majority of the Lodges. He also conferred with
the Grand Master Octavio A. Serrano, Past Grand Master R. H.
Fernando F. Dworak and other officers of the Grand Lodge. His
impression was most favorable. He found those Masons with whom
he · came in contact to be mostly men of prominence and standing in
their respective communities and his inquiries and observations
induced him to believe that they were good Masons and that they
were loyal to the tenets of our profession and were doing a splendid
work in their jurisdiction. At Nogales, Hermosillo, Mazatlan, Los

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

715

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

714

Mochis, Navojoa, Culiacan and Ciudad Obregon he found Americans
who had been raised in the United States and had cast their lot with
the Masons of the Grand Lodge of the Pacific and without exception
the expressions of these Masons were commendatory of the work and
the spirit of their Mexican brethren and their Lodges. There is a
strong American spirit on the west coast of Mexico and the influence
of the American Masons there is evident.
The Grand Lodge of the Pacific confines its authority to the
states of Sonora and Sinaloa and the central district of Lower California. It exercises its right and authority over the three degrees of
symbolic Masonry only. It requires of its initiates a belief in God
and the immortality of the soul and displays the Great Light upon
its altars. In 1923 the Grand Master Dworak represented to this
Grand Lodge that the then newly created Grand Lodge of the Pacific
had no treaty or other connection with the Supreme Council of
Mexico, nor any other Masonic body, but that it was sovereign and
absolutely independent. The application for recognition has been
before us from that time until this and the same representations have
been repeatedly made to us.
We find that the Grand Lodge of the Pacific has fourteen Lodges
with more than fourteen hundred members and that all of . the Lodges
in its territory are of its obedience except a Lodge at Cananea, which
is subordinate of the York Grand Lodge of Mexico. Recognition of
the Grand Lodge of the Pacific has been deferred until this time
because the York Grand Lodge of Mexico, with which · we are in
amity and concord, claims exclusive jurisdiction throughout the
Republic of Mexico and we were not disposed to take any action that
might be objectionable to that Grand Lodge. It appeared to your
committee that the only reason for denying the application for recognition would be an objection from the York Grand Lodge and that
otherwise the Grand Lodge of the Pacific was justly entitled to our
fraternal regard and recognition. With this in mind, we asked the
Grand Master of the York Grand Lodge to give us a frank statement
of his disposition in this matter, assuring him of our desire to work
in full harmony and accord with the York Grand Lodge of Mexico
and its members. We have now had a reply to our inquiry, made by
the Grand Master through Brother M. A. Loeby, Chairman of the
Committee on Foreign Relations of the York Grand Lodge, in which
we are advised that it cannot and will not embarrass or hurt York
Grand Lodge for the Grand Lodge of California to enter into fraternal
relationship with the Grand Lodge of ·the Pacific.
Your committee respectfully recommends that fraternal recognition be accorded to the Grand Lodge of the Pacific.

Home Fees by Prior Members
In the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes in r ecommendation "j," the Grand Master gives the true interpretation intended as to the payment of the $25.00 fee by a non-resident
Mason upon affiliating with a Lodge within the jurisdiction of California.
We urge Master Masons residing in California to affiliate with
the local Lodge. Should business, or other circumstances require a
change . of residence outside of the State for an appreciable length of
time, it is natural that the member may desire to transfer his Lodge
membership. Later he may be fortunate enough to again return to
California and desire to again affiliate with a California Lodge. He
has once paid the $25.00 fee because of non-residence. We feel that
a double payment should not be required. One payment of the fee
is sufficient.
We therefore approve of the recommendation that section 41,
subdivision 1, of the Constitution be amended by adding the words,

Adopted and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which committee recommended the proposed addition
and section 41, subdivision 1, was accordingly amended by
unanimous vote.

Selection o : Trial Commission by Lot
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration the proposal of F . L . Holmes, N . G. Matthews, and
A. A. Lund, all Past Masters of Lassen Lodge No. 149, to amend
sections 1940, 196 and 200 of the Constitution to provide for the
selection of trial commissioners by lot instead of by ballot.
Your committee does not feel that this method would insure a
greater degree of justice than that afforded by the present system. It
would leave to chance entirely the selection of the commissioners and
deprive the members of the Lodge from expressing their wishes on
this very important matter. We do not believe this proposed legislation to be desirable and recommend that it be not adopted.

The report was adopted.

Committee on Necrology
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to whom was
referred the resolution requiring the Secretary to report to Grand
Lodge with his annual report the names of brothers lost through death
during the year, favor this amendment. Masonry teaches a due observance of our deceased brothers, and it is entirely fitting that even
during the busy sessions of Grand Lodge a memorial service be held
for those who have passed beyond. The list of names of deceased
brothers furnished by each Secretary annually will make available to
the Necrology Committee information they should have. The importance of this work, in our opinion, requires that the Necrology
Committee be made a Constitutional committee.
Be it therefore resolved, that the Necrology Committee of Grand
Lodge be made a Constitutional committee and arrange for a fitting
memorial service at each communication of Grand Lodge under the
direction of the Grand Master.
·
Be it further resolved, that section 150 of the Constitution be
amended by adding there.to the following:
"7a: To transmit to the Grand Secretary with the annual return
the names, dates of initiation, passing and raising and the dates of
death of all permanent members of Grand Lodge as enumerated in
section 3 of the Constitution, and,".

Adopted and referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which committee reported back with its approval, and
section 150 of the Constitution was accordingly added to
by a five-sixths vote; and on the recommendation of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, section 27 of the Constitution
was amended by a five-sixths vote by adding "on necrology,
to consist of three members."

and b~nefit, not only from a historical point of view, but in making
accessible to all members of the craft a feeling of contact and
acquaintance with Grand Lodge.
The first provision of the resolution reads as follows:
"T.he ~dministration of each Grand Master advances the objects
and objectives of our great fraternity. Each Grand Master at considerable sacrifice, contributes in large measure to that advan~ement and
leaves the stamp and imprint of his own character and personality on
t~e .hearts and i~ .the minds of the craft throughout this great jurisdiction. Be as diligent and untiring as he may, he obviously cannot
contact al.I of our members; but science has provided a means of not
only n:akmg the Gran? Master available to all the craft, but of per- ·
petuatmg the personalities of our Grand Masters, thus rekindling in
the hearts of those who know them the affection and esteem we have
for ~hem and creating a like feeling on the part of men yet to ·be
admitted."

In conform.i ty therewith we offer the following resolution :

Physical Qualifications
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
the Grand Master's recommendation " a,'' relating to physical disqualifications. In 1928 our law was changed by amendment of section
94 to provide that the physical sufficiency of a candidate "shall be left
to the sound discretion of the Lodge," the Master, before ordering a
ballot, to state the nature and extent of a candidate's disability in
case he is unable to "comply literally" with the physical requirements
of our degrees.
The Grand Master finds , and so reports, that under the 1928
amendment aforesaid, there has been "flagrant violation of the Constitution by Masters and Lodges," and that the discretion granted by
the present wording of section 94 has been exercised, not soundly but
unsoundly in many instances.
In the judgment of your committee the Grand Master's views,
based upon very painstaking observations of what has occurred,
deserve the support of Grand Lodge and we "therefore recommend
that section 94 be restored to its language and provisions as the same
existed preceding the 1928 amendment.
T he Committee on Jurisprudence, to which the Grand Master's
recommendation was also referred, has likewise considered the same

72i

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

at great length and will submit a majority and minority report. We
are advised that the majority report will oppose the Grand Master's
proposal.
We therefore recommend that consideration of the matter be
deferred until the Committee on Jurisprudence shall have reported,
when all viewpoints will be available to the members of Grand Lodge.

idea that it is the internal and not the external qualifications that make
a man a Mason has been continually kept in mind. In the 'Old days,
and according to the strict ritualism of the fraternity in its earliest
periods, a~ shown by the old Constitutions, a candidate must have
been "a perfect youth," "without blemish," "having his right limbs as
a man ought to have," and having "the full and proper use of his
limbs." But as was suggested by the Committee on Jurisprudence in
1864, page 363, insistence upon such a requirement would long ago
have "proved the death of the fraternity." In the same spirit we th ink
that an insistence upon "literal" conformity on the part of the candidate to the requirements of the several degrees, while it might not
spell the death of the fraternity, would undoubtedly spell the death
of the ambition to become a Mason on the part of many a deserving
son of the Republic whose presence in, and contribution to the fraternity would be of inestimable value. Under our former law and in
complete support of the literal conformity required, it was solemnly
decreed by thi.s Grand Lodge that a man having "a stiff knee" cannot
be made a Mason, "for reasons which we may not express in words
but which will occur at once to every brother." (Proceedings 1864,
p. 364.)
In his argument in support of his recommendation, the Grand
Master states that the word "substantially" has no force; a candidate
"either conforms or does not conform." That is, if there be no strict
and · literal conformity there is no conformity at all, and that our
Constitution as phrased at present is meaningless. We cannot believe
such to be the case, and we find ourselves unable to agree with the
suggestion made which would involve a return to the old practice
wherein it was held that ineligibility resulting from inability to conform comprehended, among ·o ther things, "the loss of the first finger
of the right hand" or the inability to walk "without the use of an
artificial foot." (Proceedings 1901, p. 311.)
We believe the answer to the problem presented is simple and
finds adequate statement and persuasive reasoning in the report of the
special com·mittee appointed by Grand Master Fischer in 1928. That
committee was composed of very able men and gave long and thorough study to the question now involved. The chairman of the committee was Brother Walter K. Tuller, and its membership included,
among others, Past Grand Master Hutaff and our experienced, widely
read and discerning Grand Secretary. The report was considered and
passed upon approvingly by the Committee on Policy and Purposes
and by the Jurisprudence Committee, and its action and proposals
were duly ratified by the Grand Lodge. (Proceedings 1928, pp. 39,
140, 262, 285.) That committee recommended that section 94 be
amended to read as it now is. We think neither time nor experience

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Physical Qualifications-Majority Report
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California.:
There has been referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence
decision 3, and recommendation "a," both having to do with the question of the physical qualifications of candidates for the degrees. The
Grand Master states that a misconception of the law "has led to the
admission of applicants physically insufficient." In the decision rendered he held that the fact for a Lodge to determine in each instance
is whether the ap,plicant is able to conform substantially to what the
several degrees respectively require of him, "without the aid 'Of an
artificially substituted hand or leg." In his recommendation "a," he
proposes to amend section 94 of the Constitution by excluding the
word "substantially" therefrom and striking out the last two sentences
therein. Section 94 would then read, in so far as physical qualifications are concerned, as follows:
"No Lodge shall receive an applii:ation for the degrees
of Masonry unless the applicant be a man * * · * having no
maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable
of learning the art and physically able to conform to what
the several degrees respectiv-ely require of him."
The question of physical qualifications-what may be required
and how conformity thereto may be .determined-has been before this
Grand Lodge on many previous occasions. The position of the Grand
Lodge as reflected by the approved reports of its Grand Masters and
Jurisprudence Committees has been a growingly progressive one. The

728

PROCEEDI~GS

OF THE

suffice to detract from the reasoning there indulged in or the legislation so proposed and enacted.
To conform to the requirements of the several degrees is to do
the things req4ired of the candidate by such degrees. To conform
substantially means to conform in all essential particulars. The spirit
and purpose accompanying such conforming constitute no inconsiderable part of the ceremony. If that conforming may be accomplished
by the aid of an artificial limb, accompanied by the appropriate intent
and purpose, is there not in the act such a conforming as to measure
up to all intended and reasonable requirements of our ritual and teachings? If absolute conformity be required, which is the only alternative
as to what we conceive to be substantial conformity, then we disregard substance and stick blindly to form. In our judgment the true
destiny of our Institution lies not along such a narrow and constricted
path.
Our laws require that a candidate for the degrees shall be able
both to read and write. I know of a Past Grand Master who could
never have been made a Mason if strict, literal conformity to that
requirement had been exacting. He could neither read nor write
without the aid of eye glasses. In the ·broad domain of Freemasonry,
seeking the best men everywhere to do the best and most for
humani'ty, what irreconcilable difference is there between an artificial
aid to seeing and an artificial aid to walking? If with the aid of either,
a candidate is able to measure up to all the requirements of what we
would like to find in a loyal, zealous, faithful member of this fraternity,
why should we exclude him?
Whether a candidate is able to conform substantially or otherwise
is a question of fact that has to be determined by somebody, and we
submit that it is best determined by those having intimate personal
knowledge of the conditions actually obtaining. The candidate is
required to state ovei: his own signature the nature of "any physical
deformity or defect" existing. (Constitution, section 246.) The examining committee is required to examine into any lack of physical
disqualification, and if it finds one sufficient to disqualify a candidate,
it shall so report specially, whereupon the Master shall direct the
application to be withdrawn. (Constitution, section 104.) And, no
adverse report having come from the examining committee, and an
impairment nevertheless existing, the Master shall state the "nature
and extent" of the same, and thereupon the Lodge in its "sound discretion" shall determine whether such impairment disqualifies or not.
(Constitution, section 94.) In addition, after all other conditions have
been met and passed, any member of the Lodge has it within his
power, as it is his bounden duty, by blackball, to relieve the fralernity
of any undesirable, unworthy, or disqualified applicant.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

729

The Lodge determines upon the physical fitness of the petitioner
just as it determines, and through all ages has determined, upon his
moral fitness. Some judgment must be left to somebody. All possible
contingencies cannot be guarded against by legislative inhibition. The
tact, if it be a fact, that here and there a mistake may be made, or an
excess of friendly zeal displayed, does not serve to warrant the fraternity in doing that which obviously would serve to keep out of our
ranks many a man whose presence and participation therein we need.
Some of us know men who have lost an arm or a leg (in the Argonne)
who would be of incalculably more benefit to this fraternity than the
finest specimen of a perfect Adonis has ever been our pleasure to
welcome. Masonry ever needs men "right" in the head and in the
heart. An artificial limb now and then can do us no harm.
We recommend that decision 3 be not approved and that recommendation "a" be not adopted.
BENJAMIN F. BLEDSOE,
FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,

J. D. MURPHY,
BRADFORD WEBSTER,

Of Committee.
Minority Report
The undersigned members of your Jurisprudence Committee,
believing that the majority of the committee has erred in overruling
the decision of the Grand Master, designated as decision 3, and dealing
with physical qualifications, present this minority report for your consideration.
The majority opinion deals not only with the decision of the
Grand Master referred to, but also argues the recommendation of the
Grand Master for new legislation.
Much of the argument of the majority opinion is devoted to a
discussion of the excellent qualities of some men whom they seem to
think ought to make goo.d Masons, rather than giving any logical
reasons why they are eligible under the present law.
The Grand Master decided that he had held "that the fact for the
Lodge to determine is whether or nci.t the applicant is physically able
to conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively
require of him without the aid of an artificially substituted hand
or leg."
·
This decision is based upon the law as it now reads ; not upon
what some . of us think it ought to be, and we must not confuse the
issues.
Section 94 of the Constitution provides that a man must "have no
maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable of learning

I

\
•

731

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GllAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the art, and physically able to conform substantially to what the
several degrees respectively require of him."
Can it be said that a man who has lost a hand or a leg is not
maimed, because forsooth he has been able to purchase a mechanical
substitute for the lost member? Does the fact that he owns the
mechanical substitute make it a part of his physical being?
If by artificial aid he becomes eligible, then by the mere removal
of the contrivance, he will render himself ineligible. Thus he can put
on or take off his eligibility as he would his wearing apparel.
It was not the intention of Grand Lodge in ·amending the Constitution in 1914 when the word "substantial" was substituted for the
word "literal" to work any such radical change in the matter · of
physical qualifications. No such construction has ever been placed
upon the word "substantial" until today, except by some who have
misconstrued the meaning, and made the decision of the Grand Master
necessary.
When the legislation was adopted in 1928 providing that the
matter should be left to the "sound discretion" of the Lodge, it made
no change in the law, but merely placed upon the Lodge the responsibility of exercising its sound discretion in determining the fact, and
did not vest in the Lodge the power to override the Constitution and
admit members who were known to be in fact ineligible. This has been
done, and if the decision of the Grand Master is reversed, we have no
reason to doubt that just as flagrant violations will occur in the future.
We are not unmindful of the fact that many good · men are
ineligible to become Masons by reason of the loss of some member
which renders them incapabie of performing the necessary ritualistic
ceremonies, but we also k.now that many other good men are barred
hy lack of permanent residence, and other reasons which Grand Lodge
has seen fit to impose.
But we are not now concerned with the question of the good
moral character or desirability of these men, but what does vitally
concern us is the question whether or not we are .g oing to misconstrue
our law so as to remove all necessity for the possession of physical
qualifications from our candidates, in utter disregard of the plain
mandate of the Constitution.
Prior to the adoption of the amendment of 1928, it was never
intended that the word "substantial" was susceptible of the construction now claimed for it. Certainly the change of the fact-finding body
has not in any manner affected the meaning of the word.
If it is desired to change the law within the limits of the Landmarks by which we are bound, and which we admit are paramount
even to our Constitution, that is a matter for future determination.

But so long as the law remains as it is, we should obey it, and not
endeavor to evade or nullify it by misconstruction.
In our opinion the decision of the Grand Master is in accordance
with our law, and should be sustained.
.
We therefore recommend that decision 3 of the Grand Master be
sustained.
DANA R. WELLER,

Status of Senior Warden on Death of Master
Your Committee on ] urisprudence, to whom was referred the
following decision of the Grand Master, has had the same under
consideration and respectfully report as follows:
"Decision No. 9: In the case where the Senior Warden had
succeeded to the office and duties of Master upon the death or disability of the Master of the Lodge, as provided in Constitution section
148 and interpreted by this Grand Lodge in 1894 (Proceedings, p. 765;
Digest, 113), I was asked if the Senior Warden automatically assumes
the title of Master? If so what happens to the office of Senior
Warden?
"My answer was that the Senior Warden, succeeding to the
powers and duties of Master, assumed that title. There is, however,
no vacancy in the office of Senior Warden. He not being able to .
physically fill the stations of Master and Senior Warden at one and
the same time, the station of Senior Warden must be filled by appointment for each meeting. Not having been elected as Master he will
not become a Past Master at the expiration of the term of the Master
whose powers and duties he had assumed.
"In construing sections 138 and 148 of the Constitution it is my
opinion that the office of Master becomes vacant by reason of the
death or resignation of the Master and that such vacancy can be
filled only by electi1;m. During the time of such vacancy the Senior
Warden (or in his absence the Junior Warden) succeeds to the powers
and duties of the Master and acts as Master pro tempore. There
would be no vacancy in the office of a Warden who was acting as
Master pro tempore, because his very right to act as such is based
upon the fact that he is such a Warden authorized by the Constitution
to exercise the functions of a Master in case of a vacancy, until the
election by the Lodge of a Master."

It is the opinion of your committee that the decision of the
Grand Master is the correct statement of the law and we, therefore,
recommend its approval by the Grand Lodge.

Right of Secretary to Furnish ·Information
Your Committee also had under consideration decision No. 15 by
the Grand Master and respectfully report as follows:
"Decision No. 15. I received the following communication from
the Secretary of Alhambra Lodge No. 322:
"We had a member by the name of.. ....................,......., who
d ied in 1923. He came in in 1920, and paid $6.00 for 1920.
He also paid $9.00 for dues for 1921. He did not pay his dues
for 1922, and prior to the ] uly meeting of 1923 he died in the
month of May, owing dues for 1922 and first half of the year
1923.
"Now his widow wants to join the Eastern Star, and the
Eastern Star wants a certificate from me to the effect that he
was in good standing at the time of his death. The question
comes up that in case she gets sick, or anything happens to
her, would the Lodge be responsible for the same, that is,
for doctors, nursing, funeral, etc.
"The Master requested me to write and ask you for a
decision."
It is apparent that in the second paragraph of the request of the
Secretary of Alhambra Lodge as t o whether the Lodge would be
responsible tp the widow in the event of the death of the husband in
good standing, has no bearing whatever upon the question as to
whether or not she is entitled to a certificate of her husband's standing.
That question is fully settled by the laws of this grand jurisdiction,
and such was the decision of the Grand Master.
The ques tion implied in the communication as to whether the
Secretary of the Lodge may communicate information contained in
the records of the Lodge to an officer of an Eastern Star Lodge, the
Grand Master reported as follows:
"Is a Secretary of a Lodge permitted to.give a certificate
to the Eastern Star t0- the effect that a member was in good
standing at the time of his death or at any other time? My
answer is that he is not."
It may be fairly assumed that the request for information by the
Eastern Star Lodge was at the instigation of the widow of the
deceased, and based upon that fact we are of the opinion, and w.e

GHAND LOUGE OF CALIFORNIA

735

assume ·that there can be no question, that had the widow herself
asked for the information it would have been the duty of the Secretary of Alhambra L odge to have given her a certificat e to that effect
in the form of section 234 of the Constitution.
Undoubtedly the decision of the Grand Master in this particular
case was correct, and we are of the opinion that the Secretary of a
Masonic Lodge would not be authorized to give information concerning the records of his Lodge to a stranger.

In view of the peculiar circumstances ot this case, we feel that
no harm could have been done to have advised the Secretary that an
application from an Eastern Star Chapter to the Secretary of the
Lodge of which the deceased husband was a member for such information, should be complied with.

Adopted.

some county, city and county, city or town thereof, or in such other
first-class stocks, bonds or securities as may be directed by the Lodge
and approved by the Master," to be eliminated from said section, and
the following substituted in lieu thereof:
"deposited in some reputable bank or invested in securities legal
for savings banks under the laws of the State ol California, or the
Territory of Hawaii."

Adopted, and section 129 accordingly amended by unanimous vote.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
No. 700, in which F. N., a member of Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625,
was expelled under July 8, 1931, begs leave to report as follows:
This is a proceeding under section 192A of the Constitution. Accused
was charged in the District Court of the United States of the District
of Arizona in two counts; one, for the unlawful possession of intoxicating liquors; two, unlawful and felonious transportation of intoxicating
liquors.
He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to the United States Penitentiary at McNeil Island for two and one-half years. A certified copy of
the final judgment of conviction was filed with the Lodge and thereupon
a notice was sent to the accused. This notice omitted to state that the
written election should be filed with the Secretary of such Lodge within
said period of sixty days. It further omitted to state that the crime of
which he was convicted, was a felony. The record also shows that the
Master neglected, at the next stated meeting, after such sixty days from
the mailing of such notice had elapsed, to announce to the Lodge the
fact that such certified copy had been filed, that the required notice
given and that accused stood expelled from all the rights and privileges
of Masonry.
For all of these errors the case must be reversed and returned to
the Lodge for a new proceeding in accordance with the constitutional
provisions applicable.
Your Committee on Grievances, therefore, offers the following resolution and moves its adoption:
Resolved, that the action of Angeles Mesa Lodge No. 625 in attempting to expel F. N. be and the same is hereby reversed and the
proceedings are r emanded to the Lodge for further action.

Adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred trial record
No. 677, from Highland Park Lodge No. 382, begs leave to report as
follows:
This is a companion case to No. 678, just reported. The charge
is that the accused, a member of Highland Park Lodge signed, as recommendor, the petition of E. M. G. for the degrees of Masonry, knowing
that the petition falsely represented that said E. M. G. had not been
previously rejected by a Masonic Lodge. The accused plead guilty and the
penalty was fixed at reprimand.
We believe the penalty to be inadequate. In some ways it should
be regarded as more serious on the part of a Mason to join in such a ·
false representation than for one not a Mason to make such a representation in his petition. At all events, he is at least as culpable and
should be punished in a corresponding manner.
