PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Masonic Homes
3. Your committee has given very thorough consideration to the
report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes and again must commend
the Trustees for the completeness of the report and for the care given
to our Homes by the Trustees as displayed thereby.
We recommend to all a thorough reading of this report. It will bring
a better knowledge of the Homes and the splendid work they are doing
as well as the problems connected therewith and incident thereto.
The many problems incident to the Homes are left in the hands of
the Trustees, knowing each will receive thorough consideration. The
financial problems presented in the report are the only ones given consideration by this committee.
The report shows an indebtedness of the Homes of $320,000-all
chargeable to the building program entered upon prior to 1929. The
amount is all due to the Endowment Fund of the Homes but as these
funds are being accumulated for a definite purpose, they must not be
permanently used for other purposes, and therefore, the above amount
should be returned when it can be done without unduly burdening the
Lodges of the jurisdiction.
For the fund to provide the amount borrowed it was found necessary
to secure $100,000 from the bank. The interest, therefore, on this sum
is being lost to the Homes.
The report also shows a payment-and the final-for buildings and
improvements of $80,000.00, and that if it had not been for this expenditure the Homes would have operated on the income received for the year
and have had a surplus of $20,000.00.
At the close of the fiscal year the Grand Lodge had-outside of its
investment in this building, which is fjxed and cannot be used for any
other purposesSecurities ................................................................$220,000.00
Cash .......................................................................... S8,000.00
Cash-Emergency Relief...................................... 18,000.00
Or a total of... .........................................................$296,000.00
which represents the surplus built up by prudence in years gone by. This
always has been regarded as a surplus for emergency purposes. We believe the emergency has now risen for the use of a part of this sum.
We also believe the $100,000.00 secured from the bank should be paid,
that the income therefrom may again accrue to the Homes.
As the final payment on additions and improvements has now been
made, and as if it had not been for such expenditure the Homes would
have operated last year with a surplus of $20,000.00, and as we believe
the Trustees will this year effect further economies and, therefore, should

be able to apply $2S,OOO.OO toward this debt ; your committee, therefore,
recommends the appropriation of $7S,OOO.OO out of the surplus funds of
this Grand Lodge which, coupled with the · $2S,000.00 which it would
seem the funds of the Homes will permit and which sum we recommend
should be immediately taken out of the funds on hand and the $100,000.00
sec.ured · from the bank settled. A proper resolution putting into effect
this appropriation will be presented at the conclusion of this report.
Your committee has also given long and serious thought to methods
of raising funds to liquidate the balance of the $320,000.00 debt of the
Homes. While we are desirous of seeing the Endowment Fund restored
at an early date, yet we are more desirous of not placing any additional
burden at this time on the constituent Lodges.
By close figuring the Club Houses at Berkeley and Los Angeles can
be maintained for the succeeding year on a lOc per capita levy. To the
credit of the Trustees of these Clubs, let it be said that they are willing
to do that close figuring. As the tax for this purpose last year was lSc,
the constituent Lodges are being saved from this source Sc per member.
By eliminating any appropriation for the George Washington National Memorial, we are saving a further tax of 20c, or a total saving
from these two sources of 2Sc per member. We believe this additional
fax can well be added to the amount contributed to the Hoines. Therefore, in the resolution providing for the levying of our annual assessment,
we are adding this amount to that previously assessed for the maintenance
of the Homes, thereby retaining the per capita levy at the same amount
that it was last year.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $7S,OOO.OO be appropriated out of the
otherwise unexpended funds of this Grand Lodge to be paid to the
Trustees of the Homes for the purpose of returning the funds secured
from the bank.
We further offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolve&, that the sum of SOc per paying member be levied upon
the membership for the maintenance of the Masonic Homes of California.

Adopted, except as to the paragraph relating to the
George Washington National Memorial, for which a resolution had been adopted providing for a ten-cents per capita
tax for the coming year.

Pay of Members and Per Diem
10. Referring to that portion of the Grand Master's address dealing
with the pay of members in attendance on Grand Lodge and his recommendation that the present method be changed to include a per diem:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

750

The present payroll for traveling expenses is made up on the basis
of an "unlimited" fare, which in cases of those whose residence is 250
miles or more distant from the meeting place of Grand Lodge, results
in payment of amounts ranging from $15.00 to $40.00 more than the
amount actually expended in such travel.
Your committee finds that the number who actually draw travel pay
is approximately 640, but that those who reside in the vicinity of the
meeting place of Grand Lodge are not now on the payroll, and they
estimate this number at about 160, which would make a total to draw
per diem, unless favoritism is to be shown, of approximately 800.
The payroll, as now made up, consists of representatives of Lodges,
Inspectors, members of all standing committees, officers of Grand Lodge
and Past Grand Masters. At the present session, the total disbursement
for pay of members will be approximately $20,000.00, and your committee, after giving effect to the saving which would be made by paying
only actual traveling expenses to representatives, estimate that the payroll
would be increased by not less than $12,000.00-or making a total payroll
of $32,000.00.
Your ·Committee on Finance is thoroughly in sympathy with the
Grand Master in his effort to discourage the subordinate Lodges in
making excessive appropriations for the expenses of Masters and Wardens who attend the annual communications. However, they are not
convinced that the change to a per diem basis would cause the Lodges
to discontinue the unnecessary expenditure of their funds.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the consideration of the subject of the pay of members and per diem be postponed until the next annual communication.

Adopted.

the corning four years, and that when the amounts are paid into
the Grand Secretary, that he be authorized to remit yearly the
amount collected to the proper authorities of the Memorial
Association."
The payments as propo!ed in the above recommendation have been
promptly met and the financial obligation of this Grand Lodge to the
George Vvashington National Memorial Association has been fulfilled.

Conference of Grand Secretaries

20. The M:. W:. Grand Master, -as well as the Committee on
Policy and Purposes, have recommended that the Finance Committee
make an appropriation to defray the expenses of our Grand Secretary
to attend the Conference of Grand Secretaries to be held in Washington, May, 1932.
The Committee on Finance have been unable to reach an agreement in this matter and, therefore, report to the Grand Lodge without recommendation.
Grand Lodge thereupon voted that an appropriation of $500.00
be included in the report of the Finance Committee, for the purpose
of defraying the expense of the Grand Secretary in attending the
Conference of Grand Secretaries.
Grand Lodge Relief
21. There has been brought to the attention of your committee
the temporary embarrassment of a worthy brother who has served
this Grand Lodge long and faithfully. It is a case which, in the
judgment of your committee, properly comes within the purview of
this Grand Lodge.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:

Resolved, that the sum of $500.00 be appropriated out of the otherwise unexpended funds of this Grand Lodge, to be expended by
the Grand Master for the relief of a worthy member.

Morning Session
Friday, October 16, 1931.
Grand Lodge was called on at 10 o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.
The minutes of yesterday's sessions were read and approved.
ANNUAL ELECTION OF OFFICERS
The Grand Master announced that pursuant to the requirements of section . 17 of the Constitution, the annual
election of officers of Grand Lodge was now in order.
Tellers were appointed, and the following was the result
of the election :
The R.". W.". Robert B. Gaylord of Oakland Lodge No. 188
was elected Grand Master.
R.". W .". Frank Mixter of Exeter Lodge N o. 424 was elected
Deputy Grand Master.
The R.". W.". James B. Gist of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202 was
elected Senior Grand Warden.
The W.". William A. Sitton of Washington Lodge No. 20 was
elected Junior Grand Warden.
.. V.". W.". William P. Filmer of King Solomon's Lodge · No. 260
was re-elected Grand Treasurer.
The V.". W.". John Whicher of King David's Lodge No, 209
was re-elected Grand Secretary.
The V.". w:. Thomas J. Baker. of Union Lodge No. 58 was
re-elected Grand Lecturer.
The Grand Master-elect caused· to be read the names of ~ppointed
officers, as follows :
Grand .Chaplain:--:-.Rev. John Snape of Sequoi~ 1:'.o~ge ~6. 349: . .
Grand Ora tor.....:.James T: Fraser of . Hum?oldt Lodg~ _N ?· 7? . .
Assistant Grand Secretary-Frank G. Hobbs of Alexandria
Lodge No. 531.

M.'. W:. Dana R. Weller, Past Grand Master, was appointed
Master of Ceremonies, and all the officers-elect and appointed, excepting only the Grand Treasurer and Grand Sword-Bearer, were
installed by the retiring Grand Master in due and ancient form.

Past Grand Master Well er then, in behalf of Grand
Lodge, presented to Past Grand Master Ross a sterling
silver coffee set.
Marquis F. Calmes, Master of Maui Lodge No. 472,
speaking for all the Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands, presented to the retiring Grand Master a silk lei bearing the
names of the eight island Lodges.
Grand Master Gaylord ann·ounced the appointment of

of the Masonic Homes for the term ending October, 1935.
The Grand Master clothed the retiring Grand Master
with the distinctive apron of a Past Grand Master, and also
presented him with a diamond-studded lapel jewel.

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
October, 1931
BY JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith is submitted my Eleventh Report as Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee. As usual, the views expressed under
the various topics are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
There continues the same general similarity as to questions and
conditions in the Craft as heretofore, with the exception that during
the past year the loss in membership, together with its accompanying results, have brought forth queries as to-"Whither are we
drifting?", "Is Masonry shifting its basis?", "What shall we do to
be saved?", etc. We believe that one of the best presentations and
suggestions along this line was the address of Grand Master Chas.
H. Johnson of New York, before the Conference of Grand Masters
in Washington, D. C., in February, 1931. We wish that space would
permit the presentation of his entire Address, but the following are
apropos:
"We heard last night a very interesting talk by the Bishop of
Washington in which he referred to certain critical situations m
which the Church finds itself at . the present time.
"The fact of the matter is, gentlemen, that it is not the Church
alone that is in a critical situation at the present time, but most
American and other institutions are also facing crises ·at the present
time; and among the institutions that are facing such a crisis is
the Institution that we represent here today."

• •. • • *
"There is nothing written on the books anywhere that Masonry
is bound to continue, any more than it is written that America is
bound to continue. Other great organizations have existed and
passed out of existence. We have lots of remains in this country
today of great mastodons and pterodactyls and many other prehistoric forms of animal life that have passed away, mighty as they

2

REPORT ON CORRESI ONDENCE

were, because they could not adapt themselves t o a new climatic
condition, to a new environment, and they died and passed out of
the picture."

*

*

*

*

*

"The Chu rch 1s not sacred to the criticism of mankind. The
School is not sacred. The fami ly is not sacred. No institution
of society today can escape. the acid test of the modern scientific
development of mind ; and this organization, proud as we are of
its antiquity, and proud as we are 'of the grand men who have lived
in the past, cannot bank on those things in the 20th century.
"We are proud of the George Washington Memorial. But who
in the modern world cares, wh en it comes to a show-down, whether
he was a Mason or not; and who cares in the outside world whether
we care that he was a Mason?
" Masonry has got to meet this situation on something other
than a historic basis, on something other· than pride in antiquity.
It seems to me th at there are certain things that we have got to
do to meet this changing world and changing conditions that face
us. A smug satisfaction over what has been done, a calm interior
of ·soul over our great history-and we are old and we are bigis not going to help us to meet the new generation of the new age;
and one of the first thi'ngs that I would like to submit to you· is
this, that in order to meet this :Situation in the future we have got
to see to it that there is a better under standing of th.e art.
"We talk a good deal about the · ignorance of people outside of
Masonry regarding Freemasonry. We might talk a great deal more
about the ignorance of people inside Masonry r egarding Freemasonry.
"What do your Members know about Masonry any more than
the three degrees they have gone through when they were partly
in a mental haze and a mental daze and it affected them merely
. as a repetition of words? What do they know about the background?
The mysticism of Freemasonry, as someone has called it here today,
is an entirely unknown territory to most of our members. H ow
many of ·them think of it as an insurance organization? They tell
their wives, 'You need not worry any more. If anything happens
to me the Ma:sons will take care of you the rest of your life. You
don't have to worry about the children. The Masons will take
care of them.' It is thought of as a grand and glorious insurance
fund at th e smallest possible per capita cost under the sun.
"You would be surprised, my friends, if you tried to make an
analysis of the mental attitude of your members, t o find how many
men consider th e Masonic fraternity purely a cheap insurance affair.
"And there are others who think of it purely as a social affair."

"Another matter which I think must concern us as we face· the
future of this organization is the financial situation. You cannot run

Masonry o n emotion: You cannot run· this organization on sentiment. You cannot run it on the glory of John Hancock and George
Washington and all the other great heroes of the past. It requires dollars and cents to carry on this organization. If w e promise
that we are going to care for them the rest of their lives, and all
of their family likewise, their sisters and their cousins and their
aunts, it is going to take a large amount of money to run t he Order,
and it means that we will have to face a financial reorgani~ation in
order to meet our financial responsibility and not have a man turn
away and say, 'Well, they promised a lot, but they d idn't m,ake
good that promise.'
"We have got to consider the same qµestion in r egard to our
charities. H ow are we going to carry on our charities? Most
organizations are th inking in terms of institutions. We all know
that the most expensive form of charity is the institutional form
of brick an d mortar and stone, with grounds to be kept up. Institutional charity is the most expensive of all.
''H ow shall the Lodges and the Grand Lodges who have
taken upon themselves this great obligation in the future meet the
expense of the proper care of those whom they have willingly
assumed as dependents and whom they have promised should be
ca.red for all their lives?"

There is, of course, no "meeting of the minds" on any particular
remedy. Grand Masters, Grand Orators, Chairmen of Correspondence Committees and others in authority, or students of the questions present different remedies. That we must hold fast to the
principles and teachings of Masonry is perhaps the main idea of
all the suggested plans. How this can be handled is, of course,
another question.
· As heretofore within the limits of this Report cannot be considered all of the questions that receive attention. A summary of
some of these are as follows:
DRAMAS: Some ~ne who claimed to know, states that 90%
of the people are " eye-minded", and that the greatest opportunity
for Education was through methods of enlightenment along that
line. The Grand Lodges of Colorado, Nevada, North Dakota and
Nova Scotia have had presented at their Annual Sessions plays
founded upon Masonic incidents or history, which have been written
by persons thoroughly conversant with the subjects. This form of
presenting information seems to be one that will produce results,
and we believe could well be embodied in a program of any Committee on Education with great profit to the Craft.
DUAL MEMBERSHIP: The discussion of dual or plural
membership, with its various subdivisions, has continued to receive

consideration from a number of Grand Lodges, in some cases resulting in the enactment of laws permitting the same.
Those who have adopted it seem to have suffered no bad results. From statistics it would appear that only a very small
number are taking advantage of this opportunity to assist or participate in the activities of a Lodge other than their Mother Lodge.
This class of Members, therefore, appear to be Brethren who are
interested in Masonry and desire to do actual work, rather than
mere "joiners."

EASTERN STAR : As one Chairman said, the Order of the
Eastern Star is still agitating the minds of some of the Jurisdictions.
Brother Darrah of Illinois, we believe, hit the nail on the head
when he wrote:
"The Order of the Eastern Star is a distinctly woman's organization and as such it has a place in the world and an opportunity
to do much good. The sooner the Order of the Eastern Star
restricts its membership to ·women only and excludes the masculine
gender the better it will be for that organization. Much of the
present trouble arises not so much from the women themselves as
from the males in the Order who, failing to acquire distinction in
the Masonic fraternity, present themselves and their offices to the
Order of the Eastern Star where they soon become 'whales among
fishes'."
I
In some of the Jurisdictions the Order of the Eastern Star has
assisted financially and otherwise in .the work of Homes. In one
place while the Grand Lodge was called from labor to refreshment,
· the ladies called and presented a check for $25,000.00 as an Endowment fund for a Hospital.
EDUCATIONAL LOAN FUNDS: This activity of some of
the Grand Lodges continues to function along desirable lines. The
Educational Loan Fund of tlie Knights Templar has reached such
proportions that the Grand Encampment recently abolished the
assessment of their individual members, the interest on the amount
so far collected being sufficient to take care of the demands upon
the fund. While an educational loan fund has never been established by the Grand Lodge of California, it should be a source of
satisfaction to know that the Educational Fund of Oregon was
created in 1852 by their Grand Master Berryman . Jennings, who
occupied an important place in the early history of California
Masonry and the formation of our Grand Lodge.
GRAND LODGE BULLETIN: ·A few Grand Lodges issue
an official Bulletin at regular intervals for the benefit of the Craft.
It is furnished free to certain classes, . and a subscription charge
made to others. One of these outstanding publications is the Grand
Lodge Bulletin of Iowa. An official organ of the Grand Lodge

GRAND MASTERS' CONFERENCE : It is to be regretted
that the general membership of the Cr~ft cannot receive the benefit
of the observations of the Grand Masters of the United States, who
annually meet in Washington in February. As one of the Correspondents has said, this meeting is generally looked upon as a
means of boosting the George Washington Memorial, and suggested
that ·perhaps an American Masonic Congress might fulfill a long
felt want. There are certain questions of general Masonic Practice
which could be standardized in all of the Jurisdictions, without
violation of the doctrine of "Stat es' Rights." Perhaps if Masonry
is going to face the future it can only be through a united effort
of all Jurisdictions working to a common end.
The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts invited the Grand Masters
1
of New England and New Jersey to a Conference which was highly
commended by some of those present. Perhaps this idea might be
followed by the Pacific Coast with good results.
OFFENSES: There seems to be a general trend towards
adopting the form of a Trial . Commission, composed of members
appointed by the Grand Master to consider particular cases.
The Committee on Appeals and Grievances of one of the Jurisdictions having a large membership reported that no cases had been
presented to them at that session for consideration. This situation
had never arisen before in that State.
In another Jurisdiction the Grand Chaplain asked permission
to offer prayer for the erring Brothers after the report of the ·
Grievance and Appeal Committee was read. In some of the Jurisdictions there seems to be an aversion to disciplining members who
have violated the Volstead Act or the Jones " Five and Ten" law.
One Grand Master was asked if an initiate who served a term in a
Federal penitentiary for violation of the Prohibition law would be
barred from advancement, and the ruling was that within itself he
would not. The Jurisprudence Committee, however, disagreed and
held that a vote for advancement covers CHARACTER as well as
PROFICIENCY.
ORDER OF DE MOLA Y: This organization generally continues to receive the praise of those who are thoroughly familiar
with its ideals and · purposes. A few uninformed persons, both
Masons and profane, still continue to speak of it as a Junior
Masonic organization. Initiates into the Order of De Molay are .
given to understand that there is no connection between the Masonic

Fraternity and the Order of De Molay, other than the interest which
the Craft takes in an effort to perform a service to the rising
generation.
Shortly after President Hoover was inaugurated he organized
what is known as THE WHITE HOUSE CONFERENCE ON
CHILD HEALTH AND PROTECTION, working under the Department of the Interior. Dr. Harry E. Barnard was given the
direction of the work. Some 1200 experts, touching the various
fields of the life of the child, have been hard at work gathering
facts and data since the organization of the Conference. When the
reports by States have been made, being the result of the work of
over 150 major committees, and the data printed it will total over
20,000 pages. Dr. Barnard in addressing the Grand Council at its
1931 meeting at Washington, D. C., stated:
"Fellowship, co-operation, responsibility, citizenship, and leadership are encouraged and developed in varying degrees through different boys' organizations. There are many organizations for the
youngsters in school. Several of them have come to our attention
and we feel that they are doing splendid work, but when the boys
come to be 15 or 16 years of age they are different boys from the
youngsters up to that time. There is a very sharp and sudden and
. definite change in their nature, and society has taken very little
thought of the nature of those boys between the ages of 18 and 21."
"The De Malay movement, as I have seen it and as I know it,
is the movement which is giving these young qien of ours their
opportunity to develop leadership. Do you know that there are
about a million gifted children in our schools today? The children
who, when they reach adult life, will be the leaders in our society.
We are not giving those gifted children the kind of education which
fits them for leadership. We are giving them just the same education that the average boys and girls get. As I study the De Molay
movement I see that you have found a way to give a select group
of our young men between 18 and 21 the opportunity to develop
the power which will make them leaders in society."
"I want to tell you how glad I am that I have had a chance in
these last few months to do what little I could to help you in your
great work. We believe that you have found a key which, when
properly used, will let us into this great opportunity where the boys
who are to be our leaders in the years to come are receiving their
finest education."
That President Hoover is in sympathy with the work of the
Order qf De Malay is evidence of the fact that on March 16, 1931
he accepted Honorary Membership in the De Malay Legion of
Honor.

TEMPLES: Regulations requmng that constituent Lodges
must submit plans for Temples to the Grand Lodge before building ·
are being adopted by Jurisdictions who have profited by the experience of those who pioneered the idea. In some cases it has too
often been "locking the door after the horse was stolen" but produced a salutary effect even in such cases.
In a number of cases Jurisdictions that have had a law that a
Temple could only be occupied by a Blue Lodge are allowing them
to be used by other organizations. In some cases sentiment has
caused the change, while in others the increased revenue appears

Some enthusiastic Masons who were all on a World Cruise
adopted a resolution suggesting that an appropriate memorial at
Jerusalem, in the form of a "Masonic structure, beautiful in appearance and of practical service to all visiting the Holy City" should
be erected. One Foreign Correspondent called attention to the
present financial condition of the Washington National Memorial,
and suggested that it would be just as feasible to plan a memorial
on the site where the " Legendary Hiram Abiff might have been

Inevitably, when such bodies attract public attention by spectacular
displays, involving huge expenditure, the uninformed multitude regard their proceedings as exhibiting Masonry in some at least of
its aspects, and so a wrong impression may be given of the aims
and ideals of the Craft. Masonry at its best has always been
retic~nt, not seeking publicity and indeed shunning and prohibiting
it. Thus the Masonic regalia is never to be worn in public except
at Masonic funerals or by special dispensation. It is a long march
from this ascetic reserve to the gorgeous pageantry on which Toronto
eyes have just been feasting; with its magnificent massed bands, its.
fl.ashing scimitars and the oriental splendor of its costumes. This
is not a development of English or Canadian Masonry as we understand it. Whether its association with Masonry adds to the influence and dignity of the Craft, or commends the Craft to the good
judgment of the sober-minded, must remain a matter of opinion.
But as those attending the convention are all our Brethren in
Masonry we may at all events congratulate them on the success it
achieved. The attendance was large, though much below extravagant forecasts; the public demonstrations made a great impression
upon vast throngs of spectators, and there was much light-hearted
foolery which for the most part stopped far short of offensive license.
We may congratulate them also upon their benevolence, particularly
in relief of crippled children, and their declarations in furtherance
of universal peace."
·

There is, of course, a difference of opinion as to whether or not
this Memorial is worth the amount expended or to be expended.
The statement in the fifth paragraph of the address of Past Grand
Master Johnson, quoted in the first part of this Report, represents
one view.

WASHINGTON MEMORIAL: It is planned to dedicate the
Washington Memorial in May, 1932. It is generally known that
in 1908 it was proposed to erect a building at a cost of not to
exceed $100,000.00 to house the valuable relics of George Washington owned by Alexandria Washington Lodge No. 22, A. F. & M.
In 19i6 the figure was advanced to $500,000.00; in 1920 it was
increased to $1,000,000.00; in 1922 it was increased to $1,S00,000.00.
The total expenditure for everything to date amounts to $3,212,575.64. The amount required to finish the project is now fixed at
$1,339,422.02, or a grand total of $4,551,997.73. This does not include
the amount that must be raised for an endowment to cover the
maintenance during the future years. It has been suggested this
should be $1,500,000.00.
California stands 33rd on the list, having contributed $130,381.10,
or 91.8% of its quota of $1.00 per member as of July, 1930.
If the money already expended, and the estimate necessary to
complete it are correct, and is not changed, it will require a levy
of $1.70 on the present Masonic membership instead of $1.00 as
originally planned.

ATTENDANCE
The present · conditions of modern day life make the average
Lodge meeting, as a means of attraction to its members of very little
moment, and particularly so in the large cities. Prescribing a remedy for this is a difficult proposition. The conferring of degrees, set
educational programs, mediocre entertainment, etc., cannot compete
with the radio, the talkie or the automobile.
Originally Masons met in Taverns because they were the meeting places for social life and where could be found a community
of interest. Ritualistic work was not the main attraction. The desire
for Fellowship was the objective. If this basic idea could be reestablished there would undoubtedly be a larger attendance. One
Grand Lecturer has suggested that the Ritual be abridged. This may
be a straw to show which way the wind will ultimately blow.
Idaho (1929):
(Chairman Correspom!cncc Committee): Within the memory of men
not yet old, conditions were much simpler. Men in those days had leisure
evenings, and the Lodge room afforded them a place to spend a pleasant
hour. Homes were much more isolated and roads were of the pioneer
type. Having little else to do in the evening, they enjoyed going to Lodge,
where· beside disposing of their Masonic obligations they met congenial
spirits and talked over the problems of the day with their neighbors.
Then came the automobile, good roads, moving pictures, radio and many
other modern forms of attraction, and the old days passed away never to
return. Men are no longer troubled with idle evenings. There are so
many things to do and so many places to go that there are not evenings
enough in the week. ·In order to attend Lodge now they must forego some
other pleasure or business engagement. It is more interesting to turn on
the radio and listen to the varied and attractive programs that are offered,
or to step into the car and speed away on a drive to the neighboring town.
Men no longer need to go to Lodge for a diversion. Those who go
now must do so for a more substantial reason. It must be more because
of loyalty to the Lodge, love of Masonic principles and teachings, or because of a deeper faith in the fundamentals of the Fraternity. These are
new conditions, and it can readily be seen t?at the problem of Lodge attendance assumes greater importance.
Illinois ( 1930) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): As is most natural, everybody seems to be offering remedies for the present Masonic decline.
Masons who are really interested in the Fraternity are trying to find out

why Lodges are not better attended. The thought has been advanced in

The Grand Lodge of New York has been giving serious attention

Lodges ar~ not better attended. He recommended the appointment
of a committee to make a general· survey, and if possible find out why
memb~rs ~f Lodges failed to attend the meetings. New York is not
al~ne .m this ~atter of Masonic remissness. The same condition prevails m . practically every jurisdiction in the United States and the
cause will be found simply in ou r different method ·of Jivin~. Nowadays men go where they are interested. The city club, the country
club, the. golf club, the church society, bridge and dancing clubs all
have the'.r devotees because the men who attend them seem to be intereste~ 111 that particular diversion. The Masonic Lodge is no longer
the social center of the community. There was a time when it was,
but that. was. before we had so many different opportunities offered
us for d1vers1on. Lodges, as a rule, hold too many meetings. Most of
them are not content to hold two stated meetings per month but
they call ~any special meetings for the conferring of single de~rees.
solu_tion of the present decli ne in Lodge attendance will be found

groupmg the work. If L odges instead of calling a special meeting
to confer .the second degree upon a candidate will be permitted to
group their work so that they will be able to confer theit degrees
upon cl~sse.s of candidates, it will be fo und that there will be a new
awakenmg m Masonry. The rule that each candidate must receive his
degree separately obtained during the period in Masonry when candidates for degrees were very few. Nowadays· when Lodges raise fifteen

or twenty candidates in a year there is every reason Why the purposes
of Masonry would be best served in grouping initiates. Whenever
Lodges are permitted to group work haste will be eliminated; officers
will try to do better work; there will be more attention to details;
proper musical features will be introduced ; and the work instead of
being a tiresome grind will become something plea.s urable to behold.
Brethren should not be blamed for not . going up to Lodge rooms
simply to hear long tiresome ceremonies of opening and closing, and
the reading of bills; nor should they be condemned for not wanting
to go up to se~ degrees conferred in a hasty, careless, slipshod manner. If Lodge attendance is going to be improved there must be a
revolution in Lodge matters. Men used to go up to Masonic Lodge
rooms because they didn't have any other place tci go, but that time
is all over and past. Very. few people go to see the finest theatrical
production more than once. It stands to reason that the number of
times that men are going to look at a Masonic degree is decidedly
limited unless that' deg.r ee is presented in a way and manner that has
a direct appeal to them. One reason why the Scottish Rite degrees
are so successful and the attendance upon the;e bodies is good is due
to the fact that they do not work two or three times a week thereby
wearing everybody out. By conferring their degrees at a fixed period
upon classes of candidates and in a most excellent manner they are
able to hold the attention of large numbers of members. The question of Lodge attendance is a big one and requires considerable study
and investigation to get at the cause of non-attendance.

CIPHER RITUALS
There are two schools of thought regarding the use of printed
Ritu'a~s, Cipher or otherwise; one represented by the majority of
American Lodges and. the other by England, Scotland and the Jurisdictions who owe their origin to those Grand Lodges. In this age
of ~rinting, nothing seems to .be sacred. Even though laws are passed
aga.mst the use of Cipher codes, Grand Lecturers complain that their
use still continues. Undoubtedly where printed Rituals are used there
is less stress placed upon proficiency in this particular function of a
Lodge and more time given to the worth while things. Read Western
Australia's excerpt.
New Jersey (1930):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee}: It seems hard work to get
rid of this Cipher Ritual business, but it can be done if the Grand
Masters will sit on it and sit on it hard. There is no need for them.
Their use is a violation of obligations and the reason for them is
only a lazy man's reason that he has not enough "industry and zeal
to gather the knowledge," but wants to read it out of a book.
.
9hio (1930):

(Grand Master): One of the District Lecturers reported that a
.Lodge in his district had been supplying leaves from a spurious
Ritual to the candidate to assist him in learning his lectures. Th.is
custom had been in existence for some time, but the Secretary felt
that it should be discontinued and so reported to the District Lecturer. When the Worshipful Master's attention was called to the
violation of Resolution 12, he replied that no such Rituals had been
supplied to candidates during his term of office and that he had
ordered all members of the Lodge to dispose of such property.
It has also come to my attention that a publishing house located
outside of the State of Ohio which publishes spurious Rituals has
been circularizi~g the candidates of some of our Lodges, eve~ before
they have r eceived the Master Mason Degree, offering to supply
these Rituals. The question naturally arises, how does this house
secure the riames of these candidates?

Texas (1929):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Grand Master of Illinois
finds that " Notwithstanding the repeated warnings that have gone
out in years gone by, the practice of using printed keys to the Ritual
has not been eradicated." He calls attention to the severe penalty
attaching to such breaches of the law, but we fail to find any administrative act tending toward its enforcement. Texas has similar laws
and has passed through like experiences. Now and then you will
find a professing student of Masonry insisting that he should be
permitted to own copies of such keys, ciphers or exposes as he may
find himself able to purchase. Somehow, he imagines these to be
quite an adjunct to his Masonic library. At this point, we confess
our obtuseness, since for the life of us we can't imagine any legitimate use to be made of such productions of the fraud. Anyhow,
the Grand Lodge is the custodian of the esoterics of the respective
Jurisdictions, and certainly has the undeniable right to say who
shall have it. Personally, we have never understood how even a
Grand Lodge could find it consistent to commi~ such work to writing in any form. Anyhow, we outlaw it and at present are not annoyed thereby.

There was not much of outside interest in the Grand Master's
address. Brother Chase (Rhode Island) offered some interesting
observations on the question of " ciphers," or Rituals, as they are
styled in most Empire Grand Jurisdictions. He communicated with
every Jurisdiction in the United States on the matter, and was able
to assure the Rhode Island Brethren that "ciphers were . permitted
in only one New England Jurisdiction ; while New York, New Jersey,
Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware, Virginia, West Virginia and
Tennessee, and 24 other United States Grand Lodges, prohibited
their use, and the remaining 15 permitted them." He expressed h imself in favor of indefinitely postponing the matter, believing that
Rhode Island could get on without the use of s uch books. The precise grounds on which opposition to the use of the "printed words"
in a more or less veiled form is raised, do not appear, as a rule,
when this matter is ventilated in various Grand Lodges. Occasionally, one finds that the existence of such a work is violative of the
obligation, which would seem to be the strongest ground, if such
were really the case; but the writer believes it would not be difficult
to prove that the obligation is not broken. The other ground sometimes presented is the danger of the book falling into profane hands,
but this idea is an exaggerated one. At any rate, in Western Australia, as in the other Australian States, it has not been fo und, up
to the present, that whatever the disadvantages may be, they have
outweighed the advantages. The Rituals are published under the
sanction of Grand Lodge, and the most scrupulous care is exercised
in order to preserve the esoteric character of the work.

CO-ORDINATE BODIES
There is no doubt but that the attraction offered by most coordinate bodies has a greater drawing power for the average Mason
than "the work" of the Blue Lodge. This, we believe, is due in a
large measure to the variety offered and the absence of continual
repetition. Even the adoption of Regulations fixing a limit between

16

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

HEPORT ON COHHESPONDENCE

the time petitioner receives his Third Degree and when he can
apply to one of the co-ordinate bodies does not appear to increase
attendance at or interest in the Blue Lodge. Perhaps in some measure this is due to the fact that after a petitioner is raised no further
attention is paid to him. If he desires to secure "further Light" he
must find it in a library or in some other organizati<?n having membership in the Masonic Fraternity as a prerequisite.
While the Blue Lodge, as a matter of fact, properly contains
all that there is in Masonry, it perhaps plays the same part to the
present Masonic set-up as the elementary public school plays in the
entire Educational System. The co-ordinate bodies may be likened
to the Junior Colleges or Universities without detriment to the elementary branch itself.

District of Columbia (1930):
(Grand Master): The fact remains, however, that in any organization composed of Masons, no matter by what name it is known
and rega.rdless of its affiliation or non-affiliation with any national
organization or federation, every Brother is responsible solely to his
Lodge and his Grand Lodge in matters of discipline, since Grand
Lodges recognize no other jurisdiction over a Master Mason. This
fact should be borne in mind by every organization predicating its
eligibility, to membership on m.embershig in a Blue Lodge, because
no Masonic offense can be dealt with save through the Lodge of
which the offending Brother is a member.

Arizona (1931):
(Grand Master): I believe that one of our present weaknesses
is the tendency on the part of our members to become affiliated with
entirely too many organizations, clubs and activities, thereby diverting their attention from the legitimate work of the Blue Lodge to
other channels. I fear that divided duty and responsibilities which
would inevitably attach to dual membership, would be just another
step in the wrong direction.
. Canada (1929):
(Chairman Corr~sponden,ce Committee): Americans have a genius
for organization. It has been said that whenever three or more of
them meet, they organize, elect a chairman, adopt by-laws and assess
dues. As a people we indulge in a peculiar passion for joining. American men also seem to possess another outstanding idiosyncrasy.
At one time or another each of us passes through a silly season, the
duration of which is controlled by the shape of the individual head.
Some men never recover from it, while others emerge in time and
are restored to normalcy. It is during this silly season that we develop a fondness for horseplay. We follow the rule of the "monkey
see, monkey do" and become imbued with the idea that the submission of our persons to slap-stick indignities so inflicted as to tickle
the risibilities of beholding multitudes, will promote . our standing
·as good fellows and thus contribute to a blissful success in life. Many
·men, eminent even in Masonry, have at one time or another found a .
drooling delight in subjecting themselves to the manhandling of
horseplay organizations, and subsequently in perpetrating hilarious
outrages upon their less informed Brethren. There is scarcely a male
intellect, no matter how brilliant or how stygian, that escapes either
a temporary or a prolonged attack of this mysterious malady.

CORRESPONDENCE REPORTS
·. It is but natural that the compilers of Correspondence Reports
believe that greater use could be made of their efforts. Whether this
will ever be done is problematical. The cost of supplying these reports to the entire membership would, of course, be, prohibitive.
One of the Jurisdictions makes it a practice to furnish the same
to their members at a small cost, and the experiment, so we are told,
has proven worth while.
Something out of the ordinary in connection with these reports
occurred in the Grand Lodge of Maryland. When the report was
submitted the Grand Lodge took exception to certain . of the opinions or criticisms contained therein and ordered them eliminated
before the same was printed in the Proceedings. This is the first
time we have heard of such action. Of course it is impossible to
tell what was expunged, but in view of the fact that comments,
criticism or opinions of the Chairman of a Committee are well known
to be those only of the individual and not of the Grand Lodge,
the establishment of a censorship or any kind, assuming that it is
based on nothing more than a difference of opinion, seems to us

Florida (1931):

Iowa (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Its report (on Foreign
Correspondence) is to give the Mason of one locality and one state
accurate information as to the achievements and accomplishments of
Masonry in other states and localities, and to show him what the
Masonic institution stands for in the world at large. * * * In spite
of a firm and solemn resolution never to deviate from the ancient
landmarks or suffer them to be infringed, we find that Masonry has
taken many and varied forms of activity in different states and jurisdictions, and that the Masonry of no two of these is exactly alike.
* * * It is the duty of the fraternal correspondent to try to picture
to his Brethren by means of extract, quotation and comment, not
only what is said and done by the leaders of the Order, but also the
mighty movements that are being carried on by the harmonious
workings of the Masonic masses, guided and inspired by th:i.t splendid
leadership. (Musings of a Fraternal Correspondent. Page 13, etc.)

South Carolina (1929):
(Chairman Correspondence Con~mittee): T he work of the Reviewer
is not au easy task. He soon discovers that he has two classes of
readers. One class is made up of ·his fellow correspondents whose
experienced insight into things Masonic is such as to demand of him
fine discrimination, keen analysis, and piquant discussion. The other
class consists of the rank and file of his own jurisdiction who are
looking to him to furnish such information as will tend toward an
intelligent comprehension of contemporaneous Masonic history, and ·
without which they have no other source of supply. He may try
to satisfy either or both of these classes. If he is ambitious to win
for himself a place of distinction at the round table he may spend his
time breaking lances with the Knights of the Goose Quill in an endless tournament. If he desires to serve his constituency according to
its need he will endeavor to give an intelligent statement of the facts,
events and departures to be found in the current history of the Masonic world. If he is unusuaJly gifted he may strike a happy balance
and please both classes. If he is not so gifted he will find himself
among those who are "damned if you do and damned if you don't."

DUES
Present conditions have brought very forcibly home to some
of the Jurisdictions that Masonry is too cheap. In the final analysis,
Masonry is a luxury and those availing themselves of the privilege
should · be prepared to pay for it. Small fees and dues not only
handicap the constituent Lodges, but likewise cause deficits in the
activities of the Grand Lodge.
One Jurisdiction has required constituent Lodges to set up a
budget and advance their dues to take care of the expenditures.
The initiation fee to be carried in a reserve fund and not used for
maintenance. Paraphrasing the general idea that there should be
"less government in business and more business in goveri)ment,"
there should be more business methods and safeguards in Masonry,
particularly in the financial department.

British Columbia (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committl'e): They have a custom in
Florida of making honorary members (or emeritus members, as they
call them) of Brethren who have attained the age of sixty years, and
this irrespective of a Brother's financial position. In some Lodges
the Grand Master found men worth anywhere from $100,000 to $1,000,000 on the "emeritus" list, for no other reason than that they
were sixty years of age. How advantageous this is to the Lodge
is evidenced by the Grand Master's statement that in some of the
Lodges from 15 to 25% of the membership was on the free list, while
in one Lodge one-third of the members were paying no dues.
Maine (1931):
{Grana SecrelMJ•): I wish to say a word in defense of the Secretaries of our Maine Lodges in regard to the charge so often made
here and in other Grand Jurisdictions, that Secretaries are very
largely, or entirely responsible for suspensions for non-payment of
dues. I honestly believe "the charge wrong and unjust. I sent a
questionnaire to every Secretary asking how many of the suspended
Brothers lived out of town, and how many within easy personal contact. All except nine Secretaries reported and the replies showed
that over 78% of those suspended lived out of town or out of the
state, and that 96% of them had been given one or more mail notices
of amount due before action was taken by the Lodge. The Secretaries of Maine are not responsible for suspension losses.

Masonry must run its organization along business lines and as

the Lodge may remit dues and this takes care of those Brethren
whom misfortune has overtaken.
To show that the step above taken by the adoption of these resolutions was well taken it may be noted that over three hundred delinquents were suspended.
Altogether the operation of these laws is very satisfactory-the
Lodges now getting the dues in their several treasudes instead of
having the debits as an ornament on their books.

Tennessee (1931):
(Grand Master): Many of our Lodges are attempting to carry on
their work without sufficient dues to meet their needs; in some instances, just enough to pay their per capita tax. In such cases I have
urged an increase, sufficient to meet the demand incident to the success of a ·well-ordered Lodge. In many cases I could trace the inactivity of a Lodge to its lack of funds, due to the ridiculously small
amount of dues charged. In my opinion, this is extremely harmful.
In other cases, well defined programs are carried out, ~uc to the
fact that adequate dues are charged.
I have tried to convey the idea that there was much more to
Masonry than the mere conferring of degrees, and that especially .in
our rural communities, our Lodges should be made the community
center. To do this they should be made attractive and inviting, and
the Lodge should also have sufficient funds to relieve distress, have
social functions, and accomplish deeds of kindness, To be leaders in
their community should be the desire of every Lodge wherever situated.
Let's raise our dues, not to the point that it will be a burden, but
in order that we might get the best out of our efforts, and by this
means, contribute not only to the relief but to the pleasure of those
with whom we come in contact.

EDUCATION-MASONIC
Up to the present time efforts along Masonic educational lines
have produced varying results. In some Jurisdictions it has been a
failure· and has developed the fact that Masons do not generally
want Education of any kind thrust upon them. We believe that the
proper time to educate . Masons is during the period between the
conferring of the first and the third degree.
· This, we believe, is best exemplified in the Jurisdictions that
present to the Candidate some recognized work on Masonry. Curiosity, in a large measure, will at least cause the petitioner to make
himself familiar with all or part of its contents.
Alberta (1930):
(Grand .Master): A speaker who will explain to a district meeting why we address the Great Architect of the Universe in the first
degree, the Grand Geometrician in the .second and the Most High
in the third; and extend his remarks by telling why the heel is slipshod, why the Lodges have a Druidistic flavor; why the Ritual
savors more of the poetry of Milton and Chaucer than the Proverbs
of Solomon, and why the secrets were lost; for he will never fail to
grip and hold his audience. These things are what the Brethren need
at the district meetings, more than listening to the parrot-like rendition of the accustomed degree.

intelligent Masons is a serious and important duty.
I, therefore, recommend that this body make ptovision in its
budget for the presentation to every candidate receiving the degrees
of Freemasonry a copy of Street's Symbolism of the First Degree

Minnesota (1930):
(Grand Master): We are taught that Masonry is a progres.sive
science, but after initiation, our newly admitted Brothers are given
little, if any, assistance in the study of this great work. Our .Brethren
agree that our ritualistic work is beautiful but that it contains much
to be explained and studied. To whom shall they turn for assistance.?
"To the officers and members of their Lodge," you may say. But
consider carefully before you make such answer. How many of us
here today could undertake such a work without rece.iving s?me
authentic 1 reliable information to form a basis for such instruction?
I firmly believe that it is not only a duty, but a privilege for this
Grand Lodge to supervise this work, that our young men may know
what Masonry is, what it means, and what to do with it.
If we delay longer, the results are obvious. We shall continue to
lose many fine young men who would otherwise remain in our ranks
and grow in Masonry and in usefulness to their fellow man, community and state.
Montana (1931):
(Grand Master): At different times I have heard speakers lecture on the history of ancient Masonry. On one occasion I listened
to a Brother who traced the origin of Freemasonry back to the Garden of Eden, and he told us that one of the ashlars symbolized in the
degrees was the stone on which Jacob slept in the wilderness. He
wandered so far into antiquity and theorized on such unsound
depths, and played with the names of the patriarchs, that the attention of the Brethren became listless and some were on the verge
of boredom.
I am not interested in knowing whether Jacob, Solomon, or any
of the ancient patriarchs were Freemasons, but I am vitally interested
in knowing whether the modern patriarchs of Masonry are measuring up to the demands of today. Modern Masonry demands modern
methods of application and the world at large is waiting for us to
adjust our Masonry to the changing conditions of a modern and
complex civilization.
Nebraska (1931):
(Grand Master): During recent years many of our Lodges have
to a great extent become degree mills only. Our candidates receive

the "work" and lectures, and if we have in ~ur ceremonies inspired
them with higher ideals and loftier purposes, we are fortunate if they
do not soon lose interest, since our officers and Brethren frequently
pay little or no attention to them and they are given nothing to do
along the line of further Masonic interpretation. In my opinion a
plan should be adopted that will first interest our officers of the
Lodge, then the newly made Brethren.
Utah (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): We were very much interested in the Address of Welcome to the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma. We imagined that the speaker took out his watch and laid
it on the table when he promised the Brethren that he would undertake to boil down to the minimum what he had to say. We do not
want even to appear to be hypercritical but there are certain of the
speaker's statements to which, speaking for ourself alone, we cannot
subscribe, Of course, this Brother spoke for the Masons of Oklahoma-we do not overlook that fact. Personally, we do not admit
to being a follower "of the Great and Wise King Solomon," or of
the "Widow's Son," or of "Hiram of Tyre." We more than question
if "the Bible is Masonry," and we cannot admit that our Fraternity
is a "Christian organization." Whatever we may think, in moments
of patriotic fervor, we should hesitate long before putting into type
the statement that the Government of the United States is "the greatest Government that was ever organized or existed in the hisfory
of the world." That statement will be read by our Brothers to the
north of us, by those in Australasia and elsewhere, and will help to
confirm them in the belief that we are a Nation of braggarts.
Passing over the picture suggested by the hyperbole of Washington coming into the Constitutional Convention with the snow of
Valley Forge yet on his trousers, we cannot accept the statement
that the Constitution of the United States is "just like it was written," aside from the ten Amendments to which the speaker referred.
Our impression is that other amendments have been added, some
of which would certainly cause the Fathers of that Document to sit
up and rub their eyes!

Hoping to be able to work out a plan of self-education, my first

and Ed~cation, a loyal, devoted and painstaking committee. A plan
was formulated and twelve months of delightful labor has been performed. The Worshipful Master of each constituent Lodge was asked

of one of the Masonic book publishing concerns told me that his company was getting more orders for books from the jurisdiction of
Washington than from any other jurisdiction in the United States.
This, of course, because of our educational program.

EDUCATION-PUBLIC
While there has been some criticism of the "Public School Observance Week" in this Jurisdiction, it has generally received approval. There is no doubt that the average Mason, the same as the
Member of 'any other organization, likes to point with pride to
some movement or work with which he is connected that has for its
object the betterment of his fellowman or his community. Interest
in the public schools we believe furnishes this, because it is a .broad
field. in which there is an opportunity for constructive work and
one that is generally free from highly controversial subjects.

Connecticut ( 1931) :

D istrict of Columbia ( 1930):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): One Grand Lodge has foi:
years celebrated a Public Schools Observance Week, annually. The
report of their Committee on the same notes the ever-increasing
interest on the part of the Lodges and stresses the zealous cooperation of a large number of non-secret societies. But the whole report
simmers down to a "pat yourself on the back." Only one item seems

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : The National League of
Masonic Clubs, with which 22 clubs in the District of Columbia are
affiliated, is carrying on a wonderfully patriotic work in the George
Washington University of this city, by supporting two chairs in the
Foreign Service Department of the School of Government recently
endowed with $1,000,000 by the Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish
Rite of Freemasonry, and for this purpose is raising an endowment
fund of $250,000, and is at present paying to George Washington
University $7,000 annually.

We question if this, like the endorsement of political measures
by one Grand Lodge some years ago, is not a radical departure from
Masonic fundamentals. We are early taught that the main object of
Masonry is "to make men wiser and better, and consequently happier." Grand Lodge endorsement is much like proceedings in a
political caucus. Whatever action is taken, it does not change the
opinion of the minority by an iota. Hence it is purely academic and
of no practical effect except at times to make us appear ridiculous.
However worthy the object, we had better leave activity in its behalf
to individual Masons. The question also arises if the organized
activity in behalf of the schools could not have been safely and more
effectively left to the largely outnumbering other societies whose
cooperation was acknowledged as above.
Brethren, let us not allow our zeal, even in a good cause, to
outrun our discretion.
Connecticut (1931):
(Grand Master) : It has come to the attention of your Grand
Master that several Lodges in this State have recently passe·d resolutions either fo favor of or against measures now pending before the
Congress of the United States, and forwarded copies of such resolutions to Senators and Members of Congress. Also your Grand Master
has been invited to attend or appoint committees to attend conferences
to promote legislation to be introduced in the General Assembly of
Connecticut in 1931, all of which invitations have been declined.
Masons should ever remember that the Masonic Fraternity is
not a political organization and as such should never interfere in
either religious, political, or legislative controversies. The foundation
on which our Order is built is freedom of thought, speech and action
in such matters, and each individual Mason in acting on such matters
should apply the principles taught him in his Lodge, but should exercise his judgment in such matters according to his own conscience,
and any action taken by a Lodge as such, in controversial matters 0f
this nature, whether by resolution or otherwise, is an unmasonic act
and, as such, subject to Masonic discipline.

Maine (1930):

(Grand Master): There seems to be a general desire among our
Lodges to increase interest among our membership. This is a very
laudable effort and when confined within proper limits and carried
out with discretion is a most excellent idea. Care should be taken,
however, that there should be no discussion of any subjects which
might give rise to "angry discussion arising which will impair the
harmony of the meetings." There can be no danger of this when
subjects discussed are those which are strictly Masonic. If, however,
avowed political candidates for office give addresses in tiled Masonic
Lodges and those addresses are wholly upon the management and
operation of the offices to which they aspire, it not only is an exhibition of execrable taste, but comes near the line of unmasonic conduct.
It is not likely that all of the members of any one Lodge would agree
with the speaker, and it· is quite likely that things would be said
which would arouse contention, and the Masonic Lodge is no place
for contention on any political or religious subject.

FUNERALS
Eliminating the harrowing and gruesome parts of the funeral
service has been done in a number of Jurisdictions. Lack of attendance at this ·s ervice, of course, occasions comment. This applies more
particularly to larger centers of population. We believe that the
Masonic Funeral is gradually becoming more of a private affair rather
than a public function.
The Funeral Service is one of the · few opportunities where the
general public have an opportunity to see a Lodge in action, and
too often an unfavorable impression is created by the manner in
which the same is handled or the reading of the ceremony, rather
than on account of the lack of attendance.
British Columbia (1930):
(Chairman Correspondmce Committee)~ As in some .other jurisdictions, the Grand Master (North Carolina), found reason to complain of the attendance-or lack of it-at Masonic funerals. He instanced a case in one city of the state where three Lodges are
located with a combined membership of about one thousand, where
the funeral of .a Past Master ·was attended by fewer than 30 members of the Craft. This state of things is found elsewhere than in
North Carolina, probably due in part to the fact that in the larger
cities funerals occur so frequently that attendance on them becomes·
a burden, and partly to the high pressure at which we live. We are
.. all . deeply immersed in business which deman_ds such unceasing
attention that we cannot afford .the time to attend funerals . Anyway, whatever the cause, the condition is there, and the suggestion
had been made that the so-called Masonic funerals should be abolished. When one sees the sorry attendance at some of these ceremonies one feels that the suggestion is worth considering.

undertakers does not allow the Brethren to cast the spade full of
dirt on the casket, etc. I recommend that the Grand Lodge specifically authorize, as it does less specifically, the use of ordinary common sense in the carrying out of the Burial Service, conforming as
nearly as possible to Ritual.
These funeral directors began, something like a decade or so
ago, to put on so much "dog" that Masonry has to get on the jump
to keep up with them. They changed their names to "Morticians,"
if you please, and built great churches of their own for funerals ;
they invented these machines which let the remains down into the
graves; they introduced end-door copper "vaults"; they developed
artificial grass to cover the red earth which comes from all open
graves in these parts; they got up tents and so forth for the bereaved; they cut out " hearses" and introduced "funeral cars" looking like end-door sedans; and last, but not least, they put in some
flower petals instead of earth for the committal, and hired colored
laborers to do the filling. As a result, one never knows what to
expect at a funeral these days; it may be a typical country funeral
of the last century in the city, where you use the spades yourself,
or it may be one of the most modern, out in the open spaces of that
area which God blessed under the name "in the country." Andworst of all, when Masons got the habit of dying while traveling in
foreign lands, they had to have the remains cremated and then came
the problem so feelingly referred to by the Texas Grand Master
(q v.), of how to give the ashes a Masonic funeral. The Tennessee
Grand Master has hit the nail on the head: "that the Grand Lodge
authorize specifically the use of ordinary common sense in carrying
out the Burial Service." Not three hours ago we were in the act of
conducting just such a service and are prepared to testify that this
is a sound recommendation.

other .Brethren who for many years have been attending Grand Lodge

the frequent temptation to stifle that inner voice. But the Lodge
representatives, who vastly outnumber the has-beens, are morally
responsible, primarily to their Lodges and equally to the Craft in
general, to enact wise and beneficient legislation. Hence, they should
always remember that they are really the Grand Lodge.
As to advice from Past Grands, we would slightly paraphrase
the wise words of Bacon: "Read (hear) not to confute, nor yet to
take for granted, but to weigh and consider."

GRAND LODGE
A Grand Lodge is composed of constituent Lodges and not
subordinate Lodges. By reason of the fact that the governing power
owes its origin directly to the Lodges that compose it, any criticism
or objection to the action of a Grand Lodge must necessarily fall,
not upon the Officers of the Grand Lodge, but the Lodges themselves.
Unfortunately in some Jurisdictions the general membership
believe that they are subordinate rather than constituent parts.
In those Jurisdicti~ns where the business is conducted through
a Board of General Purposes, as in England, or handle the business
at quarterly communications, as in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and
other Masonic Jurisdictions there is more opportunity for fellowship
and social activities.
In a large number of cases the Proceedings of a Grand Lodge
read like the minutes of a meeting of the Board of Directors of a
business corporation.

Oregon (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): I want to again call your
attention to the careless way in which Investigating Committees
work. This is the most important Committee the Master appoints,
and upon their reports depends largely the bringing in the right kind
of material and the excluding of those not worthy. The most flagrant
case brought to my notice was from a report of Brother W. F. Kress,
Secretary of the Masonic Board of Relief of Pasadena, wherein he
stated, "I know of a Lodge which initiated a man who with five
children, was receiving aid from the county charities at the same time
he was taking the degrees, and .within a year, the Lodge was called
upon to care for his family."
No man honors our Fraternity by petitioning to become a member, but we confer certain honors upon him by receiving him into our
organiz~~ion. So why should we not make a careful investigation of
the petitioner. Some of our Lodges, in order to protect themselves
from being imposed on, have a special committee before whom the
applicant is required to appear. In my opinion our present form of
petitio~ s?ould be c?anged and also the method of appointing the
Investigatmg Committee.

South Dakota (1929):
(Grand Master): Because appreciate that this message is addressed to those whose understanding and estimate of the worth of
Freemasonry equals that of my own, I propose to waste no part of
our valuable time in extolling its virtues anew, or in dealing with its
glorious history. Neither do I propose to use space in lengthy report
of my formal official acts. This great responsi~ility has given birth
to a solemn conviction that we, as the present leaders of Freemasonry
in this Grand Jurisdiction, can fashion a future far surpassing the past
in effective and practical service if we will cease to blindly follow
custom and organize ourselves under an aggressive program of doing.
Texas (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Grand Master Biggers
(Missouri) reports having adopted something of a unique policy which
he presents under the heading "Business in Masonry." In short, this
policy consists of his having called into council the other three principle Grand Officers and having had their approval <ind acceptance
of the duties and responsibilities proposed, Grand Master, with these
councillors, proceeded to lay out a progressive program covering a
period of four years, thus establishing "a successive policy, and effecting a permanency and continuity of effort." To the end that efficient
and capable chairmen and committeemen might be secured, each of
these officers, the D. G. Master and Se.nior and Junior Grand Wardens
were given the privilege of naming a member of each of the committees. In addition, each of these Grand Officers were assigned to
certain official duties, such as the visiting of district meetings, etc.,
and often called into council with Grand Master. Out of this policy,
practiced throughout the year, Grand Master finds and reports results
satisfactory in the highest degree.

(Chairma11 Correspondence Committee): Grand Master Reid

INVESTIGATION
We believe that the lack of attendance, suspensions, dimits and
expulsions can in a large measure be traced to laxity on the part
of· the Investigating Committee. Too often this is only a perfunctory matter. As stated in some of our previous reports we
believe that this could largely be overcome by having an Advisory
Committee, composed of Officers and Past Masters of the Lodge,
examine the petitioner and the members of the Lodge who recommend him, before the petition itself is present~ to the Lodge.
This would mean that the investigation would be handled by
"experts."
One Jurisdiction solved the problem by making the Investigating Committee one of the standing committees of the Lodge,
which also possesses a great deal of merit. It would of course
depend as to results on the character and ability of the Committee.

duties, the failure of the Master and other officers to impress upon
him the importance of his mission, is downright laziness, and to say
the least, inexcusable. The code advisedly employs the word "diligently" to emphasize the importance of the duty of the Investigating
Committee. If it were necessary to define the intent of that word in
our code, one need only to take the dictionary's definition of " diligent."
Let me quote that definition: "Diligent-constant in study or effort
to accomplish what is undertaken; attentive and persistent in doing
anything prosecuted with care and constant effort; careful, painstaking."
An examination into the r oot of some of the infractions brought
to my attention indicate to me that if a "diligent iniquiry" had been
made into the qualifications of the petitioners whose subsequent acts
as members of the Fraternity have given rise to the necessity for
trial and discipline, those petitioners would have been kept far from
our Ancient Fraternity and the necessity of trial or discipline, with
the attendant unpleasantness, would have been avoided. It would be
far more honorable for a Mason who is placed on an Investigating
Committee to ask to be excused from duty on that Committee than to
make an "investigation" which is indifferent, careless, and inadequate
and therefore useless, if not dangerous, to the Fraternity. T he members of the Lodge and the Fraternity generally are entitled to and
expect the protective concern and the fidelity to duty of the members
of the Investigating Committee.
So-called "good fellowship" which encourages a member of an
Investigating Committee to favorably recommend an unworthy. petitioner or make report without diligent inquiry into, or actual knowledge of, the quality of the petitioner, not only fails to manifest
Masonic good fellowship, but is directly violating a definitely prescribed Masonic duty and may subject the Brethren of his Lodge and
the Fraternity at large. to the association of one unfit for the Masonic;
Fraternity and who may in time injure the good name of Masonry.
I urge upon the officers of Lodges a careful consideration of this
subject and a constant vigilance against all laxness in investigating
and ascertaining the qualifications of all petitioners to our Fraternity.

Illinois (1930):
(G1·and Master): The violations of Masonic propriety which have
been brought to my attention have impelled me to study the sources
from which they arise and ho~ best to prevent their recurrence. That
study has satisfied me that many of the causes for trial and discipline
can be traced to the indifference or carelessness of the committees
appointed to investigate the original petition for degrees or membership. It has been said-often and correctly-that Masonry is a progressive moral science. The successful practice of that science can be
accomplished only by men possessing integrity of character and purpose. It is intended that the portals of Masonry shall be opened only
to men of good character and intentions.
It was never Masonry's purpose to admit to its fraternity unwholesome or weak characters in the hope that they might be
reformed into good Masons. The offenses requiring discipline are
in many cases caused by those whose minds were never prepared
to be admitted to Masonry, and a careful investigation of their petitions for admission would have shown that they were not of good
report.
Our code provides that every petitioner for degrees shall be
recommended by ·three members of the Lodge, each of whom has a
personal aciquaintance with the petitioner. The inescapable ·burden is
upon the recommending Brethren to know that the petitioner possesses qualifications of character and is in other respects fitted to
receive the degrees. No Mason should recommend a petitioner unless
he knows or learns by careful investigation that the applicant pos~
sesses the necessary moral, physical and mental qualifications. When
a Mason recommends a petitioner for the privileges of Masonry, he
does so on his honor as a Mason. As a further safeguard against
improper persons joining our ranks, our code provides that an Investigating Committee of three members of the Lodge must be appointed
who "shall see the applicant personally and diligently inquire intQ
his moral, mental and physical qualifications, etc.,'' and make report
to the Master. It has come to my attention that at times some
members of .Investigating Committees fail to "diligently" inquire
into the qualifications of the applicant and some do not even see the .
applicant personally. Such conduct by a member of an Investigating
Committee, whether due to indifference, lack of understanding of his

Nevada (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The lodges of Netherlands do not put candidates through the degrees in the "degree-mill"
style so prevalent in many American jurisdictions. If a petitioner
succeeds in being elected by the Lodge to which he applies, his petition is then placed before the Grand Orient, which has a committee
of eleven men to pas.s upon petitions. If these ele'(en men are not

50

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

satisfied there is no recourse; but, if they are, then the petitioner will
receive his degrees. The Lodges meet for degree work but three
times in each year, and the candidate has to await a period of one
year between each degree. Should he desire to take the so-called
"higher degrees" after taking his Master Mason degree, he must
await three years before petitioning to become an eighteenth degree
Scottish Rite Mason. One year each must elapse before taking the
22nd, 26th, 28th, 29th and 32nd degrees. It thus takes eight years for
an .Entered Apprentice to become a thirty-second degree Scottish
Rite Mason.

LEGISLATION
The general idea "there ought to be a law" still finds favor
and is lived up to in some Jurisdictions. The late Vice-President
Marshall perhaps advanced too radical a theory when he stated that
"All the existing laws should be repealed and the Declaration of
Independence and the Ten Commandments substituted." There is
no doubt but what the excessive legislation has
tendency to bring
an O•rganization to the level of mediocrity. Again, no sooner is a
law passed than some one finds a way to avo.id it, which calls for
another law or another decision, which calls for more legislation or
decisions.
