Western Australia (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In reviewing the Proceedings of American Grand Lodges, it is impossible to avoid a
feeling of amazement at the prodigious amount of legislation continually taking place. With a few exceptions, all the Grand Lodges
share this predilection. Some Constitutional section seems to outlive
its usefulness not long after it is ushered into the Constitution, and
the need for further legislation suggests itself to the authorities. Also,
new quesions arise, and the seeming inelasticity of existing law impels
the authorities in the direction of a new one to meet new circumstances. In either of these cases the matter _usually runs the gauntlet
of a Grand Master's recommendation, the proposal of an amendment,
its reference to the Jurisprudence Committee, that body's report to
Grand Lodge, the latter's adoption of the report, 'and then, the infant
is either ready to crow at once, ·or it is laid over for a year till it is
strong enough to crow constitutionally. In a year or so, it is found
that the youngster has not developed the desired number of teeth,
and it goes back to Doctor Grand Lodge for further treatment. One
sometim·es wonders where this legislative urge will end-whether the
time is not approaching when American Masonic law will meet the
cynical gibe an American Senator uttered to me concerning the public
legislation of the United States. Said he: "Uncle Sam has millions
of statutes, thousands who know of them, hundreds who understand
them, and units who obey them."

Illinois (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): One Grand Master came
out boldly this year an.d said that in his opinion many of the L_o dges
in his jurisdiction were too large. In trying to find out why Masonry
was not making the progress he thought it should, he had come to
the conclusion that it was because many of the Lodges were so big in
numbers that they afforded the individual member very little opportunity for Masonic practice, and there is a good deal of truth in this.
It is believed that genuine Masonry receives better practice in the
small Lodge of two or three hundred rather than in the big Lodge of
two thousand. While the small LodgR may have its financial problems yet there is afforded an opportunity for better acquaintanceship,
and those who want to work in the Ritual and other departments of
Lodge affairs are given more chance to do so. The larger Lodge has
a greater opportunity for Masonic exploitation than the small Lodge.
It has a larger financial income; it probably has. more men of executive force to draw from in the selection of those who are to govern
its enterprises. The theory is correct, but it does not work out in
· practice. In nearly every large Lodge it will be found that just a

chance to reach the individual member. A Master can keep track of

perhaps the small groups have a better opportunity to attain this state

During the Revolution one of the patriots made the statement:
" These are times that try men's souls." The same might .also be
said as to the membership of the Masonic Fraternity at the present
time. It may resolve itself into the "survival of the fittest," which
will require leadership with perhaps a r adical change as to general
policy, and the adoption of new ideas.
We speak with .pride of the antiquity of Masonry. It is a golden
cord that connects us with the remote past. Abetting nothing of
respect for our Ancient Craft, we are conscious that we cannot fix
our eyes on the past without walking backward into the future. If

British Columbia (1930):
(Chairman Correspotidrnce Committee): In a general way it may
be said that Brother Darrah (Illinois) takes the stand that times have
changed and Masonry should change with them. For instance, there
is probably no point in Masonry w hich has been more strongly
stressed and we believe more generally observed, than that solicitation of candidates is absolutely barred, they must come of their own
volition. Brother Darrah, however, thinks that in selected cases
solicitation is quite proper, and goes so far as to say that he believes
that four-fifths of our candidates are solicited anyway. . He plainly
says that he "does not believe in revival meetings, he does not believe
in membership drives; he does not believe in going up and down the
street proclaiming the virtue of Freemasonry and inviting everybody
to come · in" but as we have said, he is in favor of solicitation in
selected cases, because: "At the present time Freeinasonry has much
to contend with. The competition which is all about it is strenuous.
Men are no longer flocking to the doors begging to be admitted. If
the Society is to go on and prosper it will have to depart from some
of its ·old methods and adjust itself to the new conditions of this
ever changing world." In respect to which, in the language of the
profane, our learned Brother is all wet.
Illinois (1930):
(Chairman. Carrespo11dence Committee): One of the predominant
-questions that has been suggested during the past year is this: Are
Fraternal Organizations on the Wane? After making a very careful
survey of the situation the writer is frank enough to say that they are.
Within the last few years many diversions have come into our lives
to take the place of things that predominated in the old order of
life; to say nothing of the pee wee golf courses. There was a time
when Freemasonry was looked upon ~s an organization of great
antiquity and peculiar charm. Membership in the Society of Free
and Accepted Masons carried with it a considerable amount of prestige in every commun.ity. There was a time when the fraternal
organization had an important place in our busy lives. It afforded an
opportunity for social recreation as well as building up a community
of interests. That was· when we had no movie theaters, no hard roads,
no automobiles, no radios, no flying machines, no golf courses and

60

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

very few country clubs. Men joined the Masonic Fraternity because
they wanted the companionship of their fellows and because the
Lodge meeting offered an opportunity for social recreation. But all
this has been changed. A man no longer joins the Masonic Fraternity
for the prestige which this great Fraternity offers. There was a time
when curiosity was the impelling instinct which prompted men to get
into Freemasonry. The unthinking world has always believed that
Freemasonry was in possession of some great secret which old King
Solomon had whispered to some of his followers, and which had been
carefully preserved and carried down through the ages by the Freemasons. Every man who went into the Fraternity with this thought
in mind was soon disillusioned. When ·Masonry was a small organization, when it did no soliciting and selected its recruits with the
utmost care, it gave high prestige to its members. Then when it tried
to popularize itself, when its idea of prosperity became the multiplication of Lodges and the doubling of membership, just that moment it
became commonplace; and as the multitude entered at one door,
prestige went out at the other. Freemasonry has learned its lesson.
Already signs indicate that there is an awakening to the fact that
Freemasonry was never intended for the many, and that its appeal.
is only to those individuals who are seeking in life the moral and
ethical.

Mississippi (1931):
(Masonic Service Committee ) : Hard times are crucibles through
which character passes and from which it emerges, dross-or pure
gold. These are challenging times, and Freemasonry must meet the
challenge as a reputed character builder. In these days of closed
banks and "frozen deposits" the real Freemason nurses closer to his
heart than 'ever, a banking institution whose every depositor is a
stockholder; whose stock never drops to par; whose time deposits
bear interest through Eternity, and whose strength is but increased
by a "run"-the Bank of Brotherhood! False values may at times be
placed on its · stock. During the feverish excitement of a World's
War, thousands may purchase its shares with a misconception, or no
conception at all, of their true value; on the same basis others purchase it for the sake of expediency. .From such speculation comes an
inevitable "crash in the stock market"-which shakes the entire structure. In my humble opinion, Freemasonry's problem is not one of
surviving financial depressions, but rather one of proving its right to
continued existence by imbedding in the hearts and lives of its votaries, her principles and ideals which have stood the test of blood and
fire and time in their unbroken march down through the ages.

This opens up a question concerning one of our ancient customs
upon which very little is to be found, but concerning which nearly

REPORT ON CORREGPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

· all Masonic teaching and traditions are agreed, that is, that one who
comes into our Fraternity must come of his own free will and accord
and not as the result of solicitation. Mackey does not mention this
in his collection of landmarks, and yet it comes as near being a landmark as most any one of our ancient usages that could be suggested.
The. rule forbidding it is not mentioned . iri Simons or in Mackey's
Masonic Juris prudence, nor can any mention of it be found in
Mackey's Encyclopedia of Freemasonry. In Anderson's Constitutions
of 1723, under the head of " Behavior in Presence of Strangers not
Masons" it is said:
"You shall be cautious in your Words and Carriage, that the
most penetrating Stranger shall not be able to discover or find out
what is not proper to be intimated; and sometimes you shall divert
a discourse, and manage it prudently for the Honour of the WORSHIPFUL FRATERNITY."
Just how far one might go without violating the rule against
soliciting membership is difficult to determine. The term "solicit" in
itself implies something more than a inere suggestion and usually
means some sort of earnest request or importunity. ·Mild as was the
Grand Master's suggestion it was disapproved of by the Grand Lodge.

role. When you hear a Past Master co~plaining of being slighted
and that his position of being a Past Master is not receiving just
recognition, you may depend upon it that . he is the victim of his
self-conceit, or that "Teckel" has been written after his name. A
Past Master can be a rich blessing to his Lodge or an unmitigated
nuisance. We, Past Masters, must recognize the fact that we have
been honored in an exceptional way by the Lodge; we have had
in an uncertain manner the confidence of the Brethren; we have
been exalted, for which exaltation only loyal service can offer a
suitable appreciation; we ought to be willing to be servants for the
Craft in all things appertaining to the welfare and glory of our
Lodge. Self-interests should be divorced from all our actions. We
have had our day; we have played our part in official position, then
why not let some other · Brother play his part? The Past Masters
of a Lodge should be the reserve, veterans' corps; the Master's counselors, not his dictators. A Past Master should be, by the very
virtue of his title, a better man intellectually and morally. He has
had his school of experience and wide reading that should qualify
him to be a · sage among the Brethren, a teacher among his pupils.
He has had an experience, a course of study, if he has had sufficient
ability, to make him a man of broad mind, altruistic, humble, willing
to assist, to bear burdens and to be a Brother among Brethren.
Official distinction and honors should make a man, more of a man,
not a snob, or a conceited ass, but one to whom service is a
pleasure and duty a reward. It is not necessary for a true Past
Master to air his titles, for he is known by the Brethren, he lives
respected and dies regretted..' "

Just what sort of honorary membership that will be will no

have inuch trouble when anything like this appears necessary. Virginia permits a Lodge to elect an}' Past Master an honorary member, by unanimous ballot of course; but he has all the privileges of

his check back with thanks, and a most. courteous admonition that
the Lodge knew, or thought it did, its full duty respecting his name
on its rolls.
Western Australia (1930):
( Chairman Correspondence Committee): The "Past Master's Degree"-a frequently recurring matter in American Masonry-again
cropped up in .N ebraska. It seems that many of the Lodges are
unable to afford the expense incurred in connection with the ceremony, thereby suffering certain disadvantages in connection with
representation at Grand Lodge Annual Communications. Consequently, the Grand Master expressed himself in favor of making the
degree optional instead of obligatory. "If a Master-elect is not duly
impressed with his duties and responsibilities by the beautiful and
majestic Ritual found 'in our installation service," he said, "the conferring of the Past Master's Degree is time wasted on him." Of
course, a way out of the difficulty should be found in the course
followed in our Empire: With us, the Past Master's Degree has
long fallen into desuetude, and a Past Master is one who has served
his term of office as a Worshipful Master duly installed in the Chair
by the Board of Installed Masters. By virtue of that service, he
becomes a Past Master, and is so recognized. Unfortunately, in the
American branch of the Craft, one not infrequently observes a tendency in the direction of what is fondly believed to be scientific
legalism, but which might be better described as over-regimentation.
Amongst the matters submitted to the Grand Master (Louisiana) was the following, which he answered in the negative: "Has

a Past Master who h:is taken the degree in a Chapter the right to
sit in a Blue Lodge of Past Masters?" This is one of those instances
where American practice is sometimes found differing from the
British. In Empire Blue Lodges an installed Master, having served
the time for which he was elected and installed, becomes thereby a
Past Master. We recognize "the Degree of an Installed Master,"
and have no place for such a "degree" as that of a Past Master.
PROCEEDINGS
Caesar said that all Gaul was divided into three parts, and the
same statement may ·a pply to the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge.
Under "Interesting" we would place the Message of the Grand
Masters, Grand Orattirs' addresses and miscellaneous matters of a
like character. Perhaps we might also add the printed prayers of
the Grand Chaplain, although in cold type these have produced less
effect than the spoken word. Under "Instructive'', we would, of
course, naturally class the Report of the Chairmen on Correspondence. Under "Superfluous" we would include the roster of members and long detailed. reports of Certified Public Accountants.
However, if ·a Grand Lodge believes that these are of value
to their general membership it, like other matters on which there
is a difference of opinion, is their individual affair and one that
should not be criticised.

PUBLICITY
Publicity given to Masonic affairs of all kinds has undoubtedly
detracted from the charm that the Organization at one time held
for the uninformed and has materially weakened its standing. It
has also had a tendency to cause the general public to consider
some of our activities, such as Homes and Benevolence, and Public
Ceremonies, the main objects of the Craft. As Will Rogers has
aptly said: "All he knows is just what he reads in the newspapers,"
and this is perhaps true of a large number of the rest of us.

Michigan (1930):
(Grand Master}: Loyalty to the lodge can never be encouraged
by an appeal to attend a ball game because it is to be known as
"Masonic Day." The inception of the idea itself is one of materialism
-to collect the admission of the Masons who attend in the guise of
supposed loyalty to the Craft.
Entertainment by Lodges of so-called distinguished guests whose
only claim to being distinguished is a vast amount of publicity obtained generally in a way wbich makes no real contribution to the
needs of humanity is to be condemned.
In other words, there is such a thing as "good taste" in Masonry,
that which is apropos. Lodges and their officers should consider this
when they arrange for their publicity and their programs.
The word "publish" clearly means a publication to the profane
through Lodge magazines, newspapers and ot.her printed material not
sent out in the usual course of first class mail.
It is obvious that in the earlier days of Masonry there was no
necessity because the Lodges were small and the petitioners well
known in the community, and, in addition to that fact, the first class
mail service was not what it is today. With the large membership in
many of the Lodges of the · State, where the personal contacts are
not possible between the members and betwe~n the officers and members, a form of notice to them of the petitioner or candidate for the
degree would not be improper if such notices were sent out to the
members under first class mail, postage pre·paid, addressed to the
last known address of the member with a return address to the constituent body on the outside of the envelop:e. The benefits of this
practice to the constituent bodies would clearly outweigh any disadvantages.

British Columbia (1930):
(Chairman Correspondmce Committee): Our Grand Master's Address is noticed at some length, and reference is made to th~ work
of our Board of Benevolence. It is observed that the Board had
disbursed about $9300 in relief "we judge in. assisting Lodges to care
for dependents instead of assuming the entire burden."
Well, that was the idea, but we regret to say that some of our
Lodges seem to have the impression that the Board of Benevolence
has taken the work of relief off their hands entirely-and they are
quite willing to "let George do it."
We think that there can be no doubt that in the beginning
(i.e., 1717) it was not considered that charity, or relief, was one of
the chief functions of Masonry. Of Masons, probably yes; but it was
several years after the formation of the first Grand Lodge that what
. one may call organized charity made its appearance. In the course
of time, however, the idea of personal charity or relief has gradually
lessened, and it is now a very general feeling that the dispensing of
charity is one of the proper (and perhaps the principal) functions of a
Lodge or a Grand Lodge. There may be good reasons for the change,
but that is not to say that this method of distributing relief has
existed from time immemorial.

Wisconsin (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Freemasonry is not a
charitable .institution, although benevolence is strongly inculcated in
our teachings. But the duty of affording relief when necessary is an
individual duty and not the duty of a Lodge. There is, however, in
these days too great a willingness to pass the buck to the Lodge and
on to the Grand Lodge. This tendency is one of the manners in
which the Institution is being gradually transformed.
RITUAL
There appears to be a tendency to seriously consider the proposition of abridging the Ritual, particularly that part of the Third
Degree which is a mere recapitulation, or reciting parts of the
Monitor which are available in printed form. While constant repetition may make for proficiency, it has no continuous appeal to the
average member. The Ritual is the development of early years, as
affected by succeeding times and conditions and the views of the
compilers. There is nothing in it that can be considered as sacred,
or "Land Marks" that cannot be changed. We believe that the
time is not far distant when the advisability of some abridgement
will become a live issue.

New York (1931):
(Grand Master) : This reference to Obligation leads me to a subject that fo r several years has interested many men and jurisdictions.
I .refer to the penalties of the Obligation. Members and initiates alike
know that these penalties are not to be taken literally, and yet they
follow Obligations that are to be taken literally. It is not sufficient
answer to say that the Obligation is literal and the penalty symbolical.
Such a reply weakens the whole procedure. Without in any wise
eliminating the ancient penalty I would re,spectfully recommend that
consideration be given to such a change as, by t he introduction of a
few words, would indicate that the penalty is not to be taken as literal
and that the · binding factor is in another part of the recital by the
candidate. As this is a matter of considerable importance and requires

careful study, I would suggest that the subject be referred to an

nothing should interfere with the regular meetings of the Lodge.
Those meetings should be given to business, social culture and

of Masonic membership . Every one attending these Degrees will
recall how the Brethren leave the Lodge room just before the Master
begins on thes.e lectures. This disheartens the Master, and the Brethren lose, too, for they have left before any opportunity to reach them
with a message has been given. And, still, they cannot be greatly ·
·blamed, for · they have heard these lectures many times before. They
come for social enjoyment, and for Masonic enlightenment. I believe
there is merit in this idea, which was developed in a conversation on
this subject with one of the high officers of this Grand Lodge.
"Those of us who love Masonry, and honor and respect the Institution, must be willing to recognize changed conditions, and prepare
to meet them. Society and civilization today is not what it was a
hundred years ago, or even fifty years ago, or even twenty-five years
ago. I am a firm believer, not only in the beauty and strength of
Masonry, but in its utility and its ability to meet the changed conditions, and serve mankind today as it has in ages past. In this respect
I liken it to the Common Law, rooted as it is in ancient civiliz.a tion
but still virile and flexible and serves mankind well today, because
those who administer it are shaping it to that end."
We believe that there is merit in the suggestion contained in the
above paragraph. We have long since been convinced that the parrotlike repetition of the lectures was enough to drive men away from
the Lodge. We have long contended that Masonry is something
more than conferring Degrees on candidates. The making of a new
Mason is incidental to the life and working of the Lodge. It is ·not
the primary object of Masonry. A Master of exceptional ability may
be able to so give· the lectures as to command an interested audience
at any time, but such men are rare. Therefore, it is better that

SUSPENSIONS
Generally speaking there are as many remedies suggested for
the handling of this question as there are solutions for improving
the present economic condition, both National and International.
We believe, however, that the cause for suspensions can be directly ·
traceable to the initial motive and financial standing of the petitioner. Too often the tendency is to resolve every question in favor
of the Individual, rather than the Lodge.
Some method should be found which will cause men to prize
and want to retain membership. There is ample provision for taking
care of a member who is temporarily and financially unable to pay
his dues. Those who care nothing about the Institution as evidenced
by asking for a dimit or allowing themselves to be suspended for
non-payment of dues, are perhaps better out than in.

Craft of its ungainly bug-bear, a heavy suspension list owing to nonpayment of dues. Various remedies for the evil continue to be suggested, and some of them are on trial, but the measure of success

become members of the world's greatest brotherhood. One is loath
to believe that their disregard for all these is wholly and solely their
own fault. Blame must attach in other quarters, and amongst those
who care there is a feeling that Masonic leaders should seriously take
this drift into consideration, and endeavor to devise some means of
remedying the evil.
THIRD DEGREE LECTURE
The requirement that a newly raised Member should become
proficient in some sort of a lecture of the Third Degree before he
can be admitted · to all the benefits and privileges of Masonry has
produced two different schools of thought. Generally speaking, we
believe that it has not been successful and some Jurisdictions after
a trial of it have repealed the regulation.
The coaching lectures are intended to provide one with the
means to prove himself a Member when visiting another Lodge
or Jurisdictiop. We believe that they now contain a lot of questions which could be eliminated. They are more theoretical than
practical, and the average Mason cannot learn from his teacher,
(and in some cases only after a great deal of study) just exactly
to wh.a t the particular question has reference or means. These ques~
tions should be explained or handled through the Masonic Educational ' Committee, or reference to standard authorities. A short
and specific catechism could be devised which the average Member
could and would learn for use when needed, without being made
obligatory. The present coaching Lectures could be modified so
as to remove the fear they inspire in the mind of the average man
both before and after committing them to memory. While these
are learned in the initial instance, we know of a number of cases
where . a Brother will not visit another · Lodge because he fears the
embarrassment of not being able to answer questions that naturally
are of no practical use when being examined and therefore forgotten.

VISITING

-

The question of the Lodge of a foreign Jurisdiction visiting
another State and conferring the degree according tp its own Ritual,
has been commented on and criticised in a number of Jurisdictions.
It appears to us that such a visitation .i s not only instructive but
entertaining and can produce no harmful results. It gives members
of one Jurisdiction an opportunity to witness the Ritual of another,
which they undoubtedly would never have an opportunity to observe.
Visitations from Lodges of Arizona and Nevada to the Jurisdiction
of California and vice versa do not appear to have produced any
disastrous results, in fact quite the contrary.
Connecticut (1931):
(Cltairma11 Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master (New
Hampshire) reports two cases where he·. had secured permission to
"invade" neighboring Grand Jurisdictions for purpose of conducting
funerals. Why this useless red tape? Masonic funeral customs are
general, and we cannot conceive of a Lodge or Grand Lodge which
would stand on ceremony. At any rate, were we a W. M., we
should waste no precious time in conferring but go ahead .on all
sixteen cylinders.
District of Columbia (1930):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee)°: The Jurisprudence Committee did not approve of inter-jurisdictional visits for the purpose of
conferring Degrees, fearing dangerous possibilities. This writer can
see no harm in such inter-jurisdictional visits, providing the visiting
Lodge takes its own candidate and confers the Degree according to
the Ritual of its own jurisdiction. The Committee did not approve
of shortening the statutory time between Degrees save for good and
sufficient reasons, believing that there were few occasions where haste
was necessary in this respect, which view ·of the matter, in the opinion
of this writer, is sound.

Illinois (1930):
(Grand Master): Our law provides that no other ritua l be used

The Eighty-first Annual Communication, San Francisco, October 14 to 17, 1930. Charles M. Wollenberg, Grand Master.
Arizona:
The event which brought to me the greatest personal pleasure
and pride of the year was the opportunity to act as Installing Officer
on the occasion of the installation of the Officers of Mizpah Lodge,
Number 378, of Los Angeles, on the evening of December 22, 1930.
At that time my beloved and only son, Forrest Art hur Betts, was
elevated to the honorable and distinguished position of Master of
that Lodge.
The occasion was made more memorable, happy and enjoyable ·
by the action of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, John Stewart
Ross, of the Grand Lodge of California, in convening the Grand
!--odge in ~pecial Communication for the purpose of officially receivmg me as its guest. Several Grand Lodge Officers, including a number of Past Grand Masters, were present. My reception was cordial
and gracious and the honor was emphasized by the Grand Master in
tendering to me the gavel and permitting me to seat the assemblage.
It was the second time within a little more than a year that
Grand Master Ross had distinctly honored the Grand Jurisdiction of

Pennsylvania:
California, unlike many other Grand Jurisdictions, gives evidence
of growth numerically as well as otherwise.
Another pointed indication of the healthful growth of our Fraternity on the Western Coast is the twenty-two Special Communications of the Grand Lodge convened during the year.
Indeed, one cannot read of anything concerning California without being impressed with its growth and development. With its great
natural resources, its health-giving climatic conditions, its rapid'!y
growing commerce with the Orient, together with the resultant
benefit to its shipping interests through the Panama Canal and the
fact that with improved facilities of transportation its isolation from
the Atlantic Coast is no longer a handicap to those seeking its vast
fields of opportunity-all give rise to wonderment as to the future
of the Golden Gate State. But we must not digress; otherwise we
shall be fairly chargeable with being a "California Booster."
Brother Whited presented his usual intensely interesting topical
Report on Fraternal Correspondence in which he freely quoted the
remarks of~:. W:. Grand Master Snyder before the Grand Lodge
of New York on the subject of the Order of Eastern Star and its
operations in Pennsylvania.

Several items found in the Report of the Committee on Masonic
History were of especial interest to us.
The Committee on Public Schools Week made an extended
report and were able to say that from "every point of view the latest
observance was the most successful ever held." For eleven years
the Grand Lodge of California has been stressing this feature and
with most gratifying results, if one may judge from t)le. character of
reports from various localities and groups. There are many reasons
why similar sustained efforts in behalf of the Public Schools should
be made in other Jurisdictions.

OLLA-PODRIDA
This Spanish term means "A dish of stewed meat," hence a
mixture. We believe it an appropriate term to cover the excerpts
which show the activities of various Grand Lodges during the past
year. In it we have endeavored to set forth the material things
from the Correspondence Report, which reviews each Jurisdiction
separately. As heretofore we made a liberal use of the excellent
Correspondence Reports of New York, the Philippine Islands and
other Jurisdictions who review the past doings of the American and
Foreign Masonic worlds in brief outline.
We have begged, borrowed and stolen from them and others
indiscriminately, and trust that the epigram of the late Grand Secretary of Nevada, "A wise borrower hath more wisdom than a poor
composer" is applicable.
Alabama:
The Gr;md Master reports that at the very beginning of his
term of office he had to borrow money on a note to take care of
maintenance · expenses of the Masonic Home. That was in January,
and he had to do the same thing every month since. Hoping to place
the Home on a pay-as-you-buy basis, he appealed to the Lodges for
contributions representing one dollar · per member. An intensive
"drive" was made at an expense of $1,796.60 for correspondence, the
salary of a drive director, etc. The total amount collected amounted
to $25,475, representing $22,879 less than the expectancy.
While grateful for the substantial material help, he finds that
many Lodges with residents in the Home did not contribute at all.
A glance at the figures shows that thirty-nine non-contributing
Lodges have 111 residents in the Home at the expense of Grand
Lodge to the amount of. $21,550 a year. Two of these Lodges are ·
defunct. The aggregate membership of the o_ther thirty-seven is
2,689.
The number of residents in the Masonic Home is 425: 59 women,
21 men, 169 girls, 176 boys. Ninety-six children attend high school
and eight are· in college.
R :. W :. Bro. James E. Dill~rd, Grand Orator, presented "A
Kaleidoscopic View of Freemasonry," enumerating various aspects
of the subject. He told a story of a small boy who fell out of bed
quite frequently and, when his mother asked him to explain, he said:
"I tell you why I do it. It is because I go to sleep too close to ,
where I get in." It's a good explanation to ren1:ember when we
wonder why so many Masons drop out.

According to the Grand Secretary's Report, the Grand Lodge

Arkansas:
The Home has on hand a school problem. One hundred and
nine of the children attend the Batesville school. As a result the
District is going deeper in debt every year. The Grand Master placed
before the State Board of Education the need of appropriating from
State funds sufficient to save this School District the added burden . .
He told that in Oklahoma the State pays $7,000 a year for the
schooling of the Masonic children there. He argues that the children
belong to the State, and just because the Masons house them, feed
and clothe them, does not relieve the State of the responsibility
toward them. He urges that all the membership should take a hand
in the matter and urge the Assemblymen and Senators of their particular districts to take action.
He does not think favorably of a Masonic Old Folks' Home,
knowing from experience that most old people do not like to be
away from their accustomed surroundings, nor will they submit to
institutional regulation of their habits and doings. Pensions have
proved more satisfactory under a plan whereby the local Lodge goes
50-50 with the Pension Board. The maximum should be increased
from twenty to thirty dollars.
Connecticut:
The Grand Secretary reports that encouraging progress has
been made in the building up of the Grand Lodge Library.
The Committee on Finance tackled the difficult problem of
meeting the needs of the Masonic Charity Foundation of Connecticut in a manner to provide for the ever increasing demands made
upon it. Under the existing plan all funds raised annually are required to take care of the needs of the year. Twenty dollars now are
collected by the Lodges from every initiate and every affiliate from
fellow Jurisdictions and are turned over to Grand Lodge for general
expenses in the administration of the Masonic Home. The falling
off of initiations and affiliations has shown the precariousness of
the plan. Besides, experience has made clear that an Endowment
Fund is an absolute necessity. Unless such fund is accumulated,
the Committee reports, "a time will come when care of the aged,
infirm and orphans will impose a prohibitive financial burden on
the individual Lodges."
Delaware:
The Masonic Home, opened in 1913, has had 81 guests so far,
of whom 27 are provided for now.

The Gunning Bedford, Jr., Scholarship Fund has supplied welcome support to six young people, all but one. (who atten~s the
State Teachers' College at Millersville, Pa.) bemg enrolled m the
University of Delaware.
Two hundred and fifty dollars was included in the budget for
the purchase of books for the Grand Lodge Library.
Among his recommendations is one asking for a regulation
forbidding, for the future of the organization, in the District. of
Columbia of any society of whatever purpose or name, making
membership in a Lodge prerequisite to admission, wit hout the formal. consent of the Grand Lodge.
He also recommends the adoption of an amendment to the
constitution requiring Lodges, before engaging in building enterprises, to submit to Grand Lodge a full stateme~t of. methods of
financing them, together with the plans and spec1ficat10ns of such
projected structure or structures.
Among the cornerstone-layings of the year was one of the new
Administration Building of the National Education Association, and
the other of the Western Presbyterian Church.
The Rev. Brother John C. Palmer, Grand Chaplain, is carrying
on the unique out-door religious services held under the auspices of
the Craft, on beautiful and spacious shaded and unused grounds near
the Treaty Oak on Temple Heights. These services in an unostentatious way have impressed the people of the District of Columbia
and the official representatives of t he various governments of the
world as giving "evidence of Freemasonry's fundamental revere~ce
for the Great Architect of the Universe, and the free, unsectarian
nature of its religious attitude." Ten different denominations were
represented amdng the speakers on the program of 1930. At every
service there have been many visitors from foreign Jurisdictions.

The family at the Masonic Home comprises 414 ; of these 141

New Jersey:
A per capita tax of five cents is levied annually on the members
for the support of the Grand Lodge Charity Fund. Every Lodge
pays 50 cents a year for each and every member toward the Masonic
Home and Charity Foundation. The latter also receives from the
Lodges $1.50 for every Brother raised to the degree of Master Mason.
A new provision was adopted reading as follows:
"Indigent or helpless Masons, their wives, widows and children
and the mother, sister or daughter of a deceased Master Mason,
provided such deceased Master Mason was, at the time of his death,
the chief support of such mother, sister or daughter, shall be eligible
for admission to such Home, or for aid and support from said charity
foundation."
Those receiving assistance in their own homes from the Charity
Foundation are four couples, 21 Master Masons, 17 widows, one adult
daughter and 14 children; a total of 57.
The family at the Masonic Home now consists of 153 adults
and 51 children. About 25 per cent of the older folks are at the
hospital or in need of medical aid.

New Mexico:
The work done by the Sojourners Club, under the auspices of
the Grand Lodge, at Fort Bayard, is bringing comfo~t to many
sufferers, of whom there arc 47 Brothers among the patients. at t~e
U. S. Veterans' Hospital at that pla&c. The Club was organized 1.n
December, 1920, by Masons who wanted to render some help to t~etr
less fortunate Brethren and comrades. Since then the undertaking
has been aided by Grand Lodge. Among the 369 ex-service men and
women hospitalized at Fort Bayard, there are 12 per cent-plus
Master Masons.
A similar work is carried on by t~e Relief and Trowel Club, at
Fort Stanton where 250 disabled seamen are receiving hospital care.
The Govern~ent supplies nothing but the hospital care, giving
neither clothing nor other comforts. The Brethren residing at Fort
Stanton did what they could to cheer the boys at the hospital. A
"Trowel Club" was formed of patients and employees w?o are
members of the Fraternity, as well as interested Masons outside the
Fraternity. Grand Lodge, Grand Chapter, and Grand Commandery
appropraited funds, Grand Lodge leading with $600, the total contribution amounting to $968.25 last year.

During the past year approximately 200 young men and women

the policy has been to place at the disposal of. the .respective educ~­

Texas: ·
The Grand Master sounds a warning to Grand Lodge that members suspended for non-payment of dues· ought not to be restored
automatically on payment of the outstanding dc;bt. He believes that
the law should be amended so that when a Brother has remained suspended for two years or more he shall not be restored to full fellowship on merely paying what he owes. At the Home for the Aged
there are indigents who got back just in time to be eligible for
entry. The same is true of the participation in relief provided for
Brothers a££licted with tuberculosis or other malignant diseases.
On desiring to return, after prolonged suspen!iion, he shall have to
be proposed and must be elected by unanimous ballot. No dues
shall be collected for the term for which a Brother shall have been
• suspended. Only the dues remaining unpaid, at the. time he was
dropped shall be required. But he must pass the ballot. The idea
is to fix firmly upon the Lodge the responsibility for any neglect
which may cause the Craft undue outlay of its already heavily
strained financial resources. Grand Lodge responded by adopting
a resolution reading as follows:
"Resolved, That hereafter when a Brother becomes suspended
for the non-payment of dues and remains so for the term of two
years or more he shall be required to make application to his Lodge
for reinstatement and pay dues up to the time of his suspension,
and no dues shall be collected by his Lodge for the time during
which he was suspended; and that he must be elected by a unanimous vote of the members of the Lodge present and voting."
The Masonic Home and School at Fort Worth has been deluged
with applications for admission during the year. Eighteen new
children were received. The total enrollme'nt has risen to 456.
The superintendent believes that it is imperative that children be not
sent to the home when they can be cared for elsewhere: A bequest
of $5,000 was received for the home and school.
The Grand Secretary was authorized to employ an expert Librarian to classify and catalogue books already acquired. A library
is to be organized as rapidly as possible.

Ohio:
The residents in the home numbered 437 during the year.
South Carolina:
There has been a campaign to raise funds for the erection of
an infirmary unit at the Hospital for Tuberculars at State Park.
While the results did not come up to expectations, subscriptions
were received amounting to about $41,000. The amount was not
sufficient to complete the building as was originally planned. About
$5,000 more are needed. Meanwhile; one wing was omitted and the
rest of the work completed. The campaign has been of much
benefit to the Craft in that it emphasized anew that Masonic Lodges
are not mutual insurance organizations, guaranteeing a member
against hard luck. It had the further effect that the "cheap" members withdrew from the Craft and left it that much stronger for
their going.

V ermont:
The Committee appointed to report on the feasibility of establishing and maintaining a Masonic Home, made a careful study of
the situation and believes that action should be taken. The pl~n
is to acquire a home fo accommodate from thirty-five to forty
residents. No start should be made till after the money is in hand.
The present Charity Fund should not be depleted for the purchase
of plant and equipment, for that fund will be needed and should
be continued to take care of those who cannot be accommodated
in a home. The first investment for the home, not including hospital features, is figured .at above $50,000 and the annual maintenance at an excess of $20,000 per year. The cost of the plant is
figured at $3 per capita on the existing membership. The maintenance cost is expected to be over $1 per capita a year.
In order to get the proposition under way, the Committee recommended a levy of an assessment in the amount of seventy-five
cents per capita annually for five years; that the monies be kept in
a separate fund to be known as the "Masonic .Home Building Fund";
that the fund be kept intact until it amounts to $40,000.
Virginia:
The fund for the higher education of children of the Masonic
Home is a splendid idea. The Grand Chapter and the Grand Commandery paid $2,000 a year each. The recommendation is made
that Grand Lodge pay $4,000 a year from the general fund to be
applied toward paying expenses of graduates of the Masonic Home
in college during the first and second years, and that loans be extended to the children in their third and fourth years.

· the pavilion. Of these sixty-two were discharged as cured or arrested, two died, fifty-three remained. Every section of the state
is represented among the patients who come from fifty-eight different Lodges.

The W.". Master of every Lodge was asked to prepare and deliver a twenty-minute talk on " Fundamentals of Freemasonry" ; each
Senior Warden, on "Masonry in the Revolutionary Period" ; each
Junior Warden, on the "Symbolism of the First Degree." .
It is a · fundamentally sound plan. The point is to get the membership . interested to want to know and then help by supplying the
desired information. Trying to force good things on adults is not
generally a popular procedure. It is like making children eat spinach
because it is "good" for them. The latter may, have to yield; our
own Brethren feel they are free Masons.
During the year the rules for admission to the Home have been
. revised and other improvements introduced to better meet the needs
of that institution. The Grand Master finds that the membership
is distributed rather unevenly. One Lodge in the state has ten per
cent of the resident s to its record. Here is a point not often inquired
into. The membership of the home increased about twenty per cent ·

The "Washington Monitor" has been carefully revised and a

West Virginia:
The Grand Master reports that West Virginia has had its shan •
of annoyance by invasion of its Jurisdiction by clandestines headed
by the notorious George C. Phillips w ith his " Grand L odge" a nd
Supreme Council. The Secretary of State issued a charter to such a
Supreme Council of the 33° , with rights to confer t he Symbolic
Degrees also. The Grand Master tells the story of how "these
racketeers of the organizing department grew more bold all the
time" until three young men who considered themselves defrauded
had them arrested. One of the regular Lodges in the state ignorantly
permitted a clandestine Mason made in Ohio to be affiliated with it,
because, it seems, there are no regulations by which such step can
be averted. The affiliated Mason was put out and declared "illegally
made and not en titled to any Masonic rights and privileges."

Manitoba:
After th e Aged and Indigent Masons Fund, which in 1917 had
to its credit $38,COO, had grown to the sum of $76,000, Grand Lodge
established its present benevolent fund which now has a capital of
approximately $200,000. Since its inception in 1917 the Committee

A Masonic Essay Competition was held. Three subjects were
announced: 1, The history of Masonry, in the writer's community
and district. 2, The place and possibilities of Masonry as a n influence
for world peace. 3, The meaning of the Third Degree.

Alberta, Canada:
The Grand Master traveled 10,059 miles during the year in the
performance of his Masonic duties.
The Committte on Benevolence reports that its total assets are
$170,328.01. The fund was established to assist the Lodges in meeting the dema nds. made upon them for relief. The report indicates
that Lodges often assume a greater burden than it is wise for them
to shoulder. A case is cited where the suffering individual should
have been taken care of by the municipality in which he resides.
In other words, the Lodge need not interpret its charitable duties
beyond the point of the particular care of those who cannot be provided for by the agencies upon which they have first claim. The
Lodge is not to duplicate but primarily to step in where other agencies prove ineffective or unavailable.

Saskatchewan:
Speaking of the Benevolent Fund the Grand Master reported
that the principal now had reached the sum of $253,483 which last
year produced an interest income of $12,569. Ten thousand three
hundred and twenty-three dollars w ere applied to the purposes for
which the fund was established. The serious problem of the trustees
at the present time, according to his statement, is how to distribute
the interest income equitably among the ever increasing number
of worthy applicants. The amounts given in most cases are too small
to afford the needed relief. Everything points to the desirability
of increasing the principal so as to assure a larger return.
Cuba:
As reported last year, Grand Lodge voted that a Supreme
Court of Masonic Justice be established. In order to carry the plan
into effect, it was found necessary to modify the Constitution somewhat. The tribunal is now in operation. It consists of a president,
a secretary and two special term courts, each with a president and
two additional judges. Seven substitute judges also have heen
selected.
Grand Lodge is endeavoring, despite existing conditions, to raise
funds to build its Temple on the grounds so generously granted
it by the Cuban Government, of which due mention was made in
our report last year. The investments of .Grand Lodge at present
amount to $200,000 and the value of the land granted by the Government is estimated to be no less than $300,000. On the strength
of this, Grand Lodge intends to form a corporation and borrow
half a million dollars for construction purposes. If the plans are
carried out as designed, the Craft will have a magnificent Masonic
Temple in Havana, which is to be devoted to Masonry and contain also a public library and an ·elementary school. The structure
will be of either Cuban colonial type or early English Renaissance
style. The formei: is favored by many for national reasons and the
latter, because England is the mother of Cuban Masonry.
Th_e w ork of the Auxilio Masonico (Masonic Relief), in its two
_years of operations, disbursed approximately $108,300 for funeral
expenses of deceased and relief to dependents. Its capital today is
about $35,000..

Grand Lodge has published a monumental his tory on "Freemasonry in Chile."
On June 21 the contents of the offices of Grand Lodge were
completely destroyed by_fire. Furniture, equipment and a number
of books were consumed. The principal archives were saved, although in a condition somewhat deteriorated by water. Thanks to
the co~operation of helpful Brethren, the offices have been repaired
and are serving their purposes again.

Queensland:
· After much debate at preceding Quarterly Communications it
was voted "That Grand Lodge can not, under · any circumstances,
allow anyone of its ·m embers to join the Order of the Eastern Star
as a Freemason." All Lodges have been instructed that no member
as a Freemason can join an association where women are admitted
as members.
In a past report we referred to what is known as the Ballot
Committee. This passes upon all applicants for initiation before the
Lodge can proceed to admit them. By this means the Lodges have
an additional protection and are kept to their prime duty in passing upon the merits of a candidate. Applications for affiliation also
have to be submitted. Further · duties appear to be to examine
petitions to establish new Lodges, to see that all conditions of the
Constitution have been complied with and to make such recommendations as may be deemed desirable. The number of applications examined ran into the . thousands during the year. Oft.e n
application forms have to be returned for correction and further
information. A " Reject Register" is kept for the entry of applicants
not admitted. No information is supplied to anyone concerning a
rejected candidate. The Reject Register is kept for the guidance
of the Committee exclusively.

and their dependents. The total .in fact amounted to about $12,000

Scotland :
The Grand Lodge of S~otland has called upon the members of
their Lodges to abstain from proposing or admitting to Freemasonry,
any men who are about to emigrate b'efore they can possibly have
become grounded in the principles · of the Craft and have been instructed adequately as to the duties <!evolving upon them as Master
Masons.
Brethren who have decided. to emigrate to any of the Dominions
of the British Empire, are to be furnished by their respective Lodge
Secretary, with the addresses of the appropriate District Grand
Lodges, where such exist, under the Grand Lodge of Scotland, and
to be advised to seek affiliation with one or the other of the Lodges
there. The addresses of District Grand Lodges and District Grand
Secretaries may be obtained from the office of the Grand Secretary,
at Freemasons Hall, Edinburgh.
The Brethren ar e to be told plainly life membership of their
Mother Lodge does not include active membership of other Lodges,
and that in order to acquire membership with Lodges in the Domin'ions, together with all the rights and privileges pertaining thereto,
they must acquire affiliation with such Lodges.
Grand Secretary Winning informs us that, while the notice sent
out by Grand Lodge refers only to the Dominions, it applies, most
assuredly, also to all other countries where Scots Masons may settle,
more particularly those holding Life Membership certificates.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and t he Scottish
Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized
proceedings only to the United States.

*

The symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is
by symbols.
The ·Capitular -degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the
Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most ~xcellent Mast er and the
Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests upon those who have
been regularly elected to preside over a, Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a
Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
· Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name K~ight Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the
temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.

James Lewis Matthews, Covina No. 334, 1925.
Newspaper Editor.

*

135

The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.

Jam es M. Ellis, Fidelity No. 120, 1891.

Twenty-three have held the position.
Three Grand Secretaries served on this Committee.
Seven Past Grand Masters.
Two Grand Lecturers.
William H. Hill was appointed for 1888, but on account of tye
trouble James W. Anderson wrote the report.
James B. Stevens made no report while Chairman in 1907.
Term of Service-Hills, IS years; Davies, 13 years; Whited, 11
years; Hart, 9 years; Stowell, Abell and Anderson, 5 years each.

The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River an d west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them, are: Lodge .o f Perfection, 4° to 14°,
inclusive; Chapter. Rose Croix, 15° to 18° ; Council of Kadosh, 19°
to 30° Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°;
In the Northern Jurisdiction (w hich includes all States north of
the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees conferred are: Lo<lge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 °, inclusive; Council Princes
of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4000--5923.
Scottish Rite-Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chroc
nology is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 3760--5683~ After
September add another year.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was
commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.)., "in the year
of discovery."
Add 530. years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.
Royal 'and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.) ,:
"in the year of the deposit."
·
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000--2923.
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization
of their order. 4.nno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
. From the · Christian era take 1118. .Thus: 1118 from 1923-805.
Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of the blessing
of Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis
(A. B.), "in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing.. Thus: 1923
anq 1913--3836.
